en: Preface to the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*).

The *Sūtra of the Ten Stages* was the first teaching expounded by Śākyamuni upon his attainment of the Way. It is the ultimate discourse that truly accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), rather than a provisional teaching adapted to the capacities of sentient beings.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed a treatise as an exposition upon it, thereby elucidating its meaning.
He expounded their essential meaning, and the two Tripiṭaka masters, Paramārtha and Ratnamati, translated them from Sanskrit into Chinese to transmit them to the world.

However, these sutras possess lofty intent and profound principles; these treatises contain obscure phrasing and deep meanings. They are certainly not something that those of shallow learning dare to fathom.
Consequently, many scholars look upon them with awe and withdraw. During the Sui dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Jingying Yuan.

The Master was a scholar who had thoroughly mastered the Tripiṭaka and whose reputation for erudition stood preeminent in his time. He delivered lectures on this treatise and subsequently composed a commentary upon it, titled the *Yiji* (Record of Meaning).

His analysis of the text and elucidation of its principles were so exquisite, lucid, and penetrating that nothing could surpass them. Consequently, readers first realized that this treatise was not difficult to understand; this was indeed appropriate.
It is no exaggeration to say that masters such as Xianshou and Qingliang drew much benefit from it. Indeed, as it is said:
This record is of great benefit to later students; how could it wait for our own arguments?

For some time, I have intended to edit and publish it for the world, yet I alone was constrained by the imperial decree and spent my years residing in four monasteries, where the duties of the Dharma were so overwhelming that I failed to fulfill my original aspiration.
Now that I am old, my life is like a lamp in the wind, unable to plan for even tomorrow; thus, [I have finally completed this work].

He then entrusted it to Dian Shou, instructing him to have it collated and carved into printing blocks. He expressed his regret that this book had undergone many years of transmission and was nearly lost by half;
he hoped that if future generations were to obtain a complete copy and carve it to continue the tradition, it would be a source of great fortune.
Preface in Six Sections, composed by the former Abbot of Zōjōkyō-ji,
the Great Sōjō Ryūzen, in the second year of Kōsei, the year of Gengxu,
in the second month of spring.

According to Master Yuanguang’s *Jingtu chuxue chao* (Notes for Beginners on the Pure Land) and Master Yuanchao’s *Wuzong zhangshu mulu* (Catalogue of Commentaries on the Five Schools), both state that the *Shidi lun shu* (Commentary on the Daśabhūmika Sūtra-śāstra) consists of seven fascicles and was composed by Master Jingying. (The above.
From this we know that at that time the complete work still existed, whereas what is currently transmitted amounts to only four fascicles; this is truly a pity.
Originally consisting of four fascicles, later generations divided them into beginning and end sections;
I have followed this convention here as well. In the transmission of this work, errors and merits have coexisted; I have now collated several versions and adopted the most excellent readings.
Where the meaning was ambiguous or where there appeared to be omissions, I have marked these in the upper margins to await future scholars.
Where the old edition contained missing characters, I have now provisionally supplied them for the convenience of beginners.
Among the cited texts, there are occasional differences from the Song, Ming, and Liao editions; I have not troubled to mark every instance, but let the reader take note of them.

In the old editions, instances such as "śrāvaka-śrāvaka" being written as "shō-shō mon-mon" and "pratyekabuddha-pratyekabuddha" being written as "en-en kak-kak" follow the conventions of ancient manuscripts; while these are not inherently errors, readers may nevertheless be confused by them.
Therefore, I have now revised all such cases.
Written on the middle day of spring in the year Kōsei Kōshu (1790), by the śramaṇa Tenjū in Edo.

Part One (This volume concludes the "Section on the Fundamental Nature").
Composed by Master Jingying Huiyuan.

Now, the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the sublime gateway to the wisdom of accumulation and the excellent treasury of perfected virtues. Great Sages have refined their spirits through them since time immemorial, exhaustively investigating their source.
Yet, wishing to compassionately spread the clouds of virtue and piteously open the sun of wisdom, the Dragon turns his head to manifest the light from his crown;
for this path of transformation, though its true meaning is difficult to reveal, could not be expounded without Vajragarbha to elucidate its profound mysteries.

It was unfathomable; only Vasubandhu was able to proclaim its essentials. Thus, while the rain of Dharma and the flow of its meaning reached the land of Tāvatṃsaka (India), the local dialects hindered universal communication and the differences in language obstructed the equalization of practice. Consequently, the teachings remained secret within the Hu script and their meaning hidden from the resonance of the Sanskrit sounds.
Then, in the first year of the Yongping era of the Great Wei dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Ratnamati...

Mokṣala and Bodhiruci, lamenting that the profound school had not yet been fully realized and grieving that its deep principles were on the verge of extinction, took pity upon those lost in the long darkness and transmitted the torch of the Dharma to them.
They exhausted their subtle spirits to translate this treatise; though the words reached the limits of profound secrecy, the essential meaning was revealed within the text.

The style of the Middle Way resounded far and wide, its influence blazing and flowing throughout the world. I, being the misfortune of having joined the ranks of scholars, have encountered this magnificent transformation.
I rejoice at having encountered this grand instruction and am delighted to have met with this profound text. Having studied it for many years, I have grasped but a single corner of its meaning;

thus, I have briefly recorded what I know to serve as a record against future forgetfulness. May this contribute, however slightly, like dust to Mount Sumeru or the glow of a firefly to the sun, providing a modest aid to those who have recently begun their studies and are yet unlearned.
(Cursive script can confuse and lead to serious errors; those who transmit it must use the true [standard] script—be careful not to use cursive.)
The holy teachings are manifold, yet their essential summary consists of only two: the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

The teachings on the Dharma of the Śrāvakas are called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, and the teachings on the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas are called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Within the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, there are two types of instruction:
first, the śrāvaka-śrāvaka, and second, the pratyekabuddha-śrāvaka. As for the śrāvaka-śrāvaka, this person has from the beginning sought [the path of the śrāvaka].
The path of the śrāvaka always delights in contemplating the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, thereby perfecting the nature of a śrāvaka.
In their final existence, they encounter a Buddha who teaches them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, whereby they attain realization of the Way;

because they originally possessed the nature of a śrāvaka and now again hear the sound [of the Dharma] and attain realization of the Way, they are called "śrāvakas" (hearers). Regarding śrāvakas, as it is said in the sūtras, those who seek the state of a śrāvaka are like...
I shall now explain for you the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths based on this. As for those who are pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas:

these individuals originally sought the path of a pratyekabuddha and constantly delighted in contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, thereby perfecting the nature of a pratyekabuddha.

In their final body, they encountered a Buddha who taught them the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, whereby they attained awakening. Their original nature was that of a pratyekabuddha; it was only at the very end that they heard the [Buddha’s] voice.

Because they attain awakening to the Way, they are called Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas. As stated in the sūtras, for those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; this is the discussion based on that.

Furthermore, regarding the general characteristics of the Dharma, Śrāvakas are dull and not sharp, whereas Pratyekabuddhas, through their knowledge of specific characteristics, are sharp and not dull. Although there is a distinction between sharp and dull...

Those of superior faculties and those of equal aspirations who attain minor fruits rely upon the teachings; because their stations are the same, what is taught for these two types of persons is combined to form the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.
Within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the teachings are also twofold: first, gradual entry; second, sudden enlightenment.

As for "gradual entry," this refers to a person who, having previously practiced the Great Dharma in the past, regressed from that study to learn the Lesser [Vehicle], and subsequently returned to enter it again.

Because "great" has been practiced from childhood, it is called gradual; thus the Sūtra says: "Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, I now cause them as well to enter into this Dharma.
This refers to gradual entry. As for those who speak of sudden enlightenment, there are sentient beings who have long cultivated roots of goodness corresponding to the Mahāyāna;
when they first see the Buddha, they are immediately able to enter the Great [Vehicle] without relying on [the Lesser].
Because "sudden" (頓) is used as a designation for this, the Sūtra says: "There are sentient beings who, throughout successive lifetimes, have always received my transformation;

upon first seeing my body and hearing what I say, they immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This refers to sudden awakening followed by gradual entry (*tongwu jianru*).

Bodhisattvas rely on shallow stages to reach afar; while sudden-awakening bodhisattvas leap over directly to understand the Great [Vehicle], although sudden and gradual differ, [the goal remains the same].
It is precisely because they received the great [teachings] at that time in one place;
therefore, although the holy teachings spoken to these two individuals as the Bodhisattva-piṭaka are numerous, none exceed these two. As Nāgārjuna said:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa and Ānanda compiled the Tripiṭaka at Rājagṛha for the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, while Mañjuśrī and Ānanda [compiled it] at the Iron Enclosure (Cakravāḍa)."
The *Shanji* (Collection of Mountains) states that the Mahāyāna sūtras constitute the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Furthermore, the *Dichichi* (Bodhisattvabhūmi) says that among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, only the Vaipulya division is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, while the remaining eleven divisions are the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.

That same text further states that when the Buddha taught the Sūtras as the path for Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas to transcend suffering, those who compiled the scriptures collected them into two piṭakas.
Because the conduct of śrāvakas is taught as the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and the conduct of bodhisattvas is taught as the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, one knows that the Noble Teachings do not transcend these two.
These two are also called the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, or the Half-Teaching and the Full-Teaching;
although their names have been altered, their meaning does not differ. Within each of these two Piṭakas, there are further three parts, namely: Sūtra, Vinaya, [and Abhidharma].

The *Abhidharma-sūtra* refers to all the various sūtras; what is called *Vinaya* refers to the various codes of discipline (*śīla*); and what is called *Abhidharma* refers to the various treatises (*śāstra*).
These three piṭakas are explained in detail in other chapters. As for this present sūtra, it is subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka among the two piṭakas;
it serves as the wheel of Dharma for those who are mature by nature and receive sudden instruction, and it is classified as *sūtra* among the three piṭakas.

This treatise is subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; since it is not an original teaching, it cannot be classified among the sudden or gradual Tripitakas, but rather belongs to the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
What is called the "Ten Grounds" (Daśabhūmi) is, in essence, a discourse on the Dharma-gate that gathers all aspects of the merit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna).
It is the profound path of noble wisdom and the wondrous abode of divine intelligence. Its substance transcends names and words and is beyond the reach of mind and intellect;

its nature is quiescent and luminous, surpassing birth and extinction. Its substance is empty yet eternally present, beyond the reach of those who perceive through the duality of exhaustion and difference.
Regarding its inclusion, the subsequent sutra states: "Subtle and difficult to know is the Noble Path," and so forth, even extending to the practices of the stages (*bhūmi*);

this discusses its characteristics. Its virtues are as numerous as the atoms of the universe, vast and difficult to calculate; regarding its function, it can ferry those drowning across the long stream, transcending birth and death.
It fully possesses all virtues and perfectly accomplishes the Way of Enlightenment. Vairocana Buddha has reached the ultimate consummation of this path. Furthermore...

Desiring to lead others, by means of what one has attained oneself, into the same state: yet the Dharma is difficult to manifest in practice, and the characteristics of practice are difficult to clarify through teaching.
Without teaching, there is no way to manifest that practice; without practice, there is no way to reveal that Dharma.
This is because the Dharma is the source of practice, and practice is the foundation of teaching. Thus, although the manifestation of the Dharma through practice is vast and all-pervading...
To summarize, there are two aspects: first, the practice of the path of expedient teaching; second, the practice of the path of realization that abandons signs to accord with truth.
The aspect of the practice of cessation cannot be discussed through the teachings of expedient practice. Expedient practice, which accords with conditions, can be manifested through words.
The sutras state that this practice is indeterminate—sometimes described as one, sometimes as two, and even as many. For now, based on a single approach, it is explained as follows:
Regarding the tenfold designation, starting from the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), these stages are difficult to differentiate;

therefore, the Sūtras and Śāstras establish ten distinct categories. These ten categories are: first, the difference in the skillful means for entering the stages; second, the distinction in the initial dwelling; third, the distinction in the actual dwelling;
fourth, the differentiation of the fruits of the stages; fifth, the differentiation of the stages of training; sixth, according to practice... [and so forth].
1. Revealing its distinctiveness; 2. Based on retribution to manifest its differentiation; 3. Distinguishing it by way of number; 4. Using metaphors to reveal its distinctiveness; 5.

Defining it in relation to obstacles as "expedient means" (*upāya*). As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, regarding the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), one relies on worldly pure dhyāna to cultivate all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), gives rise to great compassion for suffering sentient beings, extensively makes great vows, and enters into joy.
From the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one generally cultivates the stages of fulfillment through skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding the distinction between the "initial dwelling" (*ādi-vihāra*) and others: within the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), the arising of the bodhicitta constitutes the initial dwelling, continuing thus up to the Cloud of Dharma, where the attainment of supreme samādhi constitutes the initial dwelling.

As for the "proper dwelling" (*samyag-vihāra*): from the first stage onward, the cultivation of faith, diligence, and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) constitutes the abiding, continuing thus up to [the final stage].
Regarding the distinction between the fruit of the stage of Abiding Securely (Anuśaya-bhūmi) and the reception of the Buddha’s office of Wisdom as the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā):

from the first stage (*bhūmi*), one generates vows and cultivates the ten practices as the fruit of the stage; continuing thus up to the Cloud of Dharma, one accomplishes the five great elements as the fruit of the stage.

As for the "factors of training" (*śaikṣa-aṅga*): on the first stage one cultivates vows; on the second stage one studies the precepts; on the third stage one practices meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and on the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages one practices cultivation.

The cultivation of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) on the seventh stage of wisdom; the purification of the buddha-field on the eighth stage; the preaching of the Dharma on the ninth stage;

and the reception of empowerment on the tenth stage—all these are the progressive practice of superior dharmas, which are described as the "division of learning" (*śikṣā-vibhāga*). Regarding the "division of conduct" (*carita-vibhāga*):

from the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) accomplished in the first stage up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) accomplished in the tenth stage, all these are taken according to what is accomplished in each respective portion.

Regarding the distinction between the names of the practices and their rewards: from the first bhūmi, one frequently acts as a king of Jambudvīpa, up to the tenth bhūmi, where one becomes a Mahesvara king.
Regarding the numerical quantities: on the first bhūmi, one attains one hundred; on the second, one thousand;
and so on, until on the tenth bhūmi, one attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of unspeakable Buddha-lands.

The term "etc. refers to the six distinct similes used for illustration: the womb, the smelted gold, the mountain, the pool, the ocean, and the pearl. These six similes are employed to illustrate the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Of these six, the first was established as a simile by the commentators (*śāstrakāra*), while the latter five were provided as illustrations by the author of the sutra (*sūtrakāra*).

Regarding the phrase "in relation to obstacles": the first stage (*bhūmi*) corresponds to the obstacle of the self-clinging of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and so on, up to the tenth stage, which serves as the antidote [to its respective obstacle].

Regarding the obstacle to mastery over the dharmas, one ascends through these ten gates to reach the ten stages. Why are they named "Joyous" (*pramuditā*) for the first and so on up to "Dharma-Cloud" (*dharmameghā*) for the tenth?

The commentary itself explains: because one has accomplished the supreme practices for the benefit of oneself and others and has for the first time realized the state of an Arya, one gives rise to great joy;
therefore, it is called "Joyous. Furthermore, one is free from the afflictions that give rise to erroneous thoughts and the violation of precepts.

It is called "Stainless" (*vimalā*) because it is fully endowed with pure precepts that are free from defilements and the like; it is called "Luminous" (*prabhākarī*) because the Dharma appears through the illumination of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
it is called "Blazing" (*arciṣmatī*) because the fire of wisdom can burn the fuel of afflictions;

it is called "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*) because, through the skillful means of supramundane wisdom, it can deliver those who are difficult to deliver; and when great wisdom manifests without interruption, it is [the stage of] *Sādhumatī*.

Therefore, it is called "Manifest" (*Abhimukhī*), because one has perfectly cultivated the practice of signlessness (*animitta-caryā*) and its merit is consummate, thereby being able to transcend both the mundane and the supramundane paths of the two vehicles.
It is called "Far-Reaching" (*Dūraṅgamā*), because the retributive practice (*vipākacaryā*) has matured and signlessness is uninterrupted.

It is called "Immovable" (*Acalā*), because one achieves the practice of benefiting others through the accomplishment of teaching the Dharma with unimpeded power. It is called "Excellent Intelligence" (*Sādhumatī*), because one attains the Great Dharmakāya and is fully endowed with self-... [benefit].
Regarding the explanation of the different interpretations of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they are divided into two groups of five and thus called the "Ten Stages.
If one follows Nāgārjuna’s interpretation based on the meaning of "abiding," as stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*: "The ten successive stages of abiding are called 'stages' (*bhūmi*).

Alternatively, according to the primary tenet of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, the term "stage" is explained by the sense of "sustaining" (*dharaṇa*); just as the worldly earth can sustain all things.

The *Dharmasthāna-nirdeśa* (Exposition on the Bases of Phenomena) is also like this. Furthermore, according to that text, the practice (*caryā*) based upon the ground (*bhūmi*) is explained as being able to produce [the fruit], and thus it interprets "ground" (*bhūmi*).
That treatise states: "Because one personally practices [the path], it is called 'abiding' (*sthiti*); because it gathers and sustains sentient beings, it is designated as 'ground' (*bhūmi*).

Now, the Master of this treatise [Asaṅga] addresses these meanings comprehensively; therefore, the subsequent treatise says: "Producing and sustaining the Buddha-wisdom is called 'ground' (*bhūmi*)," thus encompassing both "producing" (*janana*) and "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*).

From the perspective of the ultimate meaning, when one first gives rise to the aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called "arising" (*utpāda*); when it is finally fulfilled, it is called "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*).

Alternatively, with respect to the fruit, the cause is termed "arising" and the conditions are termed "accomplishment. "Abiding" (*sthiti*) refers exclusively to the correspondence within the causal stage, specifically its non-retrogression;

"sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*), however, applies universally to both the cause and the fruit. This is explained by taking the first bhūmi as the standard in relation to the subsequent two bhūmis, and so on up to the Buddha.
The meaning of the various stages (*bhūmi*) follows this same principle for subsequent sequences.
Regarding the *sūtra*: its foreign name is *sūtra*, which is translated here as "thread" (*tàn*). What is the meaning of "thread" such that it is so named?
The explanation states that a thread has the sense of "pervading" and "upholding. Because the speech of the Sages can pervade all phenomena (*dharma*), it is so named by way of analogy.
It is designated as "sūtra" (yarn). If that is so, why is it not called "yarn" but rather "sūtra"?

The commentary explains that because the function of yarn is to string together flowers, while the function of a sūtra is to hold together the warp [of the teaching], their utility is similar; therefore, it is termed a "sūtra.

Furthermore, according to the conventional definition, "sūtra" means "constant" (*nitya*). Because this one dharma of the teaching persists through antiquity and the present without ever ceasing, it is called "constant."

The commentator explains that there are three types of treatises (*śāstra*) according to their meaning: First, those called "treatises" by way of exposition, such as the treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

According to this definition, the *sūtras* are also called treatises. Second, those called "treatises" by way of debate, such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*. These are termed "treatises" because they establish proponents and opponents and set forth a process of dialogue.
Third, those called "treatises" by way of commentary; this present work is an example of such a commentary-treatise (*vyākhyā-śāstra*). It is a commentary-treatise.

There are three types of exegesis: first, exegesis of meaning (*artha-vyākhyāna*), such as the *Vibhāṣā* and other works, which provides a general explanation of the meanings of all sūtras and dharmas;

second, exegesis of tenets (*siddhānta-vyākhyāna*), which relies solely on a single division [of a scripture] to explain its fundamental purport, such as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* explaining the meaning of the thirteen stages within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
and third, exegesis of the text (*grantha-vyākhyāna*), which analyzes and explains according to the specific wording, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. As for this present treatise:
The commentary on the text is titled *Śāstravyākhyāna*.
Among the ten sections, the first is designated as the "Initial Stage" (*Prathamabhūmi*), as explained previously; its "Joy" (*pramuditā*) is the same as above.

Throughout this treatise, the text is divided into two parts: the introduction (*nidāna*) and the main body (*śarīra*). At the beginning, there are two verses which constitute the introductory section.

The prose section having already concluded, this constitutes the main body (*śarīra*) of the treatise. Since the arising of the treatise has its specific causes and conditions, the introduction (*nidāna*) is first elucidated. Once the introduction has been established, the formal presentation of what was composed is called the main body. Both the introduction and the main body possess the single purpose of universal dissemination (*saṃprakāśana*). While all sūtras invariably possess these [two parts], it is not necessarily so for all śāstras. Why is it that this one lacks them? Someone explains, saying: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the intervening text.* Regarding why this is so, someone offers this interpretation: "In the case of sūtras, the Buddha himself is the speaker; therefore, the introduction must first clarify the time, place, and assembly. In the case of śāstras, however, the author is a human being, and the treatise is composed based on the sūtras. Consequently, there is no need to separately establish an introduction. Furthermore, some say: "Sūtras are the word of the Buddha, whereas śāstras are the word of humans. Because they are the word of humans, they do not require an introduction. Yet others say: "Sūtras are the ultimate teaching, while śāstras are the provisional teaching. Because they are provisional, they lack an introduction. Still others say: "Sūtras are the direct teaching, while śāstras are the indirect teaching. Because they are indirect, they lack an introduction. Finally, some say: "Sūtras are the teaching for those of sharp faculties, while śāstras are the teaching for those of dull faculties. Because they are for those of dull faculties, they lack an introduction. These are the various explanations offered by others. However, this is not the correct principle. Why? Because the sūtras themselves state: "If there is a sūtra that lacks an introduction, one should know that it is a counterfeit sūtra. If this were truly the case, then the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and other such works would also be counterfeit sūtras. Therefore, we know that the absence of an introduction in this śāstra is due to the fact that the sūtras upon which it is based already contain introductions; thus, there is no need to repeat them here. This is the meaning. Furthermore, some say: "Sūtras are the teaching for those of superior capacity, while śāstras are the teaching for those of inferior capacity. Because they are for those of inferior capacity, they lack an introduction. This is also incorrect. Why? Because the sūtras themselves state: "If there is a sūtra that lacks an introduction, one should know that it is a counterfeit sūtra. If this were truly the case, then the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and other such works would also be counterfeit sūtras. Therefore, we know that the absence of an introduction in this śāstra is due to the fact that the sūtras upon which it is based already contain introductions; thus, there is no need to repeat them here. This is the meaning. Furthermore, some say: "Sūtras are the teaching for those of superior capacity, while śāstras are the teaching for those of inferior capacity. Because they are for those of inferior capacity, they lack an introduction. This is also incorrect. Why? Because the sūtras themselves state: "If there is a sūtra that lacks an introduction, one should know that it is a counterfeit sūtra. If this were truly the case, then the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and other such works would also be counterfeit sūtras. The author of the treatise is the one who performs the dissemination; thus, when viewed in relation to the root sūtra, the treatise itself constitutes the dissemination.

For this reason, there is no separate section for dissemination at the end of the treatise. If that is so, why does the treatise composed by Vasubandhu to explain the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* establish a separate section for dissemination?
Furthermore, why does the *Bhūmivyavasthāna-śāstra* composed by Maitreya also establish a section for dissemination?

It is certain that human speech is erroneous and difficult to rely upon; for when a proponent establishes a doctrine, there is no other meaning beyond shifting positions, whether following existence or non-existence, both of which are harmless.

Separately, within the introduction, there is a fivefold analysis: first, clarifying the similarities and differences between the sūtras and śāstras as introductory texts; second, a general clarification of the śāstra...

First, the meaning of taking refuge and paying homage; second, the characteristics of what is honored according to various treatises; third, the different ways in which various treatises pay homage; fourth, the analysis and explanation of the text;

fifth, the distinction between similarities and differences. Regarding the similarity and difference: while the form of the prologue differs, the intent of the prologue is the same. As for the difference in form, there are two types of scriptural prologues.

First is the "Initiation" (nidāna) and second is the "Certification of Faith" (saddharmaparyāya-sampratyaya). When the Tathāgata was about to preach, he first manifested various signs as the cause for his preaching;
this is called the Initiation. Ānanda, having received the transformation [of the teaching], wished to transmit what he had heard to future generations;

thus, he first stated, "Thus have I heard from the Buddha," which serves to certify that it is trustworthy—this is called the Certification of Faith. The Discourse (Sūtra), however, is not like this: first, it is not the Master of Transformation.
Because it cannot manifest signs through supernatural power to initiate the teaching, there is no "initiation" [by the Buddha himself].

Furthermore, because the two [the Buddha and Ānanda] are inherently different in their composition—Ānanda merely transmitting the Buddha’s words—there are no phrases such as "Thus have I heard" to serve as a certification of faith.

One can only pay homage and thereby effect the initiation; this is the difference. As for the meaning being the same: although the sūtras and śāstras differ, they are identical in their purpose of bringing forth [realization].
Faith is that by which one enters the initial gate of the Dharma; it is the foremost for encompassing the teachings.
Because one who wishes to enter the Buddha-dharma must first give rise to faith, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "Faith is like a hand.

Just as a person with hands can take whatever precious jewels they desire upon reaching a treasury, yet cannot do so without hands, the same applies to entering the sea of the Buddha-dharma. One who possesses the hand of faith can gather [the teachings] at will."
To take up the jewels of the Dharma, nothing is obtained without faith; because faith possesses this capacity, both the Sūtras and the Śāstras work together to engender it.

Regarding "respectful intent," there are six aspects of respectful intent: first, paying homage out of gratitude for the reliance upon the treatise as its source; second, requesting [the teacher] to accept [the request].
First, it serves to provide protection; second, to inspire faith in sentient beings; third, to establish the etiquette of respectful service; fourth, to manifest the marks of excellence;
and fifth, to open up for sentient beings the recollection of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. Regarding the basis of this treatise: if there were no Buddha, there would be nothing to explain;
if there were no Dharma, the treatise would have no basis; and if there were no Saṅgha to transmit it, it would not be heard today. It is by relying upon these three that this treatise now exists.

Because [the teaching] has been established, it is fitting to offer salutations and request protection. In this degenerate age of the *mofa*, the propagation and transformation of the Dharma are not easy;
if not aided by the majestic power of the Triple Gem, there would be no way for it to prevail on its own. Therefore, one must pay homage to request their assistance.
To establish credibility, the author of the treatise—being himself a person of insufficient merit—must show respect so that people will believe and accept the work he has composed.
The Three Jewels manifest a lineage of transmission and established institutions, whereby people may place their trust; therefore, they should be venerated.

Regarding the ritual of reverence: just as in the world a filial son or a loyal minister must first inform their sovereign or parent before acting, so too this Bodhisattva, out of profound respect for the Three Jewels that surpasses even a sovereign or a parent, now intends to compose a treatise to explain the Buddha’s sutras.
I respectfully submit that, as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*, the Three Jewels constitute the auspicious realm;

they are placed at the beginning of this treatise to manifest its excellence. Thus, one first pays homage in order to arouse in sentient beings mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, as explained in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*:
"To cause sentient beings to give rise to the aspiration within the Three Jewels, seeking liberation and cultivating faith."
Having examined that making offerings and taking refuge necessitate prostration, the characteristics of the third object of veneration—the Three Jewels—are as detailed in a separate chapter.
Regarding the fourth point, the differences among various treatises: at the beginning of these works, the expressions of homage vary; some include full reverence for all Three Jewels.
In works such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, one may revere only the person and the Dharma; in treatises such as this present work, one may revere only the Buddha;

and in works such as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, one follows the specific intention of the author in choosing which to emphasize. Thus, the complete reverence for all six objects is the same as before. Furthermore, for what reason does one revere only the person and the Dharma?
Because the Dharma relies upon the person for its transmission, it is necessary to revere both the person and the Dharma; this is the principle that ought to be explained.
Regarding the reason for returning to the practice of prostration, one pays respect solely to the Buddha because he is the Teacher; thus, one must prostrate to him.
Others who are not teachers are set aside and not revered. If one were to follow [the practice of] mutual prostration, there would be no harm.
As stated previously, this treatise honors only persons and the Dharma. Who is the person? It refers to those who requested the teaching, transmitted it, and upheld it—the Buddhas.
The Dharma of the Bodhisattvas refers to the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). If this is so, then one is already fully honoring the Three Jewels:

the Buddha is the Jewel of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva is the Saṃgha, and the Dharma-gate is the Dharma. For what reason, then, is it said that "one honors only the person and the Dharma"? To explain: how could these be different from the Three Jewels?
It is simply that at present, one does not perform the prostration with the intention of [them being] the Three Jewels. How is this known? It is because now...

There are three arguments proving that [the object of veneration] is not the Triple Gem: first, by seeking it through its characteristics; second, by seeking it through its universality and particularity; and third, by seeking it through its sequence. Regarding the argument by characteristics:

the characteristics of the Triple Gem are distinct and do not involve a mutual merging or separation. Yet, in this instance of respectful exhortation and petition, the term "Buddha" is used interchangeably with "Bodhisattva" among the assembly without distinction;
therefore, it is not the Triple Gem. Regarding universality and particularity: while the characteristics of the Triple Gem are universal, the term "Buddha" [is specific].
In this way, one’s reverence for the Dharma and the Saṃgha is likewise. Now, regarding this ground-dharma (*bhūmi-dharma*), all Buddhas have taught it together.

While the Buddha may be universally revered, the Dharma alone is the ground-dharma; the rest are not. Bodhisattvas revere only those who request its teaching, transmit it, and uphold this ground-dharma;
they do not revere others who are merely beginners and unfit to proclaim or transmit the ground-dharma. It is clearly understood that [reverence] is not based on these three.

Regarding the sequence of the homage spoken by Bao-yi, according to the characteristics of their manifestation, the order of the Three Jewels should necessarily place the Buddha first, followed by the Dharma, and then the Sangha.
In this current text, however, the Buddha and the Sangha appear before the Dharma;
it is therefore clearly known that although the Three Jewels possess three meanings, it is sufficient to verify this based on the initial perspective alone.
Within the explanation of the fifth section, first the introductory text is analyzed, and then the text itself is interpreted according to its wording.
Regarding these two verses, they are divided into two parts: first, citing the person and the teaching to manifest one’s own expression of respect;

second, explaining the meaning below to clarify the intent of one’s respect, which serves to elucidate the wondrous meaning so that the Dharma may endure for a long time. This latter part can also be divided into three sections, the first of which is citing the object of respect.
Second, having already manifested [the homage], there are three parts concerning the intent of the homage; if divided according to the individual phrases, there are five:

first, citing the person and the Dharma to praise their excellence; second, prostrating; third, explaining the wondrous meaning; fourth, causing the Dharma to endure; and fifth, benefiting both oneself and others.
Among these five, the first interrogates the preceding to initiate the subsequent, as they arise in successive order. Why is the person cited at the outset?
The praise of the Dharma is for the purpose of wishing to pay homage; why pay homage? It is for the purpose of understanding the sublime meaning. Why understand the meaning?
It is for the purpose of causing the Dharma to endure. Why cause it to endure? It is for the purpose of giving rise to practices that benefit oneself and others.

These two [latter points] subsequently corroborate the preceding sequence. First, regarding the act of paying homage, one in turn questions the preceding: "For the purpose of wishing to pay homage, why does one first offer praise?"

Regarding the superiority of both person and Dharma: the person is the supreme teacher and the Dharma is the wondrous medicine; because both the person and the Dharma are honored, one pays homage by joining the palms at the crown of the head.

Next, in order to explain the meaning, one turns back to question the preceding: if one wishes to explain the wondrous meaning, why is the person designated and the Dharma cited to praise their excellence and manifest one’s own homage?
Now, since the Dharma being explained originates from the person and is heard through them, one must designate the person and praise them with verbal action.

Since this Dharma is what is to be explained, one must first mention the Dharma; because the excellence of the physical act of prostration is praised through verbal expression, one must perform prostration.

Furthermore, since the ground is profound and deep, if one does not pay homage and rely on the assistance [of others], there would be no way to independently analyze and explain the Dharma of the ground;
therefore, one must prostrate. Next, regarding the abiding of the Dharma, one returns to question the preceding point: if one wishes to cause the Dharma to abide, for what reason does one prostrate?
The ritual prostration clarifies the profound meaning; yet for the Dharma to endure long, it must depend upon sentient beings having faith and understanding.
If one does not perform prostration, it shows a lack of lineage transmission, and there would be no way to cause the assembly to develop faith in what is taught.

If one does not understand the meaning, the sutra remains obscured and hidden, and there would be no way to cause people to develop understanding of the meaning. Since the Dharma will quickly perish in the absence of both faith and understanding, prostration is necessary.
Ritual serves to produce faith; the explanation of the wondrous meaning serves to produce various understandings. Because it produces faith and produces understanding, it causes the Dharma to abide.

Next, regarding the practices for one’s own benefit and the benefit of others, [the text] returns to interrogate the preceding point: for what purpose does one explain the meaning for the sake of benefiting oneself and others?

It is so that the Dharma may endure for a long time. Abiding must rely upon understanding, as it arises by depending upon the Dharma; if one does not understand the meaning, there is no means by which [abiding] can be attained.
Regarding the understanding that because phenomena do not abide and have no basis for movement, one must understand their meaning so that the Dharma may endure for a long time;

only then is the path of benefiting oneself and others accomplished. Furthermore, within the preceding section, the first verse cites the two characters "person" and "Dharma," using these two terms to praise the most supreme aspects of the honored teachings and the person who proclaims them, thus extolling both the person and the Dharma together.

First, regarding the indefinite location among human beings: (1) if one explains it according to the specific teaching of Śākyamuni, then Śākyamuni is the teacher of the Dharma, the Buddhas of the ten directions, Vimukticandra, and others are the assembly requesting the Dharma, and Vajragarbha is the person who analyzes it;
subsequently, other masters of treatises are responsible for its dissemination and so forth. (2) Regarding Vajragarbha: [the text continues].
Regarding the oral proclamation and verbal explanation: if one follows this meaning, then Vajragarbha is the speaker of the Dharma;
the other bodhisattvas are the assembly requesting the Dharma; the various masters of treatises are the persons who analyze and distinguish it;

and Ānanda, along with the disciples who received and transmitted these masters' teachings, are those responsible for its dissemination. Below, the text will be explained according to the words. As for what is called "speaking," if we refer to Śākyamuni:
To bestow empowerment and proclaim it extensively is called "teaching" (*deśanā*); to chant it according to the vocal modulations of Gaṅgottara is also called "teaching.

This [term] serves to distinguish it from the words of refutation regarding the Dharma; it distinguishes what is being taught here—the Dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)—from that which is to be refuted below.
To ask what constitutes this distinction: it is said that its meaning is not fixed. If contrasted with the Hīnayāna, it is said that this [belongs to] the Mahāyāna Dharma-gate.
Therefore, that which Vajragarbha enters is called the Mahāyāna Samādhi. If this is contrasted with the mundane, it refers to the supramundane Dharma-gate;
thus, the subsequent treatise states that "inconceivable dharmas" refers to the supramundane factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
If this is contrasted with the fruit of Buddhahood, it refers to the Dharma-gate of gathering all aspects of the qualities of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna).
It is not a gate of fruition; if contrasted with other virtues, it refers to the dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Radiance;

if contrasted with other abodes, it refers to the dharma-gate of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva. Regarding the term "dharma" as used in the phrase "the dharmas spoken of as being of the nature of lineage," there are two interpretations:
first, "dharma" means a rule or norm; second, "dharma" means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The "dharma" mentioned here possesses both of these meanings. As for what is said...
The term "gate" (*mukha*) also has two meanings: first, it is called a "gate" because it can lead the mind toward practice;
second, it is a "gate" in the sense of the specific name for the self-substance of a phenomenon, such as the "Dharma-realm gate" (*dharmadhātu-mukha*) and so forth mentioned in the sutras.
Regarding what is discussed here, which fully contains these meanings, there are two senses: first, it is a term that cites a phenomenon, just as when one says, "form" or "mind," and so on.

"Kuan-yü" (綰御) is a term meaning "to guide and control"; it is merely another name for "I" (the self). Now, this is the meaning of "guiding and controlling," which is similar to the meaning of "discriminating person" mentioned below.

As for why this stage is not explicitly named [by the Buddha] but is referred to generically as "the teaching" (*shuo*)—it is because this stage is vast and universally shared, such that all Buddhas teach it together.
To speak of it as "the teaching" is a mark of reverence, and thus it is not appropriate to specify a particular name.

The partial ritual is like that; when Maitreya composed his treatise, he explained that the stages of the *bhūmis* universally honor all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and this case is likewise so.
Because the former encompasses the latter, it is termed "and" (*ca*). Since the number of those who request is not one, they are called "various.

To earnestly incite [others] is termed "exhortation," and to seek an answer is termed "request. Regarding these two distinctions in the explanation, it is stated from the perspective of the superior looking down upon the inferior.
To encourage those below to address those above is termed "requesting" (*yācana*). When the Buddha speaks to Gaṅgottara, it is for the sake of the assembly below;
when he speaks to Gaṅgottara, it is for the sake of those above. If this were the case, why does the Buddha also speak of "requesting" within the section on the request from below?
Furthermore, it is explained that the teacher of all Buddhas is the Dharma. Thus, even the relationship between the Buddha and the Dharma is like this.
If this meaning were to exist in the higher [levels], then all the disciples of the Buddha would, day and night, practice the path while speaking of "exhortation" (*adhyeṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, how could this serve as an exhortation directed toward the lower? Since the sense of "exhortation" toward the lower is not established, the principle of "requesting" (*yācanā*) toward the higher is likewise untenable.

These are merely provisional distinctions made according to the context; they do not lack novel significance. The Dharma is explained as before. As for the term "discrimination" (*vibhaṅga*), if one proceeds from...

Vajragarbha’s thorough exposition of the stages of the path (*bhūmi*) is called "Analysis" (*vibhaṅga*). If one follows the masters of the treatise in their analytical breakdown of the words and meanings, it is also termed "Analysis.

There is a profound reason for designating this as "Meaning" (*artha*): it encompasses names, which are called "Treasury" (*piṭaka*); its sovereign function is called "Person" (*pudgala*); its reception is termed "Experience" (*anubhava*);

its warm preservation is called "Retention" (*dhāraṇa*); its dissemination is called "Flow" (*pravāha*); its unimpeded nature is termed "Penetration" (*prativedha*); and since those who transmit it are not just one, it is "Comprehensive" (*saṃgraha*).
Regarding the names and so forth within this verse: if one follows the first line, they should all be expressed as "should be said";

if one follows the third, "person" (*pudgala*) should be placed in both. However, because the requirements of the verse are concise, the second and fourth lines lack the word "person," while the first and third lines mention it alternately to form a varied composition.

The explanation of the term "Dharma-gate" (*dharmaparyāya*) is no different from what preceded. Regarding the phrase "supreme" (*parama*), both person and Dharma are honored; thus it is called "equal and supreme.
The head is the crown of the body, and to bow down with the crown of the head is termed "prostration" (*namas*). Having already expressed this prostration, one manifests the height of devotion.

To "expound the subtle meaning" means to bring forth the aforementioned respectful intent and provide an exposition; this is termed "subtle meaning" because that which is explained is refined and profound, as previously explained.

The intent behind the "Explanation of Meaning" (Vyākhyā) is to ensure that the Way of the Earth is transmitted for a long time without falling into decline; thus it says, "wishing to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time.
Because the Sūtra has commentaries (*śāstra*), its meaning is easy to understand; because there is this explanation, the Dharma abides for a long time.

Regarding "benefit for oneself and others," it means that by relying on the Dharma of this stage, one is able to accomplish the practice of benefiting both sentient beings and oneself. Alternatively, it may mean that the author of the commentary composes the treatise to explain the Sūtra.
Benefiting the world is called "benefit for others" (*parārtha*); having a virtuous refuge for oneself is termed "benefit for self" (*svārtha*).
As for the word "therefore," it expresses the intention that the Dharma may long endure; for the sake of accomplishing both benefits, one causes the Dharma to abide.
Within the section on the Ten Grounds (Daśabhūmi), this is the main treatise; therein, the orthodox teaching is analyzed through three sections: first, identifying the essential purport;
second, opening up and judging the textual meanings; and third, providing a word-by-word commentary.

What is the essential purport? If we consider the fundamental meaning of the sūtra, there are three points: first, that which is "spoken," namely the practices of the causal stage prior to all the grounds (*bhūmi*), which are cultivated according to their characteristics and can be expressed in words;

second, that which is "revealed," namely the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) manifested by the two paths of teaching (*deśanāmārga*); and third, that which is "indicated," namely the dharmas of the grounds.

As for what is called "spoken," it refers to all the practices of the causal portion prior to the grounds, which can be discussed because they are constructed according to their phenomenal characteristics. As for what is called "revealed," it refers to the fruition within all the grounds.
The practice of virtue, relinquishment, cultivation, and realization is free from characteristics and beyond words; it can only be provisionally designated through its causal aspects.

Because the characteristics of the practice manifest and indicate the true virtues, these virtues are spoken of as that which is "manifested" or "expressed. Although the preceding discussion manifested these virtues, the intention was not directed toward phenomena themselves;

rather, it was intended to rely upon the pure, characteristic-free realization of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to represent the dharmas of the stages. Thus, these virtues are said to be what is manifested and expressed.

The reason for explaining the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) as that which is manifested (*lakṣya*) is precisely because these dharmas are the true reality of sentient beings, yet they remain objects of deluded and erroneous conditions from which they do not awaken.

Now, wishing to immediately dispel delusion within those very conditions and manifest the reality, and desiring to lead people toward entry [into the path], it is difficult to clarify the principle of truth by means of delusion alone;
therefore, one relies upon pure realization (*viśuddha-sākṣātkāra*) to manifest the dharma. As for this treatise, its essential tenets are fourfold: first, ...

First is the scriptural teaching of the original text as it is explained; second is the practice of the path of the teaching as it is established; third is the true realization of the departure from signs as it is revealed;
and fourth is the essential nature of the stages as they are manifested. Briefly stated, this explains the primary teaching of the initial stage and establishes the latter three;
the specific characteristics of these latter three are fully detailed as previously analyzed in the *Zongyao*. Such is the case.
Next, regarding the analysis of the textual meaning: first, we shall distinguish its characteristics based on the *sūtra*, and subsequently, we shall examine it according to the *śāstra*.
Within the *sūtra*, there are two parts: first, manifesting virtues by means of persons; second, distinguishing [the teachings] according to the dharmas.

Regarding "manifesting virtues by means of persons," there are two distinct types of persons: first, the principal teacher, Vairocana Buddha; and second, the assistant teacher, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva. Concerning these two individuals...

This reveals each of the three [aspects]: first, manifesting the substance of the virtues; second, manifesting the characteristics of the virtues; third, manifesting the functions of the virtues. Regarding the Buddha, there are three parts:

first, manifesting the realization of the substance of the Dharma upon attaining perfect enlightenment; second, manifesting the supreme characteristics of the virtues through seven days of contemplation—hence the treatise below states that "contemplating the causes and conditions" reveals the uncommon dharmas; and third, manifesting his virtuous functions by having Vajragarbha enter samādhi.
Regarding the three aspects elucidated by Vajragarbha: first, he enters samādhi to manifest and realize the essence of the Dharma;

second, because all Buddhas collectively bestow their empowerment to manifest the supreme marks of his virtues, the Buddhas below join in praising him so that he is able to enter this Mahāyāna samādhi;

third, from the section on "arising" (*utthāna*) onwards, it clarifies its virtuous functions. As for speaking in terms of the Dharma, according to the meaning, there are various ways of expansion and contraction, as well as opening and closing, which are not uniform. Or...
It is explained as three, or again as six, or divided into nine, or judged as ten, or further separated into forty-eight parts.

As for the "three," they are the introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*śarīra*), and the dissemination (*pariṇāmana*). Within these three, the essential dharmas elucidated consist solely of realization (*adhigama*) and teaching (*deśanā*);

since realization and teaching differ, the three parts also differ. Regarding the three divisions of the teaching: from the beginning up to the "Section on Arising" (*utpatti-vibhāga*) is the first part.
This is because the sequence [of the text] initiates the formal exposition from this point onward. From the "Fundamental Section" (*mūla-bhāga*) onwards constitutes the "Main Body" (*śarīra*);
although within it there are both concise and extensive expositions, the shared teaching on the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi-dharma*) is judged to be the Main Body.

The section on the benefits for those below, which encourages faith and the transmission and maintenance [of the teaching] to reach future generations, is judged to be the "Circulation" (*pariṇāmana*). Regarding the three divisions based on their function, the first is the "Introductory Section" (*nidāna-bhāga*), which is thus determined.

The section on "Entering Samādhi by Way of Sequence" constitutes the cause for realizing the main body of the teaching, as it is through entering samādhi that the actual realization is clearly manifested;
hence, the subsequent treatise states, "This samādhi is the essence of the Dharma. Regarding the meaning of "circulation" (*pravartana*), there are two interpretations:

first, to cause one's own virtues to flow out and benefit those on the stage of faith is called circulation; according to this sense, from the "Section on Additional Qualities" (*Anuśaṃsā-vibhāga*) onwards, all [sections] constitute circulation.
The "Circulation" (Pravartana) is so called because it explains one's own virtues in order to inspire faith in the Bodhisattvas' entry into the stages (*bhūmi*).
Alternatively, in the final age, this [section] is termed "Circulation. According to this meaning, the portion concerning the benefit of the stages is called "Circulation.

As for its division into six parts, the first, up to the "Initiation" (*ārambha*) section, establishes the reasons for initiating the transformation in order to produce faith in sentient beings; the second, the "Fundamental" (*mūla*) section, provides a brief explanation.
Section Three: Praising the Excellence of the Ground-Dharmas to Arouse Aspiration; Section Four: Clarifying the Ground-Dharmas through Speech to Produce Correct Understanding; Section Five:

Explaining the Ten Grounds to the End to Elucidate the Characteristics of Cultivation and Inspire Practice; Section Six: Manifesting Virtues by Means of Parables through the Image [of the Ground]; Section Seven:
The Benefit of the Ground, wherein since the virtues have been perfected, one accords with and realizes the Ground-dharmas. Therefore, below...
The *Śāstra* states that there are nine sections based on the words "attaining the power of the Dharma," "the great earth shaking," and so forth:

from the Introductory Section (*nidāna*) through the Requesting Section (*adhyeṣaṇā*), these constitute six; the Explanatory Section (*ākhyāna*) is judged as the seventh; the Section on the Images of the Grounds (*bhūmi-pratibimba*) is stated as the eighth;
and the Section on Benefits (*anuśaṃsā*) is the ninth. Within these nine, three types of analysis are presented: first, [analysis] with respect to...

First, regarding the commonality of the manifestation of signs for the purpose of initiating the discourse; second, regarding the commonality of the intention behind the manifestation for the purpose of revealing the proof; third, concerning the dual examination of the essential proofs and teachings according to the school’s tenets.

As for "initiating the discourse": when the Tathāgata was about to speak, he first relied upon time and place, manifested signs, assembled the multitude, and initiated what was to be taught, using these as the introduction.
Once this introduction had been established, and he was about to speak for the sake of the assembly, Vajragarbha entered into silence.

The third [section] clarifies that one’s own realization manifested through samādhi can be explained to the assembly; furthermore, because one receives empowerment, the second part next elucidates the section on samādhi.
By entering samādhi, the Buddhas of the ten directions mutually praise and bestow power and empowerment. Consequently, the third part elucidates the section on empowerment.
Having obtained the power of the sages, when one wishes to explain it to the assembly, since concentration alone is without speech, one should follow [the Buddha].
Because it arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the fourth [section] clarifies its "arising division" (*utthāna-bhāga*);

having arisen from concentration, the *dharmas* of the stages (*bhūmi*) are briefly proclaimed, and since they will be explained extensively thereafter, the fifth [section] clarifies its "fundamental division" (*mūla-bhāga*). However, within that fundamental section, the names of the stages are stated only briefly without detailed analysis;
because the great assembly yearned to hear them and desired their meaning, they collectively requested an explanation, and thus the sixth [section] clarifies its...

Having requested that the assembly be divided, and having already requested it, [the Buddha] proceeds to explain it extensively; therefore, next, the seventh section clarifies the exposition of those divisions up to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Since these expositions are difficult to understand, they should be illustrated through metaphors; therefore, next, the eighth section clarifies the "images of the stages" (*bhūmi-pratibimba*).
Once the exposition is complete, it is appropriate to manifest the benefits of the stages and encourage faith and transmission; therefore, next, the ninth section clarifies the stages.
The term "benefit" (*artha*) reveals the intention of the author to provide proof; its primary purpose is to establish that proof.

Within this, the first section establishes the proof by way of the introduction, while the subsequent eight sections explicitly establish the proof. Of these eight, the first three establish the proof by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); the next four establish the proof by way of exposition (*deśanā*);
and the final one establishes the proof by way of the disciples to be converted (*vineya*). Regarding the first three of these, the initial two...
The second section, "Entrance by Relying on Obscurity," reveals the characteristics of attaining realization through the application of grace;

thus, the subsequent treatise asks: "For what reason is there this application? It is because one has attained the Dharma of the Radiance of the Mahāyāna. The third section, "Arising," relies on the emergence of the manifest to reveal that speech must necessarily arise;
it thereby reveals that the entry into quiescence is beyond words. Thus, the subsequent treatise states: "It is certainly non-existent [in terms of verbal expression]."

Because such is the nature of verbal expression, one should now proceed from among the four subsequent sections. First, the "Fundamental Section" (Mūla-bhāga) provides a brief explanation that reveals the proof [of the stages].
Second, the "Section on Requesting" (Adhyeṣaṇā-bhāga) sweeps away conceptual marks to reveal quiescence.

Within the "Section on Exposition and Reflection" (Deśanā-pratibimba-bhāga), the reflection of the stages is used as a metaphor to manifest virtue; finally, the last section reveals the proof by way of those who are to be converted.

For the sake of benefit, the subsequent text states that by attaining the power of the Dharma, the earth shook and flowers rained down, and so forth. These various distinctions collectively serve as manifest proofs (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the statement that one should "discriminate both proof and teaching according to the essential tenets" (*siddhānta*): the essentials of this sutra do not exceed these nine points of proof and teaching. Of these, the first is the introduction (*nidāna*), while the remaining eight correctly reveal the characteristics of proof and teaching. As for the eight [points]: 1. The Buddha’s manifestation of the body; 2. The manifestation of the Dharma-body; 3. The manifestation of the transformation-body; 4. The manifestation of the land; 5. The manifestation of the assembly; 6. The manifestation of the time; 7. The manifestation of the place; 8. The manifestation of the teaching. These eight are the actual manifestations of the Tathāgata’s great compassionate skillful means, which are the causes and conditions for the arising of the Mahāyāna teachings. They are called "manifestations" because they are all produced through the power of the Tathāgata’s original vows and his sovereign mastery over all phenomena. Furthermore, the term "manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*) signifies that these are not the Tathāgata’s own true body, but rather bodies manifested through his transformative power. This is because the Tathāgata’s true body is eternally quiescent and transcends all conceptualization. It is precisely because he manifests such bodies that sentient beings are able to perceive and hear them. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata “manifests” these forms. Because these eight manifestations are the primary causes and conditions for the arising of the Mahāyāna teachings, they are termed the "eight manifestations. The first section of the middle part, "Entering Samādhi," reveals correct realization; the subsequent seven sections clarify the sequential arising of verbal teachings.

Regarding the sequence of these verbal teachings, their meaning is as explained in the initial gate. As for the "ten" mentioned, they are divided into ten according to the differences between the stages (*bhūmi*).
As for the "forty-eight distinct textual divisions," there are eight divisions for the first stage, two for the second stage, and so on, up to eight for the tenth stage.

Regarding the classification into sections, there are forty-eight parts in total. Above, the characteristics were distinguished according to the *sūtra*; below, they are analyzed according to the *śāstra*.

Within the *śāstra*, there are two parts: first, the analysis of the textual passages; second, from "In this way" onwards, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text. Thus ends the third [section].
Regarding the "Ten Grounds" (*daśabhūmi*) within the explanation, these are divided into ten distinct stages according to each respective ground. Ten.

The Dharma-gate of the Grounds is fully explained as previously set forth. Regarding the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), which subsumes those below, the text is analyzed by first stating the number and subsequently listing the eight names, as interpreted in other treatises.
There are three ways of explaining the meaning: first, the "superior-to-superior" gate, where the subsequent text arises from the preceding in a sequential manner;
second, the "general-and-particular" gate, as described below in the section on the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) and so forth; third, [the gate of]... [text fragment].
Regarding the inclusion of the gates according to their corresponding meanings, they are mutually subsumed.

Now, concerning the statement that "the eight [factors] subsumed by the first stage" are included within the gate of inclusion, there are two ways of explaining this: First, inclusion is defined as the general encompassing of particulars;
because the first stage universally includes all eight specific divisions within itself, it is called "inclusion. Second, inclusion is defined as the particular encompassing of particulars.

Taken collectively, these are termed "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*). Because they are subsumed into eight divisions according to their distinct meanings within the initial stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), it is said that "the first stage comprises eight parts.

Here, "parts" (*aṅga*) refers to the individual distinctions. Among these eight, why is it stated that the first stage comprises [all] of them, when the latter two can be included in the first stage while the meaning of the former six applies throughout?
In this text, there are three senses of inclusion: first, inclusion within its own level (*svabhūmika*).

Regarding the analysis of inclusion: as in the case of "Free from Defilement" (*vimalā*), the eight intermediate stages are included in two preceding ones, just as the latter two divisions of the tenth stage, though they pertain to all ten stages, are collectively termed "included in the tenth stage. Conversely, the three subsequent stages include the preceding ones;
thus, although the first six stages prior to this [seventh] stage pertain to all [ten], because they follow the latter two, they are also said to be "included in the first."

Regarding the following eight names for the introduction (*nidāna*): it is said that by means of the introductory words, through the samādhi, once the introduction has arisen and [Vajragarbha] desires to preach for the sake of the assembly, Vajragarbha enters samādhi in silence to manifest the realization of his capacity to teach.

Furthermore, desiring to receive empowerment, this samādhi is named "the samādhi of the samādhi-portion" (*samādhi-aṃśa-samādhi*). This is the Chinese term for it; its name is *samyak-samādhi* (Right Concentration).

Because the mind abides in the Dharma and is free from deviant distraction, it is called "Right Concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*). Regarding the "Section on Bestowal of Empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna-vibhāga*):

having previously entered samādhi with the desire to receive empowerment, once he has entered meditative absorption, all Buddhas collectively empower him; because this matter of empowerment is clarified, it is called the "Section on Empowerment.
Regarding the "Section on Arising" (*vyutthāna-vibhāga*): after that Vajragarbha has obtained supreme power, desiring to preach for the sake of the assembly, he emerges from his concentration.

It is called the "Section on Origination" (*utthāna-bhāga*) because it clarifies the process of arising. As for the "Section on the Basis" (*mūla-bhāga*), once one has arisen from meditative concentration, the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi-dharma*) are briefly explained;

since this serves as the basis for the extensive exposition, it is called the "Section on the Basis. As for the "Section on the Request" (*adhyeṣaṇā-bhāga*), after the brief explanation of the stages has been given, the great assembly remains silent;

hearing the name [of the teaching], they feel a thirsting longing and desire to understand its meaning, so they join together to make a formal request—therefore, it is called the "Section on the Request. As for the "Section on the Exposition" (*deśanā-bhāga*):...
Since the conditions for the request have been fulfilled, it is possible to provide an extensive exposition; therefore, it is called the "Exposition Section.

As for the "Comparison of Excellence," this is also a form of exposition, but it specifically employs comparisons and measurements based on the fullness of the ground to manifest its superiority; the preceding section was thus termed the "Comparison of Excellence."
Having thus concluded the preceding section, we shall now provide an exegesis based on the text itself, beginning with the initial preface.

Within this preface, the treatise (*śāstra*) is concise; therefore, it should be explained by relying upon the sūtra. The sūtra consists of two parts: first, the *samyak-prasāda-anuśaṃsā-nidāna* (the sequence for establishing faith);

second, the *nidāna* (the introductory narrative). There are five general gates for analyzing these two sequences: first, explaining the names of the sequences and the reasons for their establishment; second, clarifying the distinctions between the names of the two sequences.

This consists of five parts: (1) revealing both the gains and losses; (2) explaining the three interpretations and two types of prefaces regarding their commonality and specific application; (3) determining the sequence of the two types of prefaces within the text; (4) providing a word-by-word commentary; and (5) interpreting the meaning according to the text.
Regarding the first section, the term "preface" (*nidāna*) is first explained: "initiation" refers to the Buddha’s preliminary reliance upon time and place before he was about to preach the sutra.
The "Preface of Exhortation" refers to the gathering of the assembly through supernatural powers and the like, which initiates what is to be taught.
The "Preface of Testimony and Faith" means that Ānanda, having received the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, wished to transmit what he had heard to future generations;

thus, he first addressed the sentient beings, saying, "Thus have I heard," thereby manifesting his own lineage of transmission to certify its credibility. This is called the Preface of Testimony and Faith.
Why are there two [versions], given that the sūtra is but one? Although the essence of the sūtra is one, it may be spoken of as two according to the time and the person.
For example, there is what was spoken by the Tathāgata and what was transmitted by Ānanda. What the Tathāgata spoke benefited those of his own time;
what Ānanda transmitted is for the sake of the future. Therefore, they are distinguished in terms of person and time.
Since these two sūtras both possess two introductory sections (*nidāna*), they should likewise be distinguished.
Within the second section, first the differences between the names of the two introductions are clarified, followed by an exposition of their respective merits and defects.

Regarding the names established for the two introductions by various schools, there are generally four pairs: first, based on the meaning of "introduction" (*nidāna*), they are named the "Certification of Faith" (*śraddhā-pratyaya*) and the "Exhortation to Begin" (*ārambha*).
1. Classified according to the person involved, they are named the Tathāgata Preface and the Ānanda Preface;
that which is the Preface of the Arousing [of the Teaching] is called the Tathāgata Preface, and that which is the Preface of the Certification of Faith is called the Ānanda Preface.
2. Classified according to time, they are named the Present Preface and the Future Preface; the Tathāgata Preface is termed the Present, and the Ānanda Preface is termed the Future. 4.
Regarding the sūtra by way of its title, the prologue and epilogue of the sūtra are designated as "Spoken by the Buddha" (buddha-bhāṣita) and thereby constitute the sūtra itself.

In contrast to this sūtra, the sequence of the prologue and epilogue is manifested: the Tathāgata’s prologue constitutes the preface to the sūtra, while Ānanda’s prologue is declared to be the epilogue of the sūtra.
This Ānanda prologue has another name: the "Prologue of the Bequeathed Teaching" (yījiào-xù), as it consists of the Buddha’s final instructions.
Because this introduction was established by the Teacher, it is called the "Bequeathed Teaching" (*yìjiào*); thus, the names differ in this way. What are the strengths and weaknesses here?

Within these four pairs, there is no discrepancy regarding the meaning of "testimony of faith" (*zhèngxìn*) and "arising of the name" (*fāqǐ*). In the second pair, the introduction by Ānanda is without fault in either name or meaning;
however, the introduction by the Tathāgata has meanings that are not fully exhausted, as seen in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, where there are transformed Buddhas, a sovereign king, and a queen.

The five individuals, including Caṇḍī and Śrīmālā, initiated various sūtras; such initiations are frequent and not limited to the Buddha alone. If one speaks only of the Tathāgata, the meaning of initiation by other persons is omitted.
Thus, there is a deficiency in the title when it refers solely to the Tathāgata’s introduction. Regarding the introduction by Ānanda, the same applies:

the first pair [of initiators] is established, but the third pair—where the present has no fault but the future would have a defect—is not established. This is so if the Buddha were speaking in the present.
Regarding the title "The Introduction Spoken by Ānanda": at the time of its transmission, it was also the present.

If one were to designate what was spoken in the presence of the Buddha as the "Ānanda Introduction" while treating it as the future, then in contrast to Ānanda’s present transmission, that "Tathāgata Introduction" would have to be called the past.
Since the time of both introductions was equally the present, it is incorrect to unilaterally designate one as the future.

Regarding the future [sections], it is logically appropriate that they not be established as counterparts to the present; thus, they should be discarded, or at least one may follow a single interpretation without harm.

Within the fourth pair, the Sūtra is clear and faultless, whereas what follows the Sūtra contains errors. If one says the section preceding the Sūtra may be called the "Introduction" (Nidāna), yet if one says it comes after the Sūtra, then it lacks the meaning of an "Introduction.
If the Tathāgata’s Introduction were spoken by the Buddha before the Sūtra, then Ānanda’s Introduction would be [the subsequent part].
Furthermore, regarding the words "before" and "after" found in the scriptures transmitted by Ānanda, if there were faults in what preceded the scripture, it would have to be discarded;
yet even the preceding discourse does not establish the principle. Now, because all these names possess such faults, we retain the title "Initiating the Proof of Faith" (Faith-Initiation).
Regarding the terms "comprehensive" (*tong*) and "restricted" (*ju*) mentioned in the third section: "Comprehensive" means that both prefaces are equally termed "testimony of faith" (*zhengxin*);
the intent of establishing the "preface of origination" (*fajqi*) is likewise the same, as both serve to engender faith. Therefore, both prefaces are given the common name "testimony of faith.

Furthermore, the "origination" is the primary meaning of a preface, as both are intended to initiate the teaching; thus, both prefaces are equally designated as "origination. Their specific distinctions have been clarified above.

Since the meaning of "introduction" (*nidāna*) applies generally to both, why is the "Initiation" (*pratimokṣa*) exclusively attributed to the Tathāgata, while the "Certainty of Faith" (*śraddhā-prasāda*) belongs solely to Ānanda?
