The storehouse of roots of goodness is firm, and because these two forms of firmness are themselves the storehouse, how much more so for that Bodhisattva whose internal virtue of roots of goodness is both firm and a storehouse?
Therefore, the third section below joins them together as "like firm" and "like a storehouse. These two are distinct;
thus, the word "this" (i.e., *iti*) applies to both phrases, meaning that the internal virtue of roots of goodness of that Bodhisattva is as previously described.
The two "stores" (*kośa*) are themselves firm; being firm like a diamond (*vajra*), they constitute the internal virtues and roots of goodness of that bodhisattva.
Since these two forms of firmness are the store, it is like the "Vajra Store" (*Vajragarbha*); thus, the preceding section has correctly explained that the diamond is the store.
From this point downward is the second section, which, by means of contrast, reveals its superiority and clarifies that the essence of this treasury has the meaning of "vajra.

Within this, there are three parts: first, distinguishing its superiority over inferiority; second, citing other inferior things to manifest its superiority; and third, concluding the preceding discussion with the term "therefore.
Regarding the first part, the statement "among all roots of goodness, these are the most powerful" relies on a contrast with other forms of goodness to manifest this [treasury].
The Bodhisattva’s internal virtues and roots of goodness, as previously described, possess a superior power to shatter obstacles within the womb;

because these roots of goodness of the Bodhisattva’s ten stages can destroy the five abodes, they are the most supreme in their power to shatter obstacles when compared to the various virtues of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.

To illustrate this, the analogy of the diamond (*vajra*) is employed; it is also used to generate a lower comparison against other virtues in order to manifest the excellence of these [Bodhisattva virtues].

The Bodhisattva’s internal virtues and roots of goodness are like the aforementioned power of the tree’s core to produce [growth]; their excellence surpasses what was previously mentioned, yet they are also capable of such power.
Just as that tree’s core is solid and substantial and thus able to produce branches and leaves, so too do these ten stages (bhūmis) produce all other virtues.

Their initial arising is called "production" (*janman*), and their final fulfillment is called "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*). Furthermore, they may be termed "production" when acting as causes, and "condition" (*pratyaya*) when acting as supporting conditions.
It is said that the practice of the paths of humans and devas is what gives rise to them; yet the practice of the supramundane path of humans and devas is even more excellent.
Within the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, regarding the inclusion of the supramundane and mundane wholesome dharmas, it is stated that "other roots of goodness cannot destroy them.
This means that the roots of goodness possessed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are unable to exhaust them.
Having ultimately destroyed the afflictions—this, compared to the first power, reveals its inferiority; yet compared to the subsequent power, it should likewise be said that they cannot be produced.
This is not discussed in detail here, as it is fully explained in the alternative translation of the root text. Therefore, it is called the "Concluding Section" (*kṣepa*).
Because it possesses both of the preceding meanings, it is termed the "Vajra Samādhi. Within this section, the initial part concludes what preceded and generates what follows.

The preceding section introduces the scriptural passage, while the subsequent commentary merely explains the intent of entering samādhi without interpreting the text; it is now appropriate to provide that interpretation.
The phrase "at that time" refers to the time of entering samādhi, meaning when the Buddha was in the celestial realm and the great assembly had gathered.

"Vajragarbha" refers to the person who enters samādhi; he relies upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as the basis for his meditative absorption. Thus, he is so named because he receives the power from above.

Regarding the samādhi called "Entering with Power and Might" (*vīryabalavegavat-praveśa*): this clearly explains entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), wherein one withdraws the spirit into the Ultimate Way;
thus it is termed "entering. What is that which is entered? What is this samādhi? It is the so-called "Bodhisattva Mahāyāna Samādhi.

To speak of "Bodhisattva" is to distinguish [the practitioner] by way of person; to speak of "Mahāyāna" is to manifest its uniqueness by way of function, as it carries all across and penetrates everywhere.
It is called the "Vehicle" (yāna) and is designated as "Great" (mahā), as explained in the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra].
It is described as "wisdom-light samādhi" (*prajñā-āloka-samādhi*) when referring to its essential substance; it is described as a "vehicle" when referring to its functional activity.

Regarding the term "light," this refers to the manifestation of its distinct characteristics, for its essence is free from the obscuration of darkness, hence it is called "light. The mind abiding in a single object is termed "samādhi"; this is that which is entered.

Since this is already a bodhisattva samādhi, why is it necessary to rely on [the power of] another? There are three meanings to this: first, because the transformation is attributed to the Tathāgata, he manifests as relying on that power;
second, although he has attained it himself, when facing a superior person such as a Buddha, he cannot act with complete autonomy and must look upward in supplication;
third, although he has partially attained and realized this concentration, its ultimate fulfillment resides in the Buddha. Now, this [samādhi] is intended to be for the sake of the Buddha.
Because it is a superior transformation, one must rely on the power [of others]; if one were capable of it oneself, one could speak of it independently.

Since the Buddha himself is present, why would one need to rely on the power [of others] and speak forcefully? This explanation is the same as the previous one. To augment the power, the treatise states that "the Dharma is not an object of thought," which carries a dual meaning:
first, from the perspective of one's own level (*svabhūmi*), it reveals that what is spoken is based on personal realization and is not something heard from others.
Regarding the two types of reflection, this stage is explained as being superior: one must rely upon samādhi and receive the power of the Buddha to be capable of proclaiming these essential dharmas;
it cannot be proclaimed through the power of one's own independent reflection. Furthermore, there are many general purposes for entering samādhi:
either to sever afflictions (*kleśa*), to generate various virtues, to experience the bliss of meditative absorption, to manifest supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), or for other such reasons.

Observing the capacities of beings, he preaches the Dharma in accordance with them; sometimes he reveals that the Dharma transcends words, or manifests the power of realization that can preach it, or bestows superior strength upon those who receive it.
Since these modes are not uniform, I shall now explain the intent of "entering" based on the latter two.

Regarding the section on "bestowing empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), first is the summary that concludes the preceding and introduces the following; next is the explanation of the text itself, which consists of three parts:

(1) because [the Bodhisattva] entered samādhi, all Buddhas praised him in unison and granted him empowerment; (2) from "Furthermore, all bodhisattvas... onwards, it clarifies the purpose for which the empowerment is bestowed; (3) from "You should discern...
onwards, it demonstrates the characteristics of the empowerment being manifested.
In the first section of the sutra, the essential points are summarized into three parts, which are further detailed as ten. To state these three summaries:

first, the Sūtra-master arranges the sequence to show that because Vajragarbha entered samādhi, the Buddhas of the ten directions manifested their bodies in unison, desiring to bestow praise upon him;

second, from the words "Excellent! (*sādhu*) onwards, the Buddhas collectively offer praise, corresponding to his prior entry into meditative concentration to manifest the realization of his capacity to preach; third, furthermore...
Regarding the Buddha’s permission to perform the empowerment, there are ten distinct sections of discourse preceding his entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to receive the Buddha’s power.
Within the first of these sections, there are five distinct phrases: (1) restating the *samādhi* previously entered; (2) clarifying the distance of the Buddhas from which they come;
(3) clarifying the number of Buddhas; (4) clarifying their manifestation of physical forms; and (5) indicating their shared names. These are the five.
In the commentary on the first section, only the third and fifth phrases are explained, while the remaining three phrases are omitted.
In the second section, there is only one phrase which the commentary explains. In the third section, there are four distinct phrases: first, the Buddhas personally state their own number;
second, "all share the same name," where they themselves proclaim their own names; third, "I grant you," where [the Buddha] grants permission; and fourth, [the phrase regarding] the assembly.
Having already performed the addition of four, this section below clarifies the basis for that addition. Among the subsequent four [verses], the commentary explains only the first two;
the final one, "I bestow upon you," is omitted from the separate explanation as it follows the general text. Within these ten phrases, six phrases are explained collectively.
Within the first section, the phrase "At that time, Vajra entered samādhi" restates what preceded to introduce what follows.
The phrase "immediately, in the ten directions, beyond worlds as numerous as the dust motes of ten billion lands" clarifies the distance of the Buddha’s presence;

this is explained by distinguishing whether it refers to a single direction or the ten directions collectively. According to the *Da ben* (Original Text), it says: "At that time, in each of the ten directions."

Beyond billions of buddha-fields, there is a Tathāgata named Vajragarbha. Likewise, in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the dust motes of ten billion fields, there are Buddhas as numerous as the dust motes of ten billion fields.
This mention of Buddhas throughout the ten directions—passing beyond ten billion times ten billion buddha-fields—is intended to clarify the vast number of Buddhas;
it refers to those who exist beyond even ten billion times the number of dust motes in such fields.
In a single location there are as many Buddhas as these, all sharing the same name, Vajra; do they dwell scattered about?
It is that beyond worlds as numerous as the dust motes of ten billion Buddha-lands to the east, there is a Tathāgata named Vajragarbha;

likewise it is the same throughout the ten directions. Thus, only when one has passed through worlds as numerous as the dust motes of ten billion lands in the ten directions does one find ten [such Buddhas].
Beyond ten billion Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms of those lands; furthermore, there are ten such Buddhas.
Thus, proceeding sequentially through the ten directions, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of ten billion Buddha-lands in total.

Each of these Buddhas is separated from the next by a distance of worlds as numerous as the atoms of ten billion Buddha-lands. This refers to what was previously mentioned regarding "beyond ten billion [lands] in the ten directions."

Regarding the statement that there is a Buddha who bestows empowerment at the time of attaining the tenth stage, this is spoken in terms of proximity using the number of particles of dust in worlds as a metaphor.
Now, in order to rely upon numbers to symbolize the Dharma, it is said that there are Buddhas numbering ten billion particles of dust. Why do all these Buddhas manifest their bodies together?

If they did not manifest their bodies, the assembly would not know [of them]; and if the assembly did not know [them], how could they [know] that they are separated by worlds numbering ten billion particles of dust? If the assembly did not...

Because there is no way to convey [the meaning] by relying on those ten numerical symbols that represent the dharmas, it is necessary to manifest the body and speech. Regarding the term "same name" (同 *tóng*), the subsequent treatise itself provides its own explanation.
In the second section, the word "well done" (*shàn zāi* 善哉) is a term of praise; "shàn" means good, and "zāi" is an auxiliary particle.

For what reason is there a double sense in the repeated exclamation of praise? First, all Buddhas have contemplated this supreme Dharma, desiring that sentient beings attain realization identical to their own;
yet no one was able to awaken to it, and now Vajragarbha has suddenly been able to enter it—therefore, the Buddhas marvel and exclaim, "Excellent!
Excellent! Second, all Buddhas desire to transmit this Dharma to sentient beings, but no one had previously expounded it.

Because Vajragarbha, having manifested realization, desired to speak [of this], the Buddha joyfully praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You are indeed able to enter and emerge from what has been praised.
The word "indeed" (*nai*) is an expression of rarity and transcendence; since others are entirely incapable while you alone are capable, it is said, "you are indeed able."

Regarding the phrase "furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) in the third section: since the previous praise has already been concluded, the word "furthermore" is used to indicate that he is now manifesting his own additional [merit].
As for the statement "Buddhas as numerous as the dust motes of ten billion lands," this is intended to cause the assembly to hear the number ten and thereby understand what it symbolizes.

Since the numerical value was already revealed previously, why is it necessary to clarify it again? This is the number personally proclaimed by the Buddha at that time; the previous instance was merely recorded by the compiler of the sutra.
Regarding the phrase "all having the same name," this expression is insufficient; it should properly state, "all having the same single name, Vajragarbha Buddha.

This reveals that his own name is identical to the name bestowed upon him, which serves to gladden them. The statement "I empower you" is intended so that the assembly may all know of it and develop faith in what he says.
The mention of "the power of Rocana’s original vow" attributes the manifestation of this Buddha to that source.
Observing the trend of this passage, it appears that "original vow" (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*) is named as the power upon which [the Buddhas] rely.

According to the subsequent commentary, "vow" refers to Śākyamuni’s past vow-power, while "intentional power" (*adhiṣṭhāna-bala*) refers to Śākyamuni’s present transformative power. It is by virtue of these two that all Buddhas know [this matter] in common.

Regarding the three sections of the treatise, they are explained in accordance with the sutra. From the beginning up to the point where the manifold [aspects] are revealed, this explains the first section of the sutra. Below the section on this samādhi...
The second section has been explained; the following explains the third section.
Within the first section, there are three questions and answers:
the first question and answer explains the third phrase of the sutra, while the latter two explain the fifth phrase. "Why many? asks regarding the aforementioned third phrase of the sutra.

If the power of one or two Buddhas were sufficient, for what reason do as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a buddha-field collectively bestow their empowerment? The intention of this question is as follows:

although this sutra directly states that there are as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten billion buddha-fields without using the word "empowerment," this question speaks of "many Buddhas bestowing empowerment" because the many Buddhas are precisely those who are capable of bestowing it;
thus, by citing the act of empowerment, the question seeks to establish the point. Furthermore, this refers to the ninth phrase.

Regarding the phrase "the empowerment of you," there is no further separate explanation; it follows each clause. Here, the term "empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is used as a formal inquiry to manifest the Dharma Master’s increased reverence:
that many Buddhas empower him together to reveal the supreme excellence of the essential Dharma, thereby manifesting his own respectability and causing the assembly to revere him.
This explains the phrase "ten billion *koṭis* of dust. The two subsequent questions and answers herein have not yet been explained.
In the explanation of the first section, the first question and answer clarify the preceding fifth phrase;
the subsequent question and answer reveal the underlying intent for establishing these identical names. Why are they given identical names? This is the initial question.

As stated previously, many Buddhas collectively bestow their empowerment to manifest the Dharma and increase reverence for the Dharma-preacher. If that is so, [what of] those with identical names or different names...?
The Buddhas all collectively increase their empowerment, making it even more sublime. For what reason now is it said that they add their empowerment through the power of the original vow?

It is because Vairocana Buddha, while formerly in the causal stage, made this vow: "When I attain Buddhahood and preach the Dharma of the stages (*bhūmi*), may all Buddhas empower me by bestowing the syllable *vajra*.
Since that vow has now been fulfilled, they are able to empower him with the same title, "Vajra."
"Kang, for what reason did the Tathāgata make such a vow? This is the second question, which interrogates the fundamental point regarding the Tathāgata Ruciraketu.
"In the past, why did he make this vow of sharing the same name to manifest many Buddhas? This answer clarifies the intent behind making the vow in the past;
these words are difficult to understand. The previous question asked why he made the vow of sharing the same name, and now the answer explains it.
If one asks, "How can this be known?"—this objection is not difficult to resolve. To speak fully, it should be stated that [the sūtra] reveals that many Buddhas equally rely upon this Dharma.
Equally relying upon what Dharma? It means they equally rely upon the Vajra-dharma of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). How does it reveal their equality?
Because many Buddhas have equally realized the Vajra-dharma, they share the same title, "Vajra. Why is this revealed? It is to reveal that many [Buddhas] are equal.

The Buddhas equally rely upon this Dharma to manifest the essential excellence of the Dharma, from which many Buddhas are born. Because many Buddhas equally rely upon it, they cause the multitude to revere the Dharma with deep respect and yearning for it;

subsequently, they may preach for them. The Tathāgatas, through their profound past knowledge, know that those who share the same name possess this essential method for manifesting the Dharma and initiating transformation.
For this reason, they make this vow of sharing the same name. Furthermore, these words accord with foreign [Indian] usage.

The reason why this discourse is difficult to understand is that, following this principle, one should say that many Buddhas have revealed it. What is it that they reveal? They reveal the Dharma-gate of the Vajra-samādhi entered by Vajragarbha. How is it revealed? It is revealed through the empowerment of all Buddhas via their respective *akṣara-vajra* (syllable-vajras). One should know that the purpose for which this is done is the Vajra-dharma. As it was said, "O Bhadrapāla, it is through the empowerment of all Buddhas via their respective *akṣaras*. "Bhadra" means "Noble One. "Empowerment" refers to the empowerment of all Buddhas via their respective *akṣaras*.

"Akṣara" means "indestructible" (*akṣaya*). Because it is indestructible, it is called a *vajra*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *samādhi*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dhyāna*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dhāraṇī*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *mudrā*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *mantra*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *vidyā*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *siddhi*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *tattva*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *jñāna*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *bodhi*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *nirvāṇa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmadhātu*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *tathatā*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-sthiti*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avasthāna*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-ananyathā*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avyabhicāra*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-asaṃbheda*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avirodha*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avikopa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-aviparyāsa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvāda*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvāditva*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatva*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha*. Because it is indestructible, it is called a *dharmatā-avisaṃvādanatā-tathatā-avikopa-aviparyāsa-asaṃbheda-avirodha-avik
At the outset, it was known that the one who acted was Bhadrapāla; when he preached the *Daśabhūmika*, all the Buddhas conferred upon him the name Dharmamati.
It was known with certainty that the one who acted was Dharmamati; at all assemblies, they were likewise unanimous. Now, this case is also the same.

For what reason must [the Buddha] now manifest [this]? Why did he remain silent and enter into this dharma before Vajragarbha? The great assembly did not know what he had entered, nor did they know what it was.
Having entered the state of no-mind, by what means could one obtain [this state]? It must be manifested for the purpose of speaking so that the multitude may know and feel yearning and aspiration.
Because the Tathāgata, in the past, knew in profound wisdom that there was a meaning of manifesting the Dharma and initiating transformation through a shared name, he made this vow.
To say that "this samādhi is the essence of the Dharma" explains the second section, the praise for entering this samādhi.

This samādhi is the essence of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) to be explained hereafter, and not the essence of other samādhis. Furthermore, this statement explains the reason why all Buddhas together praise it:
because this samādhi is the essence of the Dharma, all Buddhas collectively exclaim, "Excellent! Excellent! (sādhu sādhu).

From "The Original Practice" (*Pūrvayoga*) onwards, the third section of the sūtra is explained in four parts. First, the second part—where it is stated that they all share the same name—is addressed;
this in turn resolves the first phrase regarding the term "one billion. Subsequently, the fourth part is explained, which concerns their original vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*);

therefore, the third part is added. [The text] says, "I add for you," yet it briefly omits an explanation. Question: Since the shared names were already explained previously, why are they now explained again?

The commentary first explains that the "same name" (*samāna-nāman*) applies to both the bestower and the recipient; this explanation differs from the previous one in its intent regarding the identity of the names of the bestower and the recipient, and therefore it is discussed again.

Within the text, there are four points: first, it clarifies that in the past, the bestower and the recipient were both named Vajra. Below this, the meaning of the Buddhas' proclamation is further elucidated.
Regarding the first of these four points, it clarifies that in the past, both the bestower and the recipient shared the same name, Vajra.
Second, it clarifies that the Dharma taught in the past is identical to that of today; third, it clarifies that what is added and what is added to today is identical to the past;
fourth, it concludes by showing that when he was practicing the Bodhisattva path in the past, his name was the same as "Vajra"—this is the first phrase.
When Vairocana Buddha was practicing the Bodhisattva path in the past, he saw Vairocana of the past...
When that Buddha taught the Dharma of the Grounds (*bhūmi*), the *sa* syllable and the Vajra of the Consecrated were both empowered.
Why is this clarified? Because the common origin of today [of this teaching] derives from that; therefore, it is cited and explained together with this Dharma. This is the second phrase.

Because it was taught in the same manner as now, it is said to be "explained together. Why is this clarified? It is to manifest that the present teaching is identical to that of the past. As for what is currently...
Since the teaching of the Dharma is not different from that of the past, how could the one who bestows the empowerment differ from the original?

Now, having attained perfect enlightenment, he is also named Vajra; this is the third phrase clarifying that the one who bestows the empowerment (the empowering agent) and the one who receives it (the empowered object) are not different from those of the past.
Therefore, he is also named Vajragarbha. Thus, "not different" is the fourth [point], which serves as the conclusion regarding the empowering agent.
The addition [of the title] is likewise the same as in the past because it is named "Vajra"; thus, there is no difference in the name. The following section explains the intent of the address:
for what reason do all Buddhas address Vajragarbha, saying, "Because we share the same name"? The subsequent passage explains this;

furthermore, when that Bodhisattva hears that all Tathāgatas have names identical to his own, he experiences an increase of exultation. Therefore, it was necessary to address him. Why is it that he hears these identical names?

The exultation of Śakra has two meanings: first, exultation for one's own sake, which means reflecting that while that Buddha abides in the fulfillment of the vajra-dharma and has become a Buddha, I too shall abide in this dharma and thus become like that Buddha; therefore, one exults. Second, exultation for the sake of others:
Vajragarbha had entered a silent samādhi and desired to speak to the assembly, yet the great multitude did not know what state he had entered.

For those who have no aspiration or wish and thus cannot attain [realization], it is taught that through the Tathāgatas’ proclamation of their shared names, they all come to know what has been entered:
this is the Vajra Dharma. Because they subsequently desire to hear it and are able to be taught, its transformative intent is fully expressed;
therefore, they rejoice. Why is it not said that [the time] has passed immeasurably? This explains the first phrase: the expression "ten billion" is used to complete the phrasing.
There are three questions and answers here. In the first two phrases, there is both a question and an answer; in the third phrase, there is only an answer without a question.
Why is it not said that he "transcends immeasurable realms"? This constitutes the first question. This text is somewhat abbreviated;

if it were complete, it should have stated: "Why is it not said that he transcends those ten billion [realms]? It speaks of "immeasurable realms" as numerous as the atoms of all Buddhas, yet it mentions only "ten billion."

The answer below explains, by means of a skillful method (*upāya*), that there are many Buddhas: it declares that where the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) are expounded, there is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of a Buddha;
this is not restricted to a specific quantity, yet the mention of "ten billion" is used as a skillful method to complete the number ten.

Because the number of atoms (*paramāṇu*) therein makes manifest the multiplicity of Buddhas, it is said that the skillful method reveals many Buddhas. Why is it specifically stated that there are ten billion Buddha-fields? This is the second question.
It is already known that ten is not said to be immeasurable; for what reason is it definitively stated as ten billion, neither more nor less?
The answer below is given because the Dharma of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) is being taught, and these are manifested by means of numbers; therefore, only "ten" is mentioned.

Regarding the question of why one is missing—if this were further questioned, one should ask: "For what reason are only the Ten Stages taught? According to the response, it should be so; such is the case in this sutra.

It is frequently stated that the number ten is used to provide a comprehensive illustration by way of analogy; this is because in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, whatever dharma is taught, ten is often taken as the standard number.

Thus, the "Ten Stages" (*daśabhūmi*) are taught because ten represents the completion of a numerical cycle. Following the frequent use of the number ten, the fourth original vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*) is explained.
To clarify the original vow of Rocana Buddha, the phrase "the former vow of that Buddha" is added. The meaning of "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) is as explained previously.
Now, furthermore, he adds his own power to explain the sūtra. Vairocana Buddha now uses the power of his intent to empower Vajragarbha, causing him to enter samādhi;
this is called "self-empowerment" (svādhāna). It is subsequently empowered by other Buddhas, which is why it is called "addition" (adhāna).

Because of Vairocana’s original vow-power, he causes the Vajra-Buddhas of the ten directions to add their empowerment; therefore, the subsequent words conclude [the section], stating that it is due to the original vow.
The "Binding" (kṣepa) refers to the power of the prior vow; the "Adding" (āveśa) refers to the subsequent addition of the empowerment of other Buddhas.

Why is there this addition? The following explains the purpose of the addition and clarifies its characteristics. First, a question and answer are provided to initiate the discussion; subsequently, a detailed explanation follows.
Regarding the purpose of the addition, there are both questions and answers; regarding the characteristics of the subsequent addition, there is only a question without an answer.
The following will explain that further questions and answers are required to fully manifest its characteristics; however, as this would be overly cumbersome, no such responses are provided here.
Regarding the purpose for which [the Buddhas] act, why is it asked? There are four purposes for which all Buddhas collectively bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*):
first, with respect to Vajragarbha, because that Bodhisattva has attained samādhi; second, with respect to the original vow of Śākyamuni.
Adding these two preceding sections fully reveals that they are taught within the first part of the sutra by way of three perspectives on the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Adding the four perspectives regarding those to be converted (*vineya*) establishes [the practice] as benefiting oneself and others.

Adding these two subsequent sections fully reveals that they are taught within the latter part of the sutra. These four perspectives also follow a sequential order: first, Vajragarbha attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding that, one might ask: why does the Buddha bestow his empowerment? It is because of the power of Vairocana’s vows that he bestows it. For what purpose is this empowerment bestowed? It is for the sake of preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, for what purpose is the preaching of the Dharma? It is for the sake of establishing the bodhisattvas in conduct that brings benefit to both self and others.

The purposes of the first two have already been analyzed in the preceding text. Now, since this *Abhidharma* (Treatise on the Dharma) further inquires into the intent behind the empowerment, we ask about it here.

Regarding the question "For what reason is there an addition? the answer below states that it is for the purpose of explaining the dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Furthermore, as to why there is an addition, the text asks about the characteristics of this addition.

In the following passage, the purpose of the addition is first explained, and subsequently the characteristics of the addition are interpreted. Within the section concerning the purpose, the scriptural text contains two parts.
Regarding the first pair, the purpose of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*): it is to cause those to be converted to enter [the path].

Within the former [of these two], the word "moreover" (*punar*) is a term used for repetition; since its fundamental vow was already explained previously, it is explained again here as the purpose for which the teaching is given—hence the use of "moreover.
"All bodhisattvas" refers to the persons for whom the purpose is intended; "inconceivable dharmas" refers to the object.
The words of profound praise stating that the Dharma taught is inconceivable (*acintya*) are also spoken in the sutras.

Generally, this is one [concept], yet it is divided into two according to its meaning. When speaking from the perspective of the Dharma in relation to the mind (*citta*), it is called "inconceivable," because fundamentally there is no mind outside of the Dharma.
What is the meaning of this? The arising of the characteristics of the mind originates from deluded conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

Due to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), signs (*nimitta*) arise; because one relies upon these signs, mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*) further arise, which are grasped as being existent and given the name "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*).
Because of these conceptions, names (*nāman*) arise; relying upon these names, mental conceptions again arise that follow after the names to grasp at reality—this is precisely vitarka and vicāra.
Relying upon this vitarka and vicāra, verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) arises; and relying upon verbal expression, [the cycle continues].

Furthermore, one gives rise to the mental conception of grasping at the teachings spoken; this is taking mere words as the Way and the mind as practice. Thus, these conceptions blaze forth without ceasing.
Now, by acceding to the reality of the Dharma, one eliminates the characteristics of deluded thought, which is the characteristic of non-arising.

Because it does not arise, it is designated "the extinction of the mind. Because it is called the extinction of the mind, it is called "non-arising. Because it is called non-arising, [it is thus realized].
When applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) do not arise, because applied thought does not arise, verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) accordingly perishes.

Because verbal expression perishes, one no longer relies on words to grasp what is expressed. Because one does not grasp what is expressed, the path of speech is cut off and the movements of the mind (*cittagati*) are extinguished.
Because the mind is extinguished, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*); because words have perished, it is termed "indiscussible" (*avācya*). Therefore, it is said to be "inconceivable."
Judging from the facts, when comparing the phenomena to the Dharma, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*) because the Dharma transcends the realm of the mind and speech;
thus it is said to be inconceivable. Now, however, we speak of the phenomena in relation to the realm of the mind; for this reason, it is called "inconceivable.

The following section explains the various *āyatanas* (entrances) as a comparative analysis of the distinctions in the meaning of wisdom (*jñāna*). It clarifies that the entrance (*āyatana*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) cannot be separated;

However, while "entrance" refers to the practice itself, the "stage of wisdom" refers to the position [of that practice]. Since both the practice and the position are presented together, it is called "entering the stage."

The remaining nine [categories] are distinct. Within the section on benefiting others, there are eleven phrases; the first statement, "furthermore, one attains the ten stages (daśabhūmi) from beginning to end," is the general summary.
Some people say that the ten stages are the dharmas attained, while "attainment" and "from beginning to end" refer to practicing in accordance with those dharmas.
This is not so. What was previously explained as the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas are the dharmas attained; the attainment of the stages and their beginning and end [are the practice].
All of these are practices accomplished in accordance with the Dharma; however, "attaining" refers to reaching the beginning and end in terms of the stages and positions.

As for the practice of cultivation, both the positions and the stages are raised together; therefore, it is said that one attains the beginning and end of the ten stages, while the other ten are distinct.

Fourth, distinguishing self and others according to the gates of practice: the gates of the six perfections and so forth constitute practices for one's own benefit (*svārtha*), while the gates of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth constitute practices for the benefit of others (*parārtha*). The distinction between benefiting oneself and benefiting others is as follows: all virtuous qualities accomplished within one's own continuum that can be used to transform others are termed "excellence in benefiting others.

Among these, all practices and virtues cultivated within the stage of further progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*) that have not yet matured or become stable for the purpose of transforming others, but are practiced solely for one's own training, are called "benefiting oneself.
This point is explained in detail below, in the section on the accomplishment of the skillful means of the Dharma Master in the Ninth Ground.

Regarding the explanation of the four [categories], they are distinguished according to their functional gates (*arthamukha*) into "self" and "other. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are of one and the same essence, mutually assisting one another.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the enumeration of phenomena is twofold: first, the small, and second, the large. When ten is used as the number ten, the scope is narrow and is called "small";

In the interpretation of the first section, the term "bodhisattva" refers back to the person for whom this is intended; "those at the stage of faith" (śraddhā-bhūmi) excludes [others] by specifying their rank.

There are two kinds of stages: first, faith (*śraddhā*), and second, realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). That which is the means for approaching realization and reaching certainty is called "faith," while that which is correctly attained is called "realization."
The great stages are divided such that those prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) are called "faith" (*śraddhā*), while those on the grounds are called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).

Therefore, the text below states that one has already entered the first ground and is no longer subsumed under the stage of faith. Generally speaking, those prior to the grounds and those on the grounds have not yet attained what is called "faith"; rather, they attain what is called "realization.
Now, this bodhisattva is in the stage of faith, not realization. Question: Why is it specifically addressed to those at the stage of faith, rather than to those who have already realized the grounds?

Since it does not rely on verbal explanation, one might ask: "If that is so, why does the subsequent passage state that for those who have already realized the stages (*bhūmi*), the Dharma of the stages is taught so that they may attain the powers of a Buddha?

To explain: those referred to as having "already realized the stages" are those from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward. As for the term "faith" (*śraddhā*) mentioned here, it refers to all stages from the tenth stage downward;

in relation to what follows, these are collectively termed "faith" because they have not yet attained [the higher realizations]. Thus, although it is called "faith," it does not contradict the aforementioned realization.
Question: Previously, it was stated that those bodhisattvas who have taken a single birth are all individuals who have fully realized the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Why, then, is it now said that they are at the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*)? Answer: Those [previously mentioned] were individuals who served as "echoes and shadows" (*pratibimba*) for the sake of the holy transformation; those now referred to as being at the stage of faith are the assembly of practitioners directly addressed by the holy transformation.
They are not the same as those [previously mentioned]. One should not consider this to be a repetition of the sutra’s description of those on the supramundane path.
Having purified the mind, one proceeds toward the path of true realization; because there are distinctions in the practice of this path, it is called a "chapter" (*varga*).

The "Chapter on the Supramundane Path" (*Lokottara-mārga-varga*) cited from the Sūtra refers to its method of practice. Because this method of practice is stainless, it is termed "clarity" (*vidyā*). Seeing, knowing, attaining, and realizing—these four aspects manifest the Dharma through practice.
Generally speaking, these four share the same meaning despite having different names; they are like "eye" and "vision," which are distinct yet synonymous.

This refers to the realization through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which attains the realization through practice (*pratipatti*). "Beginning" and "end" refer to the initial vision and the final wisdom;

seeking [the truth] is called vision, while decisive resolution is termed wisdom. Regarding the practice having a beginning and an end: attaining the beginning and realizing the end, such that the Dharma manifests within the mind, is termed "attaining the mind.

When the mind is in profound union with what has been taught, this constitutes realization. "What has been taught" reiterates the words of the Sūtra. "Discrimination" refers to [the analysis] among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*).
These are explained and proclaimed as the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

In the following section on the practice accomplished in reliance upon the Dharma, there is first an explanation of the text concerning self-benefit, which is divided into four parts: (1) explaining the initial summary;

(2) explaining the remaining nine individually; (3) from "All these entries... onwards, manifesting the particulars within the general to dispel the notion of sequential gradations; and (4) [the fourth part].
Each of the ten phrases contains six aspects; the following is a detailed analysis of the six lower aspects. First, regarding the general section, I shall first explain the text:

"Entering" (*praveśa*) refers to the sūtra’s mention of "faithful aspiration and attainment of realization. To explain the meaning of "entering": faithful aspiration marks the beginning of entry, while the attainment of realization marks its culmination.

This determination regarding the Dharma is called "faith" (*śraddhā*); the intensification of faith is called "aspiration" (*preman*); and the attainment of realization is as previously described in the stage of knowledge (*jñānabhūmi*). This concludes the citation of the sūtra.
The "Ten Grounds" (daśabhūmi) refers to the wisdom of the ten grounds as established according to the Dharma. The ten names are as explained in the "Section on the Fundamental" (mūlāṅga).

This is the "fundamental entry" (mūlapraveśa), which establishes the fundamental by distinguishing it from the derivative; it is spoken of as the "fundamental" in contrast to the other nine phrases, yet it is not the fundamental of cause and effect.

As for the term "as in the sūtra" (yathāsūtram) used below, it indicates the name of the sūtra; alternatively, it may refer to the commentary that resembles the sūtra, following the sequence of the sūtra's text.

In the treatise, it can be understood that the remaining distinctions are explained as follows: regarding the statement in the *Sūtra* that there are nine types of entry based on the fundamental [ground], this refers to the general opening of the specific.
That is to say, within these *Sūtras* of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), based on the initial general entry, the remaining nine specific entries are opened up.

This is to demonstrate how, by relying on the fundamental, the remaining nine are opened; this is the explanation of the *Sūtra* compiler and was not created by the treatise itself. Therefore, it is said: "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) provides a detailed commentary on this. Regarding the actual practice, from the stage of "Joy" (*pramuditā*) up to the "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmameghā*), every moment of thought is endowed with all the virtues of practice.

To summarize these essentials, they are comprised of nine phrases. Although there are nine distinct phrases, the practices themselves consist only of hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization.
Of these, the first is hearing; the next two are reflection; the next one is cultivation; and the final five are realization. This is the summary.

The four virtues are accomplished simultaneously and are difficult to distinguish individually; therefore, they are categorized by assigning them to specific stages. There is a distinction between the mundane and the supramundane:

prior to the stages, there is the mundane; upon the stages, there is the supramundane. "Hearing" (*śruta*) refers to the wisdom derived from hearing, which is mundane, while "contemplation" (*cintā*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) are supramundane.

By assigning these to their respective stages, the mundane is explained as being subsumed within the supramundane realization. Within the explanation of the wisdom of hearing, the names are listed inclusively because it fully encompasses all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
This is called "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*). Within the general category of "entry," this inclusion is further differentiated; taking the general name as a specific name, it is termed "inclusion.

This principle of entry applies analogously to all subsequent phrases. Next, its characteristics will be explained. Regarding the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), that which can include the essence of practice includes everything;
this explains the meaning of inclusion. By means of the gateway of the wisdom of hearing, all practices are comprehensively gathered so that none fail to enter therein.

Therefore it is said that they are subsumed as heard; since this is so for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the following section uses the sūtra to apply [this principle] to reflection (*cintā*).

This section has two parts: the first is the actual reflection, and the second is the completion of that initial reflection. Within the actual reflection, there is reflection on the enumeration and reflection on the meaning.

Regarding the reflection on the meaning, the text explains its characteristics: "As for the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*)," this identifies the essence of reflection; "the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and so forth" refers to its application.

"Discerning the meaning" (*arthapravicaya*) refers to all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which are the objects of reflection. As for the "factors of enlightenment," they are as previously explained.

"Wisdom" (*jñāna*) regarding the inconceivable qualities of the Buddha is the characteristic of reflection; the clear vision (*pratyavekṣaṇa*) of these factors of enlightenment is called wisdom, and the skillfulness (*kauśalya*) of that wisdom is therefore called "skillful means" (*upāya*).
Below, the Sūtra provides a summary: "Skillfully distinguishing and selecting" summarizes the aforementioned wisdom. (1)

The "All Buddha-Dharma" section corresponds to the "Chapter on the Path" (*mārga-varga*). Later, when contemplating the establishment of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) therein, one lists their names.

If categorized according to that which enables knowledge, it should be named "Entry into Knowledge" (*jñāna-praveśa*); now, categorized according to that which is known, it is named "Entry into the Characteristics of Phenomena. Next, its characteristics are explained.

Since the "Chapter on the Path" is not of a single name, its various meanings are extensively interpreted according to their distinctions; thus it is named "Immeasurable Knowledge. Below, the sutra passage is cited: the term "extensive knowledge" (*vipula-jñāna*) serves as the commentary.
Regarding the phrase "immeasurable knowledge of all dharmas": it refers to the teaching and guidance of those who enter [the path] according to their respective meanings;

this constitutes the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). Cultivation possesses both benefits; here, the benefit for others is briefly clarified. First, its names are listed; next, its characteristics are explained.

"According to what is contemplated" refers back to the meaning of the contemplation mentioned previously. "Names and words are complete" refers back to the second point, the entry into the characteristics of dharmas. This transformation is based on the preceding two.
Therefore, the phrase "one who speaks the Dharma well" refers precisely to teaching through transformation that does not contradict the meaning; thus, it is called "well.

Below, the sūtra applies the term "one who speaks the Dharma well" to the act of contemplating the meaning, which is termed "complete"; because this restates the aforementioned dharmas, there is no separate sūtra passage to apply.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Stages*, Fascicle One, Part One;
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Stages*, Fascicle One, Part Two.
Regarding the five proofs at the end, the first is situated within the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and the second is situated from the Second Stage upward.
Up to the third stage of "far-reaching," which is provisionally situated in the eighth and ninth stages; the fourth stage of "provisional residence," which is situated in the tenth stage;
and the fifth stage of "provisional residence," which is situated in the Buddha-stage.
First, their names are listed for the initial entry into realization; next, their characteristics are explained. Regarding the "wisdom of equality toward all phenomena":

Regarding the direct realization of the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-explainer), the wisdom of equality that realizes all phenomena as being equal to their names is thoroughly purified during the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

To clarify the distinctions within this pure path according to its stages, there are three: first, seeing; second, cultivation; and third, the effortless (*anābhoga*). Seeing occurs in the first stage (*bhūmi*);
cultivation occurs in the second through the seventh stages; and the effortless occurs from the eighth stage upward. Such are their characteristics.

The details are as explained in a separate chapter. What is now referred to as "the time of seeing" (*darśana-kāla*) pertains to the first stage (*bhūmi*). This section on the "division of practice" (*caryā-bhāga*) is situated here within the context of the "time of seeing," where one is wondrously detached from grasping and defilement;

thus it is termed "excellent purity. Below, the sūtra provides annotations: "non-conceptual wisdom" (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) annotates [the former], while "equalizing wisdom" (*samatā-jñāna*) annotates "purity" and "non-mixture.
Following this, "subsequent excellent purity" is annotated. Below this, there is a further detailed analysis of the aforementioned teaching on entering the transformation-born state of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the phrase "thus spontaneously accomplished," these ten phrases clarify the primary theme of self-benefit (*svārtha*). Why is the fourth [phrase] explained as entering through transformation and instruction?
It is because for a Bodhisattva, transforming others is itself the spontaneous accomplishment of oneself; thus, although one transforms others, there is no contradiction with self-benefit.

If it were not so, why would the previous explanation of transformation not have immediately followed with the explanation of this "realization and entry" (*praveśa*), instead waiting until later to provide such an analysis? This would be the case if realization were not clearly understood.
One must not manifest [the practice] merely for the sake of transforming others while remaining self-centered; this is why it is explained thus.

Therefore, in the conclusion below regarding non-negligence (*apramāda*), first the names are listed: "cultivating the path" and "leaving behind faults" are termed non-negligence. Next, its characteristics are explained:

when practicing, "elevating one’s station and leaving behind afflictions" clarifies non-negligence. Below, the scriptural passage is applied: the phrase "dharmas of Māra" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

"Untainted" (*anāsrava*) refers to being far removed from defilement. Regarding the "progression through the stages" (*bhūmi-bhūmi-parāvṛtti*), first the names of the eight stages and above are listed;

this is called "spontaneous ascent within the flow of the Dharma. Next, its characteristics are explained: the "supramundane path" (*lokottara-mārga*) refers to the supramundane, untainted, true path.
This distinguishes it from the pure states of non-attachment and so forth prior to the stages, and distinguishes it from that which is not effortless (*anābhoga*).
This refers to non-attachment and so forth; because the stains and obstructions of the wholesome roots of non-hatred and non-delusion are completely exhausted, they are called "pure.
From the seventh stage downward, one has not yet abandoned the longing for nirvana and the aversion to the world, and thus the three wholesome roots are impure.

From the eighth stage upward, these are entirely abandoned, and therefore they are pure. Below, the sutra applies the term "supramundane dharma" to the supramundane path, wherein the wholesome roots are pure.
The commentary on non-attachment and the others further explains that there are wholesome states at the lower levels;

by contrasting these with worldly wholesome conduct, it shows that those which give rise to the supramundane path may also be called "supramundane roots of goodness. However, here they are not designated as such because they are intended to be the "roots" of the supramundane.
Regarding the "Bodhisattva’s exhaustion," the names are first listed to indicate the final stage of study, which is termed the "Bodhisattva’s exhaustion"; next, its characteristics are explained.

In the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), its positional division is designated as "entering secret wisdom" (*guhyajñāna*). Because it faces the ultimate limit of the Buddha-realm and is profound and subtle, it is called the "Secret Ten Stages.
One who is able to enter this is named a Bodhisattva. Below, the sutra provides the topical headings (*uddāna*); by means of these headings, one attains entry.

Regarding the heading of the "inconceivable realm of wisdom," within the "exhaustion of the Buddha's secret wisdom," although the names are first listed even while still in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), [they are fully realized upon reaching the fruit].

Fully encompassing the virtues of a Buddha is called "the Buddha’s exhaustion" (*buddha-kṣaya*). Next, its characteristics are explained: "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) refers to the Buddha’s wisdom regarding phenomena.

"Entering into knowledge" means being able to enter into the aforementioned Buddha-wisdom. Below, the sutra provides the textual correspondence: "even attaining" corresponds to the preceding "entering into knowledge";
because one reaches the ultimate limit within the attainment of knowledge, it says "even unto the sphere of all-knowledge," which corresponds to the first [point].
The "person of all-knowledge" (sarvajñajña) is the Buddha; the specific measure of the Buddha’s wisdom is termed the "domain of wisdom.
The preceding section explained the distinctions [of the entries]; from here below, we shall demonstrate the distinctions by way of the general, thereby brushing away the gradations.

These "entries" refer to the nine kinds of entries, such as the *saṃgraha-vastu* (bases of inclusion). As for the phrase "in order to compare the distinct meanings of wisdom," this is done for the sake of a provisional comparison.

Because there are distinctions in the qualities and meanings within the stage of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*), one relies upon the successive stages from the mundane world up to the Buddha-stage, which become increasingly superior.

It is not that those who have not originally entered [the stage of wisdom] can rely upon those progressively superior positions to manifest the distinctions in the qualities and meanings within the stage of wisdom;
rather, those progressively superior positions relied upon are not the fundamental entry into the ground of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*), precisely because they exist on the grounds (*bhūmi*).

Because every moment of thought is fully endowed with all the virtues of practice, there is differentiation; yet because these are not acquired only through a sequence of prior and subsequent stages, there is no characteristic of progressive superiority.
Since there is no gradation of levels, this [differentiation] must be swept away. Alternatively, this statement concludes the end differently from the beginning:
the preceding nine entries were intended to compare the distinctions in the qualities and meanings within the stage of wisdom, which progress in a sequence of increasing excellence.

This refers to the branches rather than the root; it is called "not the root" and "not the entry. This differs from the previous summary, which concluded by distinguishing the root from the branches, though their wording is similar.
In the fourth section, there are six distinct points: first, a general enumeration of all ten phrases, each of which possesses six characteristics;

second, applying these six characteristics to these ten entries; third, explaining the six characteristics based on these eighteen [entries]; and finally, exhorting one to understand all ten [entries] through these analogies.
Section Three clarifies the boundaries of its six characteristics; Section Four lists the six names; Section Five provides the formal explanation of the ten entries regarding the six characteristics;
and Section Six uses what has been explained to formally exhort one to understand all ten phrases by analogy.

Regarding the "ten" mentioned at the beginning of all that has been taught: since the *Avataṃsaka* frequently employs "ten by ten" as its thematic gates, it is said that all the ten phrases taught therein possess six [aspects].
Because these six meanings apply universally, it is said they "all possess" them; yet because their thematic gates differ, there are six kinds.
These six are all the essential characteristics of all phenomena, which are designated as "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*); as distinct meanings, they are termed "gates."
This statement below constitutes the second section; within these eighteen modes of discourse, one should understand that the six aspects explained therein apply to all ten phrases mentioned.

The section beginning with "excluding the matter" constitutes the third segment. Because the matter is obstructed and lacks the six characteristics, it is excluded; the specific reasons for this exclusion are set forth below.

These refer to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). The aggregates refer to the five aggregates; the elements refer to the eighteen elements; and the bases refer to the twelve bases.
This is explained in detail in other chapters. Why are they not complete? As in the case of the five aggregates, form is not feeling, perception, and so forth.
It is not that consciousness is like this; because they are distinct, there is no universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

Since there is no universal characteristic, one cannot take the particular (*viśeṣa*) to correspond with the universal to establish [the former] as being produced or destroyed. Therefore, it is said to be "incomplete.
If one considers their essential nature (*svabhāva*), each aggregate (*skandha*) fully possesses the six characteristics; the same applies to the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).
"What are the six? This is the fourth section, which poses the question and enumerates the names.

"In total, these are the fundamental... This is the fifth section, which properly explains the six characteristics by means of the ten entries; within this explanation, they are briefly analyzed according to four gates.

First, to clarify the intent: because there are those who grasp at fixed characteristics—such as totality and particularity, or identity and difference—with respect to phenomena, these six gates on the mutual establishment of the dependent origination of all phenomena are elucidated;
it is not that they are refuted as being fixed, but rather to break through their fixed attachments.
Second, to clarify the basis upon which this is established: the author of the treatise relies on what to establish these six characteristics? He states that he relies on this sutra;
as explained in the fourth vow of the first stage (*bhūmi*), all practices possess six gates as their means (*upāya*).
Therefore, the treatise relies upon this to provide a comprehensive explanation for all things.

Third, regarding the general explanation of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) across all phenomena: although phenomena are distinct in their facts, their underlying principles and meanings are equally pervasive. For now, we shall explain the six characteristics by taking form (*rūpa*) as the illustration;

other categories may be understood accordingly. What are these six characteristics? For example, within a single instance of form, its own substance inherently possesses all such meanings as suffering (*duḥkha*), impermanence (*anityatā*), and so forth.
It is because these various meanings collectively constitute this single form that it is distinguished according to those respective meanings.
When form is divided, it is immeasurable—namely, the distinctions such as impermanent form, suffering form, empty form, and selfless form.

Regarding its totality: outside the total there is no separate [part]. Regarding its particulars: outside the particular there is no total. The total is a single form, which is called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*);
the particulars are many forms, which are called the "specific characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Within those particulars, one considers [the categories] such as impermanence and so forth.

The aforementioned meanings of "form" (rūpa) are called "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Although these meanings of form are common, their specific distinctions—such as impermanence and so forth—are each different;
thus, they are termed "distinctive characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The two gates of formation and destruction explain the preceding two [categories] by means of commonality and difference.
Because those distinctive characteristics, such as suffering and impermanence, are inseparable from the essence [of form], various forms according to those distinctions can be subsumed [within them].

Because they are one, they are termed "formation" (*saṃskāra*); because their characteristics—such as suffering, impermanence, and so forth—are not identical, they are termed "dissolution" (*bhaṅga*).
This dissolution does not mean total annihilation, but rather that a single form is divided into many forms.

To speak according to reality, the first four gates reveal the meaning of the phenomena (*dharma-artha*), while the latter two gates, by means of difference, reveal sameness and thereby establish the preceding general and specific categories; thus, there are six.
Regarding the characteristics applied to form (*rūpa*), it is thus; the teaching that "form is impermanent" applies to the six [sense bases] in the same way.

When one speaks of impermanence as a general term, its specific divisions according to phenomena are manifold—namely, the impermanence of form, the impermanence of suffering, and so forth—which are termed the "particulars.
Within these particulars, because the quality of impermanence exists upon each phenomenon such as suffering and the rest, they are termed "common. Although impermanence...
The various aspects of suffering and so forth are each individually termed "differentiation" (*visesa*).

Because the essence of those differentiating characteristics is inseparable from them, they are subsumed under the single gateway of impermanence according to those distinctions; thus, it is called the "establishment of differentiation.

Because the meanings are distinct, within one gateway of impermanence, the various divisions are numerous; therefore, it is called "disintegration. This is as with the six gateways of the impermanence of form. Since—
However, all other dharmas of the same essence, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are likewise one by one;
since this is the case for the essence of form, it is the same for all dharmas, even up to nirvāṇa.
The fourth section, "Explaining the Text," concerns that which is "entirely based on the fundamental. This refers to the first of the ten phrases, which is "causing entry into the stage of wisdom.
The remaining nine are distinct from it, being divided according to their specific practices into the [remaining] nine entries such as "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "based separately on the fundamental to fulfill that fundamental": this means that by opening up the general into the particular, the particular is said to be based on the fundamental; thus, through the particular, the virtues inherent within that general are manifested.

Regarding the statement that "the names are identical" (*pūrṇa-samāna*): although they are identical in being "entrances" (*praveśa*), within the nine distinct categories, each individual phrase contains the sense of "entrance";
thus, they are termed "identical. Regarding "increase" (*vṛddhi*): although the entrance is the same, the sequence of "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) and so forth proceeds to ever-greater excellence;

this is called "increase," and "increase" signifies "difference. Regarding "accomplishment" (*siddhi*): it is "concise" (*saṃkṣipta*) because, within that difference, the essences of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*) are inseparable.
Therefore, because the nine bases (*āyatana*) as they were explained are subsumed into one, it is called "abbreviated";

whereas that which is "extensive" refers to the fact that within those differences, the nine types of meanings such as hearing and so forth are distinct, and thus they are collectively included within their respective categories to form nine, which is why it is called an "extensive explanation.
This is like the worldly analogy of formation and destruction, used to illustrate the unification of ten billion worlds into a single Sahā world-system.
Therefore, it is named "Accomplishing One Part. To call [the state of] the four heavens "the destruction of all" constitutes one set of ten phrases;

according to their respective categories, this is the sixth section. By means of the characteristics of these six gates thus explained, one is exhorted to understand by analogy that all sets of ten phrases are likewise so.

Regarding the benefit of others hereafter, first the initial general [explanation] is expounded, followed by the detailed explanation of the remaining particulars. Within the general section, the initial statement, "The twentieth phrase attains the beginning and the end," cites the scriptural text;

this "original beginning and end" (ben-shi-zhong) clarifies that the original is distinct from the derivative, and it is designated as the "original beginning" in relation to the subsequent ten phrases.
Below this, the meaning of "beginning and end" is explained, wherein it is first discussed in terms of the teaching and practice.

Subsequently, the distinctions are made by contrasting realization (*adhigama*) with teaching (*deśanā*). Within the section on teaching and practice, "the beginning" cites the sūtra’s terms "faith" (*śraddhā*) and "desire" (*chanda*) to distinguish their characteristics through the act of approaching.
A mind that is resolved regarding the Dharma is called faith; when faith increases, it is called desire. To rely upon desire and proceed toward it in accordance with it is called "approaching.

"The end" cites the sūtra’s terms "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) and "retention" (*dhāraṇā*) to distinguish their characteristics. Because the encompassing dharmas are held within the mind, it is called mindfulness.
Because mindfulness of the Dharma does not lose it, it is called "retaining" (*dhāraṇī*). The various stages (*bhūmi*) are the dharmas that are retained therein.

Regarding the subsequent section which distinguishes [the stages] by correlating realization (*adhigama*) with teaching (*deśanā*), the word "furthermore" (*punar*) is used because previously the beginning and end were explained in terms of the practice of the teachings;

now, this is once again distinguished by correlating realization with teaching, hence the term "furthermore. The *āgama* (scriptural transmission) and the realization—the fundamental nature of the dharma from beginning to end—are as previously described regarding the beginning and end.
All are termed *āgama*, which is generally explained as the beginning being the proof of the end. *Āgama* is a term from the Middle Kingdom (China); it signifies "pure teaching.

"Proof" (*sākṣāt*) carries the meaning of knowing and attaining. These two [terms] are discussed broadly; in terms of their specific meanings, there are nine [categories]. First, regarding the contrast between practice and teaching:
verbal instruction consisting of sounds and speech is called *āgama*; all practices and virtues are expounded as [the fruit of] this.
"Realization" (證) refers to what is explained below; it signifies both the meaning of the middle [term] and the two collections (*piṭaka*). Regarding the two stages in relation to one another:

prior to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), practicing in reliance upon the teachings is called "Scriptural Transmission" (*āgama*). From the first bhūmi upward, being free from verbal expression and in accord with reality, it is called "Realization.
This corresponds to the second request, where the assembly is praised as being liberated. That which arises prior to the bhūmis—namely, hearing, reflection, and cultivation—is called *āgama*.
Including the pure [wisdom] from the first bhūmi upward, all practices and virtues are collectively termed "verified purity" (*avetyaprasāda*).

Within all stages, where the true and the false are contrasted, the four types of mind—consisting of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as the consciousness and gnosis born of maturation—and their illuminating understanding through objective conditions are called "scriptural knowledge" (*āgama*).
Because they take verbal expression as their basis for verification, the subsequent treatise states that these are the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Thus, that which can be explained by means of what can be explained is called the stage of *āgama* (scriptural transmission). That which transcends words is termed "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).

Regarding the fourfold cultivation, when the true and the false are cultivated in relation to one another across all stages, it is called *āgama*. Abandoning the false to accord with the real is termed "realization.
This corresponds to the meaning explained below regarding the two great expositions: the exposition of the Great *Āgama* and the skillful cultivation of its methods.

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the accomplishment of realized practice (*adhigama*). Regarding the five aspects, when they correspond to reality within mundane cultivation, the attainment of those realized characteristics is called "scripture" (*āgama*).
When they correspond to the fundamental [truth], it is termed "realization" (*adhigama*). This is as explained below in the *Dharmaparyāya of the Radiance of the Sublime Dharma*:
"The superior" (*adhipati*) is realization, and "radiance" (*prabhāsa*) is teaching. Regarding the six bodies, their correspondence to virtue is established therein.
Within the practice accomplished through the signless (*animitta*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) that was originally hidden is now revealed; this is termed "realization" (*adhigama*).

The virtues of the skillful means (*upāya*) accomplished based on the essence are produced through cultivation according to the teachings; these are termed "scriptural authority" (*āgama*). This is analogous to the example of refining gold given in the subsequent text:

the essence of the gold is a metaphor for realization, while the ornaments such as bracelets and earrings are metaphors for scriptural authority. Thus, the essence and its function correspond to one another.

The essence (*tattva*) and its qualities (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) are explained in terms of realization (*adhigama*). Based on this, the function of the wisdom that accords with worldly teachings which arises therefrom is called *āgama*.

This is as illustrated in the following passage by the analogy of the light of a jewel; the "jewel" represents the essence of realization, while the "wheel," "light," and "flames" serve as pure metaphors for *āgama*.
Eighthly, regarding the distinction between the state of abiding in one's own level (*svabhūmi*) and the state of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*), [the former] is... [self-].
The essence, qualities, and functions produced by these divisions are all termed "realization" (*adhigama*).

Within the factors conducive to advancement (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), that which can receive the Buddha’s teachings is called "scriptural authority" (*āgama*), as illustrated in the later passage praising the two powers of Vajragarbha.

Sublime wisdom and eloquence are termed "power of realization" (*adhigamabala*), while firm and pure mindfulness regarding the Buddha’s teachings and the Dharma is termed "power of scriptural authority" (*āgamabala*). The ninth [point] is based on the expressive terminology.
Speaking in terms of the essence of true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) as it relates to reality, this very essence of realization is divided into ten categories for the sake of explanation;
these are called *āgama*. This is because, as in the passage below, the dharma is illustrated by the analogy of the tracks left in space;

since the ground of realization-wisdom is like the equality of space, the treatise below states that the "abode of the body of syllables" is subsumed within realization-wisdom, serving as the tracks in the sky as a metaphor.

Because the *Śrāvaka-āgama* exists, the subsequent treatise states that it is not the case that there is no knowledge of the stages (*bhūmi*). "Names, phrases, and phonemes" (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) refer precisely to the *āgama*-dharma.
Now, with respect to their cultivation and realization, the preliminary practices (*prayoga*) cultivated prior to all the stages are called *āgama*.
