"attaining the three kinds of transformations such as the Buddha-body" is explained in contrast to what precedes it. By mentioning the "body" and so forth, one includes both speech and mind; therefore, it says "body and so forth.
These three are the transformative activities of all Buddhas, termed the "three types of transformative functions. When performing these transformations, at that time—

His lack of timidity is called "fearlessness. Regarding the phrase "according to those to be saved" (*yathā-vineya*), this clarifies that the transformation [of the Buddha] accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
To manifest body, speech, and mind according to those to be saved is called "manifesting the three karmas. Because what is manifested is preeminent, it is termed "extraordinary" (*viśiṣṭa*).

That which is manifested is difficult to fathom, hence it is called "miraculous transformation" (*ṛddhi-vikurvita*). Below, the sutra passage "together with the Tathāgata" serves as a commentary on the previously mentioned "attaining Buddhahood" and the "three [karmas]."
The term "manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*) is spoken of as being directed downward toward those to be converted; it is said to be "bestowed" because it proceeds from the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "well-discriminating," this refers to the fact that one speaks by relying on the power of the Buddha, specifically the Vajragarbha Bodhisattva. The phrase "according to those to be saved" means that one well discriminates the body, speech, and mind of the sentient beings to be converted;
this indicates the three karmas. The term "ornamentation" (*vyūha*) refers to excellence; it signifies excellence in function.
It is said that what is called "arising" (*utthāna*) refers to the manifestation of spiritual transformations; because skillful means appear before one, it is designated as "arising.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha possesses power," this explains why the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is mentioned first. As for the reason why the question is asked first and the answer follows later within the sutra:
it is because [the author] intends to explain the purpose of the question. Now, the author of this treatise first takes up the underlying intent of why that question was asked within the sutra.
I anticipate that in the subsequent commentary on the sutra, one might simply explain the text of the answer and consider it redundant;

or, having already clarified the addition previously, one might again explain it redundantly, thereby questioning the reason for this partial addition. Therefore, the word "also" (yòu) is used: there is power because there is compassion.

The inquiry as to why there is power and the ability to add, and why there is compassion and the ability to be universal, is expressed by the phrase "for what reason? (hé gù), which serves as the term of inquiry.

The passage beginning with "By means of the ten bodies" serves as a phase of inquiry. Since the Buddha possesses both power and compassion, for what reason does he bestow [the title] "Ten Bodies" only upon Vajragarbha and not upon the others?
That "only Vajragarbha" constitutes one phrase; "only" (*yu*) means "exclusively.
That "he does not bestow it upon the others" constitutes another phrase; those named Ratnagarbha and so forth are considered "the others."

These two lines pose a question which the subsequent treatise answers specifically. Regarding the first question in the Sūtra, it is answered by what follows. Within that answer, there are ten phrases:

the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific. Since it is the Bodhisattva who attains samādhi—and because it is Vajragarbha who has attained samādhi—the Buddhas bestow their empowerment solely upon him.
Thus, within the subsequent specific section, the text concerning the Bodhisattva also appears in the first phrase.

The meaning applies to the latter eight; if expressed fully, one should say that they are also the bodhisattva’s well-purified mind, and so on, up to the final one, which is also the bodhisattva’s seal of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-mudrā*). These are not discussed in detail here.

What is now stated—that they also arise from original vows—is said "also" in comparison to the preceding samādhis, meaning that these too are what are called "arising from original vows," whereby one attains the samādhi.

Because they have attained samādhi, the Buddhas bestow special empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon them; furthermore, because this is the seal of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-mudrā*), they attain samādhi.
Because they have attained samādhi, the Buddhas bestow special empowerment. Every phrase [of the sūtra] is entirely established as the "samādhi of remote correspondence" (*dūra-pratibimba-samādhi*).

In the treatise, first, based on the initial general phrase, the answer to the preceding question is explained; subsequently, the remaining specific points are elucidated. This is how it is for the bodhisattva.
Regarding those who have attained samādhi, the initial general statement is cited as the answer to the preceding question; "only Vajragarbha" is added because others did not attain it.
Regarding those who did not attain it, no others are added to the answer to the preceding question because Ratnagarbha and the rest did not attain samādhi, and thus they are not included.
Yet, since Ratnagarbha and the others were all individuals who had fulfilled their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), why is it said that "others" did not?
There are two meanings for [the statement that they] "attain" liberation: first, because it is taught that others do not attain it in order to promote the transformation of Vajragarbha;

second, because each of the bodhisattvas attains it according to the specific dharma-gate in which they abide, whereas this is distinct from other "treasure-store" [realms], and since their virtues are not being manifested through this particular gate, their attainment is not mentioned.
If one enters this gate, in principle one truly attains it; even down to a blade of grass, one is empowered by the holy power.

Since wood can also preach the Dharma, why is it said that [the Buddha] bestows empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) specifically upon those who have attained realization? To explain: if one discusses the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), that is one distinct meaning;
that he empowers those who have attained realization so that they may preach is another form of transformation. If there were no such attainment, what would there be to empower?
As it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that he empowered Subhūti—a person who understands emptiness—so it is here as well. The following section explains the remaining cases.
Regarding the statement that there are two kinds of initial attainment of samādhi: this refers to the general opening of the specific. The "initial attainment of samādhi" is the general category;
it is divided into two kinds based on the distinction between the essence and the qualities within that general samādhi. "The fulfillment of original vows manifests as the essence of this samādhi":
"essence" refers to the supramundane bodhicitta; from "deep mind" (*adhyāśaya*) onwards, it encompasses both self-benefit and benefit for others.

He is the one who manifests the original vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*) as listed in the *Samādhi-guṇa-vyūha*. The essence of the bodhicitta that arises in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is called the "original vow" (*mūlapraṇidhāna*);

now, having reached the culmination of study, it is called "manifestly accomplished" (*abhinirvṛtta*). The scripture states "original vow" (*mūlapraṇidhāna*) and "manifestly accomplished" (*abhinirvṛtta*);
these are abbreviated terms for "arising" (*utthāna*) and "accomplishment" (*nirvṛtti*), respectively, which are not explained here.
In the second section of the text, there are five distinct parts: first, the general; second, the specific; third, the concise; fourth, the detailed;
and fifth, the explanation that has already demonstrated the meaning of the function of practice as a cause. The initial statement, "the samādhi-body encompasses all merits," is the general part.
It is called "the samādhi-body encompassing merits" because it fully contains all virtues within the essence of samādhi. Regarding the eight kinds [of these merits]:
The second [set] is distinct because it relies on benefiting both self and others; the third is concise. The first four rely on benefiting oneself, while the latter four rely on benefiting others.

Because these eight qualities are explained based on benefiting both self and others, they are called "reliances" (*niśraya*); alternatively, the concentrated body relies upon these various qualities, and thus they are also called "reliances."

From "Because of purity" (*viśuddhi-hetu*) downward is the fourth section, which provides an extensive explanation of the preceding [section on] self-benefit. Among these, the first is the foundation for initiating practice, while the latter three constitute the very essence of the virtues of practice.
Regarding the explanation of "purity of cause" (*hetu-viśuddhi*), the names of the causes are listed; under "profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*), the profound mind is explained.

Because it is characterized by intense longing and earnestness, it is called the "profound mind. To reach the ultimate, the "profound mind of the first stage" (*prathama-bhūmi-adhyāśaya*) is explained.

At this point, having exhausted study, it is called "reaching the end" (*niṣṭhāgata*); because it is the exhaustion of [all] ends, it is "purity. Next, the sutra passage on purity is applied to the term "reaching the end.
Regarding the phrase "profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*), it is again applied to the section on the profound mind to provide a further explanation of the sutra and thereby establish the treatise.

The mention of the "profound mind" in the sutra refers to "faith, joy," and so forth, which distinguishes the essence of its practice; this is the interpretation of the sutra. Furthermore, it is the root of all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).

Explaining the meaning of its cause establishes the preceding treatise; it is called a "cause" simply because it is the root of goodness. The latter three are its common characteristics (*sādharmya*). Regarding the three paths:
the first is realization (*adhigama*), the second is assistance (*sahāya*), and the third is the meaning of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhāna*). These should be discussed in detail as in other chapters.

Within the section on the purity of wisdom (*jñānaviśuddhi*) under realization, its names are listed. Below, under "tending toward exhaustion" (*kṣayaparyanta*), the term "tending toward exhaustion" is explained, and "purity" (*viśuddhi*) is interpreted.

The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) explains that wisdom (*jñāna*) by way of its function; since wisdom penetrates both the paths of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation, it is distinguished here as "cultivation.

It is subsequently applied to the sutra’s terms: "purity," "application" (*prasthāna*), and "the application toward the knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*). The phrase "perfection of wisdom" has not been explained above;

rather, it was introduced here following the momentum of the preceding discussion and will now be explained in detail. This consists of a primary teaching followed by a simile; this is the contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*).
The perfection of internal wisdom is the perfection of the essence of wisdom; the illumination of the Dharma-realm is the perfection of the function of wisdom. This is like the orb of the sun:
the former is compared to the perfection of the essence, while the light pervading the world illustrates the perfection of the subsequent function.

Among the practices that assist the Way (*anuloma-pratipatti*), the purity of the body is listed as a name for these assisting practices, because one can thereby attain the supramundane Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), which is superior through its transformation. Because the auxiliary practices are pure, it is called the "purity of the transformed body."

Furthermore, because the body that serves as the basis for supportive practice gives rise to increasingly superior practices, the purification of those practices is called the "purification of the body.

Next, to explain its characteristics: the "body that produces birth after birth" refers to the fact that from the first bhūmi upward, the bodies one receives are not limited to one; thus it is called "producing birth after birth," and because these become increasingly superior, it is called "transformation.
To explain the purity of understanding: this can be known by correlating it with the sūtra. Regarding the "mind of non-abiding on the path," the names are listed in their proper order.
Having mastery over emptiness and existence is called "taming the mind. Next, its characteristics are explained: because one does not cling to existence, coarse afflictions are severed;

because one does not dwell in non-existence, those subtle habitual tendencies are abandoned. Since what is to be severed is brought to exhaustion, it is called "wholesome. Furthermore, according to the sutra, regarding the cultivation of fundamental karma:
the understanding of non-dwelling can give rise to merit, wisdom, and the factors conducive to the path; therefore, it is called "fundamental karma."

Furthermore, grasping at existence is the dharma of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while grasping at non-existence is the dharma of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*); because they do not abide in either existence or non-existence, this is called the Bodhisattva’s true path.

Thus, within the section on benefiting others (*parārtha*) in the *Mūlakarman*, the first [of the four] is the skillful means (*upāya*) for benefiting others, and the latter three are the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the practice of benefiting others.
Within the preliminary skillful means, "hearing" is listed as the inclusion; according to what is heard, one is able to include [the other factors].

Therefore it is said: "Hearing" refers to the inclusion; "explaining its characteristics" means that which is capable of being upheld is the act of inclusion, while "all teachings" and so forth are the objects included.
"All that is taught and all that is included" refers to the breadth [of the teachings]. "The secret" refers to the depth of what is included. Below, the sūtra provides the topical outline:
"mindfulness" corresponds to the inclusion, and "capable of upholding immeasurable dharmas" corresponds to the teachings spoken. Regarding "immeasurable," there are two types.
1. "Vast and immeasurable" corresponds to the preceding [section on] "all. 2. "Profound and immeasurable" corresponds to the preceding "secret" and the subsequent three phrases.
Regarding these three, first is the body, next is speech, and the third is the mind. Within the body, purity is established by listing its names;

"supreme penetration" and "mastery" explain its characteristics. Below, the sūtra provides the correspondence: "the pure light of faith and understanding" refers to stainless supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
It is called "Radiance. This Dharma of Radiance can cause sentient beings to believe and understand it without doubt; thus, it is designated as the "Dharma of Pure Radiance of Faith.

To definitively explain and harmonize this with the sutras and treatises: the masters of the sutras call it the "Dharma of Radiance through Belief and Understanding," while the masters of the treatises call it "Pervasive [Understanding].
Because these terms do not accord with one another, they must be explained and reconciled through the power of definitive faith.
The *Śāstra* explains that the term "penetration" (*pratisaṃvid*) applies here as well. Why is it called the "Dharma of the Radiance of Pure Faith"?
Because this penetration is the power of definitive faith, it is named the "Dharma of the Radiance of Pure Faith.
The faith of sentient beings is called "definitive faith," and because the power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) can generate that faith, it is therefore termed the "power of definitive faith."

Regarding "embracing the supernormal powers" (*abhijñā-parigraha*): when explaining the sūtras and reconciling the treatises, since the sūtra-author names this "pure light of faith" (*śraddhā-viśuddhi-prabhā*), why does the commentator call it "supernormal power"?
It is because this light embraces the supernormal powers; thus the commentator names it "supernormal power.

Since the essence of that [light] is no different from the supernormal powers themselves, it is called "embracing. This is analogous to how, in the two lower stages, ten names are subsumed under a single category.

The meaning of this is similar to that explained in the section on verbal karma (*vākkarma*). Among the enumerations of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), it is explained as "skillfully knowing" (*suvidita*) without contradiction.

Regarding the explanation of its characteristics, it is subsequently sealed by the *sūtra* with the phrase "having attained *dhāraṇī*," which seals "skillful knowledge. The term "unfailing speech" (*abhedyavākya*) seals "non-contradiction.
Below, there is a further detailed analysis; the first chapter therein concerns that *dhāraṇī*, which, through metaphorical illustration, clarifies the Dharma within the fourteen chapters.
The letter *si* (ṣa) is at the beginning and is called the "first chapter" because it can give rise to all other letters; thus it is raised as a metaphor.

The various *dhāraṇī* gates illustrated by this chapter are indeed *dhāraṇīs*, which is why it says "this is so. The section beginning with "each and every one" explains the metaphor to reveal the Dharma:
just as these letter-gates encompass immeasurable letters, so too does a *dhāraṇī* each and every one encompass immeasurable teachings.

The meaning of the "gate of syllables" (akṣaramukha) should be explained here in detail. It is called "unfailing" (*abhedya*) because it does not contradict the preceding or following sections of the sūtra;

since the treatise is cited to clarify this and there is no discrepancy between them, it is named "unfailing. Regarding the explanation of the mental action (*manaskarma*), it is called "free from pride" (*nirmāna*) because it lists the names [of the stages] as proof that false attachments have been eliminated.
Next, its characteristics are explained: for one who possesses true knowledge, their own realization is free from pride, and the instructions they provide do not differ [from the truth].

"Having gathered beings to be the same as oneself" and below refers to applying the sūtra to the Seal of the Wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna-mudrā*), which applies true wisdom. Wisdom realizes the Dharma-realm;

as for the term "seal," it means that the teaching is not different [from realization]. This is called a "good seal" because one uses one's own wisdom to seal those sentient beings, causing them to become the same as oneself; this is termed a "good seal."

The preceding section has extensively explained [the topic]; the following section reveals the meaning of how practice functions as a cause. Within this, first, the self-practice is elucidated, which contains four parts:

(1) a general restatement of the preceding four [points] to generally demonstrate their function as causes; (2) "Well-purified" (*suviśuddha*) and so forth, which specifically restates the scriptural text;

(3) "Sūtra" (*sūtra*) and so forth, which generally restates the preceding scripture to point toward the subsequent treatise—namely, that which was taught in the aforementioned scripture; and (4) [the conclusion].
In the subsequent discussion of the four phrases, they are explained in sequence as causes. Regarding the four causes of diligence (*vīrya*):
first, the cause of diligence is that the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) is able to initiate the practice of diligence, serving as the cause for progress.

Second, the cause of non-forgetfulness is that, by relying on that wisdom (*jñāna*), one does not lose mindfulness regarding all phenomena; thus, that wisdom serves as the cause for non-forgetfulness. Third, the cause of momentum...
As for the cause (*hetu*): it refers to the power of mastery in the auxiliary practices of the path that can encompass superior retribution;

this serves as the cause for that power. Regarding the "cause of non-attachment" (*asaṅga-hetu*): it is the path of non-abiding, which is able to remain unstained by and unattached to both emptiness and existence;
this serves as the cause for that non-attachment. Below, the cause is further distinguished through the benefit of others; moreover, it exists based upon the cause of benefiting others.
These four types are first presented collectively as a general heading, and then subsequently cited individually for detailed exposition.

Regarding the question of why, in the preceding section on self-benefit (*svārtha*), all four practices were raised together to explain the four causes, whereas it was not so for benefiting others (*parārtha*): it is because within the practice of self-benefit, the Sūtra contains four phrases and the Śāstra likewise contains four [points];
therefore, they may be raised together and their causes explained together. Now, regarding the latter part of the section on benefiting others...

Since all three phrases must be explained with further emphasis, they are separately cited and addressed. Regarding the statement of the cause for "recalling immeasurable dharmas," this refers to the first phrase of the sutra;

it is called the "cause for severing doubt" because by recollecting the Dharma oneself, one is able to sever the doubts of others, and thus, in relation to the severing of doubt, it is designated as the cause.
Regarding the statement of the "cause for reverent respect" through the clear illumination of the Dharma, this refers to the second phrase; it causes others to manifest supreme radiance.

"Because of reverence, it acts as the cause for reverence. The following explains the meaning of reverence: by manifesting inconceivable states through supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), one causes others to give rise to faith and enter [the path];

therefore, it is called the "cause of reverence. Because its universal application is difficult to fathom, it is termed "inconceivable"; because it is the domain of supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*), it is termed a "state.
By manifesting these superior powers, those who behold them witness these miraculous transformations, thereby gaining faith and entering the Buddha-dharma to attain *dharani*.

Regarding the third phrase of the *dhāraṇī*, "the cause for turning the Dharma": because one relies on the *dhāraṇī* to turn the principle of the Dharma, it is designated as the "cause" in relation to the turning of the Dharma.
Here, "Dharma" refers to the teaching (*dharma*), while "principle" refers to the meaning (*artha*). "Turning" refers to the flow of transformation;

thus, when the Dharma is about to perish, one provisionally takes up the recitation and preservation of other [teachings] to explain and manifest its characteristics. When the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is extinguished, one provisionally takes up the recitation that permeates other external teachings.
Regarding the fourth line of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samaya-mudrā*, the instruction on the cause is as follows:

because one relies upon the seal of one’s own wisdom (*svajñāna-mudrā*) to teach sentient beings and enable their deliverance, this is designated as the "cause" in relation to the teaching of deliverance. Such a transformation does not forget self-benefit;

by citing the former to manifest this, it attains the second [aspect] within self-benefit: the non-forgetfulness of the wisdom of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Because of this, it is able to act as [the cause].
Regarding this transformation:

within the section on the empowerment of the Śākya-body, first the preceding [context] is concluded and the subsequent [topic] is introduced by briefly manifesting its characteristics. That is to say, he touches the crown of the head to cause [the disciples] to awaken from meditative absorption;

because power is increased through this touching, it is called "empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The four phrases in the Sūtra are: first, not departing from the original [state]; second, by means of the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*)...

Regarding the third power, "extending the right hand" and the fourth, "rubbing the crown of the head": extending the right hand follows worldly convention; the right side is used because it is more convenient to extend.
Rubbing the crown of the head is also a sign of consolation according to worldly custom; because rubbing the crown of the head can bring benefit, it is called "skillful.
Below, the commentary explains this by not departing from the citation of the sūtra to demonstrate the superior power: [the Buddha] rubbed [him] from a distance.
"This is called 'indicating superior power'—this is an expository interpretation. 'Coming here is not extraordinary'—this is a counter-explanatory interpretation.

By stating that coming is not extraordinary, it conversely reveals that not coming is extraordinary. Why reveal this extraordinariness? To manifest the excellence of one's own virtue. Why manifest this superiority?
Because those of superior virtue bestow their grace upon the Dharma; by manifesting the excellence of the Dharma, one causes the assembly to revere it. This is the first [section].
The appearance of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna from afar likewise manifests the gravity of the Dharma; each represents a distinct meaning.
If one is to earnestly encourage the mind that seeks the Dharma, it is necessary for [the Buddha] to come from afar and manifest the essential Dharma through supernatural power;

this must be the *ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna* (the supernormal power of psychic transformation), and not any other power. This explains that within the sūtra, "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*) is used. There are four kinds of such powers: first, the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi*).

1. The supernormal power of transformation of one's own body, whereby a great sound is heard everywhere; such as these, there are two types of illusory supernormal powers. 2. The supernormal power of transforming external objects. 3.
The supernormal power of knowledge regarding phenomena (*dharmajñāna-abhijñā*), which is unimpeded with respect to all dharmas. 4. The supernormal power of noble mastery (*āryavaśitā-abhijñā*):

being able to produce the perception of pleasure within suffering, to produce the perception of suffering within pleasure, and to produce the perception of equanimity within both suffering and pleasure. Thus it is.
"All this now is precisely the power of *ṛddhi* (supernormal power) according to one's will, and not other powers.

In the "Exegesis on the Section on Arising," first there is the summary of what preceded and the introduction of what follows; next, regarding the arising [of the discourse] after the Sūtra, the Treatise cites the Sūtra and explains it through four phrases.
The statement "the matter is concluded" refers to the first phrase: having entered *samādhi* above, in order to manifest his own realization, he was able to proclaim [it].
The first phrase, "having finished explaining," means that because the explanation has already been fully revealed, the matter is concluded;

"attaining superior power" refers to the second phrase, wherein the previous entry into samādhi was for the purpose of receiving empowerment, and now that the Buddha’s empowerment is complete, it is called "attaining superior power";

"the time for speaking has arrived" refers to the third phrase, wherein the previous entry into samādhi was for the purpose of observing the capacities of sentient beings to grant the Dharma accordingly, and since the awakening of those beings is now present, it is called "the time for speaking."
The fourth phrase, "reaching the state where there is no speech," refers to the previous entry into samādhi, which manifested the realization that transcends speech;

now, it describes emerging from samādhi to conversely reveal that the state entered—the quiescent transcendence of speech—is such that the meaning of words is thus [inapplicable]. Below, the text explains this passage:

previously it was asked, "When the time arrived, why did you not speak immediately while in samādhi? Because samādhi is without speech, one cannot speak immediately; this [response] follows the needs of those to be converted.

If one relies on the actual practice of these characteristics, then quiescence and constant function are inherently present; how could they wait for one to emerge from meditative absorption? Because these four meanings are complete [within the state of concentration], one arises from that concentration.

This explains the initial section of the "Fundamental Division," which concludes the preceding discussion and introduces the subsequent inquiry. In the sutra, this is fully analyzed through five phrases.
First, the text is divided into three parts; second, it reveals the Dharma taught therein; third, it clarifies the practice accomplished thereby;
fourth, it demonstrates how these mutually arise and are established in relation to what follows; and fifth, the text is briefly analyzed and its points pointed out.
Regarding the "three parts": the preceding four parts, which explain the reasons for the arising of the teaching, are collectively judged as the introduction (*nidāna*).

From this point onward, the exposition of the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) constitutes the main body (*śarīra*). Some people claim that the section on the explanation of the person constitutes the main body;

however, this is not the case here in the same manner as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In that sutra, the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) is judged to be the introduction, while from the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*) downward, there is a brief praise of the Buddha’s wisdom.

The three requests made by Śāriputra for the Tathāgata’s extensive response constitute the primary authentic teaching (*samyag-śāsana*). By analogy with those [sections], although the initial part and the section on the request do not provide an extensive exposition, they are nonetheless the primary authentic teaching.
As for the Dharma elucidated therein, its essential nature (*dharmatā*)—which is quiescent and transcends verbal expression—is revealed within the subsequent section on the request.
To manifest the characteristics of this stage (*bhūmi*), both its essence (*tattva*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are presented together within this section on the fundamental division.
The six determined matters constitute the essence of this stage, while the ten enumerated names constitute its characteristics; this is the Dharma.
Regarding the practice to be accomplished (*sādhya-caryā*): the preceding four sections have explained the reasons for its arising in order to inspire faith in sentient beings;
now, within this fundamental text, the stages (*bhūmi*) are presented and their excellence praised to arouse a desire [to practice], which constitutes the practice to be accomplished.

Regarding the "arising through the establishment of characteristics": first, within this initial section, the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the stages (*bhūmi*) is presented as the basis for the subsequent request for explanation;

subsequently, in the section containing the request, the essential nature of the stages is further revealed. Furthermore, the excellence of the stages is praised so that the assembly may develop a desire [to hear], thereby giving rise to the words of the subsequent request and the ensuing exposition.
Now, within this initial section, ten names are briefly listed to give rise to the detailed explanation that follows.
This means that what precedes arises from what follows. Below, the request for an exposition clarifies this fundamental section; what are its characteristics?

Because the subsequent assembly requested a broad revelation of the reality of the stages (*bhūmi*) as being quiescent and devoid of marks, the essence of the stages elucidated in this fundamental section is established.

From the "Exposition Section" (*vibhāga-bhāga*) below, the characteristics of the stages are extensively proclaimed, which constitute the characteristics of the stages represented by the ten names within this fundamental section.
Originally, this is the fundamental ground (*dhātu*); everything below is established upon it. This constitutes the mutual arising and establishment of both the fundamental and the derivative.

To explain the text by its divisions, there are three parts within the sūtra: first, clarifying that the excellence of the vow constitutes the essence of the ground; second, enumerating the ten names to manifest the characteristics of this ground;
and third, citing the Buddha’s shared praise to manifest the essential superiority of the ground. Within each of these three, there are further [divisions].
Regarding the first of the two sections: first, he initially cites those six determined matters as the substance of the ground;

second, after these ten grounds have been explained, he reveals below that the matters of the Bodhisattva grounds herein taught are spoken of in common by all Buddhas, and further clarifies the reason for his own proclamation of them.
Within the former [of these two], the determination of the initial vow is the general [principle]; it is not mixed with what follows.

The sixth is its specific distinction. Regarding "having arisen, he addressed [the assembly]": this refers back to what was previously generated and introduces what follows. As for the term "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*):

it arouses the minds of the multitude, for since the practices of all bodhisattvas are capable of succeeding to the lineage, they are called "Sons of the Buddha. This "bodhisattva's vow" is a general enumeration of the essence of the stages (*bhūmi*).
This statement does not mean that it refers to a single bodhisattva; rather, it refers to the vows of all bodhisattvas as being unmixed and so forth.
In the *Pṛthak-vyākhyā* (Separate Commentary), the second section is explained in detail.

Regarding the statement "I speak thus because of this matter," it means that because all Buddhas speak of the stages (*bhūmi*) in common, what is now being transmitted by that Buddha Vairocana may likewise be spoken of as common across the three periods of time.
This is also the case for the phrase "I too shall speak," which follows below; the explanation of the second section appears to be thus.

The Chinese text is divided into two parts: first, the listing of the names of the grounds; second, the further clarification that these were taught identically throughout the three periods of time, thereby manifesting the essential excellence of the grounds.

Within the third section, there are again two parts: first, "I have neither seen nor praised the speaker," which cites the Buddha’s own praise to manifest the essential excellence of the grounds—this is merely a negative expression (lit., a reversal of speech).
By stating that he has already neither seen nor praised [the speaker] within the middle way, it manifests what is being described.
"Seeing that all [the Buddhas] sighed in unison"—from here below, Vajragarbha clarifies the essential excellence of the stages (*bhūmi*) and explains the reason why all Buddhas sigh together.
Why does he ask? Because the Buddhas are distinct, for what reason do they sigh for the stages without distinction? From "This is...
below is the explanation of the reason for the sighing; there are four phrases, the first of which is the "superior dharma," which serves as the proof.
Regarding the phrase "practicing this," it refers to the practice that serves as the proof for explaining how the Buddha likewise praised [this teaching].
The second point, "it is also a dharma of illumination," refers to the *āgama* (scriptural authority). By citing this *āgama*, it explains that the Buddha likewise spoke of it;

the word "also" (*api*) indicates that while one aspect is the dharma realized through supramundane realization, the other is also practiced through mundane skillful means. Therefore, it is called "also."
In this cultivation, one attains the signs of supramundane realization, which are called "light.
It is like a person drilling for fire who first perceives the sign of warmth, or like digging for water who first perceives the sign of moisture; this is also like that.

The third stage is what is called the "Stage of Discernment" (*vibhūti-bhūmi*), which clarifies the preceding second "Dharma-gate of Light. The fourth stage is "The Inconceivable Nature of Things," which clarifies the preceding [third].

The phrase "the first, the supreme, wondrous Dharma, inconceivable" is an expression of profound praise. Although the stages (*bhūmi*) manifest their characteristics within worldly cultivation, their essence is wondrously transcendent;

therefore, it is said that "this matter is inconceivable. This refers to the wisdom of the various stages, which excludes [worldly] modes of practice and denotes the supramundane realized wisdom of the ten stages.

In this treatise, first there is a question-and-answer analysis regarding the reasons for the Buddha’s own proclamation; subsequently, the scriptural text is explained. Why does he proclaim it himself? This is the initial question.
The subsequent passage explains extensively that it is necessary for the assembly to request [the teaching], yet here too he speaks—why does he not wait for a request but proclaim it himself?
In the answer, there are two points: the first clarifies that because the great assembly did not know [the reason] for the teaching, it was necessary for him to speak of it himself.
Second, it is explained that because the great assembly does not know the Dharma, they must request [the teaching] themselves;

if they do not request it, the assembly will not know whether he will speak or not—this is the first point. Although the previous Buddhas have empowered him to speak, it is still unknown whether Vajragarbha will speak by virtue of that power.
If he has the intention to speak, then one may request it; if he is determined not to speak, then making a request would be of no benefit.
Because the assembly has this intention to request [the teaching], yet there is no fixed time for it, he must speak of himself in order to initiate the subsequent request.

Furthermore, they do not know what dharma he intends to preach; this refers to the latter part of the sentence. Even if they knew he wished to preach, they would still not know which specific dharma he intended to preach or how they should formally entreat him;
therefore, he must speak of himself so that the assembly may know. Question: It was stated above that he speaks of the inconceivable.
Regarding the "Illumination of the Dharmas of All Buddhas," why is it said that one does not know? Because within the inconceivable dharmas, the gateways and distinctions are not singular;

thus, even if one does not know, if one were to say as above that by adding the capacity [of the empowerment] to the Buddha, they are likewise named "Vajra," thereby knowing what is intended, how could it be said that one does not know?
This is known through the indication of signs rather than through certainty; yet, it is still permissible to say that one does not know. What, then, is being said?

Because it must be explained by oneself due to ignorance, the commentary on the text follows the sequence of the three divisions of the sūtra. In explaining the first division, the sūtra text contains two parts, which are categorized as before:
first, clarifying the essence of the stage (*bhūmi*); second, clarifying the shared exposition. The treatise (*śāstra*) has three sections: first, explaining the essence of the stage.
The two commentaries agree in explaining that the third section analyzes the preceding substance by means of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).

In the first part of the sūtra, "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) and "wholesome" (*kuśala*) constitute the general [definition], while "unmixed" (*asaṃbhinnādi*) and so forth constitute the specific [explanations]. Within the initial general section, there are four distinct points: first, the explanation of the meaning of "vow"; second, the explanation of the meaning of "wholesome";

third, the explanation of "certainty" (*niyata*); and fourth, from "having entered" (*praviṣṭa*) onwards, the manifestation of its stage (*avasthā*). Regarding the former, "vow" and "wholesome" cite the wording of the sūtra.
This correctly raises the vow as it arises in conjunction with certainty, just as the generation of the bodhicitta occurs in the first bhūmi.
Here, "this vow" refers to the essential nature of the vow; it is not a case of explaining a name or a meaning.

"As" is a term used to point to the phenomenon itself, just as in the section on the dwelling of the first bhūmi below, where the arising of the bodhicitta constitutes the first dwelling, and that mind is precisely [what is meant].

It should be understood that this vow is referred back to in the subsequent explanation of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), because the text below states that "one who gives rise to this mind" refers to the vow within the section on the fundamental nature.
This is because the essence of the mind and the vow are one; thus, the two refer to each other so that both meanings are revealed.
"Essence" (*tattva*) refers to the supramundane roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of true realization, which are able to increase and lead toward and accord with *bodhi*.
Therefore, it is called a "vow" (praṇidhāna) and also termed the "essence of the arousal of the mind" (cittotpāda). Since their essence is not different, why are the names "mind" and "vow" distinct?
Although their essence is one, they differ according to their respective meanings; thus, the names are not the same. As for the difference in meaning:
to direct one's intention toward great enlightenment is the meaning of "arousing the mind"; that this [enlightenment] belongs to oneself is the meaning of "vow. Question: Is the vow wholesome?
Regarding the essence (*tattva*) of these stages (*bhūmi*), why is it specifically pointed to as the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*) of the first stage?

The explanation says: "O Śūraṅgama, the essence of all stages is now indicated by pointing to the first stage; this is merely spoken from the perspective of the beginning. Furthermore, it was previously stated that the essence of the stages consists of vows and goodness (*praṇidhāna-kuśala*).

From the section on "divisions" (*prabheda*) onwards, however, only the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the stages are clarified. How can the characteristics be used to manifest their essence? The explanation says: "By indicating the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of that [the first stage], this [the essence of all stages] is manifested."
Within this, the analysis points to the "fruition aspect" (*phalāṃśa*) manifested by that [bodhicitta] to reveal this vow.
Next, the meaning of "virtuous" (*kuśala*) is explained: "Virtuous determination" (*kuśala-niścaya*) cites the scriptural text;

"subsumed by the subsequently attained true knowledge" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-tathatājñāna-saṃgṛhīta*) explains why the mind of the virtuous vow is called "virtuous," because this mind of the vow is subsumed by true knowledge and is therefore designated as "virtuous."

Although the two meanings of "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) and "true wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna*) differ, their essential substance is not distinct; therefore, they are subsumed [under the same category] in this way.

If this vow-mind were subsumed under false wisdom (*mṛṣājñāna*), its characteristics would accord with it while its nature would conflict, and thus it could not be called "wholesome" (*kuśala*). Because it is subsumed under true wisdom, its substance accords with it and is thus named "wholesome.

Next, regarding the determination of "definitive wholesomeness" (*niyata-kuśala*): "definitive" refers back to the scriptural text, specifically citing the term "definitive wholesome," following the sequence of the passage.
This constitutes a definitive explanation that clarifies its characteristics; this interpretation takes the preceding vow as the meaning of "definitive.

Regarding the general explanation of the meaning of "definitive," there are three types as stated in the *Bhūmivastu* (*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*): first, the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*) is called "definitive" because it is fixed as the seed of Buddhahood;

second, the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) is called "definitive" because it is certain to give rise to the resolve for enlightenment; third, the stages from the first bhūmi upward are called "definitive."
Now, that which is discussed here is the third question: "How is it that there are five meanings of 'definitive understanding' regarding the stages (*bhūmi*)?
First, in terms of the essence of practice, it is definitive non-retrogression; second, in relation to the objects of faith and the dharmas realized, it is definitive freedom from doubt;

third, in relation to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it is definitive non-creation [of further karma]; fourth, in relation to *bodhi*, it is definitive orientation toward it; and fifth, in relation to sentient beings...
Because it is definitively able to benefit and possesses these various meanings, it is called "definitive" (*niyata*). The preceding "vow-mind" (*praṇidhāna-citta*) is not merely wholesome;

it is also its definitive meaning, and is therefore described as "definitive. Below, the section on stages is shown: having already entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is no longer comprised within the level of faith (*śraddhā*).
This initial stage and above is the mind of true realization (*sākṣāt-pramāṇa-citta*); it is not the distant aspiration of the stage prior to the grounds (*pūrva-bhūmi*).
Therefore, it is not subsumed under faith.
Within the detailed explanation of the lower [stages], there are six determinate categories; these are further divided into general and specific aspects, which are explained extensively below.

Among these six, the practice according to cultivation is divided into two: the first five are self-perfection (*svabhāva*), and the last one is superior progress (*viśeṣa*). The practice according to conduct is divided into three: the first four are self-practice (*svacaryā*).
The fifth [point] concerns benefiting others; the sixth clarifies the attainment of all Buddha-dharmas.

Its meaning is similar to that of the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* regarding the "upholding of the true Dharma. Among the preceding four [points], the first two clarify the essence of the vows and virtuous practices;

the next one clarifies the excellence of the qualities of those practices, which may also be termed the broad and extensive meaning of practice; and the final one clarifies the sense of being able to act as a cause.
Regarding the essential nature of these practices, the various gates differ; yet the conduct, virtues, and capacities of the higher and lower stages are similar.
As for the ten great vows explained below, the essential nature of the practice within each individual vow is distinct, though they are equally vast and identical.

Within the former two [categories], first, "contemplating the characteristics" clarifies the understanding of contemplation—discarding appearances to enter into suchness—while second, "the ultimate reality" manifests the virtues of practice.
The distinctions regarding the realization of reality and the departure from characteristics are thus.

In the text, the "characteristics of contemplation" (*guanxiang*) are listed by name; because it illuminates principle, it is called "contemplation" (*guan*), and because it is the essential form of that contemplation, it is termed "characteristics of contemplation.

This contemplation is extracted from within the general determination (*zhongjueding*), and since the general term is being applied to the specific, it is called "determination. This applies to all subsequent phrases.

It is determined that this is necessarily so. To explain its characteristics through the analogy of "contemplating a single flavor" (*ekarasa*): contemplating the principle means severing emotional delusions;
to speak of it as "true" is to describe the essence of all phenomena as identical, which is termed "suchness" (*tathatā*). Contemplating this identity is explained in the same manner as before.

Regarding the phrase "explaining the characteristics of the single flavor," it clarifies those characteristics. Realizing suchness as a single flavor is the essential nature of contemplation. The term "single flavor" is applied metaphorically.
Just as the ocean, though vast, has but one taste—salt—and just as various medicines boiled together in a single vessel have no difference in their flavor, so it is with all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Although their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are numerous and distinct, when one exhaustively contemplates their reality, they are not different from the principle (*tattva*). Therefore, it is called "one taste.
As the Sūtra says, "without admixture" refers to this one taste.
The "True Reality" (bhūtatathatā) is listed among the names because its practice brings about the departure from delusion; thus it is called "True Reality. The following explains its characteristics:
it is not the realm of the world (*loka-viṣaya*). Because correct understanding of True Reality does not perceive [it] through conditioned observation, it is named "not the realm of the world.

To further explain why it is "not a realm," this refers to conforming with reality and turning back from emotional appearances, which have never existed from the outset. Since there is no characteristic (*animitta*) that can be apprehended, it is termed "transcendent" (*lokottara*).
There is no world that emerges in opposition to it. Regarding the phrase "cannot be seen" at the end of the sutra passage: it cannot be seen because it is not an object of the mundane world.

In the explanation of the superior virtues (*viśeṣaguṇa*), first their names are listed; subsequently, they are explained, and finally, the section below provides a detailed analysis. First, the names of the superior virtues are listed.

Because the practice accords with the *dharmadhātu* and its virtuous qualities are vast and great, it is called "supreme. This explains its characteristics: "Great *dharmadhātu*" is stated to manifest the greatness of the supreme practice.
Because the practice is profound, it is called "greatly great. It is designated as the *dharmadhātu*, and thus termed the "Great *Dharmadhātu*.

It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas. To explain this extensively: it is called "vast" because the Buddha’s virtues are broad and manifold, and his vows are excellent and capable of serving as the fundamental source for all Buddhas.

Because it is vast, it is called "the supreme category" (*viśeṣa-gotra*). One should have stated previously that the Buddha's fundamental nature is the *dharmadhātu*, but it was omitted there. Below, the Sūtra provides both a concise and an extensive commentary.

The phrase "the Buddha's fundamental greatness" returns to the term "great. Regarding the term "*dharmadhātu*": the "Dharma" refers to its own essence; within the *tathāgatagarbha*, all dharmas are fully present.
Although they share a single essence, their aspects are eternally distinct; because they are distinct, they are called a "realm" (*dhātu*).
The practice is identical to the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it is said as follows. Within this, there are two parts: first, a general explanation of its vastness being like the *dharmadhātu*;
second, from "furthermore, the *dharmadhātu*" onwards, a specific explanation of the vastness of various practices being like the *dharmadhātu*.
In the general section, the initial phrase "great, supreme, equal, etc. explains the meaning of "vastness," while "all phenomena" and so forth explain "like [the *dharmadhātu*]."
The Dharma-realm is supremely victorious, lofty, and vast; its transformation is called the manifestation of the characteristic of greatness.

It is not that the name and meaning are explained by the scripture’s statement "the treatise on greatness reveals loftiness and victory," for it is by means of that loftiness and victory that greatness is manifested and established.

What is meant by "great"? It refers to loftiness and victory. What is meant by "vast"? It refers to loftiness and victory. The manifestation of the characteristic of greatness and the meaning of the term are likewise identical in essence.

The meaning of the previously established "greatness" (*mahat*) and other characteristics being made manifest is as follows: although names such as "great," "supreme" (*viśiṣṭa*), and so forth differ from one another, their essence (*tattva*) is one;

therefore, they are said to manifest the same characteristic. Because they share a single vow and excellence, they are termed a "single essence. Yet, because they are distinguished as "great," "supreme," and so on, they are called "different names. This is because the meaning of the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) is distinct.

Thus, while the essence remains one, the meanings of the *dharmalakṣaṇa* are differentiated; for this reason, the previous [statement] regarding different names is explained. Their essence is indeed one, yet the meanings of the *dharmalakṣaṇa* are distinct. Therefore...

What is meant by "different names and different characteristics"? "Profound" has the meaning of being great; "vast" has the meaning of being broad. "Surpassing the lower" is named "victorious," and "emerging above" is named "lofty.
"All phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) is an explanation of the *dharmadhātu*. Because the *dharmadhātu* is not one, it is called "all phenomena.
Thus, they are understood as such; "such as" (*tathā*) means "just like. Because all phenomena constitute the virtues of practice, and because that practice is vast and great, it is so described.

It is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that although it was previously stated in general terms that all dharmas such as the "Great," the "Victorious," and so forth are by their very nature vast, this was not yet explained in terms of their actual practice;
thus, the following clarifies how they are vast according to the Dharma. Although practices are immeasurable, they are essentially comprised of only three paths:

the path of realization, the path of non-abiding, and the path of assistance. Regarding these three, only the following is clarified: [The text continues with the specific analysis of these three paths.]
Regarding the "Great Meaning" (*mahārtha*), as with the *dharmadhātu*, other aspects such as "superior," "lofty," and "vast" are not discussed here in detail.

How is this known? Because the text simply states, "Furthermore, the *dharmadhātu* is great," and does not mention the others. What is the reason for this? The preceding text has already stated that "great," "superior," "lofty," and "vast" are synonymous terms for the same essence;
it clarifies them by way of the "Great Meaning" as being like the *dharmadhātu*, and the other categories can be understood accordingly. Therefore—

It does not say that the beginning and middle first clarify the practice of the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*) and the great pure dharma; rather, what follows explains it as being like the *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the previous section, the initial statement "furthermore" serves as a general heading to introduce the *dharmadhātu* above, which has already been explained in summary. Now, it is explained again specifically;
therefore, the meaning of "furthermore" in the two subsequent phrases is identical, signifying that within the *dharmadhātu*, there is furthermore one kind of path of realization.

The practice of the "Great Name" (Mahānāman) is the Great Practice of the Dharma-realm; it is only by being commensurate with the Dharma-realm that it can be called "Great. Thus, the Dharma-realm is cited to manifest its greatness.

This means that through the contemplation of True Suchness (Tathatā), its great essence is revealed. This contemplation is superior to that of ordinary beings and the Two Vehicles, thereby manifesting its great significance.
Below, this greatness is clarified in relation to the Dharma-realm. When the term "pure phenomena" is used, it refers to the Dharma-realm. The preceding section was general.

To explain this, it is said that "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*); here, in this specific interpretation, it refers to "pure phenomena" (*viśuddhadharma*). This means that within the *dharmadhātu*, one realizes the gates of pure phenomena;

by the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one understands suchness (*tathatā*), and thus those pure phenomena become practice. Regarding the "Great Non-abiding," it is first clarified as the practice of non-abiding. "Great" refers to what follows;
having explained [the title], the subsequent section interprets it according to the *dharmadhātu*. Within the preceding part, it first states "furthermore, the phenomena."
To summarize the *dhātu* (element) by way of its general indication: within the *dharmadhātu*, there is furthermore a type of non-abiding practice characterized by great understanding.

The text is the same as before. Regarding the "assemblage of skillful means" (*upāya-saṃgraha*), it reveals the essential nature: because skillful wisdom (*kauśalya-prajñā*) moves simultaneously through both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhava*) without attachment, it is called "skillful means.

Because it does not abide in emptiness, it is able to encompass merit (*guṇa*); because it does not cling to existence, it is able to accomplish wisdom (*prajñā*). It is for this reason [that it is so described].
The stage of the path where the fulfillment of virtuous wisdom is attained is called the "Collection of the Grounds" (*jñānabhūmi-saṃgraha*). This is explained as being as vast as the *dharmadhātu*.
When speaking of the Mahāyāna, one cites the *dharmadhātu* because it was previously explained in a general sense; thus, it is called "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*).

Now, because this is a specific explanation, it is called the "Great Dharma" (*mahādharma*, i.e., the *dharmadhātu*). Within this *dharmadhātu*, what is the skillful means of the Mahāyāna—the non-abiding dharma-gate? Why is this alone singled out for exposition?
The three greatnesses must all be explained as clear evidence and aids; each has its own distinct substance, yet they do not abide separately.

Based on the two preceding [greatnesses], one discusses them according to their respective meanings; thus, the three paths are specifically manifested as the "Great" because they are non-abiding practices that transcend both emptiness and existence, surpassing the ordinary and distinguishing them from the sage.
Because this reveals the profound meaning of greatness, it is specifically termed the "Great Dharma. One should understand the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena in this way.

Because the Mahāyāna dharma within the *dhātu* (realm) is accomplished through practice, it is "Great. Within the section on the aids to the path (*pakṣa*), it first clarifies those great wholesome dharmas that serve as aids to the path.
The subsequent explanation is as follows: as previously stated regarding the *dharmadhātu*, the initial phrase "furthermore, the *dharmadhātu*" serves as a general heading;

that is, within the *dharmadhātu*, there is furthermore a specific type of aid to the path that is "Great. The commentary on the text is the same as before: [it refers to] the "white dharmas" (*śukladharma*).

Regarding the "dhātu" (element/realm): it reveals its essential substance. Since all three paths are white, they assist in practice to counteract defilement; because the meaning of manifesting whiteness is thus revealed, it is specifically so designated.

The true and the false are the conditions for counteracting delusion; when delusion is determined to be identical with reality, it becomes the True. What is now being distinguished is the True and not the False.
Taking the dharmas as the basis for this distinction, "whiteness" refers to the Dharma-realm, hence it is called the "White Dharma-realm. Furthermore, "white" is that which...

The meaning of purification, the auxiliary practices, and the removal of hindrances enable the purification of the *dharmadhātu*. The following clarifies this great [nature] as it pertains to the *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the term "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), this refers to the *dharmadhātu*; since it was explained in general terms previously, it was called "all dharmas," whereas here, because it is explained specifically, it is called "wholesome dharmas.
This means that within the *dharmadhātu*, those wholesome dharmas that assist the path—since all such dharmas are wholesome—they serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for assisting the path.
Because the meaning of "constructing and cultivating that which is conducive and beneficial" is clearly manifested, they are specifically termed "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*).

Furthermore, because wholesome dharmas that assist the path are established as practice within the *dharmadhātu*—which is suchness as it is—the three paths are collectively called "great" (*mahā*). Therefore, one cannot speak of "great" exclusively as the path of realization;

rather, it is broad only in the sense of assisting the path and lofty in the sense of non-abiding. One should know that all three paths are both broad and great; thus, [the term "great"] is applied below.
The practices sought within each of the ten vows are vast and expansive; they cannot be divided separately.

Regarding the explanation of the causes within the section on "Wholesome Causes," there are two parts: first, the general enumeration of the names, and second, the detailed explanation of those names.
Within this, there are briefly three gates for analysis: first, the certainty [of the result]; second, the fruit; and third, the discernment of its cause.
Third, the explanation according to the text. However, regarding these two fruits, interpretations by various individuals differ.

Some explain that the *nirvāṇa* of skillful means (*upāya*) is an impermanent fruit, while the *nirvāṇa* of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is its permanent fruit. Why is the *nirvāṇa* of skillful means said to be impermanent? Furthermore, it is called a "fruit of affection" (*priya-phala*).
This fruit was originally non-existent and is produced through the cultivation of skillful means; therefore, it is termed "impermanent. Its beneficial qualities (*anuśaṃsa*) are clearly manifested.

Because it is characterized by emotional craving and attachment, it is called "the nature of the fruit of craving. Although the pure *nirvāṇa* manifests through conditions, its essence is inherently existent and does not arise from conditions;
therefore, it is called "eternal. Because those with subtle craving and attachment are rare, it is not termed "craving.

While this principle is not absent when discussing the general characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is not what is being elucidated here. How is this known? It is because the Sūtras speak of an "eternal fruit."
Is it not the case that the *upāya-nirvāṇa* which extends to the end of the future is a fruit of the posterior limit (*paścimānta*) rather than an eternal fruit?

Some further explain that both of the two aforementioned nirvāṇas are eternal fruits. [They argue that] the "excellent rewards" (such as those of the ten kings) are called "unconditioned love" (*anāsrava-tṛṣṇā*), yet because they are worldly conditioned fruits, they are termed "unconditioned.
These superior rewards are desirable and are thus called "fruits of love" (*tṛṣṇā-phala*). This interpretation of them as eternal fruits accords with reason.
"Impermanence" is too narrow; how is this known? The commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* explains that the fruit of craving is like the production of form from space—it is inexhaustible.
The retribution of the Ten Kings is limited to the causal stage; it distinguishes the ten stages up to Buddhahood but does not discuss [the ultimate state], which would be far too narrow.
Now we shall properly discuss it: the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain Great Nirvāṇa yet do not abandon the world; this is impermanent craving.
Because it arises and ceases in accordance with the world, it is called impermanent; because the principle of the activity of great compassion is delightful, it is named a "loved fruit.

The two kinds of nirvāṇa are its permanent fruits. These two are still the two types of practice and virtue—namely, the permanent together with the impermanent, and the impermanent together with the permanent—found within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
They are also the two kinds of adornments of that sūtra; the permanent fruit is that [of the latter].

Because it is adorned with wisdom, that sutra states: "The adornment of wisdom is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), untainted (*anāsrava*), unimpeded (*apratigha*), eternally abiding, and has the fruit of being cherished.

Because it is adorned with merit, that sutra states: "The adornment of merit is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), tainted (*sāsrava*), impeded (*sapratigha*), impermanent, and has the characteristics of two fruits.
These passages are clear. Since the fruits are thus distinct, what are the characteristics of their causes?

Discussing its causal essence, it is fundamentally one; yet, according to the meaning, it may be divided into two. In relation to that constant fruit, the aspect of the arising of the direct cause is incomplete and thus termed the "cause," while the aspect of its fulfillment is termed the "fruit.
In relation to the impermanent love, it is produced by the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), just as form arises from space;
thus, cause and fruit are simultaneous, with no distinction between before and after. Although they are conceptually divided, for now they are treated together as the cause.
In the following commentary on the text, first the impermanence [of the cause] is clarified. Initially, its names are listed; next, its characteristics are explained.
This is because the cause is like space, manifesting the same nature as the dharma, and the effect is impermanent because the cause can produce it inexhaustibly.

Just as space is the basis upon which form arises, and that form is inexhaustible—this distinguishes the metaphor to reveal the dharma: just as space gives rise to form that cannot be exhausted, may [the practitioner's] vows be likewise.
The phrase "the capacity to produce fruits of affection that is inexhaustible" is stated below because the cause is revealed through its fruit;
since the produced forms (*rūpa*) are inexhaustible, it demonstrates that the space (*ākāśa*) which produces them is likewise capable of producing the inexhaustible.

By this analogy, since the produced fruits of affection are inexhaustible, it demonstrates that those vows (*praṇidhāna*) are well-capable of producing the inexhaustible. Below, the sūtra provides the definitive conclusion (*niṣṭhā*) following the subsequent section.

The arising of form is inexhaustible, like space; this preceding section concerns the cause, which is like space. Regarding the constant fruit, the initial enumeration of names is followed by an explanation of their characteristics.
To say it is "the cause" refers to the cause of the constant fruit. The fruit of cessation attained thereby is termed *nirvāṇa*.
The wisdom and virtue of *bodhi* are spoken of as the "path. Furthermore, the fruit of intrinsic purity that is attained is also termed *nirvāṇa*.
The Bodhi of skillful means is called the Path; that which exhausts [all things] down to the very end of the future is called "Exhaustion" (kṣaya).
The profound pointer takes the fruit as the "future," and the place where the future is attained is called the "limit" (koṭi).
This "limit" is like a boundary. At the time of attaining Nirvāṇa, one looks back upon saṃsāra and sees that it has never existed from the beginning; how then could there be Nirvāṇa?

Regarding the explanation of the limits: here, within the cycle of birth and death, one looks far toward nirvāṇa; since nirvāṇa is yet to be attained, it is said that nirvāṇa constitutes the "future limit.
In the explanation of "Great Goodness," first its names are listed: because this benefit for others is vast and its moistening influence is boundless, it is called "Great Goodness."

Next, the explanation of its characteristics states that "benefiting accordingly" means benefiting sentient beings in accordance with their needs. Next, the sutra passage [is cited] to cover and protect them:

"protecting all within the realm of sentient beings by causing them to increase in goodness and guarding them so they depart from evil. Below this, in contrast to the preceding cause, its non-abiding is clarified.
Regarding the phrase "the one immediately preceding," it refers back to the cause of goodness; since that text is adjacent to the present one, it is called "the one immediately preceding."

Regarding the statement "this vow," it refers back to the aforementioned great goodness; it determines that what was previously called a "vow" is merely a figurative expression for this [great goodness].

Regarding the statement "in the world and in nirvana, not exclusively," because the cause of goodness constantly results in the fruit of nirvana, one does not abide exclusively in the impermanent fruit within the world; furthermore, this great goodness is able to accord with the world.
Therefore, among the six [types of non-abiding], these two specifically manifest the functional capacity of practice to produce benefit;

for this reason, they alone are taken up to explain non-abiding. If that is so, since the practice of being undaunted and capable of entering the Buddha’s wisdom is also a form of non-abiding in the world, why is it not mentioned?
In truth, the principle applies equally to all, but it is not discussed here simply because the text has not yet reached it.

Furthermore, one may not fear [the teaching] because it penetrates the five sense-bases (*pañcāyatana*) and reaches the Buddha-realm; thus, it is explained that one does not dwell in the mundane world.
Regarding the explanation of "not fearing," first their names are listed. Because one is able to enter deeply, it is called "not fearing. This is the explanation of being able to enter.

From the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*) upward, the mind of cessation and contemplation manifests, reaching the stages of the Buddha-realm, which is termed "entering the Buddha-ground. Below, this is corroborated by the sutra.

Furthermore, regarding this section below, the second part explains the reason for the simultaneous exposition. Again, as for these "ten stages" (*daśabhūmi*), the text cites the scripture stating that they "generate and maintain the Buddha-wisdom.
Some say: "This is an explanation of the meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*). Indeed, the explanation of the meaning of the stages does not differ from this;
however, the intent of the present text is not to explain the stages themselves. This citation of the stages is intended to explain the three periods of time.

Regarding the explanation of how it arises and is perfected: in relation to the fruit of Buddhahood, its initial emergence is called "arising" (*utpāda*) and its final fulfillment is called "perfection" (*niṣpatti*).

Alternatively, it may be termed "arising" when acting as a cause (*hetu*) and "perfection" when acting as a condition (*pratyaya*). As for a single dharma of the stages (*bhūmi*), how can it be both a cause and yet also called a condition?
To explain: the virtues of a Buddha do not yet exist [in this stage]; since the dharma of the stages can cause that which does not yet exist to come into existence, it is so named.

Therefore, it is said that they serve as causes (*hetu*) because they provide the basis for seeking the fruit of Buddhahood; they are called conditions (*pratyaya*) because they are capable of making manifest those dharmas that can be attained.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes: first, realization (*adhigama*), and second, teaching (*deśanā*). The fruit also has two aspects:

first, intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*), and second, purity through application (*prayoga-vyavadāna*). In relation to the fruit of intrinsic purity, the path of realization serves as the cause and the path of teaching serves as the condition.
Regarding the path of means (*upāya-mārga*) as the cause and the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*) as the condition, it is because this fruit exists that it is said to "generate" and "abide.
When speaking of "abiding" (*sthiti*) in terms of the correspondence within the causal stage alone, it refers to maintenance;

however, when considering both cause and fruit, it is like the first stage (*bhūmi*) being viewed in relation to all subsequent stages up to the Buddha-stage, wherein the meaning of "maintenance" is explained. Thus, the various stages are viewed in relation to those that follow.
The sequence follows this same principle. Why is it called "holding" (*dhāraṇī*)? It is because it has the sense of ascending and holding.
Just as the earth in the world is called "holding" because it can support all things, so too, for these reasons, since the Buddha spoke of these various meanings, I likewise speak of them;
the application of this in the sutras is thus to be understood.

The two preceding sections have provided an exegesis following the sūtra; now follows the third [section], the "Sixfold Analysis. Regarding the phrase "because of the distinct characteristics and specific characteristics":

this borrows terminology to demonstrate that while these are the true characteristics of contemplation and so forth, they are termed "specific characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) because they differ from the single determination of the second section, which is divided into six names. This constitutes the "specific characteristics."

Why is it that the commentary definitively explains the second section of the sūtra on the characteristics of the second bhūmi? Within that section, there are two parts: first, the listing of the names of the bhūmis;

second, the clarification that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have spoken [of them] in common. However, the present commentator only explains the first part and does not explain the second, as the latter is similar to what preceded it.
Within the portion being explained, there is first the teaching and then the simile. Regarding the teaching, one first distinguishes the number [of perfections] in relation to the obstacles.

Why is the first of the ten stages named "Joy" (*pramuditā*)? Below, the names of the stages will be explained according to their respective positions; first, we shall address the question of why they are so designated.
Why are there exactly ten stages, neither more nor less? This is explained by way of their opposition to specific hindrances (*āvaraṇa*).

While this sutra and its commentary extensively analyze the ten stages through ten gates, as demonstrated above, the present discussion refers specifically to the single gate concerning the opposition to hindrances.

Question: Why is it definitively taught that the ten obstacles correspond to the ten stages (*bhūmi*)? Through this correspondence between the obstacles and the stages, they further illuminate one another.
Question: Are these obstacles illusory or real? Answer: It is not fixed. Those who possess these obstacles cannot attain the ten stages; for this reason, they are called "real.

Conversely, from the perspective of realization, one looks back and sees that these obstacles have never existed; they are merely established as a provisional designation to manifest the virtues. For this reason, they are called "illusory."

The names of the following obstacles were previously raised and will now be analyzed; their meanings are explained extensively in a separate chapter, which should be studied in full. For now, we shall merely explain the terminology.

First, regarding the "obstacle of the ordinary person’s mark of self" (*pṛthagjana-ātmagrāha-āvaraṇa*): this is contrasted with the realization of non-self (*anātman*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*), where the notion of a self is explained as an obstacle.
There are two kinds of "self": first, that which is called "self" in the sense of sovereignty, such as the eight forms of mastery (*vaśitā*); this refers to its functional application.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of "self" based on reality: this refers to the substance [of the self]. There are two types of real self: first, the ultimate reality, which is what is called the Buddha-nature;

therefore, the Sūtra says that "self" refers to the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha. Second, the conventional reality, which refers to the false grasping of ordinary beings toward the self-nature of arising phenomena.
The self of ultimate reality is attained by the sages, while the self of false grasping arises in ordinary beings.

In the mundane world, there is a distinction between "self" (*ātman*) and "person" (*pudgala*). These are distinguished by means of human beings to make them manifest. The term "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) refers to the ordinary:
"ordinary" refers to the vulgar dharmas of birth and death; "person" (*jana*) refers to a man or individual. Because these vulgar dharmas constitute a person, they are called an "ordinary person.

This is merely another name for the distinction between "self" and "person. To cling to names as real is "self-grasping" (*ātmagrāha*). To take up the characteristics of the self's substance and state is termed "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*). To obstruct the noble path is termed "obstructing wrong conduct" (*mithyācāra-vibandha*).
Regarding the phrase "obstacles to the arising of the body and so forth": this is taught in contrast to the purity of ethical conduct (*śīla*) maintained on the second stage (*bhūmi*).

It explains that non-virtuous karma (*akuśala-karma*) constitutes an obstacle; because such karma deviates from the correct path, it is termed "perverse" (*mithyā*); because perverse karma accumulates and arises, it is termed "activity" (*caryā*).

Since activity arises in dependence upon conditions, it must rely upon "requisites" (*sambhāra*). The term "arising" (*utpāda*) refers to its conditions, while "the body and so forth" refers to the requisites; here, "body" is mentioned as a representative example.
The phrase "equally encompassing speech and mind" refers to those factors that obstruct the precepts and are termed "obscuring darkness.
