Regarding the statement that one "forgets various dharmas such as what has been heard," this is explained in relation to the third stage (*bhūmi*) as the obscuration of the mind’s understanding of the Dharma through hearing. Because the mind lacks the illumination of wisdom, it is called the "aspect of darkness"; this constitutes the essence of the obstruction.

Since darkness necessarily involves delusion regarding its object, the following clarifies this: among the processes of hearing, reflection, and so forth, these are the dharmas that are the objects of delusion. In this context—
Because one cannot clearly retain it in mind, it is called "forgetting. Because of this forgetting, it constitutes an obstacle to the pride of understanding the Dharma (*dharmajñāna-māna*).
This refers to the supramundane true realization of the Fourth Ground; it explains that within the Third Ground, the mind of understanding (*jñāna-citta*) acts as an obstacle.

Although this understanding on that ground can cognize phenomena, because it grasps at signs (*nimitta*), it is termed the "pride of understanding the Dharma" (*dharmajñāna-māna*), and thus it is an obstacle. Question: Previously, you spoke of the self (*ātman*)...
The obscuration of misconduct and forgetfulness is now explained; why is it said here that understanding [the nature of things] is an obscuration?
Because the first three stages involve worldly practice, one abandons transgressions through merit; from the fourth stage upward, practice is supramundane, and one abandons signs through wisdom.
Therefore, these are not comparable. Regarding the pride of bodily purity: this refers to the fifth stage’s mind of equal purity, whereas on the fourth stage one still grasps at purity.

Because one conceives the pride of "purity of body" by grasping at the signs of purity within the body attained during the first four stages (*bhūmi*), this constitutes a subtle affliction and habitual tendency.
This refers to the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) in relation to the ten dharmas of equality;

it explains that in the fifth stage, the prideful mind that discriminates between defiled and pure dharmas is taken as an obstacle. Furthermore, there are three grades of pride—superior, middling, and inferior—as explained previously.

The pride of regarding the Dharma as supreme acts as an obstacle to the lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) of the fourth stage; the pride of regarding the purity of body and mind acts as an intermediate obstacle to the middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*) of the fifth stage;
and the pride of grasping at defilement and purity is the lowest among the prides, acting as an obstacle to the superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) of the sixth stage.

This superior patience can eliminate it. Regarding what was previously stated, the subtle nature refers to the obstructive dharmas consisting of the delusion of pride; this is explained in terms of its faults.

The explanation of "affliction" (*khila*) refers to subtle [afflictions], while the explanation of "obstruction" (*nīvaraṇa*) reveals the coarse [afflictions]; this applies similarly to the categories of "hindrance" (*paryutthāna*), "fetter" (*saṃyojana*), and so forth.

Since all these are afflictions (*kleśa*), why are the first two specifically designated as "pride" (*māna*)? It is because pride follows the path of grasping at [objects] with attachment, which differs from [the other afflictions] such as ignorance (*tamas*), whose nature and characteristics are entirely contrary [to the path].
Thus, based on the objects grasped, their respective hindrances are distinguished and designated as "pride. These subtle afflictions are the coarsest among them.

The residual habit-energy is termed "subtle habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). Regarding these subtle tendencies, it is said that in contrast to the superior practices initiated by the wisdom of the ten skillful means of the seventh stage, the delight in emptiness within the sixth stage constitutes an obstruction.
Because one attains equality regarding phenomena in the sixth stage and dwells with pleasure in emptiness, one is unable to immediately give rise to superior practice from within emptiness;
therefore, this is considered an obstruction. It is characterized by grasping at conditioned existence as coarse and grasping at emptiness [as a fixed state].

That which is subtle in form is called the "residue" (*vāsanā*) of the coarse [characteristics of name and form]; it is rejected as such because, although the objects grasped—emptiness and existence—are distinct, the nature of the attachment is the same.

Thus, it can be described as a residue. Regarding the statement that there is an obstacle to practice within the signless (*animitta*), this is said in contrast to the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) of the eighth stage;
the effortful practice of the seventh stage is the obstacle, while the eighth stage consists of the practice of natural fruition (*vipāka-caryā*).
The complete mastery of relinquishing effort is called "signlessness" (*animitta*). Yet, even in this stage of signlessness, there still remains the practice of effort;

therefore, this constitutes an obstacle that prevents one from effectively benefiting sentient beings. This "obstacle" is contrasted with the unimpeded preaching of the ninth stage, for the eighth stage cannot act as an obstacle to it.
Although within the first eight stages one can purify lands and transform sentient beings, [this specific capacity is absent here].
That sentient beings are unable to employ eloquence (*pratibhāna*) to teach the Dharma for the benefit of others is called "inability. Because of this inability, it is described as an obstruction.

Regarding the statement that they lack mastery over all phenomena, this is said in contrast to the wisdom of mastery belonging to the tenth stage; it indicates that within the ninth stage there is a lack of such wisdom which acts as an obstruction.
Although those in the preceding nine stages may indeed possess eloquence, teach the Dharma, and benefit sentient beings, they have not yet attained [this mastery].
Receiving the Buddha’s cloud-and-rain-like preaching of the Dharma, which pours down the rain of Dharma to extinguish defilements and give rise to goodness, is called "lack of mastery.
Because there is a lack of mastery, it is described as an "obstruction.

From here on, the second section explains the meaning of the names of the stages (*bhūmi*); first there is the inquiry, followed by the explanation. The meaning of the ten stages is explained in detail in a separate chapter.
This should be explained in detail within the exposition on "joy": the initial realization of the noble state is that which is to be rejoiced in;
the accomplishment of unsurpassed self-benefit and benefit for others constitutes its practice.

Because the virtues cultivated previously have now reached maturity, it is called "accomplishment"; it is not that what was previously capable of being added is designated as "unsurpassed self-benefit and benefit for others."
That which emerges as the first realization of the state of sainthood (*ārya*) is its realized practice; this principle is the state of sainthood.

Because one realizes this ground for the first time upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*), it is called the "first realization. To distinguish it from previous first realizations and to differentiate it from subsequent births, it is termed "joyful" (*pramuditā*).
One gives rise to joy because the unsurpassed state is accomplished; one gives rise to much joy because it is the first realization.
Therefore, it is called the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Regarding the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), according to one of Nāgārjuna’s threefold explanations:

first, freedom from the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*); second, freedom from the defilement of karma; and third, the purity of the essence of practice—this is termed "Freedom from Defilement. Here, too, it is the same:
first, by abandoning the affliction of violating the precepts through mistaken intent, it clarifies the distancing from the defilement of afflictions. [End of section on] Afflictions.

There are two types: first, the subtle; second, the coarse. The coarse arises as the transgression of precepts, whereas the subtle does not. This is because the coarse is distinguished from the subtle by its nature of manifesting the afflictions that give rise to the transgression of precepts.
There are two kinds of such transgressions: first, intentional; second, unintentional. The intentional is grave while the unintentional is light.

Thus, the afflictions that arise intentionally are coarse rather than subtle, whereas the afflictions that arise unintentionally are subtle rather than coarse. This is the "coarse" [aspect] of the preceding stage.

Having already eliminated the subtle [faults] that give rise to errors, this stage is far removed from them because it distinguishes the subtle from the coarse; thus it is said to be "free from the arising of errors.

Since even the afflictions that lead to erroneous transgressions no longer exist, how could there be actual transgressions? Nevertheless, what is here abandoned has the power to cause agitation and confusion, and is therefore called an "affliction" (*kleśa*), a "defilement" (*mala*), or a "stain" (*kaṣāya*).
As for the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes being free from the stains of karma. One who is "endowed with pure precepts" refers to the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*).

It is called "Stainless" (*vimalā*) because it is pure. The first "stainlessness," which is the departure from afflictions (*kleśa*), is its cause; the second "stainlessness," which is the departure from karma, is its result;

and the third "stainlessness," which is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), is its antidote. Regarding the explanation of the third stage, the "Luminous" (*prabhākari*), there are three parts:
first, it is called the Luminous Stage because one attains the characteristic of the light of wisdom of the fourth stage. Therefore, below...
The Treatise states: "The wisdom of non-arising therein is called 'light' (*āloka*); because it is light, it is named the 'Luminous Stage' (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).

Second, having attained this stage, the wisdom of the skillful means of dhyāna is termed 'clarity' (*vidyā*); thus the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* says: "Because samādhi illuminates, it is called the Luminous Stage.
Third, within this stage, the mind that understands the Dharma heard eliminates the obscuration of darkness; therefore, it is described as 'clarity. Thus says the *Bhūmi*.

Because one holds the clouds of the Dharma and illuminates with the Dharma, it is called the "Luminous Ground" (Prabhākarī-bhūmi). In this present text, we rely only on the latter [explanation] and do not discuss the former two.

Regarding "illuminating the Dharma in accordance with what is heard": hearing, reflection, and cultivation are the dharmas that are to be known; correct understanding in accordance with those dharmas is termed "illuminating in accordance.
When this illumination is distinct and clear, it is called "manifestation. The fourth ground, the "Blazing Ground" (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), provides a complete explanation.
There are two ways of explaining [the term *jvālā*]: first, by way of internal realization as an antidote, it is explained that it is called "flame" (*jvālā*) because it is like fire burning objects;
second, by way of its function, it is explained that based on the clarity of the realized essence, the flame manifests externally and is thus termed "flame. Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
"The jewel of realized wisdom emits the light of the *āgama*, illuminating the world; this is called 'flame'. Here, we rely on the former explanation.

The omission of the discussion regarding the fire of wisdom that burns the non-forgetfulness of afflictions is because, in the first three stages, the nature of understanding derived from hearing, reflection, and so forth constitutes this "non-forgetfulness.
Since it is an object of perception and a conceptualization of delusion, it is termed an "affliction.

Because it is consumed by the fire of wisdom in the fourth stage, it is called "fuel. Wisdom burning the fuel of afflictions is designated as "fire"; thus, because wisdom burns the fuel of afflictions, it is called fire.

It is said that it receives its name from the mutual relationship between the ability to burn away these hindrances and their remedies; however, this fourth stage should properly be called the "Fire Ground" (*tejodhātu*).
While fire can burn, it does not necessarily illuminate; since "blazing" (*jvalana*) possesses both capacities, the term "blazing" is retained.

Regarding the explanation of the "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjaya*), some commentators state that by attaining supramundane wisdom and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), one explains the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and is able to deliver those who are difficult to deliver.

Regarding the difficulty of the meaning, it is explained that this does not accord with the treatise; rather, one attains supramundane wisdom through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). This resolves the objection. There are two types of such objections:

first, in contrast to the preceding three stages, it clarifies the difficulty of attaining the supramundane, as the treatise below states: "The ten minds of equality are extremely difficult to attain.
Second, in contrast to the fourth stage, it clarifies the difficulty of its skillful means in accordance with the world, as the treatise below states: [the ten kinds of skillful means].
Furthermore, because it is the most difficult to attain in the world, the first difficulty in this present text is that which pertains to the supramundane.
The second difficulty is that within these five stages, the ten minds of equality and the contemplation of reality are termed "supramundane wisdom" and "skillful means.
In the subsequent five stages, compassion for benefiting sentient beings and the five types of clear wisdom accord with the world.

It is named "Skillful" because it possesses these two meanings; therefore, it is called "Difficult to Attain. It is difficult to cross over, yet it can cross over what is difficult to cross. Because it distinguishes the superior crossing amidst difficulties, it is called "Attainment.
Regarding the term "Manifest" (*abhimukhī*): the former two stages are difficult to reach, yet one can reach this stage; therefore, it is called "Superior Attainment.
It is superior to the first three stages because it is supramundane, and it is superior to the fourth stage because of its skillfulness. This explains the meaning of "Manifest."
Prajñā has intervals; it is contrasted with what follows to reveal its inferiority. The realization of emptiness that is actual wisdom is called *prajñā*;
because from the seventh bhūmi upward it is constantly manifest in every thought-moment, whereas this [prior stage] is not yet so, it is said to have intervals.

As for "the manifestation of great wisdom" (*mahājñāna*), it is contrasted with the former to highlight its superiority; the preceding *prajñā* is designated as "great wisdom. Why is this termed "great"? As Nāgārjuna says:
Wisdom is twofold: the small and the great. Contemplation of the eighteen emptinesses is termed "small," referring to the wisdom of objective illumination within the causal stage (*hetubhāga*).
The true realization of *prajñā* is termed "great," referring to the wisdom of the cessation of contemplation within the resultant stage (*phalabhāga*).
What is discussed here is the great and not the small; therefore, it is called "Great Wisdom" (*mahājñāna*), based on the understanding of the self-nature within this stage.
Because it shatters all signs (*lakṣaṇa*) to the ultimate degree, causing the aspect of true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) within the resultant portion to manifest, it is called "Manifest" (*abhimukhī*).

Examining this text through both its hidden and explicit aspects, both [the preceding and succeeding stages] possess intervals; thus, for those who argue that both are manifested, the terms are merely elegant and alternating expressions.

It is named the "Manifest Ground" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*) by concluding from the subsequent stage; however, following the previous [logic], it should be called the "Ground with Intervals. This concludes the explanation of the Far-Reaching (*Dūraṅgamā*) stage.

"Skillfully cultivating the signless (*animitta*) explains its practice. From the preceding stages onward, existence and non-existence arise alternately; therefore, it is not called "skillful cultivation.

In this stage, both arise simultaneously, and thus it is called "skillful cultivation. Because of this skillful cultivation, one is free from the signs of the separation between existence and non-existence;
hence, it is called "signless. Furthermore, because within the seventh stage one cultivates the wisdom of skillful means and does not cling to emptiness, it is so named.

Because one skillfully cultivates signlessness and initiates superior practice, it is called "the stage of functional effort" (*prayoga-prayukta*). The following section explains its meaning of "remoteness.

"The culmination of functional effort" is stated in contrast to the preceding six stages to demonstrate its remoteness; for within those six stages, functional effort was not yet complete, whereas in this stage it reaches its ultimate limit, hence it is called "culmination.
"Able to transcend the world" is stated in contrast to ordinary beings to clarify its remoteness; it refers to being beyond the three [lower] stages.
Because its mode of practice accords with that of ordinary beings and it has not yet transcended this worldly stage, it is called "transcending" (*atikrānta*).

Regarding the phrase "surpassing the two vehicles": while the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) through the causal conditions of analytical contemplation on the truths in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages is similar to that of the two vehicles, it is not called "distant.
Because this stage can give rise to all Buddha-dharmas and surpasses those [stages], it is called "transcending."

Because it has transcended [the lower stages], it is called "distant. Regarding the explanation of the immovable [stage]: because the ripening of the fruit is signless (*animitta*) and free from the movement of effort (*prayoga*), all the qualities of practice arise through prior cultivation;
thus they are called "accomplished through ripening" (*vipākaja*). Because they are currently designated as "matured" and are free from the characteristics of effort, they are called "signless.
This is precisely the stage of "effortlessness" (*anābhoga*) within the explanation of the names of the lower stages, wherein the path is well-established.
Regarding "uninterrupted" (*anantara*): because it is free from separation and because both the empty and the existent manifest simultaneously, it is called "uninterrupted.
This is what is referred to as "ground-to-ground" (*bhūmi-bhūmi*) within the explanation of names in the lower stage. It refers to the power of unimpeded mastery among the excellent wisdoms.
That which accomplishes the benefit of others through the forty kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is called "unimpeded," and the sovereign freedom in initiating discourse is termed "power" (*bala*).

Because he proclaims the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, it is called "knowledge for the benefit of others" (*parārtha-jñāna*). Because his skillful means are supreme, it is named "Good Intelligence" (*Sādhumati*).

Regarding the initial correct explanation of the meaning of the name "Dharma Cloud" (*Dharmamegha*) within the *Śrīdharmamegha* [stage]: having received this, one manifests distinction through comparison;
possessing the great Dharma-body and mastery, the Bodhisattva of this stage has a Dharma-body that is universally identical with the entire Dharma-realm, and is thus called the "Great Dharma-body."
With this great body, one extensively receives many teachings; the rain of Dharma descends to extinguish defilements and generate goodness.

Being endowed with these three meanings is called "possessing mastery. These [qualities] are like clouds; thus, both the phenomenon and the metaphor are presented together, and it is named the "Dharmameghā-bhūmi" (Cloud of Dharma Stage).

Regarding the subsequent section on "demonstrating differences through correspondence," the first correspondence below highlights superiority, while the second correspondence above reveals inferiority. Why is this explained here? This is the preceding explanation.

Regarding the phrase "possessing mastery" (*vaśitā*) within the middle [of the three categories]: if it were simply "possessing," it would be redundant with what precedes; therefore, it must be contrasted with what follows.

If it were simply "possessing" in relation to what follows, it would be confused with the Buddha; therefore, it must distinguish itself from what precedes. Thus, in this middle category relative to what follows, one receives the position. To illustrate this, the tenth stage is cited; within this stage, one attains the office of Buddha-wisdom, which is termed "receiving the royal throne.
This is like the following passage which contrasts the inferior to manifest the superior: "The Buddha is like a great king, and the Dharma-cloud..."
Because the Bodhisattva succeeds to the station of the Buddha next [after the ninth stage], he is like a crown prince; from the ninth stage downward, they are called "other princes.

In comparison to that [tenth stage], the Dharma-cloud stage attains the highest mastery; therefore, it is said that [the lower stages] are fully accomplished. Regarding the phrase "in this place there is a subtle cognitive obstruction," this means they lack mastery.
By citing the inferior to manifest the superior, it is shown that even in the tenth stage, a subtle darkness still persists, and thus [mastery is not yet complete].

Subtle obstructions have not yet been equalized; although one acts with unimpeded spontaneity like a Tathāgata, this is termed "lack of mastery. To counteract this, the following section distinguishes between superiority and inferiority.
After the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), all subtle obstructions are completely dispelled and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) manifests;

this is designated as the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). Why, from the perspective above, is it definitively stated that there are ten stages? Regarding the explanation of the ground of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), the preceding dharma-explanation is further divided by means of a metaphor to clarify its correspondence.

Regarding the two points of comparison: while the preceding stages were previously described as being "obstructed" and not yet emerged, here in this analogy, they are described in relation to what follows as being "located therein.

Although there is this difference—namely, that in the former case the obstructions for the first stage were explained prior to the first stage, and so on up to the obstructions for the tenth stage being explained prior to the tenth stage—these are merely relative distinctions made in comparison to one another.

Below, [it says] "the two collections have ten. *Note: This passage appears to be a commentary on a structural outline (mātṛkā) concerning the stages (bhūmi) of the Bodhisattva path, specifically addressing the relationship between the "obstructions" (āvaraṇa) of various stages and their respective positions within a sequential framework.*
Regarding the virtues manifested by the ten names, first it clarifies that the Bodhisattva while still obstructed is like a child born;

next, it raises the excellence of the Buddha’s emergence to show that all preceding stages are still within [the realm of obstruction]. Within the category of Bodhisattvas, the analogy of being "in the womb" is established to illustrate the Dharma;

thus the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are analyzed according to this shared metaphor. Furthermore, the fact that each stage possesses obstructions serves to explain the commonality between the Dharma and the metaphor.

Regarding the clarification of the Buddha, first among the manifestations of his virtues, there is a metaphor followed by its application. Within the "Treasury" (garbha), there are ten stages; this is the general overview of the metaphor.

As for a person dwelling in the womb, the explanations in the various sūtras differ: the *Pañcarājopama-sūtra* (*Wǔwáng jīng*) states there are thirty-eight seven-day periods, while the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that from the initial stage of consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), there are ten stages within the five phases of the womb.
The emergence from the womb is likewise so; now, ten stages are explained. Advancement is not like the former [stages], and regression is not like the latter;

these are described in relation to the thirty-eight weeks (forty-six days) and can be understood as being divided into ten periods. Calculated, there are twenty-six days and a half, which together constitute one period.
The ten months constitute the ten periods. The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are like the ten months; their names are listed below. Among the ten, the first three are in the Hu language (Sanskrit).
Regarding the difficult-to-understand latter seven [stages] expressed in the Chinese language through metaphors for the Dharma: what is *tārapa*? This dialectal term means "milk.

Just as the physical characteristics of an embryo in the first month of gestation are faint and subtle, like milk in the world, so too is the wisdom that first realizes *tathatā* (suchness) in the first stage (*bhūmi*);
because its form is similar to the Buddha-wisdom, it is called "faint and subtle. What is *vālapa*? This refers to "thin curd" (*takra*), which is a metaphor for entering the second stage.

In the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the mind of liberation becomes increasingly powerful and superior; "curd-like milk" refers to the fact that in the third stage (*bhūmi*), one is fully endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), skillful means (*upāya*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the roots of goodness for transforming sentient beings have already become thick, which is described as being "firm.
"Solid body" refers to the supramundane *dharmakāya* in the fourth stage, which is firm and indestructible. "Similarity of form" refers to the fifth [stage].
"Abiding not within the stages" refers to the practice of the path resembling the nature of the higher stages;

"nature" refers to the manifestation of the characteristics of the various faculties, such as the eye, which is metaphorically illustrated by the unobstructed wisdom opening and clarifying before one in the sixth stage.

"The body moving through karma" metaphorically illustrates the arising of great skillful means and the performance of distinguished practices in the seventh stage. "The body of fulfillment" metaphorically illustrates the virtues of practice in the final three stages.
The fulfillment of the three faculties represents the maturation of the conduct of retribution in the eighth stage;
the distinction between male and female forms represents the differentiation of the two practices of self-benefit and benefiting others in the ninth stage;
and the breadth, length, and fullness represent the perfection of all virtues in the tenth stage. Thus, these dharmas are presented collectively for all the stages.
"I do not see anyone who has not praised [this]"—this refers to the third major section, the "Explanation of the Buddha’s Joint Praise," which is explained in two successive parts.

Regarding the first part, the statement "I do not see anyone who has not praised" cites the scriptural text to clarify that this supreme dharma causes those among the assembly who are thirsty for it to understand what is meant by the words "I do not see anyone who has not praised. Why did that Vajragarbha address the assembly in this way?
When it says, "I do not see the Buddhas," this is stated to manifest the excellence of the Dharma and to inspire longing within this great assembly.

Regarding the "Buddha-realm" (*buddhadhātu*), the text first cites the scripture and subsequently explains its characteristics. First, it is explained in terms of the place where it is established. Initially, there is the Dharma and then the metaphor;
for example, that which is like a rice field: just as a place where rice is sown is called a "rice field," so too is the realm of all Buddhas.

The place where a Buddha appears in the world is called a "Buddha-world. Just as [the text] previously explained the Buddha-world by taking Jambudvīpa as an example, it now explains the Buddha-world by taking his field of transformation (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*) as the basis.
Regarding the praise and citation of the sūtra from the other three directions, there are two parts: first, citing the number, and second, praising the two divisions;

thus, there are two types. Below, their characteristics are distinguished: "for the sake of explaining the Āgamas" refers to the explanation of the sūtras. As for those Buddhas of the ten directions...
In the section on "Explanation" (*vyākhyāna-bhāga*), for the sake of the great assembly, he proclaims the section on "Causes" (*hetu-bhāga*) by means of what is called the *Āgama*;

this is the "Entrance through Realization" (*praveśa-prativedha*), which praises the sūtra so that those who enter may realize it. Regarding those Buddhas of the ten directions, within the section on "Requesting" (*adhyeṣaṇā-bhāga*), they praise the "Fruit of the Ground" (*bhūmi-phala-bhāga*) as subtle, ineffable, and beyond verbal expression, causing people to achieve realization;
this is named "Entrance through Realization. Below, [the commentary] explains the passage where Vajragarbha interprets the text of the praise.
The sūtra contains questions and answers; here, we shall provide only the answers, explaining them according to the sequence of the four phrases found in the sūtra.

Regarding the first phrase, "Mahā" (Great) is cited from the sūtra. There are three [categories], which state the number. "Mahā" is a term in the language of the Hu (Sanskrit); this is translated as "Great.

It distinguishes many types, yet according to the essential points, three are taught. First, the greatness of the vow (*praṇidhāna-mahattva*): listing the names, it refers to the vast and expansive resolve to seek great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), which is called the greatness of the vow.

The vast accumulation of the various perfections (*pāramitā*) is termed the "Great Practice" (*caryā-mahat*), while the benefits such as the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) are termed the "Great Benefit for Beings" (*sattvārtha-mahat*).

Regarding the citation of the Sūtra as being most excellent: even when compared to the Small Vehicle from the perspective of the stages prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi-pūrva*), these are called "excellent"; because this excellence surpasses that [of the Small Vehicle], it is named "most excellent.
Next, in explaining the second "light" (*prabhāsa*), the citation of the Sūtra states: "This Great Vehicle" refers to the dharmas of the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) as the Great Vehicle.
Regarding the illumination of all other dharma-gates: because the characteristics of the supramundane true path manifest within the mundane skillful means of cultivation, it is called "illumination.
This refers to the cultivation of mundane practice; although these other dharma-gates belong to the stage of cultivation, they attain the characteristics of reality.
It is like drilling for fire where one first obtains the sign of warmth, or like digging for water where one first obtains the sign of moisture. What is the meaning of this?
When practicing generosity, not perceiving the giver, the recipient, the material gift, or the karmic fruit of enlightenment is precisely attaining the characteristic of true generosity;
the same applies to all other practices. Regarding this dharma-gate, the term "dharma" refers to the essential nature of the gate, for it is not merely the explanation of names and meanings;
rather, because the dharma can lead people to enter the supramundane, it is called a "gate. Next, the third [point] is explained.

The detailed citation of the sutra reveals the characteristics of "worldly knowledge" (*loka-jñāna*) as true realization; it is explained as tenfold according to its cultivation so that the world may understand it.

Furthermore, within the context of worldly cultivation, the partial attainment of those characteristics is also termed "worldly knowledge. Below, the fourth [point] is first cited from the sutra text, and then its characteristics are explained:
this demonstrates supramundane understanding and the wisdom of the various stages (*bhūmi*). The phrase "this is not worldly, etc. explains the inconceivable (*acintya*).
The mind that contemplates through conditions is called "worldly discrimination" (*loka-vikalpa*); because it cannot accomplish that supramundane pure path, it is termed "inconceivable.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Stages*, Fascicle One, End;
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Stages*, Fascicle Two, Beginning. (This fascicle concludes with: "By what cause...")
*Jingying Shi* (Commentary by Jingying), composed by Huiyuan.

In the "Request" (*qing*) section, first, the preceding [text] is concluded and the subsequent [text] is introduced; below, the text is explained according to its phrasing. Within this explanation, it is briefly analyzed by means of four gates:

1. Clarifying the Dharma manifested within the "Request"; 2. Clarifying the practice accomplished in reliance upon that Dharma; 3. Dividing the "Request" [into sections]; 4. [The fourth gate is omitted in the source fragment].
The subsequent detailed exposition consists of a four-part textual explanation on how [the stages] arise and are established in mutual relation.
Regarding the "dharmas revealed," this section of the request precisely clarifies the essence of the *bhūmi* (stages). "Essence" refers to the supramundane;

it accords with true realization, and because this essence transcends the characteristics of the mind and speech, it cannot be reached by them. Therefore, in the subsequent request, through silent consent, the dharmas of the *bhūmi* are extensively revealed.
Being free from names and transcending marks, it cannot be proclaimed; by means of these words that still leave behind traces of marks, the reality of the stage (*bhūmi*) is revealed.

Such is what is manifested. As for the practitioner who has achieved this, in the preceding "Section on the Foundation" (*mūla-bhāga*), the stage was presented with praise for its excellence to inspire the desire of the assembly; now, the reality of the stage is being revealed.

To generate various understandings regarding the previously explained dharmas of the stage of the departure from signs (*lakṣaṇavigata-bhūmi*)—which are thus established—the following is now first stated to establish the section on the request (*adhyeṣaṇā-vibhāga*).
Subsequently, through that section on the request, the extensive explanation below is initiated. As for "establishing the request":

within the request, the actual substance (*svabhāva*) of the stage revealed therein is difficult to manifest as being free from signs; it cannot be made manifest without verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).

There are two ways of explaining and distinguishing [the truth]: first, through practice; second, through teaching. Regarding "explanation through practice," this refers to the practices of the causal stage and the means (*upāya*).

Because these practices arise by following conditions and relying upon the teachings, they are said to be "subordinate to the [true] part. Because one initiates practice based on words, it is used to manifest true virtue.

Regarding "explanation through verbal teaching," this refers to using verbal teachings to distantly point toward true virtue; therefore, it is said to be "subordinate to the [true] part. Because one initiates speech based on practice, it serves as a manifestation of the ultimate.
This reveals that Dharma. Regarding the statement "arising of the teaching," there are two parts therein: first, clarifying the causal arising of the subsequent practice;
this means that the understanding produced during the request gives rise to the practice cultivated during the subsequent teaching.

If there were no true understanding, one's practice would be inverted and could not serve as a skillful means for realizing that goal; therefore, it is by means of the true understanding produced during the request [that the subsequent practice arises].
Regarding the arising of that practice, there are two parts corresponding to the subsequent teaching that clarifies the causal conditions for its arising. Within this, there are three sections:

first, concerning the request made by the assembly of bodhisattvas to initiate the subsequent exposition; regarding that Vajragarbha’s desire to expound the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*), if the assembly did not request it, he would not reveal the gravity of the dharma, and thus it could not be taught.
Therefore, the subsequent exposition arises due to the request of the assembly. Second, concerning the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha.

Please explain how the subsequent discourse was initiated. Regarding this, there are three points: First, concerning the request made by the Buddhas to initiate the subsequent discourse—Vajragarbha desired to expound the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*), yet because the Buddhas had not requested it, he did not reveal them.
This was due to the gravity of the Dharma, which required that the assembly be inspired with reverence;

otherwise, to speak of it in vain would have been useless. Therefore, he remained silent. Because the Buddhas then made their request, the gravity of the Dharma was revealed, causing the assembly to revere it.

Because it was only through the Buddha’s request that [Vajragarbha] was able to proclaim it, the subsequent exposition is initiated by the Buddha’s invitation. Second, regarding the Buddha’s addition of the initiation for the subsequent exposition:
Vajragarbha, wishing to expound the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*), feared that the assembly would be unable to bear it and thus could not proclaim them;

he remained silent. It was only because the Buddha emitted light and empowered the listeners, enabling them to hear it, that [Vajragarbha] was finally able to proclaim it; therefore, it is due to the Buddha.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent discourse on the three [vajras] based on the Buddha’s teaching: Vajragarbha, wishing to speak for the sake of the assembly, remained silent and did not speak out of fear that the assembly would not believe him.
Once he had been exhorted by the Buddha according to the prescribed ritual, the great assembly understood that these were the teachings of the Tathāgata;
although the words were transmitted through the mouth of Vajragarbha, they were all the speech of the Buddha and could certainly be relied upon.

It is through faith that one attains the teaching of the stages (*bhūmi*). These preceding three phrases are combined to form the second section, which, by means of the Buddha’s empowerment and request, initiates the subsequent exposition.
Thirdly, from the perspective of meaning, these two [sections] give rise to the subsequent exposition.

That Vajragarbha, wishing to expound the dharmas of the stages, feared that people might grasp at and become attached to them as they were being taught, thereby preventing the full proclamation; thus, in the following text, he elucidates the subtle reality of the stages.

The subtle [truth] transcends verbal expression and exists only within the causal conditions; it is only after causing the assembly to have correct knowledge that one may subsequently speak of its arising. This constitutes the subsequent teaching.

Regarding the analysis of the text, there are two main divisions within this request: first, after Vajragarbha has finished speaking and remained silent, the Bodhisattvas and the Buddha all join in requesting him;
second, from "Observation" (*vīkṣaṇa*) onwards, it indicates the limits of the teaching to cause the assembly to have correct knowledge.
Regarding the preceding section on "invitations according to the person," there are three types: first, the invitation by *Vimukti* (Liberation); second, the invitation by the Great Assembly;

and third, the invitation by the Buddha’s empowerment. Within these three, they are distinguished by three gates. First, regarding the distinction between the primary and auxiliary invitations for one person versus many people:
the single individual, *Vimukti*, represents the primary invitation, while the Buddha and the multitude represent the auxiliary invitation. This refers to *Vimuktisena*.
The leader of this assembly, knowing that the assembly harbors doubts, makes a formal request on their behalf. However, within that request it is said, "the assembly is capable of hearing.
If the assembly did not manifest its own capacity to hear and understand, Vimalakīrti’s (Vimukticandra’s) words would be false and erroneous;

for what reason would Vajragarbha be willing to speak? Therefore, the great assembly must manifest their own capacity to hear in order to assist in fulfilling that request. Furthermore, Vimalakīrti...

In the request for permission to speak, it is said: "If the Buddha bestows his power, people will believe and understand; if the Buddha did not bestow his power, the words of Vimukticandra would otherwise be false.
How could that Vajragarbha be willing to speak? To cover these words, the Buddhas jointly requested him.

Thus, the two Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas engaged in mutual deliberation; the previous request by the Bodhisattva was to clarify the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) and what is to be studied by Bodhisattvas.
Subsequently, the Buddha’s request was made to manifest that this Dharma is what has been realized by the Buddha;

because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas alike rely upon this, the excellence of the essential Dharma is revealed to inspire profound respect in others before it can finally be taught. Thirdly, there is the distinction between a single person, many people, and the Buddha.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the motivation for the teaching; second, the manifestation of the gravity of the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of speaking," it refers to that [assembly] of gold...

Having finished speaking, Vajragarbha remained silent and did not elaborate further. Since it was appropriate for the leaders of the assembly to voice the intent of the multitude, he first requested one person to do so;
yet, the influence of a single individual is not equal to that of many, and thus secondly, the request of the entire assembly is clarified.

Furthermore, because a request made by those of similar status carries only slight influence, thirdly, the request of all the Buddhas is clarified for the sake of those who revere the Dharma, as they would not otherwise request it.
Because it was taught that there is no means by which the majesty of the Dharma could be manifested, Vimukticandra first requested one person to manifest the Dharma;
because that single request was insufficient to manifest the Dharma, next the second assembly collectively requested the Bodhisattva practitioner;
and because the manifestation of the Dharma was still not ultimate, thirdly, all the Buddhas bestowed their empowerment and made the request.

The analysis of the request for liberation is divided into three sections. First, regarding the analysis of the methods of requesting according to the various sūtras: the methods for making a formal request do not exceed three. Why is this so?

Because more than three would be cumbersome and prolix, while fewer would lack sincerity and devotion. Thus, depending on the specific circumstances of the conversion, the extensive, the intermediate, and the concise are established as the three.
Now, Vimukticandra, following the threefold method of requesting according to the Dharma, makes a request on behalf of the assembly and the Buddha combined.
52. Analysis of the Ritual for Invoking. Regarding the ritual for invoking found in various sutras, it does not exceed praising the person or praising the Dharma.

Among these, there is nothing superior to praising both the speaker and the listener. Now, within the three invocations made by Vimukticandra, the first two praise the person and the last one praises the Dharma.
Such is the ritual for invocation; the invocations made by the assembly and by the Buddha follow this same ritual. The text is analyzed and explained according to these three parts.
Regarding the three pairs of questions and answers within the Chinese text, in each case the first speaker remains silent after speaking, while the latter clarifies the request for instruction.
In the first pair, after Vajragarbha has finished speaking, he remains silent; subsequently, Vimukticandra, perceiving the doubts in the minds of the assembly, asks him on their behalf:
"O worthy one, you are capable of speaking and the great assembly is able to hear; for what reason do you not speak? This constitutes the first pair.
Of the two pairs [of interlocutors], in the first, Vajragarbha, following the previous inquiry, reveals his own intention of silence as a response;

because the Dharma is difficult to expound and faith and understanding are difficult to attain, he says, "I do not speak of the vehicle of liberation. This is a praise of the assembly’s repeated request.

He asks, "O Noble One, what further intention do you have that you say faith and understanding are difficult to attain and that you do not speak now? [The assembly] praises this Bodhisattva as being excellent.

This assembly is pure, gathered together with realization and faith; O worthy one, you should speak. Regarding this second pair [of verses], following the previous two pairs which praised the person to make the request:
herein, first, Vajragarbha takes up the words of the prior request and cites the disadvantages to show that although this assembly is pure, there are others who delight in the lesser vehicle;
if they hear this, they will give rise to doubt and confusion, and for a long time suffer decline and affliction. Because these two disadvantages exist, [he speaks thus].
"I do not say that liberation is attained by this; I praise the Dharma and entreat you, O Benevolent One, to speak further.

Do not worry about the doubts of the assembly, for the Buddhas protect and mind them, making it easy for people to understand. Furthermore, as there is great benefit in speaking, do not fear decline or affliction.

However, although Vimukticandra’s request was not yet fully satisfied, Vajragarbha’s exposition of the principle reached its limit. At this point, he ceased speaking; out of reverence for the Dharma, he remained silent.
Waiting for other requests, after the first Vajragarbha had finished his initial discourse on the stages (*bhūmi*) within the *Sūtra*, he remained silent.

From this point onward, it clarifies how the doubts of the assembly were resolved through their request. Of the two preceding lines, the first—where Vajragarbha spoke of the names of the stages—cites what preceded to introduce what follows.

The second—his silence and refusal to speak—indicates that he was waiting for a subsequent request. Below this, the assembly, facing him, gave rise to a desire to hear and began to harbor doubts. Regarding this:

In the first part of the "Request" (*adhyeṣaṇā*), it is explained that when the great assembly heard the names [of the bodhisattvas] and desired to understand their meanings, they fell silent and gave rise to doubt.

In the subsequent section, it is explained that Vimukticandra, knowing their doubts, made the request. Regarding the former [section], first, having heard the names and desiring to understand their meanings, they had this thought;
next, because they did not discern [the meaning], they fell silent and gave rise to doubt. The words expressing their wonderment—"For what cause and for what reason?"—are as follows.
Vajragarbha remained silent and did not understand; thus he set forth his doubts: "By what cause and by what condition is this explained as being one and the same?

This "one" (*eka*) is a common expression used by worldly people when they are perplexed or astonished. Whenever worldly people have a doubt, they say: "What is the cause of this? What is the condition of this?
Within this, there are indeed no differences in the distinct classifications; how then can their characteristics be different?
Regarding the phrase "for what reason," it is addressed to those people to resolve their doubt as to why he does not speak; it does not mean that Vajragarbha is incapable of speaking.
Regarding the phrase "for what cause," it is addressed to the audience to resolve their doubt as to why he does not speak;

it does not mean that we, this great assembly, are incapable of hearing it. Such is the intent of the inquiry. This is understood within the context of Vimukticandra’s request arising from his awareness of these doubts.
There are three distinct sections: first, identifying the requester, the Bodhisattva Vimukta;

second, knowing the doubts of the assembly and requesting [the teaching] through verse on their behalf—since Vimuktacandra, as the foremost among the multitude, had already anticipated the sentiments of others, he knew that the assembly harbored doubts;

yet because the causes and conditions were fully present, he remained silent and did not speak, which was truly lamentable, and thus the assembly’s deep suspicion arose; third, presenting the words of the request, which follows these three points below.
One should carefully examine and memorize the treatise according to its topical divisions (*kośasthāna*).

Within the verses of this request, there are five couplets analyzed through two gates: first, the analysis of the inquiry (*praśna*) and the request (*adhyeṣaṇā*); second, the analysis of the inquiry itself. Regarding the inquiry:

"inquiry" refers to questioning Maunīndra (the Silent Lord) to dispel the doubts of the assembly; "request" refers to entreating him to speak so as to fulfill the desires of the assembly's minds. Among the verses, the first two constitute the inquiry regarding silence.
The phrase "What is the reason? (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) is a word of inquiry. The third single verse contains the request for its proclamation; the words "I pray" (*vaktum arhasi*) are the words of entreaty.
Regarding the latter two verses, they lack the inquiry and the request, which logically ought to be present in both; however, because the verses were compressed, they are absent.

As for the explanation of what is praised, there is a distinction between the speaker and the listener. First, the initial verse praises that speaker as being capable of speaking, in order to dispel [any doubt regarding] his greatness.

Regarding the doubt concerning the assembly, the four subsequent verses praise the assembly’s fitness to hear [the teaching] in order to dispel the doubts of the great multitude as to the cause [of the teaching].
Within the praise of the speaker, first, the phrase "for what reason" (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) is a term of inquiry; the following statement does not provide an explanation for that inquiry.
It should be said: "For what reason is there no explanation? The passage beginning with "pure awakening" (*viśuddhabodhi*) inquires into the reason why, O Benevolent One (*mānava*), within...

Regarding the phrase "there are those with pure awakening" (*viśuddhabuddhi*), for what further reason would it not be explained? The characteristics of the question are as follows: in this text, "pure awakening" is the general term.
Because the pure mind contemplates the Dharma, it is called "pure awakening. One who has perfected pure awakening is called a "person of pure awakening.

Alternatively, because such a person possesses pure awakening within, they are named a "person of pure awakening. "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) and so forth are the specific aspects of pure awakening. There is [a distinction].

2.1. Comprehensively encompassing the remedies within oneself while being endowed with all virtues; 2. Being free from all faults so that there is no loss of mindfulness when teaching. "Possessing wisdom" refers to the comprehensive encompassing of the remedies.

"Mindfulness" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, and "wisdom" refers to the knowledge of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*). Being "endowed with virtues" as described below refers to being free from faults.

There are three faults to be abandoned: first, the fault of stinginess and envy; second, the fault of indolence in teaching; and third, the lack of delight in teaching. Being "endowed with virtues" [refers to] possessing these qualities.

The phrase "one who is free" removes the first fault; the phrase "one on the ground of verbal expression" removes the second fault; and the phrase "one whose speech is powerful" removes the third fault.
Within the latter four verses, the first two verses praise the assembly of those of like dharma, while the following one verse praises the assembly of those of different dharmas.
The final verse offers a general praise of the two assemblies; this is also known as "those of common birth and different births" and "those of common dharma and different dharmas.

These assemblies are distinguished according to the basis of their practice: those from the first bhūmi upward who have realized the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) together with Vimukticandra are called "those of common dharma," while those prior to the bhūmis who have not yet attained this are called "those of different dharma. "Those of common birth and different births" are distinguished according to their karmic retribution.

There are two general ways of understanding this: first, distinguishing between identity and difference based on the actual nature of retribution; second, differentiating identity and difference according to the characteristics of retribution. Regarding the first:

from the first bhūmi upward, those who share the same *dharmatā-kāya* as Vimukticandra are called "beings of the same class" (*sajāti*). Prior to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*), because various karmas have not yet been abandoned, the retribution is not pure, and one does not share the *dharmatā-kāya* with Vimukti;
thus, they are called "beings of a different class" (*vijāti*). Regarding the second: one distinguishes identity and difference according to the marks of retribution.

Do not inquire whether they are worldly or supramundane; those who receive human rebirth from the same teacher as Candrasama are called "those of similar birth" (*sabhāgaja*), while other dragons, ghosts, and so forth are called "those of different birth" (*visabhāgaja*).
Because this assembly contains a mixture of various destinies (*gati*), although there are differences in their status—superior or inferior—they are all equally capable of receiving the Dharma.
Therefore, in this praise of those who share the same Dharma, the first verse praises their faculties (*indriya*) and the subsequent verse praises their aspiration (*chanda*).

The faculties (*indriya*) are habitual tendencies from the past, while desire (*chanda*) is what arises in the present. If those listeners possess only desire but lack the faculties, they will not understand even if they hear [the teaching].

Conversely, if they possess the faculties but lack desire, they will not accept it even if they hear it. Therefore, both must be praised. Regarding the initial praise of the faculties, the phrase "for what reason" (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) is an interrogative term used to pose a question;
the subsequent statement, "he does not expound," corresponds to that interrogation, meaning "for what reason does he not expound? its intended sense being as follows.

Regarding the reasons for these further inquiries concerning certainty and so forth: since the great assembly already possesses those who are vessels of certainty, why does the Venerable One not expound their meaning?
Such is the nature of the inquiry. Furthermore, as for the word "why" (*kasmāt*) in this verse, if one follows the preceding verse, it should be construed with the beginning of the verse;
yet, if treated as a separate question, every line contains it. Here, however, we address the subsequent line to inquire: "Why?"

The preceding cases are all like this. Regarding the term "definitive" (*niyata*): because their faculties and natures are clear and they are free from the darkness of doubt, they are called "definitive.
This refers to the assembly of those with similar dharmas who are all definitively so; thus it is called "all these. This phrase is a general heading, within which there are three [categories]:

first, the "superior definitive," referring to the Bodhisattvas. Because they inwardly harbor the resolve for the Way, they are called Bodhisattvas. Second, the "name-based definitive. Third, the "hearing-based definitive."
"Samādhi" (concentration) refers to "great renown" (*mahāyaśas*); it is termed "name" (*nāman*) because it reveals the essence, and "renown" (*yaśas*) because it marks its virtues.

Generally speaking, these three are unified, yet they are distinguished according to their specific determinations. To speak of "stages" (*bhūmi*) is to explain this within the treatises where their characteristics are extensively elucidated.
As for the phrase "not expounding," it is synonymous with the term "not explaining" found in the preceding verse; the wording of the verse is merely skillfully and elegantly interwoven.

In the following verse, this assembly’s delight in hearing [the teaching] clearly demonstrates that this assembly of those who share the same Dharma possesses desire [for it], whereas those of a different Dharma do not.
The three subsequent lines are an exhortation to speak; "O Son of the Buddha, be fearless" is the language of the exhortation.

Addressing Vajragarbha as "Son of the Buddha" is not intended to address the entire assembly. When the wise say "this assembly is wise," they refer to its wisdom; when they say "fearless," they mean the same.
This is an exhortation for Vajragarbha not to fear that this assembly is incapable of hearing [this teaching]. Thus, he requests him to analyze and explain the meaning of these stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the praise of this extraordinary assembly, the first phrase is a general statement; because the faculties and inclinations of these ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are free from turbidity, they are described as "pure."
The remaining phrases clarify that within each respective category, the assembly is free from the six kinds of turbidity and thus attains purity:
"free from laziness" means those who seek the mind with diligent exertion; "free from the turbidity of lack of desire" means those whose majestic deportment is strictly orderly;

"pure" means those whose minds are pure as they listen to the Dharma, being far removed from the turbidity of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); and "firmly established" means those who dwell without malice.
One who possesses the merit of eliminating the turbidity of divergent perceptions has deep-rooted past roots of goodness and is thus far removed from the turbidity of deficiency in merit.
One who possesses wisdom has sharp and keen faculties and is thus far removed from the turbidity of delusion.

Among these six types, the initial elimination of indolence—namely, solemnity and steadfastness—is their aspiration (*chanda*); the possession of pure merit and virtue is their faculty (*indriya*); and the distinctions in their practice are their application (*prayoga*).
Therefore, they are divided into six.

In the subsequent general praise, "mutually gazing at one another" means that those who share the same Dharma and those who follow different Dharmas look toward each other with a unified mind to seek the Dharma;
because their sentiments are without discord, it is called "abiding in mutual gazing. "Abiding" refers to abiding in the mind that seeks the Dharma, as there is naturally a seeking of the Dharma.

Because they harbor jealousy and pride, it is further necessary to state that "all revere," where "all" means everyone without exception. The latter half of the verse illustrates the characteristics of reverence:
with a unified mind they strive for realization, just as bees desire ripe honey; they focus their intent on seeking the teaching, just as the thirsty long for nectar;
furthermore, they approach the Dharma with their minds like the thirsty longing for dew, seeking the Dharma so that it enters their hearts.

Because the *Vimukticandraparipṛcchā-vidhi* explains that the three assemblies are disciplined below, it clarifies the discipline of the assembly;
as for the others, if the assembly is not requested and is not disciplined, one does not avoid the disorder of the assembly.

Next, regarding the explanation of the verses of request: first, we shall pose the introductory question. Why are they called "verses of request"? Below, the explanation consists of three parts: first, defining the characteristics of the verses;
second, clarifying the intent of the treatise; and third, elucidating the purpose. Regarding the definition of the characteristics of the verses:

in general, there are three types. First, a verse is defined by its lines (*pāda*); provided that several syllables together form a single line, four such lines constitute one verse, regardless of their length.
Regarding the distinctions among verses (*gāthā*), the foreign method consists of eight syllables forming a line and four lines forming a verse (*gāthā*).
Such verses are those where the lines are equal; as for "unequal verses," the number of lines is indefinite. Second, regarding the meaning of the term *gāthā*:

regardless of whether it is in prose or verse, one must not concern oneself with the length of the words; rather, once a single meaning is fully expressed, it is then called a *gāthā*. Third, [the definition of] a verse...
The term "verse" (*gāthā*) is used here as a synonym for "stanza" (*śloka*); it is called a verse because it expresses all phenomena through metrical composition.

Regarding the purpose of establishing these verses discussed here, there are two: first, the skillful composition of the words, wherein a few syllables are able to encompass many meanings, making them easy to understand and easy to retain; second, the excellence of the phrasing, which is employed for the purpose of praise.
Therefore, it is necessary to establish this. To say that "few words encompass many meanings" refers to the first intention:
because few words can extensively encompass the virtues of the Bodhisattvas who preach and those who listen. As for the second intention, it is because those who offer praise mostly do so in verse;

this is because one must employ verses when wishing to extol the virtues of the preacher and the listener. Furthermore, the purpose for which these words are spoken is for the sake of sentient beings.
First, for the benefit of others, the method of explanation is stated briefly without requiring extensive exposition; hence it is expressed in verse.

Second, for those of dull faculties who do not grasp it upon hearing it once, it is repeated in verse. Third, for the sake of future sentient beings who wish to hear the previous teachings, they are repeated in verse, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Fourth, because there are sentient beings who delight in elegant speech, [the teachings] are presented in verse.
The five verses are for the purpose of refuting the wrong views of sentient beings. Some say that while the teachings of non-Buddhists contain elegant words, the Buddha-dharma does not;
it is to refute this view that they are expressed in verse. Furthermore, these verses are composed in metrical form to reveal the Dharma concisely for those of sharp faculties.
The following is the commentary on the verses, which consists of four parts: first, a brief presentation of the characteristics of the verses along with the intended meaning of the verses;
second, a structural analysis of the verses; third, an explanation according to the text; and fourth, a comprehensive examination through both general and specific distinctions.
Regarding the meaning of the verse in the first section: the question is raised to initiate the discourse on the faultlessness of speaking and listening.
In analyzing the characteristics in response to this question, although there are five verses, they essentially clarify only the faultlessness of speaking and listening, as previously determined.

The statement that "if there were faults, one should not speak" clarifies the intent of the verse; since the purpose is to request the teaching, it demonstrates faultlessness. However, within this text...
By returning to the objection that there is a fault and that it should not be proclaimed, it is shown that because there is no fault, it ought to be proclaimed.

In the second section, the statement that the speaker is without fault constitutes the first verse; furthermore, the fact that the listener shares the same dharma (*samāna-dharmin*) and is certain constitutes the second verse.
The mention of "the listener" distinguishes this from the first verse, while the term "sharing the same dharma" distinguishes it from the latter two verses.
Regarding the term "definitive" (*niyata*), this distinguishes it from the third verse. The third verse indicates those who have a desire to hear; the fourth verse further shows others;
and the fifth verse clarifies that all are capable. The phrase "mutually gazing at one another" cites the verse to demonstrate the meaning of being "all capable.
Because both assemblies—those of similar dharma and those of different dharma—are able [to listen], they are said to be "all capable."

From this point downward is the third section: the detailed explanation following the text. Within the commentary on the first verse, there is first the introductory question. Below that, the verse and the treatise are presented for explanation.
In the treatise, there is first the explanation of the term "pure awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi*), followed by the interpretation of the verse.

As for why the subsequent part of the verse is not explained first, it is because the latter part—concerning the possession of mindfulness and wisdom—is explained later. Within the explanation of "pure awakening," there are two distinct sections. The first is the explanation of the partial praise of the object.
For what reason is this question asked? Since the noble virtues are not singular, why is liberation praised specifically as "pure awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi*)?

To explain the cause of this "pure awakening" in response to the question: awakening is the cause of teaching; therefore, it is praised specifically. Because speech arises from awakening, it is called the "cause of teaching.

It is praised as the cause of teaching because it gives rise to that teaching. Regarding the two types of awakening, they are termed "awakening"; below, the name "awakening" is explained according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*. As for the name "awakening": [text follows].

Vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are the explanation of the sūtra; they are also the oral expression of conduct, which constitutes the treatise (*śāstra*). Conduct is causal action;
because speech arises from vitarka, it is called *vitarka-vicāra* as oral expression of conduct. Because it is oral expression of conduct, the treatise is termed "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*).

Regarding the phrase "having the cause of pure explanation" (*viśuddha-vyākhyāna-hetu*) in the subsequent verse, why is it not explained? It is because explaining what follows based on what precedes constitutes the cause of pure explanation; this is the restatement (*uddeśa*).
Why was this not stated previously? This question serves to clarify what follows. Since you, O Benevolent One, possess pure awakening (*viśuddha-bodhi*), why do you not speak of it?
Why is it still not mentioned within these verses? Why is it still not explained within these verses? There are two types of awakening:

first, the awakening of mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth; second, the pure awakening. Having cited the general [category], the specific [types] are now opened up: namely, *saṃgraha* (comprehension), *vyūhana* (development), and *pariṣkāra* (purification).
"Free from faults" lists their names; mindfulness and wisdom are the remedies for cultivation and accomplishment. "Greed and so forth" refers to the faults;

their removal and abandonment is called "freedom. Since there are specific things to be abandoned within the former category of "remedies," and specific remedial powers within the latter category of "freedom from faults," these are divided into two gates.
Because the internal virtues of mindfulness and wisdom—the meaning of the remedies—are explicitly revealed, they are specifically named [as such].

Regarding the summary of the treatment of stinginess and so forth, it is taught that there is no fault when speaking, as this demonstrates the meaning of detachment and clarifies the specific name "detachment from faults.

Below, its characteristics are explained. Within the first section, the sutra text is first cited and contrasted with the treatise to reveal mindfulness and wisdom. Because the sutra summarizes the antidotes, the treatise is cited for comparison.
Regarding the two objects to be treated, obstacles are established in relation to conduct; there are two types, and their number is stated as "various discursive thoughts."

Furthermore, when one enumerates names such as "permanence" and so forth, seeking them out through inverted cognition, this is called "defiled and turbid. To perceive the mind and its objects as pure is what is meant by "mixed.

This cognition is the delusion regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa-viparyāsa*); the three inversions of thought, perception, and view are the minds capable of producing the four inversions, which are termed the cause of mixed cognition.
By means of recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, one discerns their characteristics; failing to see the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*), one falsely grasps at them.

The phenomena of the causes and effects of defilement and purity are designated by names and concepts through discrimination; this cause is an inversion that deludes one regarding the principle. Below, the text turns to clarify the practitioner of mindfulness.
This passage cites the four foundations of mindfulness from the Sūtra to explain them, yet the text here is insufficient; if it were complete, it should state:

"The wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness is so named because they give rise to mindfulness regarding the body, feelings, mind, and dharmas. To illuminate this understanding is the fourth [foundation]."

Mindfulness (*smṛti*) serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to discursive thoughts; by reversing obstacles, it reveals the remedy. Contemplating the impurity of the body is the antidote to the inversion of purity;

contemplating that feelings are suffering is the antidote to the inversion of pleasure; contemplating that the mind is impermanent is the antidote to the inversion of permanence; and contemplating that phenomena are selfless is the antidote to the inversion of self.

The wise one cites the sūtra and explains its relative antidotes according to the "wisdom of signlessness" (*animitta-jñāna*), thereby clarifying how mindfulness counters the causes of discursive conceptualization.
The section "Distinguishing the Reversal of Obstacles to Reveal the Antidotes" below explains the abandonment of faults. This also first cites the Sūtra and presents the Śāstra to clarify it;

as for "the rest," this refers to citing the Sūtra, meaning that within the verse text, the remaining qualities fully describe the higher stages and so forth. To explain the "abandonment of faults," the Śāstra is cited to clarify them:

there are three types of faults, which correspond to the three obstacles established in relation to practice. Regarding the enumeration of these three faults, they are as follows: [faults] do not exist.

Because it can explain the characteristics of those faults and obstruct the discourse, the names of the faults are listed following the [explanation of] faults. First, the question is asked, and then the terms are listed:

"One who is stingy regarding speech" refers to one who is parsimonious with the Dharma; this is called stinginess (*mātsarya*). "One who is envious regarding speech" refers to one who resents the excellence [of others]; this is called envy (*īrṣyā*).

"One who is indolent regarding speech" refers to someone who, although lacking a stingy or envious mind, is lazy in expounding [the teaching]; this is called indolence regarding speech. "One who does not delight in speaking" refers to someone who, although diligent, lacks [the desire to speak].
The skillful wisdom that causes others to find no pleasure in whatever one says explains the characteristics of faults; it merely clarifies the first fault while not discussing the other two.

Regarding those who are stingy with the Dharma—those who cherish what they themselves know and harbor envy toward others—it refers to envying the superior wisdom of others and desiring not to be surpassed.

Above this, the faults were established; below this, by reversing [the previous points], the virtues of being free from them are clarified. This fully cites the sutra’s statement "not being angry" and so forth, providing a complete explanation to manifest its meaning.
Regarding their characteristics, among the three roots of goodness, non-attachment comes first, non-hatred is next, and non-delusion is last.

Why is it that [the text] does not mention the first and instead takes up the middle and the last, and then mentions non-hatred and the other remaining virtues? The explanation is that hatred is a grave transgression for a bodhisattva;
therefore, it is singled out for mention. Furthermore, in order to distinguish it from the root of goodness that is non-delusion, non-hatred is mentioned first.

Why must the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*) be included by way of "etcetera" (*ādi*)? Because non-delusion (*amoha*) is subsumed under the preceding category of wisdom (*jñāna*), it is excluded here as it does not belong to the gate of abandoning faults.
Now, in order to counteract the two faults of stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and so forth are cited;
specifically, non-attachment counters stinginess, and non-hatred counters envy. Since stinginess is a form of greed and envy is a form of hatred, this demonstrates their absence.

First, the refutation of the first objection to demonstrate transcendence: the preceding section cites the sūtra to proclaim the sublime and wondrous dharmas of the ten stages, which is called "proclaiming the higher stages.

It demonstrates that there is no second [stage]. Second, the refutation of the second objection to demonstrate transcendence: by citing the sūtra, it is stated that there is the power of skillful means and eloquent exposition;

this demonstrates that there is no third [stage]. Third, the refutation of the third objection to demonstrate transcendence: because there is the power of skillful means, others do not delight in the second [stage].

In the verse, the first part—“concluding the preceding and generating the subsequent two kinds of pure awakening”—constitutes the conclusion of what has gone before. Previously, from “pure awakening,” two types were opened out:

“comprehension and cultivation” (*saṃgraha-pratipatti*) and “separation from faults” (*doṣa-viveka*). Since these general names are now being applied to specific instances, they are referred to as the “two kinds of pure awakening.

Alternatively, the two kinds [of pure awakening] may be restated as the two types of pure awakening already mentioned: “comprehension and cultivation” and “separation from faults,” with these being restated at the beginning.
The general "pure awakening" (viśuddha-bodhi) refers back to the preceding text, which is termed the "praise"; next, the praise of the listener follows, which constitutes the subsequent section.
Below, the verse and its commentary are raised for explanation. First, regarding the initial "general determination": citing the sūtra, "the wise and clear-minded" explains its characteristics.

"Determination" (*niścaya*) refers to the faculty (*indriya*); the essence of this faculty is wisdom (*prajñā*). Within the context of wisdom, knowing the teachings is called "clarity" (*medhā*), while entering into realization is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

Because this is free from the two kinds of darkness, it is called "clarity. The following section explains the remaining distinctions, which consist of four parts. First, regarding the determination of the superior [vehicle], there are three sections:

(1) opening the general into the specific; (2) listing the names and providing their definitions; and (3) the aforementioned determination of the superior. "Superior" refers to the excellence of the seeking mind;

because that which is sought is more sublime than that of the Two Vehicles, it is termed "superior. Within the determination of the general, this "superior" is further distinguished and thus named "superior."

In the two final phrases, "decidedly" (*niyata*) applies by analogy to both. "Wishing for enlightenment" (*bodhiprārthana*) explains its characteristics; that is, the intention of all Bodhisattvas to seek Buddhahood.
All these virtues are explained from the perspective of the primary subject. The term "wishing" (*prārthana*) is used to manifest the excellence of their virtues.
Since their internal virtues are full, their beautiful reputation resounds far and wide; therefore, by citing their renown, one manifests their internal virtues and other excellences.

"Veneration" (*gaurava*) explains its characteristic; because its name signifies beauty and greatness, it causes others to hold [the teaching] in high esteem and to definitely receive the excellence of the Dharma.
It is called "reception" (*parigraha*) because one is capable of receiving and assimilating the ground that has been taught.
Thus, it is known that the speaker, being well-versed in manifesting the capacity of the recipient, teaches the ground by knowing that the listener is capable of receiving it. This is the meaning.

The great assembly is now capable of receiving the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*). Among these three types, the first two gates are distinguished individually as "determination through realization" (*adhigama-niścaya*), while the latter one is "determination through scripture" (*āgama-niścaya*).
