Alternatively, according to the general rule, all three are both determination through scripture and determination through realization.
These two types of determination constitute the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and they are explained as being based upon the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta*).
Because supreme wisdom and virtue are established within and fame manifests without, it is called "fame" (*yaśas*).

Because one is able to encompass and receive [the teachings] upon realizing the *āgama*, it is called "encompassment" (*parigraha*). Third, regarding the application of the sūtra [to the treatise]: following this sequence, compare the sūtra with the treatise.

The sūtra has three phrases, and the treatise has three phrases; apply the first [phrase of the treatise] to the first [of the sūtra], and the latter to the latter, so that the textual order does not deviate.

Therefore, it is said that they follow a sequence. Why does this not expound the meaning? It is because it is abbreviated and lacks detailed explanation. Regarding "desire" (*chanda*) within the section on "aspiration" (*chanda-ruci*):

first, the preceding faculty (*indriya*) is excluded to clarify the necessity of the subsequent desire as the catalyst for arousal. Although there is determination, this excludes the preceding faculty; it distinguishes both attainment and loss, hence the use of the word "although" (*sui*).
"Having the faculty" constitutes attainment, while "lacking desire" constitutes loss. The passage "the mind does not desire" below clarifies the necessity of the subsequent [desire].
This is merely a counter-statement; if one were to speak correctly, one should say that it is only when there is a mind desiring to hear that one may proceed to explain.

Below, the verse and its commentary are raised to interpret the first phrase. Within this, there are three distinct parts: first, distinguishing the differences between the desire for present happiness and the three dharmas through the *āgama* and definitive realization;
second, "If not present before," which is a counter-argument showing there is no fault; third, "Manifesting," which follows the sequence.

To clarify that there is attainment, for what reason is this [distinction] made here by way of the three? If these three were not different from what was previously explained—namely, that the possession of faculties (*indriya*) is itself the possession of desire (*chanda*)—then why would this verse be necessary to further clarify the possession of desire? It is precisely because they are distinct; for although one may have possessed the faculties previously, it does not follow that one lacks desire.
Therefore, it is clarified once again. As for the term "definitively" (*niyata*), it refers back to the previous definitiveness of desire, correlating it with the preceding faculties.
This is stated in order to distinguish [the two types of evidence]; hereafter, the actual distinction is made.
First, there is the *āgama* that is not definitive proof (*aniścaya-pramāṇa*), which clarifies that the *āgama* roots are distinct from the proofs of the roots.

That is to say, while there exists an *āgama* that is not definitive proof, it does not state that such [proof] is non-existent—just as one says "form is not mind" without saying "mind does not exist"—and it clarifies that there are two kinds of *āgama* that are not manifest direct evidence (*pratyakṣa-sākṣāt-pramāṇa*).

There are various faculties and roots that do not possess the desire for present happiness; namely, the two types of certainty—realization through one's own experience (*svaprativedha*) and reliance on scripture (*āgama*).

Since these do not involve a desire for present happiness, it does not mean they are non-existent. Why, then, is "desire" termed "present certainty"? It is because the faculty and its dharmas, through past habituation, have become established as a desire;
this [newly arisen] desire is produced in the present moment in response to conditions. To distinguish it from the former faculty, it is called "present" (*pratyakṣa*). This is the meaning.
Because there is also the sense of a definitive inclination toward the Dharma, it is called "definitive. The preceding section was the first part, which distinguished the three dharmas;
from here below is the second section, which returns to the point that there is no fault in their absence. Regarding "absence" (*an-abhimukha*):

when the mind of desire is not present and the vessel of the Dharma is incomplete, one is unable to listen. Having the faculty [of hearing] but lacking desire is called an "incomplete vessel"; the vessel is incomplete.

Because they are dissatisfied, they are unable to hear and accept [the teaching]. What follows below constitutes the third section, which sequentially demonstrates that there are those who have attained [realization].

This means showing that the assembly in this gathering, whose faculties and inclinations are all complete, is called "equipped with the implements of the Dharma" and is thus capable of receiving [the teaching].
The verse beginning from here explains the second phrase; first the verse is cited, and below it is explained in detail. Only the character *jñāna* (wisdom) is explained, referring to the Buddha.
"Subhūti, do not fear"—this is a brief statement that does not yet explain. "Wisdom is twofold" is a citation used to present the number;

this clarifies that there are two kinds of wisdom among the great assembly. Below, its names are listed: "those who have realized the Dharma" clarifies that the assembly of those with common Dharma have first realized the Dharma.

By citing their prior realization, it is shown that those who realize later are likewise so. "Those who currently receive" clarifies that the assembly of those with common Dharma possesses realization of the *āgama* (scriptural transmission). These two [categories] are explained.
The various roots [of merit] are capable of realizing the teachings in this very life; thus one knows. Below, the latter half of the verse is explained.
Within that, the preceding is restated to manifest the subsequent request for clarification regarding the distinct dharmas. First, the preceding is concluded and the subsequent is introduced.

Next, the verse and commentary are cited for explanation. First, the initial "total purity" is interpreted: the sūtra states "not turbid," which explains the first "purity" by means of "non-turbidity."
The following section explains the remaining distinctions, which consists of two parts: first, a general enumeration of the six turbidities (*ṣaḍkaṣāya*) in contrast to them to reveal purity;
second, a specific enumeration of the six turbidities in contrast to them to reveal purity. Within this, the first part begins with a specific enumeration of the six turbidities.

What is being asked? Below, their names are listed: "turbidity of desire" refers to having no intention to consume or gather [objects]; "turbidity of deportment" refers to the physical form not being respectful or solemn, and speech...

Regarding "defilements" (*kaṣāya*): the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) that shroud the mind; the defilement of "diverse thoughts" is explained in the text itself; the defilement of "envy" refers to the desire for superiority and the destruction of the *Abhidharma*;

the defilement of "insufficiency" refers to having many illnesses and the like; and "delusion" (*moha*) refers to hearing [the teaching] without understanding, which is to say, ignorance and darkness. This explanation clarifies their characteristics:

being deluded regarding the teachings is called "ignorance," while being confused regarding the principles is called "darkness. When taken collectively, these meanings are equivalent to the six [defilements].
In the middle, there is no desire for distinctions in majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), nor is there any such desire; the rest are "without roots" (*amūla*). Reversing this constitutes the "roots";
because desires are fully present while practices (*caryā*) vary, they are divided into six. Below, the reversal reveals purity, which contains five parts:

first, it is stated that these remedies are sixfold and untainted, which serves as a general heading; second, the specific explanation of "firmness," which is precisely for the purpose of cultivation.
Not mixing with other thoughts is called cultivating firmness; because this [cultivation] is subtle and hidden, it is specifically explained in three ways.

Thus, fourthly, the sequence is clarified by viewing the obstacles and their remedies in relation to one another. Fifthly, the characteristics of the remedies are extensively revealed. Sixthly, these six phrases conclude the section as a whole.
Within the fifth verse, first the preceding is concluded and the subsequent is introduced, stating that these two verses praise those born together.

The two verses that conclude the praise of those of the same Dharma (*sahadharma*) are as follows. Next, the praise of others refers to the single verse that concludes the praise of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The statement that "the final verse reveals the two purities" refers to what follows [the preceding section]. Below, the verses are cited and can be understood through the commentary.
Thus ends the third section, which provides a detailed analysis according to the text. What follows below is the fourth section, the general and specific classification.

Among these, first, regarding the fifth verse, its general and specific aspects are explained. As for the remaining [verses], they follow the pattern of the preceding four verses, all of which possess general and specific aspects, as well as similarities and differences, and the processes of formation and destruction, as previously stated—just as it was already explained at length within the "Six Determinations" concerning the ten bases (*āyatana*) mentioned above.
Although these five verses have already been discussed, one may fully comprehend them by seeking their meaning according to the principles set forth herein.
In the first, second, and fourth verses, all six characteristics are fully present; in the remaining two verses, there are only the general and specific aspects and they cannot be complete.
For this reason, the author of this treatise did not provide separate [explanations] for them.
From "The Great Wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*) onwards is the second pair. Within this pair, first Vajragarbha, following the previous [request], reveals his intention for silence;
subsequently, Vimukticandra, following the words [of the request], requests again. Regarding the former, there are six verses:
the first verse clarifies the intent of Vajragarbha’s response as recorded by the sūtra-narrator (*sūtrakāra*), while the remaining five are the actual [response].
Regarding the words of response, within the first verse, the first and third lines precisely convey the intended meaning of the reply;
the subsequent commentary explains that the second and fourth lines are easy to understand and thus are not further explained.
Regarding the meaning of the commentary, the intention of the general response is to cause the assembly to rejoice; "rejoice" (*yue*) here means "to be glad. Why is this called a general statement?

It is because the verse was spoken generally for the joy of the assembly, and thus this "joy" is designated as the general [purpose]. For what reason was the verse spoken generally for the joy of the assembly?
It was because of the doubt and distress of the great assembly mentioned previously. Previously, the great assembly had witnessed his silence and became doubtful and distressed.
Liberation is the request; this present recitation of verses is for the purpose of removing that doubt and causing the assembly to rejoice.
"Great wisdom" and "fearlessness" are its specific attributes. To achieve that general rejoicing—namely, to cause the assembly to rejoice—is the intention of the speaker at that time.
"Wisdom" and "fearlessness" are words of praise added later by the compiler of the sūtra. How can one take those later words of praise [as the primary meaning]?
To establish the preceding general satisfaction: although this is stated here as appearing later in the discourse, its meaning was fully present at that time;
therefore, based on the original intent, it establishes the general satisfaction. What is meant by "great wisdom and fearlessness"?
"Great wisdom" refers to Vajragarbha’s declaration in verse that he possesses the wisdom capable of expounding [the teaching]. "Fearlessness" refers to that same Vajragarbha...

He spoke this verse to demonstrate that he himself was not afraid, yet the assembly was unable to receive his teaching. Why? Because he used this to bring general satisfaction to the assembly, whereas previously they had been displeased.
Previously, when the great assembly saw him remain silent, they were filled with doubt and distress; there were two kinds of such doubt and distress:
first, the doubt that the speaker lacked wisdom and was incapable, thus having no day for preaching; second, the doubt that the great assembly was incapable of hearing the teaching.

If he were not made to speak, there would be no prospect of hearing [the teaching]; thus, because the assembly harbors these two doubts regarding liberation, Vajragarbha first offers praise for both the speaker’s and the listener’s capability, and then requests silence.
By means of this, in response to the two preceding questions, he dispels the two doubts of the assembly;
therefore, he speaks in verse to manifest his own wisdom and capability to teach, thereby removing the doubt of the great assembly as to the cause [of his silence].
This demonstrates that he himself does not fear this assembly, thereby removing the doubt previously held by the great multitude as to the cause [of his confidence].
Within the verses, when has it ever been said that "possessing wisdom and fearlessness" constitutes the speaking of verses to manifest one's own possession of these qualities?

Although these words do not appear within the verses themselves, their meaning is revealed in response to the aforementioned doubt: that the assembly was previously incapable of either speaking or listening.
Vimukti requested that this Vajragarbha speak, and in his verse reply he stated only that it is difficult to explain, and thus he did not say that he himself lacked wisdom or was incapable;
rather, this was to manifest that he possesses wisdom and is capable of explaining it.

He stated only that it is difficult to hear, because those who hear it in the world find it difficult to gain verifying faith; therefore, he did not say that this assembly was incapable of hearing and receiving it.
This demonstrates that he himself does not fear this assembly; it clarifies that the compilers of the sutras possess clear discernment of this intent and raise it to bring about joy.
Within the final five verses, the first two clarify that the Dharma is difficult to expound, while the following one verse reveals that the Dharma is difficult to hear.
Next, there is a verse that uses a metaphor to illustrate the difficulty of explaining and hearing [the teaching]. In the final verse, the objection is raised and the silence is concluded;

within the preceding two verses, the Dharma has four layers: first, a general presentation of the difficulty of the Dharma; second, its being "most rare" to manifest the characteristics of its difficulty;

third, "the practices of Bodhisattvas and so forth" to bring forth the essence of the difficult Dharma; and fourth, "subtle and difficult to see" and below, to demonstrate its difficulty. Regarding the first verse:

Regarding the first three layers, within the second verse there is a fourth layer. The initial statement concerning "difficulties" (duskarāḥ) generally clarifies that the dharmas of the stages (bhūmidharmāḥ) constitute these difficulties.
Because the dharmas of the stages as explained are difficult to realize and difficult to believe, they are termed "difficulties. Because they are difficult, they are hard to expound;

yet, although they are called "difficult," the nature of the difficulty has not yet been fully manifested. Therefore, it is clarified below by the term "first," which indicates the dharma being taught.

The essence transcends names and forms, making it difficult to verify. To speak of "rareness" clarifies that the Dharma being taught is absent from within the realm of signs, making it difficult to believe.

Within the third section, first the difficulty of the essence is presented; below, by turning back to point out what is practiced, the "demonstrator" (the one who shows) is revealed—this is the path of realization.
This is precisely the emergence of the first Dharma-essence mentioned previously, wherein the realized mind engages with its objects.

Therefore, it is named "practice" (*caryā*), which is a manifest designation for that which is shown; if one follows the previous translation, it is called "the object of practice" (*caryā-viṣaya*), where "viewing" (*darśana*) likewise signifies what is shown.

Regarding the "matters of the stages" (*bhūmi-vastu*), these refer to the path of teaching (*deśanā-mārga*). This constitutes the differentiation of the ten distinct positions within the body of the previously mentioned marvelous Dharma, categorized according to teaching and practice;
this is termed the "differentiation of the matters of the stages. The term "superior" (*uttara*) clarifies the aforementioned matters of the stages by indicating their excellence.
Taking the Dharma of equality as the ten distinctions for the purpose of discerning the original source of all Buddhas, one proceeds to point directly to that which is the root of all Buddhas;
this is what is meant by "discerning the superior. When it says "this is the Buddha-root," it distinguishes this from the practices of counteractive cultivation based on conditions (*pratyaya*).
While such conditional and counteractive practices ultimately cease and cannot serve as the ultimate foundation of Buddhahood, what is now called the "Buddha-root" is [the true source].
Clarity is the true virtue; since both this realization (*pratyakṣa*) and the teaching (*śāsana*) are the true virtue, it is said that the Buddha’s fundamental nature is true virtue.
How can it be called realization or teaching? Abandoning the expedient means (*upāya*) to discuss the reality, the true essence is of a single flavor, which is designated as "realization.

When the truth follows the differences of the expedient means, it is spoken of as the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which is termed "teaching. Because all of these are the True [Dharma], they are entirely ineffable.

In the second verse, the first three lines correctly reveal the reason why the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) are difficult to explain, while the fourth line cites the confusion and distress caused by hearing them to manifest that difficulty.
Within the first three lines: the initial two lines demonstrate profundity in contrast to inferior levels;

the third line—referring to "the object" (*viṣaya*) and "wisdom" (*jñāna*)—manifests their excellence from the perspective of superiority. The two characters "untainted" (*anāsrava*) provide a dual explanation for the preceding two [terms].
To clarify and establish the difficulty of explanation, in the first two lines, "difficult to attain" is the general [term], while "subtle," etc., are the specific [terms].

Within each of these, there are four aspects: first, "subtle" (sūkṣma) is distinct from the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā); second, "difficult to see" (dur-darśa) is distinct from the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā);

third, "beyond thought" (amanasikāra) is distinct from the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā); fourth, "not of the mind-ground" (acittabhūmi) is distinct from the consciousness-wisdom born of supramundane retribution. Next, [the text] proceeds to the superior [aspects].
This is to reveal its wondrous realm. Following the foreign language, it should properly be called the "realm of wisdom" (*jñāna-gocara*).

As for the stage (*bhūmi*) and the dharmas, they are exclusively that which is illuminated by true wisdom; therefore, they are called the "realm of wisdom. Furthermore, because they constitute the limits and extent of that wisdom, they are termed the "wisdom-realm.
The term "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) explains that this is the realm of wisdom and not any other realm.
In the first part of the third verse, up to the phrase "capable of hearing," the difficulty of hearing is clearly elucidated; the subsequent section explains the reason for this difficulty.

Within that [explanation], the capacity to hear is first restated in reverse order to manifest the difficulty of hearing. Why not discuss this directly? It is because one wishes to cause people to train in the capacity to hear as well.

Within this, there is first a general [summary] of deep faith and so forth, followed by a specific [analysis] of the capacity to hear, and finally a general statement regarding the maintenance of the mind.

"Like a diamond" means that one who upholds the mind for hearing the Dharma is as firm as a diamond. This "firmness" refers to having realized faith and deep belief in the Buddha’s wisdom; this is the firmness of faith.
This is called the "Dharma of the Ground," for the ground of the Buddha's wisdom is selflessness; this is the firmness of realization.
Only when these two types of firmness are possessed can one begin to hear [the Dharma]; it is revealed that those lacking them are incapable of hearing it. This is why it is difficult [to hear].
The wise, moreover, distinguish this stage as supreme, excellent, and sublime, clarifying that its phenomena are exclusively the domain of realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*).
Because they are subtle, they manifest as profound in contrast to inferior states; since these phenomena are not the objects of the four types of mental consciousness, they are called "subtle.
Being the domain of wisdom and not the domain of anything else, they are difficult to hear.

In the first part of the fourth verse, the difficulty of seeing the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmidharma*) is clearly elucidated; the phrase "the Buddha’s outflow-free [dharmas] are difficult to hear" demonstrates the reason for this difficulty.

Within this section, first a simile is presented, followed by its application to the Dharma. According to the Dharma, the simile is insufficient because it is too limited—specifically, it is limited in its analysis of what is difficult to see.
This refers precisely to taking the space where a painting is made and the space of the wind as the metaphors.
Regarding the phrase "the wisdom that accords with the lower [realms] is thus," this refers to the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which is like the wind or a drawing in space.
The term "difficult to distinguish" clarifies that it is difficult to explain; the term "difficult to see" indicates that it is difficult to hear.
This single character "difficult" applies in both senses. As for why it is "difficult" even for a Buddha, it is because the realm of a Buddha consists of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
It cannot be said that it is heard.

In the first three lines of the fifth verse, the preceding difficulties regarding the Dharma are restated; in the final line, the intention of one’s own silence is concluded by reflecting upon the Buddha’s wisdom.
Because the Dharma of the preceding stages was the path originally traversed by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, it is called "Buddha-wisdom."
This sentence is a general statement. "The first" refers back to the difficulty of explaining, specifically citing the word "first" from the initial verse.

"Difficult for the world to know" refers back to the difficulty of hearing; this addresses the aforementioned difficulty of hearing by clarifying that the "mind-ground is without self," meaning that worldly sentient beings are unable to realize it.
"Rare" refers back to the difficulty of explaining, citing the initial verse.

"Rare indeed are these words"—this statement regarding what is difficult to believe restates the aforementioned difficulty of hearing, and through the phrase "deep faith amidst what is difficult to hear," it clarifies that the sentient beings of this world are unable to believe.
Within the preceding sentence, the first point is raised first, followed by the manifestation of its being difficult to know;

within the subsequent sentence, the difficulty of belief is clarified first, followed by the revelation of its rarity. Thus the text serves as both left and right ears. Furthermore, within the preceding sentence...
To speak directly, regarding the phrase "rare dharma" within the latter part of the first line, there is a matter of textual concealment and manifestation;
furthermore, while the preceding line states that it is "difficult for the world to know," the subsequent line omits the mention of "the world" because the verse was too concise.
Below, the commentary explains the first verse. First, it explains "universal delight" (*saṃmodana*), as this is the intended meaning of the verse;

thus, it is said that this is a general statement made with respect to the meaning, not with respect to the literal phrasing. The answer is twofold. Below, the explanation of the terms "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*) is divided into five parts:
(1) opening the general into the particular; (2) enumerating the two names; (3) explaining that what is capable of answering is its "knowledge"; (4) [the capacity of] knowledge to...
To arise and speak thus is called "being capable of speech" and "not being timid," which is fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).

This means that Vajragarbha does not fear that this assembly is incapable of hearing and receiving [the teaching]; it is not like the dread of the great assembly’s majestic power or the like, where one fears others out of self-doubt.

These two constitute the initial general response, and are therefore both termed "responses. Alternatively, these two may be extracted from within the responses themselves to serve as a general summary.

Because their names are distinct, they are collectively referred to as "the three. The verse [verse 4] provides a summary, while the commentary explains their characteristics. "Unable to endure" (*akṣama*) refers to the first type of knowledge (*jñāna*).

"Free from what is improper" (*viśārada*) explains fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*). If one fears this assembly and, unable to listen and receive [the teaching], speaks deviously according to one's own whims, this is called "improper knowledge" (*asamyag-jñāna*).

That the assembly is able to hear [the teaching] without fear, and that one is not intimidated by their inability to receive it, but imparts the Dharma correctly—this is called being "free from [what is improper]."
If that is so, why does he not proclaim it? Because he fears that the people of the world would lack faith and conviction.
Fifth, regarding the manifestation below, there is a double conclusion to the preceding two points: "having no fault oneself" means being free from incapacity;

"others having no fault" means being free from what is improper. Others have no fault because they are capable of receiving [the teaching]; it does not mean that one has no fault of fear toward others.

Regarding the initial question-and-answer in the remaining verses, which briefly reveals what constitutes the "characteristic of the answer" (*uttaralakṣaṇa*), it was already stated in the preceding text that "the delight of the assembly" is the characteristic of the correct answer.
Why, then, is it asked again, "What is the characteristic of the answer? There are two types of characteristics of the answer:

first, the characteristic of the intention (*abhiprāyalakṣaṇa*), and second, the characteristic of the expression (*vyañjanalakṣaṇa*). Previously, causing the assembly to rejoice was the characteristic of the answer’s intention; the characteristic of its expression has not yet been presented.
To clarify this question—that this Dharma is difficult to explain and even more difficult to hear—a brief answer is provided to reveal it.

Regarding the difficulty of explanation and hearing, it is fully categorized as previously stated. As for how it is difficult, the following provides a detailed explanation based on the text. First, "difficult to explain" is explained; the phrase "how is it asked?
introduces the response to that.
In the explanation of the first verse, the [subject] is first presented and then subsequently explained. Within the verse, the threefold sequence is analyzed and explained.
Regarding the "difficulty of being attained" (*duradhigama*), it is said to be difficult because it is hard to realize and hard to believe.

Because it is difficult to attain, it is said to be "without benefit" (*anartha*) and "inexpressible" (*anabhilāpya*). There are two types of difficulty; the following explains the second type, wherein first—

The general statement introduces the specific; "most" (*parama*) and "never before" (*apūrva*) are presented by listing their names and defining their characteristics, which is why they are called "most.

Since these two do not exist within the [standard] characteristics and have never existed before, both are extracted from among the difficult points (*duskarāṇi*). Therefore, they are both termed "difficult.
As in the sutra, the first section below is the "Most Rare" (*parama-durlabha*) section; this "never before" section presents the difficulty and establishes the specific as the general.

Because these two [points] specifically clarify the initial general objection, it is said: "To demonstrate the objection. Regarding the phrase "What is it?", the following explains the nature of the third layer of objections.
Within this, first the bodhisattva’s practice is explained, and subsequently the Buddha’s original explanation of that practice is clarified. Regarding the question "What is the objection?

within the explanation of the practice, this interrogates the preceding to initiate the subsequent; the verses that follow cite the latter in contrast to the former. Below, the text is interpreted according to its wording.
"Practitioner" (*yogin*) refers to the sūtra; "supramundane wisdom" (*lokottara-jñāna*) is the wisdom of realization (*adhigama-jñāna*).
"Demonstrating" (*darśana*) refers to the sūtra; "manifesting the characteristics of realization" is called "demonstrating. "Grounds and activities" (*bhūmi-kriyā*) refers to the sūtra;

"the practice of the path of instruction for the ten grounds" is what is meant by "activities," and "discriminating the distinctions" is the specific name for these activities. "Superiority of verbal expression" (*vāk-sampad*) refers to the sūtra.

Regarding the explanation of the analysis of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), it is said that the superior realization of those very same dharmas through the equality of realization constitutes the ten distinctions;

thus, it is called "superior explanation. In the Buddha’s own words, what is the bodhisattva’s practice? This interrogative phrase initiates the subsequent section. The verse that follows cites the latter in contrast to the former.

Below, the text is explained according to the scriptural passage. "Buddha" (*buddha*) refers to the sūtra; "Awakened One" (*jñānin*) refers to the Master of the Treatise, who explains through awakening and understanding.
"Buddha" (佛) means "awakening" (覺), which refers to discernment. Judging by this according to foreign terminology, "awakening" (覺) and "Buddha" (佛) each have distinct names;
yet although the names differ, their meaning is not different. It is like the case of "eye" and "organ of sight" (眼目); thus, one may explain the meaning of "Buddha" by means of "awakening.

If there were no distinct designation, the Master [of the Treatise] would never have translated the foreign term into Chinese on his own; had it not been so, he would not have rendered it thus. Therefore, we know that [the two] are not the same.

Regarding the phrase "because it is the principle and the Buddha’s wisdom," this explains that the Buddha is awakening (*bodhi*) because the Buddha is wisdom; thus, he receives the name "Root of Awakening.
The words are abbreviated and not further explained.

In the second verse, there are three distinct parts: first, the conclusion of the preceding and the introduction of what follows; "that which was difficult to explain" refers to the conclusion of the preceding.
Next, the reason why this arising is difficult to explain after [the preceding discussion] will be set forth. This consists of two parts: the question and the brief explanation.

What is the question? What is the reason it is difficult? "The practice of the Bodhisattva" and what follows is the answer. Regarding the meaning of the phrase "practice" (*caryā*): "practice" (*caryā*) reiterates the practices previously performed;

"matter" (*vastu*) reiterates the matters of the previous stages (*bhūmi*). This is the explanation of the reason for the difficulty. Regarding "practice" (*caryā*), it refers back to the practices already undertaken. Regarding "matter" (*vastu*), it refers back to the terminology of the previous stages. This concludes the section.

The practice and the activity are established as the principle, and thus they are termed "abiding in meaning" (*artha-vihāra*). Because they are identical to the principle, they cannot be expressed in words.
The phrase "it cannot be spoken of in this way" concludes the difficulty of explaining it; this statement is inverted—if the text were correct, it should say, "in this way it cannot be spoken of.
Thus, by restating that the previous practice, activity, and abiding in meaning are inexpressible, the conclusion is reached.
Regarding the detailed explanation of the three questions and answers concerning the difficulty of exposition, the question is: "In what sense does it abide?

Since only the first gate was asked—namely, that it is "inexplicable"—the others were omitted for brevity; had they been included, one should have asked: "In what sense does it abide? In what way is it thus inexplicable?
Below, a verse is cited in response to these questions, after which the text is explained.
In this treatise, the first part initially explains the preceding three phrases. If one hears [this teaching] and becomes confused or faint-hearted, that will be explained separately later.

Within the first section, the scriptural text is subsumed into three parts: from the beginning up to "difficult to obtain" constitutes one part; the section contrasting the inferior with the superior "sphere of the wise" (*jñānagocara*) constitutes another part;
and the section revealing the excellence of the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) as superior constitutes one final pair. The preceding two arguments of the treatise rely upon these three.

The sequential and specific explanation is as follows: first, there is the correct interpretation of the text according to its literal meaning; next, the profound [meaning] is explained; finally, these are sequentially summarized.

Within the explanation of the first section, there are four distinct parts: first, the determination that the general and the specific are difficult to attain—here, "general" refers to the whole, while "subtle" and so forth refer to the specific;

second, the explanation of the general which opens up the specific. Regarding the first point, "difficult" means it is difficult to realize or attain; this is the explanation of the general, and it is difficult because...

The "four kinds" constitute the opening of the specific classification. The three [categories] follow the specific enumeration of names; "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and so forth all emerge from within "difficult to obtain.
Taking the general name and applying it to the specific, they are all termed "difficult to obtain. Fourth, the extensive explanation based on the names: "Subtle" refers to the first gate;

"not the object of hearing" (*aśravaṇa-viṣaya*) means it is not an object known by the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). Alternatively, it may mean that it is not the domain or limit of the wisdom of hearing, and is thus called "not the object of hearing."

In the following sentences, the examples where [the object] is not the domain [of hearing] are likewise so. When it is said that "coarse matters do not require reflection," this is stated to highlight the subtlety of the Dharma-teachings;

because coarse matters do not depend on reflection, they can be attained through the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). However, because the reality of the stages (*bhūmi*) is subtle, it is not within the domain of the wisdom of hearing.

The phrase "difficult to see and difficult to attain" reiterates the second point—that it is not the domain of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); since it was previously stated that it is subtle, it is not the domain of the wisdom of hearing.
Because it should be attainable through reflection (*cintā*), it is now stated that because it is difficult to see, it is not the object of reflection.

Regarding the statement that it is "difficult to attain apart from thought" (*amanasikāra*), this restates the third point—that it is not the object of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The questioner asks: since it is difficult to see, it is not the object of reflection; therefore, it should be attainable through the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
To this, it is now stated that because it is free from thought, it is not the object of cultivation. Hearing, reflection, and cultivation all belong to the mundane realm.

For what reason does the commentary on the middle [verse] specifically mention "the world"? It explains that this refers generally to both the consciousness and cognition born of retribution (*vipākaja*) as well as true cognition (*tattvajñāna*), all of which are cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Now, in order to distinguish these, it says they are not the objects of cultivated wisdom belonging to the world.

By stating "below the three realms," it further analyzes the worldly cultivation, showing that the three realms are the world. The various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) are the analytical cultivated cognitions.
This is the mundane path-cultivation wisdom (*laukika-bhāvanā-mārga-jñāna*). "Mind" refers to the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness;

the essence of mind consists of mental factors (*caitta*) such as perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*). The wisdom that arises within these mental factors is called "discriminating mundane cultivation-wisdom.

It is not the true ground-dharma (*bhūmi-dharma*); it is not the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*). This [phrase] "not the mind-ground" reiterates the report-generating consciousness-wisdom (*vipākaja-vijñāna-jñāna*) from the fourth section.

Regarding that which is "not within the sphere": it was previously stated that this is not the sphere of mundane cultivation; since those from the first bhūmi upward possess the cognitive wisdom born of retribution (*vipākaja-jñāna*), they should be able to know it.
Therefore, it is now said that because it is "not within the sphere of the mind-ground," it is also not the object of the cognitive wisdom born of retribution. What is the meaning of this?

It is that for the sages who have transcended cultivation, the mind of the fruit of transformation (*pariṇāma-vaipākika-citta*) from the first bhūmi upward is the wisdom born of retribution. What does this signify? It signifies that [this realm] is beyond the reach of such wisdom.

When the cause of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) arises, one immediately perceives the meanings of phenomena such as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; this is called the "wisdom born of retribution" (*vipākaja-jñāna*).
Its accomplishment and manifestation is termed "skillfully attaining increased illumination," which is also called the "wisdom of the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga-jñāna*).

Furthermore, on the stages of the *bhūmis*, when the physical retribution first arises, it is called the "retribution-born mind of the transformation-fruit" (*pariṇāmi-phala-vipākaja-citta*), which arises simultaneously with the retribution and is attained as soon as it is produced.

Because it does not need to be practiced through present cultivation, it is called "arising as fruition" (*vipākaja*). One attains the cultivation of wisdom; this is because it is a mind that discriminates impermanence.
Therefore, the earth is not its object. When it says "the realm of the mind is the ground of the mind," this is to further clarify that the limit of the deluded mind is the ground of the mind.
Within the explanation of the realm of wisdom, there are two questions and answers; the first question and answer uses wisdom to manifest the Dharma.

"Whose object is this? is the question. Since it has been stated above that the four minds are not its objects, and it is still unknown what the *dharmas* of the stages (*bhūmi*) are the domain of, this question is asked.
The verse below provides the answer by citing the Sūtra: because they are illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), they are called the "domain of wisdom" (*jñānaviṣaya*).
Furthermore, they may also be termed the "sphere of wisdom" (*jñānagocara*) as the limit (*pramāṇa*) of that actual wisdom. This concludes the first question and answer.

Regarding the discernment of wisdom through the summary of the Dharma, the question is: "What is wisdom? The preceding four minds are identical in being the ground of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*), yet they are not its objective domain (*viṣaya*).
Now, when it is said that this is the objective domain of wisdom, what is it? The one who perceives the true meaning answers by distinguishing it:
the realization of the true meaning is precisely what constitutes wisdom; it is not the same as the preceding four. Thus far, the meaning of abiding in the practice of activity has been clarified.
Why is it not explained below that the untainted (*anāsrava*) is established as being thus inexpressible? Why is it not [explained] by other questions?

Because it is raised to initiate the discussion of the untainted; by citing the verse in response to the question, it is shown that because it is untainted, it is exclusively the object of gnosis (*jñāna*) and not the object of the four minds.
Even if it were untainted, what would hinder its being known by the world? Therefore, he further explains: "This is the meaning of supramundane (*lokottara*)."
Therefore, because it is supramundane rather than mundane, it is the domain of wisdom alone and not of the mundane;
thus, it is not the domain of the other four types of consciousness, such as that derived from hearing and so forth.

The above was the first section, which explained the text according to its words regarding this profundity. Next, the following section summarizes this profundity in sequence: "Thus profound" means...

The preceding section concludes by resolving the difficulty that [the object] cannot be the mental object of the four consciousnesses; this is thus explained. The phrase "the second stage of the preceding" refers to the wisdom of the objective realm (*viṣaya-jñāna*).

"Inexpressible" (*anabhilāpya*) concludes the discussion on the untainted (*anāsrava*). Below, the confusion and bewilderment are first cited and then explained. "What is confusion and bewilderment? asks the question.

The explanation of confusion and bewilderment begins with "arising from attachment to what is heard," which means grasping at words and seizing upon phenomena (*dharma*), thereby obscuring and obstructing the reality (*tattva*).
Therefore it is said: "Deluded and distressed, one speaks of 'hearing,' yet 'hearing' means that it is not that one does not hear. This reveals the meaning of grasping through attachment;
to speak of grasping at reality is called "hearing," yet one does not know that the reality of the ground is quiescent and beyond words, which is why it is called "not not hearing."
In the explanation of "difficult to hear," first the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent one is introduced; below, the verse and commentary are cited for explanation.

First, "the wisdom that is difficult to hear is subtle" explains the difficulty of hearing; it follows that this is discussed later as a separate topic. Within the preceding section, there are four parts:

(1) explaining the general opening and the specific "firm as a diamond," which explains the general; "firmness" has two types, which opens up the specific; (2) listing the names according to their particulars.
Because the two types of "firmness" (*dṛḍha*) are extracted from within [the category of] "evidence and faith" (*śraddhā-pratyaya*), they are both termed the "vertical three divisions.
Regarding these three phrases: in this verse, the first three phrases state that "firmness" is the general [category] and the remainder are the specific [instances].

Here, the initial "firmness" is the general, while the two types of "evidence and faith" are the specific instances. Fourth, following the specific [explanations], there is the sequential interpretation; first, the explanation of "faith" (*śraddhā*).
"Vajramati asked thus" introduces the inquiry; "below, its characteristics are explained" refers to the fact that these are known only by the Buddha and are not within my own sphere of experience.

This demonstrates the depth of his faith, as he reverently defers to the Tathāgata’s own domain of non-cognition; thus, his faith is profound. "The Bodhi of the Buddha" and so forth manifest this profundity.

Bodhi is the Dharma realized through his own practice; because it exhaustively penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is called "boundless. The various [teachings] spoken... are the seeds.
The various distinctions among the gates of the teachings for the benefit of others are called "various preceding words" (*pūrvavākya*);

the subsequent mention of "various elegant phrases" (*vicitrapada*) refers merely to their mutual interweaving. Within this, that which is definitive is termed "faith" (*śraddhā*). Regarding the stages of understanding and realization, first, two questions are posed together to initiate the discourse:
"What is the ground of the mind? asks regarding the dharma to be realized; "What is selflessness? asks regarding the means of realization.

The commentary on the term "ground of mind" (*cittabhūmi*) below explains it as follows: it refers to the body of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which is the retribution received within the three realms according to the mind;
and it refers to all objective spheres (*viṣaya*), the phenomena of the six dusts (*ṣaḍ-rasa*), which are what the mind engages with.

Because these twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) are the places where the mind arises, they are called the "ground of mind. All phenomena are thus included, though this is merely an illustration. [Next is] the wisdom of non-self.

This refers back to the subsequent question that there are two [types of emptiness]. To enumerate them: "knowing self-emptiness and dharma-emptiness as they truly are" distinguishes their characteristics.
In terms of the general meaning, among the twelve *āyatanas* which are merely provisional designations, to attain emptiness therein is called knowing self-emptiness;
to attain the actual absence of self is called knowing dharma-emptiness. Specifically, regarding the internal six sense organs and the body...

Attaining the equality of emptiness within the internal [aggregates] is called knowing the emptiness of the self (*ātma-śūnyatā*); attaining the equality of emptiness within the external six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the phenomena of "mine" (*ātmīya-dharma*) is called knowing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This meaning is explained as in the latter two stages (*bhūmi*). Next, the subtle meaning of wisdom (*jñāna*) is explained. First, the scriptural text is cited:
herein, one should properly raise the subtle nature of wisdom; because it is capable of hearing, it follows along with the preceding characteristics.

The coming [of these states] is difficult to discern; a brief explanation is as follows. These are subtle in the manner described above. As indicated by what was previously stated, they are shown in detail according to the preceding verse, for since the four minds cannot reach them, they are called "subtle."
In the fourth verse, the analogy is now briefly introduced to inspire [the understanding]; following this, the verse and its commentary are presented for explanation.

Within this, first the characteristics of the dharma and the analogy are clarified, followed by a formal analysis and subsequent exposition. Regarding the characteristics of the dharma and the analogy:

here, we specifically take the space where a painting is drawn and the space occupied by wind as the analogies, because a location must necessarily depend upon space; thus, the manifestation of the realm of empty space is necessarily established in relation to wind, and the drawing is based upon that space.

Therefore, this treatise clarifies that wind, painting, and their respective metaphors fully demonstrate the emptiness that serves as the proof for the essence [of the ten stages]. The metaphors of wind and painting illustrate the dwelling places of wind and painting;

the distinctions of what is illustrated are like space. Although they are equal in terms of the essence being proven, there are distinctions among the ten stages based on words and expressions—just as space is equal, yet there are distinctions regarding wind, painting, and dwelling places.
Thus, although the essence is proven to be equal, the distinctions of the ten stages are like empty space.
Although the locations of wind and the locations of painting differ, because they have emptiness as their essence, they are difficult to perceive as having distinct characteristics.
Likewise, although the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) differ, because they have realization as their essence, they are difficult to perceive as having distinct characteristics.

Furthermore, just as the locations of wind and the locations of painting within space are difficult to see, yet they exist and are not non-existent, so too the ten stages, though difficult to see, nevertheless exist.
The "Inability to Illustrate" (Anupama) is divided into three sections in this treatise: first, the explanation of the illustrative text;

second, the explanation of the corresponding text beginning with "Thus the Buddha’s wisdom has been revealed"; and third, the brief omission of the explanation for the Buddha and the untainted [wisdom].
Regarding the first section, because the metaphor is obscure and difficult to recognize, the author of the treatise provides an extensive illustration.
Broadly speaking, within these there are four types of threefold propositions (*trikoṭika*): first, three based on the painted; second, three based on the wind;
third, three based on the combination of wind and the painted; and fourth, three based on the combination of the metaphor. These categories are roughly divided for the sake of convenience.
Next, I shall explain the text. Regarding the three based on the painted: "like painting colors in space" is the first proposition, which cites the metaphor.
This is an illustration using the strokes of a moving brush as a metaphor. It differs slightly from the previous metaphor regarding the traces left in empty space;
the phrase "like on a wall" refers to the second line, clarifying that the place where the stroke is made is neither existent nor non-existent.

Because the characteristics of the place where a stroke is made in empty space are difficult to clarify, it is manifested by means of the place where a stroke is made on a wall. Since this [place] does not abide therein, it cannot be grasped.
"Seeing" is the third phrase, clarifying that the place of painting is difficult to perceive apart from its marks.
Regarding the three analogies for wind: "wind in space" is the first phrase; "like tree leaves" is the second phrase; and "not abiding and not being seen" is the third phrase.
The meaning is the same as the previous painting. This movement is divided below into three phrases: this "agent of movement" is the first.
The first phrase cites the first of the two preceding points. "Movement" cites the preceding wind; "drawing" cites the preceding lines.
It is not that these two things do not exist within space; this is the second phrase, citing the second of the two preceding points.

It clarifies that it is not that wind and drawing—these two types of objective phenomena—are absent from empty space. Thus, the location of such spatial phenomena cannot be described; this is the third [phrase].
The third phrase of the two preceding pairs is called "wind-painting in empty space.
Taking these two locations as the objective phenomena (*vastu*), with emptiness as their essence, one cannot distinguish:
"this is the painted area," "this is the wind area," "this is the high area," or "this is the low area. Because all such things are thus, it is called "ineffable" (*anabhilāpya*).

In the preceding section on "Distinguishing the Middle," it was stated that the metaphors are invisible and the Dharma difficult to hear; here it says they are "inexpressible" (*re-se*), let alone the fact that the Dharma is difficult to explain.

This "left-and-right" [structure] is the "wind of painting. Regarding the three phrases in the middle of the synthesis: first, the initial phrase is synthesized; next, the third phrase is synthesized; finally, the second phrase is synthesized.
This "wind of painting" is like the explanation that synthesizes the initial phrase above; "is this" (*ni-tshe*) refers to the restatement of the Dharma (*dharma-nirdeśa*).
These words are like the previous metaphor of wind and painting; "painting" is a single phenomenon.
How can it be joined with the two metaphors of wind and painting? Because within the explanation there are sounds, names, and so forth, they can be joined.

As in the metaphor of the bird's tracks in space, the location of the tracks serves as the metaphor to be joined, in order to prove that the strokes made by the moving brush here are fleeting and transient.
Using the wind as a metaphor, these two aspects are combined to explain its existence; this should be noted and understood.

It is not because its nature is inferior that it is difficult to perceive, but rather because the ten stages (*bhūmi*) described differ from one another in their designations (*vyañjana*), and thus they cannot be seen.
However, in the preceding metaphor, its difficulty of perception was established simply through its non-abiding; now, in this application (*yoga*), there are two meanings.

The explanation is as follows: because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they cannot be seen; this is the first meaning. As in the aforementioned metaphors, wind and drawings are two different things;

because they lack the intrinsic nature of wind or a drawing, they cannot be perceived. Likewise, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are similarly distinct from the nature of the expressive sounds (*vyañjana*) and so forth, and thus they cannot be seen.
Therefore, the subsequent metaphor of the bird’s tracks in the sky states that it is "not like" [the preceding cases].
The second meaning is that because the nature of sound is invisible, it does not abide; it is like space, which is equal and has nothing upon which to rely or abide.
Just as wind, a place for painting, or a location cannot be perceived within that space, so too is the reality [of phenomena]:
being free from characteristics and equal, it has nothing upon which to rely or abide. Therefore, within that reality, the distinctions of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) cannot be perceived. Because...
The guest, having descended, coincides with the second [category], which is "both existent and non-existent.
As in that analogy, space is said to exist first and is designated as the "host," while wind and painting are subsequently designated as "guests" based on their meaning;

because wind and painting are both guests, the locations for wind and painting within space are not non-existent. In the same way, the earth is actually the "host," while verbal expression is the "guest," because...
The guest [the interlocutor] thus maintains that while the ten stages are realized as equal within the Middle Way, the distinctions between the ten stages are not non-existent;

this is because they are differentiated by words, and since their meaning follows from the designations used, they are called "verbal expressions" (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, this passage is brief and insufficient; if it were complete, one should say:

"It is not that there are no such verbal expressions regarding these ten stages. The subsequent explanation of the ten stages should be combined with the text in this manner, as explained by the Buddha’s wisdom.
In the verse, "wisdom is thus" refers to the fact that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the wisdom originally practiced by the Buddha; therefore, it is called "Buddha-wisdom.

The phrase "the discourse reveals equality" explains and distinguishes how the various stages gradually increase and are measured as superior; because this discourse reveals such [distinctions], it is said to be "distinguishing.

Regarding "difficult to see," there is no further separate explanation beyond what is cited from the sutra. From here below is the third section, which again combines with the preceding metaphors. Why?

The preceding section combined [the examples] to explain the general synthesis; because the specific characteristics of the wind-like sound had not yet been distinguished, the following section distinguishes them by applying them individually according to their metaphors.
First, it applies the metaphor of painting; the metaphor of painting refers to names and so forth, which directly correspond to the previous metaphor.

Why is this? The subsequent question-and-answer provides an analytical explanation. "Why? is the question. It is asked now in order to clarify that the Dharma is difficult to explain, and that this explanation is a metaphor for the wind-like sound.
[Question: "If this is sufficient, why is it that the painting is used as a metaphor for the names (*nāman*) and so forth, which depend on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)?

[Answer: It is explained by way of manifestation; for it is only by depending on the characteristics of names and so forth that sound can express the earth. Regarding the metaphor of the painting, the metaphor of the wind is joined below it.

The metaphor of the wind corresponds precisely to the preceding metaphor. The two lines following this explain the reason for the correspondence. If the text were to be fully expanded, it should also be as follows:
The previous question asked how it is that merely using the analogy of painting to illustrate names and so forth as a means of revealing the Dharma would suffice;
why then take the trouble to use wind to represent those sounds? This line of questioning is briefly absent from the text, but below is a direct explanation:
speaking and listening must rely upon the two factors of sound and characters; therefore, the analogy of wind is established to represent those sounds.
To explain the fifth verse below, first the initial question is restated to serve as an introduction:
"In this way it can be explained" restates what was previously stated regarding these two matters; "in this way it can be heard" restates what was previously heard regarding these two matters;
"in this way it is difficult to see" restates what was previously shown regarding the distinction of the stages (*bhūmi*) and their comparative excellence. Why, then, is it not mentioned?
After the inquiry was raised, it was stated as above that the Dharma is difficult to see but not difficult to explain and hear;

for what reason was it not explained? Next, a verse is cited in response: "Because it is difficult to obtain faith and understanding, I have not spoken. Below this, the treatise provides an explanation for the latter three phrases.
The first phrase is not discussed [here]. The term "difficult to realize" (*duradhigama*) explains the second phrase, and "difficult to determine" (*durniścaya*) explains the third phrase.
From this verse downward, the fourth phrase is explained. Within this, first, by citing what can be spoken and heard, the meaning of silence is explained through contrast;
with the line "difficult for the world to obtain" and below, the necessity of silence is explained in accordance with the context.
With the line "liberation from hearing" and below, this is the second request. Within the sūtra, there are three parts: first, Vimukticandra hears the repeated request that was declined.

This is a general praise of the assembly’s purity. Having heard this, they were startled and silent; because what was heard contradicted their expectations and because the preceding verses were difficult to understand and difficult to believe, they remained silent—thus it is a praise of the assembly.
The request to Vajragarbha is a repeated request. "The great bodhisattvas, the well-purified assembly having gathered" is the general praise.
Regarding the two points of "well-purified mind" and below, there is an extensive praise of the assembly’s purity, which consists of ten [sections].

The purity of the mind regarding the phrases is the general [category], while the remaining nine are the specific [categories]. Question: Why, in the previous request, were the two assemblies—the *sahaja* (co-emergent) and the *anya-jāti* (other-born)—praised separately, whereas here they are praised together? Explanation: Previously, there was a concern that Vajragarbha might be biased in his fear, thinking that the *anya-jāti* assembly was incapable of receiving and retaining the teaching; therefore, he remained silent and did not speak. Consequently, it was necessary to praise the purity of the *anya-jāti* assembly specifically. Now, since that concern has been resolved, they are praised together. Furthermore, the purity of the *anya-jāti* assembly is superior to that of the *sahaja*. Thus, it is said: "Vajragarbha, having heard the praises of the purity of the minds of the *anya-jāti* bodhisattvas, spoke thus to the Tathāgata. This indicates that because the purity of the *anya-jāti* assembly is superior, they are praised together. It is like the analogy of a king who, when accompanied by his ministers, is praised as a "king with his retinue. Because the retinue is pure, the king is also praised as being pure. Similarly, because the *anya-jāti* assembly is pure, the *sahaja* assembly is also praised as being pure. Therefore, the two are praised together. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the assembly. Next is the section on praising the purity of the Dharma. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, praising the purity of the Dharma itself; second, praising the purity of the Dharma’s function. First, praising the purity of the Dharma itself: "O World-Honored One, the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is profound, subtle, difficult to see, difficult to understand, and beyond the reach of logic. This means that the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is profound and subtle because it transcends the realm of all sentient beings. It is difficult to see and difficult to understand because it transcends the realm of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. It is beyond the reach of logic because it transcends the realm of all heterodox teachers. It is not something that can be grasped through mere reasoning. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the Dharma itself. Next is the section on praising the purity of the Dharma’s function: "It is realized through the internal realization of the Tathāgatas, and is not within the sphere of the world. This means that the Dharma realized by the Tathāgatas is realized through their own internal realization and is not something that can be known by the worldly. It is not something that can be understood through the common consciousness of ordinary beings. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the Dharma’s function. Next is the section on praising the purity of the teacher. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, praising the purity of the teacher’s body; second, praising the purity of the teacher’s speech. First, praising the purity of the teacher’s body: "The Tathāgata is one who has attained mastery over all dharmas. This means that the Tathāgata has attained mastery over all dharmas, such that he can manifest them according to his will. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the teacher’s body. Next is the section on praising the purity of the teacher’s speech: "He is skilled in explaining the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. This means that the Tathāgata is skilled in explaining the Dharma according to the various capacities and dispositions of sentient beings. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the teacher’s speech. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the teacher. Next is the section on praising the purity of the time. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, praising the purity of the time of the teaching; second, praising the purity of the time of the assembly. First, praising the purity of the time of the teaching: "This Dharma is taught at a time when the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable. This means that the time in which this Dharma is taught is a time when the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the time of the teaching. Next is the section on praising the purity of the time of the assembly: "At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas was immeasurable. This means that the time when the assembly of bodhisattvas is immeasurable is the time when this Dharma is taught. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the time of the assembly. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the time. Next is the section on praising the purity of the place. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, praising the purity of the external place; second, praising the purity of the internal place. First, praising the purity of the external place: "That place is adorned with various precious jewels. This means that the external environment of that place is adorned with various precious jewels. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the external place. Next is the section on praising the purity of the internal place: "Within that place, there are immeasurable lion thrones. This means that within that place, there are immeasurable lion thrones for the bodhisattvas to sit upon. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the internal place. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the place. Next is the section on praising the purity of the audience. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, praising the purity of the audience’s faith; second, praising the purity of the audience’s practice. First, praising the purity of the audience’s faith: "The audience has deep faith and respect for the Tathāgata. This means that the members of the audience have deep faith and reverence toward the Tathāgata. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the audience’s faith. Next is the section on praising the purity of the audience’s practice: "They have long cultivated the roots of goodness. This means that the members of the audience have long cultivated the roots of goodness. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the audience’s practice. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the audience. Next is the section on praising the purity of the Dharma being taught. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, praising the purity of the Dharma’s profundity; second, praising the purity of the Dharma’s vastness. First, praising the purity of the Dharma’s profundity: "This Dharma is profound and subtle. This means that the Dharma being taught is profound and subtle. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the Dharma’s profundity. Next is the section on praising the purity of the Dharma’s vastness: "It is vast and extensive. This means that the Dharma being taught is vast and extensive. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the Dharma’s vastness. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the Dharma being taught. Next is the section on praising the purity of the fruit. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, praising the purity of the fruit of liberation; second, praising the purity of the fruit of merit. First, praising the purity of the fruit of liberation: "It leads to the attainment of the unconditioned. This means that the fruit of this Dharma is the attainment of the unconditioned. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the fruit of liberation. Next is the section on praising the purity of the fruit of merit: "It brings about immeasurable merit. This means that the fruit of this Dharma is the production of immeasurable merit. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the fruit of merit. This concludes the section on praising the purity of the fruit. This concludes the section on praising the purity. Next is the section on the request for the teaching. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, the request for the teaching; second, the granting of the teaching. First, the request for the teaching: "World-Honored One, please teach us this Dharma. This means that the assembly requests the Tathāgata to teach this Dharma. This concludes the section on the request for the teaching. Next is the section on the granting of the teaching: "The Tathāgata, having accepted the request, remained silent. This means that the Tathāgata, having accepted the assembly’s request, remained silent to grant the teaching. This concludes the section on the granting of the teaching. This concludes the section on the request for the teaching. Next is the section on the introduction to the teaching. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, the introduction to the teaching; second, the introduction to the meaning. First, the introduction to the teaching: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas. This means that at that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas. This concludes the section on the introduction to the teaching. Next is the introduction to the meaning: "O sons of the Buddha, listen well and attend closely. This means that the Tathāgata exhorts the assembly to listen well and pay close attention. This concludes the introduction to the meaning. This concludes the introduction to the teaching. Next is the section on the actual teaching. Regarding this, there are two parts: first, the teaching of the Dharma; second

In the midst of the response, the *Kangyur* (Tibetan canon) merely states that it is difficult for those in the world to attain conviction; it does not say that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are incapable of hearing and receiving [the teaching].

Therefore, this general praise is likewise applicable to the subsequent request by the assembly. Regarding the three "Excellent! (*sādhu*) at the end, which conclude the request for the teaching to be spoken:
"Excellent" is a praise of the assembly's virtue. Since this assembly is virtuous, it is appropriate for the Benevolent One to speak; thus it may also be so named.

He explains that the ground is virtuous; because it is virtuous, the Son of the Buddha should say that those capable of realization will be able to enter realization upon hearing this, and those capable of knowing will be able to believe and understand upon hearing this.
In this treatise, only the first two sections are explained, while the final conclusion is not discussed. Within the explanation of the first section, why is there a repeated praise?

It is to stimulate the assembly by posing a question. Since there was no separate [explanation] for the previous request which already included praise, why is there a further repetition of praise here?

The answer below clarifies the intent of this repetition: the previous statement that “it is difficult for the world to have faith and conviction” explains the passage in the Sūtra regarding hearing this teaching.

"Realization is difficult to attain" refers to what was called "difficult for the world to know" in the preceding verse. "Faith is difficult to attain" refers to the phrase "difficult to believe" in the preceding verse.
"Showing those who are capable to the assembly" is an explanation of the passage in the sutra: "a well-purified assembly has gathered. Below this, the extensive praise of the pure mind is explained;
this generally reveals both the general and the specific purity. There are two types of purity; below, they are explained according to their specific distinctions, first citing the two numbers.

Next, two names are listed: that which is practiced prior to the stages (bhūmi) is called "purity of scripture" (āgama-viśuddhi), and that which is accomplished upon the stages is termed "purity of realization" (adhigama-viśuddhi).
Among the preceding nine types of realization and teaching, this is the second section.

Below, following the text, the *Āgama* is explained and interpreted. Within it, there are five enumerations, which are subsequently explained individually. Of these five, the first three constitute *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing);

the fourth is *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection); and the fifth is *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation). In the text, "desiring purity" (*chanda-viśuddhi*) refers to the mind seeking the Dharma and its thirst for the Dharma;
this "desire" (*chanda*) is extracted from within the general category of "purity," and because the general term is applied to the specific, it is designated as "purity."
In the subsequent phrases, the meaning of "purity" (*viśuddhi*) follows this same pattern. Regarding the explanation of "recollection according to tradition" (*yathāśrutānusmṛti*):
since the dharmas sought and recollected are not limited to one, it is called "according to what has been obtained. The "skillful means" (*upāya*) and so forth refer to the mind that seeks;

"recollection" (*smṛti*) refers to the desire for awakening (*bodhicchanda*), and "awakening" (*bodha*) refers to volition (*cetanā*). Because this recollection and awakening serve as the basis for hearing [the Dharma], it is called "the purity of the awakening of recollection through skillful means" (*upāyasmṛtibodhaviśuddhi*).

Because one accomplishes this awakening of mindfulness, it is called "attainment," as can be understood from the scriptural citations. To speak of "seeking purity" means seeking the practice of the Dharma;
because it involves initiating practice and gathering the Dharma, it is said that "seeking purity" results in "conformity. This explains and clarifies its characteristics:

reverence of body and speech constitutes the practice of seeking the Dharma, and is therefore called "reverent practice. Because one conforms to all Buddhas by seeking the Dharma through this, it is called "conformity."
The accomplishment of respectful conduct through body and speech is designated as "attaining the sutra" (sūtra-paryāpti), which can be understood as the practice of upholding with purity.

One who has accomplished the wisdom of hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā) is said to "uphold"; this is explained by the following terms. Regarding the meaning of "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*), it is explained by the phrase "recollection and retention" (*smṛti-dhāraṇa*).

This means that one has heard [the teachings] over immeasurable lifetimes for a long duration; thus, "much-hearing" (*bahu-śruta*) refers to the vastness of what has been heard. This statement explains the term "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) below. As for "recollection and retention," it means:

"Not causing forgetfulness and not erring in speech" does not mean there are few errors; rather, the sutra’s statement is made because it mostly pertains to the skillful means of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), as one has frequently approached the Buddha.
Because one is able to extensively receive the teachings spoken by the Buddha, that which is "naturally pure" refers to the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
This is named after the skillful means of the wisdom derived from reflection. If this were [meant] correctly, it should instead be stated as follows:
"Attaining birth in purity" refers to the superior supramundane retribution; it is called "attaining birth" because one generates the aspiration for such a birth prior to the [first] stage.
Because the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) arises based on this aspirational mind, it is designated by the name of its "skillful means" (*upāya*).
The following explains its characteristics: "aspiring to attain" interprets the aforementioned "attainment," while "superior higher birth" explains the aforementioned "birth."

Because the retribution of birth increases further and further from the first bhūmi upward, it is called "superior and superior. As for the phrase "recollection of excellence," this refers precisely to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

it is the thought that arises in seeking an excellent birth, the thought that gives rise to the aids to the path (*pakṣya-dharma*), and the thought that initiates the path—this is termed "recollection of excellence.

When the Sūtra says "accumulation," it means that the mind of reflection is able to accumulate the practices that aid the path. As for the phrase "purity of conduct," this is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); because it is produced through cultivation, it is termed "conduct" (*caryā*).

The following explains its characteristics. "Seeking excellent realization" refers to the beginning of the practice; realization occurs on the [first] stage (bhūmi), whereas here one is still prior to the stages.
"Aspiring for that realization" and practicing few desires (*alpeccha*) and so forth refers to the sequence of the practice.

Few desires and the dhūtas are practices for detachment. "Few desires" is the literal meaning of the term; "dhūta" is a foreign word (Sanskrit) which means "to shake off. This shaking off is the practice of detachment.
It is named after its metaphor: just as shaking out a garment can remove dust and grime, practicing these twelve *dhūta* (ascetic) observances enables one to abandon greedy attachment;
therefore, they are called "shaking off" (*dhūta*). The meaning of *dhūta* is extensive, as detailed in other chapters; the phrase "this should be fully discussed, etc.
refers to the inclusion of other practices for accumulating wholesome deeds. To "accomplish many virtuous qualities" means to cultivate them to completion. As the Sūtra says, "endowed with."
The phrase "immeasurable merit" applies only to the final clause.
