The meaning of "collection" (*saṃgraha*) in the subsequent phrases follows this same pattern. As for "retinue-holding morality" (*parivāra-śīla*): this explains its characteristics. "Skillful cultivation" refers to the excellent application of wisdom as the primary factor, with morality acting as its attendant.

Because they assist [the practice], they are called "retinues" (*parivāra*). Below, the sūtra is cited to collect the various practitioners; since these three groups are not one, they are termed "various practices.

Having definitively collected and enumerated their names as "well-performed" (*sukṛta*), the following provides an analytical explanation of their characteristics. The meaning of "retinue" does not differ from the previous explanation.

Below, the word "practice" (*caryā*) from the sūtra is cited; as it has not yet been explained, it is restated and then analyzed. Regarding the practitioner of *samādhi*, the term from the sūtra is restated once more.
Regarding the passage "The practice of samādhi increases as it follows the performance of the text": *samādhi* is *śamatha* (calm abiding) and the practitioner is *vipaśyanā* (insight).
These two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* constantly assist one another. In this specific text, *śamatha* is primary, while *vipaśyanā* is employed to bring it to completion.

Because *vipaśyanā* can give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called the "practice of insight" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). Since insight is predominant, the concentration is profound and superior. Having thus approached [the practice],...
The final four lines concern wisdom within wisdom: first hearing, then reflecting, and subsequently practicing; the last line concerns realization.
"Cultivating intimacy through hearing" means that because the wisdom of hearing is obtained by drawing near to spiritual friends, it is termed "intimacy" from the perspective of its skillful means.

"Accumulating goodness and habituating oneself to hearing" excludes the essential nature of the practice itself. As the Sūtra says, "making offerings to the Buddha" refers to cultivating intimacy; one seeks the Dharma by making offerings to the Buddha.

The accumulation [of wisdom] refers to the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); the mind of the wisdom born of reflection is able to gather all the perfections (*pāramitās*), and thus it is termed an "accumulation" (*caya*).
Because one cannot repeat the same name, it is called an "accumulation. To contemplate all phenomena is to explain the meaning of "accumulation.

As the Sūtra says, "skillfully accumulating pure and white dharmas," the practices of the perfections can counteract defilements; therefore, they are called "pure and white. This is the cultivation of the accumulation of protection.

Regarding "the cultivation of wisdom through the practice of wisdom": it is called "protection" because one follows virtuous friends above and is sustained by their guidance; below, its characteristics are explained.

Because the supramundane true realization can be entered through cultivation, it is termed "cultivation and realization. Being well-received by a teacher means being sustained by the instructions of those virtuous friends;

the application of the sutra is as may be understood. Thus far, the three types of wisdom have been presented as the skillful means for approaching realization; below, the actual [realization] is revealed.

The "Certainty of Purity" (*avetyaprasāda*) lists the names; it is called "pure mind" because it realizes and transcends defilement. This explains its characteristics through supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), as can be understood from the sutra citations.
Regarding the extensive collection [of practices] below, three aspects clarify the protection against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*):

therein, the first two protect the mind from the Lesser Vehicle, while the last one, through present application, protects the practice from the Lesser Vehicle. Within the former two, the first protects against a narrow mind, and the latter protects against [selfish] benefit.
That which is called "the extensive gathering of mind and speech" refers to a vast mind. To give rise to such a vast intention is also termed an "extensive mind.

According to the subsequent scriptural text, one should also speak of it as "deep," yet here only one aspect is mentioned, referring to it simply as "extensive. The following section on the "deep mind" explains and reveals its characteristics:
because the arising of the mind is earnest and ultimate, it is called "deep"; because it acts for the benefit of all, it is designated as "extensive. The scripture says "entering."
The phrase "deep" in the preceding section refers to the "vastness" of the deep mind (*adhyāśaya*). The subsequent passage, "to benefit all," should be noted here as it will be required below.

The "collection of faith" (*śraddhā-saṃgraha*) refers to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*). Within the scriptural text, there is both faith and seeking: faith in the great cause and seeking for the great fruit.
In this present text, we refer to the former alone and designate it simply as "faith"; yet it is the seeking for all [benefits].
This explains its characteristics. Within the scriptural text, there is both faith and seeking; here we explain only seeking and do not briefly explain faith.
"The knowledge of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*) refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. The scripture says, "faith and delight," which reiterates the preceding "faithful mind.
"The Great Dharma" refers to the Mahāyāna that is the object of that faith. "Those who seek the Buddha-wisdom on the causal ground" reiterates the subsequent "desiring to seek all-knowledge."

Furthermore, the preceding discussion regarding the "Great Dharma" and the "Buddha-wisdom" was merely an elaborate exchange of terms. What has been explained above extensively concerns protecting the mind from the Lesser Vehicle;

the following single phrase clarifies its protection of the practice of the Lesser Vehicle for the sake of benefiting others. Since those of the Lesser Vehicle exclusively cultivate their own self-benefit, cultivating the benefit of others is termed "protecting the Lesser Vehicle.
Why is the protection of the Lesser Vehicle through self-benefit not explicitly stated? If it were to be further...

Since it is not distinct from the preceding six [types of mind], it is omitted and not discussed. If that is so, why does the text separately clarify the mind of self-benefit within the mental continuum?
It is because those of the Two Vehicles lack the aspiration for Buddhahood; therefore, by means of the intention for self-benefit through the Great Mind, one protects their limited minds.

Furthermore, since those of the Lesser Vehicle possess the practices of the Three Trainings, even if one were now to clarify that their modes of practice are identical to theirs, would this not protect the meaning [of the Great Vehicle]?

This demonstrates that regardless of whether they are currently assembled or listed by name, those who mutually benefit through compassion are termed "present. As for the term "many practitioners," this explains their characteristics:
because there are never times when suffering sentient beings do not exist, and because there are never moments when one does not provide compassionate rescue and deliverance, they are called "many.
Alternatively, they may be called "many" because they arise extensively within the objects of perception; thus, the sutra text below is further divided into sections.

Because the other types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are coarse, they rely on rescuing from the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); because the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*) is subtle, it relies on rescuing from the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). The meaning of these three types of suffering is analyzed in detail within the chapter on the Four Noble Truths. It was previously stated that the causes and effects of loving-kindness and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are the same as those for compassion regarding the extraction of sorrow and suffering; why, then, is it now said in all cases that they "rely on suffering"? To explain this: [The text continues with the explanation: This refers to the fact that while the former two [loving-kindness and joy] take pleasure as their fruit, compassion takes the removal of sorrow and suffering as its fruit; however, since both share the same causal basis in the perception of suffering, they are here categorized together under the heading of "relying on suffering. Furthermore, because the object of compassion is vast—encompassing all sentient beings who are submerged in the ocean of birth and death—it is said to be superior to the other two.

Moreover, because the nature of compassion is subtle and difficult to realize, it is said to be superior to the other two. Finally, because compassion is the antidote to the affliction of anger (*dveṣa*), it is said to be superior to the other two. Thus, although the causes and fruits of the three immeasurables are distinct, they are all subsumed under the single category of "relying on suffering" based on their shared causal basis. This concludes the explanation.

There are two senses in which these meanings are both general and specific. Specifically, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness upon beings, while compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract them from suffering.

Generally, both kindness and compassion are alike in their ability to bestow happiness and alike in their ability to extract one from suffering. As for the bestowing of happiness, it is as explained in the Third Stage (*tṛtīyā bhūmi*):
its loving-kindness is vast and immeasurable; it extensively bestows the pleasure of desire and greatly bestows the joy of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), being immeasurably joyful.

The same applies to the categories of joy, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; thus, these two types of mind equally bestow happiness upon beings and equally extract their suffering, as explained in the context of the third stage (*bhūmi*).
Because one enters into compassion based on sentient beings who are suffering, it relies on the latter gate [of extracting suffering].
Since the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are all equally for the benefit of others, why is it that only loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is clarified here?
The Compassionate One [the Buddha] spoke in response: Although the four immeasurables all benefit others, compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are the foundation;
therefore, joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are explained only as secondary supports, and thus are not discussed here.

Within this, the first two of the nine points are analyzed together as the practice of the retinue (*parivāra-caryā*), while the subsequent four phrases are analyzed together as the essence and meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*). The final three...
The meaning of the phrase "the accumulation is a single entity" can be understood by analyzing the textual characteristics;
what has been explained above is the extensive exposition of the "accumulation" as a whole, and this is the third section, the beginning of the formal teaching on the sixfold classification.

The six aspects are distinguished here, and the same applies to all other categories. Regarding the "thick accumulation" as a whole, it refers to the comprehensive synthesis of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) into one thick accumulation.
Therefore, it is called the "General" (samuccaya). The remaining nine are all derived from the General and are designated as "Specific" (vyavasthāna).

They are "the same" in that each of the nine specific categories contains the sense of "collection" (samuccaya), which is why they are termed "same. They are "different" in that although the sense of collection is the same, they differ in their particulars such as morality (śīla) and meditative concentration (samādhi);
thus they are called "different. Their formation and destruction can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the meaning already explained concerning the basis of the body (*āśraya*), what follows next concerns what fetters (*saṃyojana*) precede and succeed one another.
Within the sūtra, there are two pairs: the first pair clarifies the mind sought by the Buddha’s wisdom; the second concerns the bodhisattva’s generation of this mind.
Following this summary of the generation of the mind, there are ten phrases; the first is the general [statement], while the remaining nine are the specific [details].

The treatise now returns to explain the sūtra in its sequential order. Within the preceding section, it first interprets the initial summary. Regarding this, the phrase "the Buddha’s wisdom" (*buddhajñāna*) cites the wording of the sūtra;
"unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) is used as a general designation to indicate that the Buddha’s wisdom has nothing superior to it, hence it is called "unsurpassed.

"Knowledge," "abandonment," "realization," and "cultivation" specifically manifest its characteristics. "Knowledge" refers to knowing suffering (*duḥkha*); "abandonment" refers to abandoning the origin (*samudaya*); "realization" refers to realizing cessation (*nirodha*).

Regarding the practitioner who cultivates the path: why is it that, concerning suffering (*duḥkha*), one speaks only of "knowing" it and not of "abandoning" it? Because this is a resultant phenomenon (*vipāka-dharma*) and cannot be abandoned;

rather, one must know its faults and thereby give rise to revulsion and detachment. Why is it that, concerning the origin (*samudaya*), one speaks only of its "abandonment" and does not say "knowing" it?
This clarifies that the origin can be eliminated, and thus it is not merely a matter of knowing it. Why is it that, concerning cessation (*nirodha*), one speaks only of its "realization"?

Regarding why it is said that "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to progressive practice while "cessation" (*nirodha*) is not so called: cessation is a non-existent dharma (*abhāva-dharma*) that can only be realized through knowledge;
because it is not a mental dharma (*citta-dharma*), it cannot be progressively cultivated. Why, then, is only the Path (*mārga*) described as "cultivation" and not as "realization"?

The Path is a mental dharma that can be progressively practiced, and is therefore termed "cultivation. Furthermore, cultivation is for the sake of attaining cessation; since its purpose does not terminate with the Path itself, the Path is not termed "realization."
Regarding the ultimate Buddha-wisdom, why is it said to be "cultivated"? It is called "cultivation" because it is accomplished through fundamental habituation;
furthermore, in relation to all dharmas, there is no virtuous quality that is not cultivation, and thus speaking of "cultivation" involves no error. The meaning of "learning" is likewise so.

This is the Tathāgata’s own removal of suffering and its origin, and his own attainment of cessation and the path; it is not a mere general contemplation of the objects of the Four Noble Truths. The essence of wisdom is one.
In terms of their meaning, there are four [categories] because they are divided accordingly. The following section explains the remaining distinctions; therein are two parts.

First, a general enumeration of the nine activities of the Buddha’s wisdom as the cause for seeking birth [in the Pure Land]. Regarding this "Buddha-wisdom," it refers back to the previously mentioned general wisdom.

As for the "nine kinds of activities," these range from the ten powers (*daśabala*) up to the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*); each possesses a specific function, which is termed an "activity. Since such [activities exist],...
Because the activity of benefiting sentient beings requires that a bodhisattva first seek to give rise to the bodhicitta, this is explained extensively below.

However, these nine kinds of qualities, when perfected within oneself, are all activities for one's own benefit (*svārtha-kriyā*); yet, when they benefit others, they are all activities for the benefit of others (*parārtha-kriyā*).

Now, regarding the essence of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*), we shall provisionally divide them according to their meaning: the first three pertain to self-benefit, and the latter six to the benefit of others. Within the first three, the first is power (*bala*) and fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
This is the third equality of the Buddha’s *jñāna* (knowledge). Within the initial practice of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there are five distinct phrases.
First, regarding the power of the Buddha’s knowledge: this refers to the power of his cognitive capacity. Among the ten powers, this specific power is extracted from within the Buddha’s knowledge;

thus, what is generally termed "power" is here specifically designated as "the Buddha’s knowledge. This same principle applies to the Buddha’s knowledge in all subsequent phrases. Second, as for the questioner: [text continues].

Clarifying its activity means that it is able to provide a prediction for all questions regarding cause and effect according to the inquiries of sentient beings; this is called "answering questions" (praśnavyākaraṇa).

To answer whatever is asked is the activity of this power. Third is the Tathāgata’s power of the possible and the impossible (sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala), which provides a dual explanation for the preceding two.

Regarding the possible and the impossible: this explains the essence of the aforementioned wisdom. Among the ten powers of a Buddha, the first power is the general correct knowledge of cause and effect.

Because it can provide a definitive answer according to the question, it is singled out as "question-and-answer" (*praśnavyākaraṇa*). This term "question-and-answer" explains the preceding category of karma.

Regarding the phrase "according to the question it can provide an answer," this refers to the *sūtra* (as indicated below by the character "xuán"). The meaning of the "ten powers" (*daśabala*) within the sūtras cannot be discussed in detail;
therefore, although it is indicated by referring to the sūtras, the specific volume (*bǐ*) is not cited, and it is not known which particular sūtra it is.

Luo says that there ought to be a separate *Daśabala-sūtra*; alternatively, one may point to those passages in various sūtras where the powers (*bala*) are manifested as being what is referred to here.
Fifth, regarding the application of the sūtra to the ten powers: "power" is used to distinguish these from other powers; therefore, they are called the "powers of the ten powers.
Within the second section on the activities (*karman*), there are three distinct phrases. First, "fearless wisdom" (*vaiśāradya-jñāna*) raises up the essence of that wisdom; this is...

The Tathāgata’s fourfold fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) consists of two parts: first, the destruction of heterodoxy; below this, it clarifies that the function of his wisdom (*jñāna-karma*) is able to crush opposing arguments, which is termed "the destruction of heterodox doctrines. This destruction of heterodox doctrines is the activity of fearlessness.

Third, by citing the sūtra to distinguish him from other bodhisattvas who are free from the five fears and so forth, he is therefore called "one of great fearlessness. Within this third activity, there are four distinct phrases; first, the leveling [of pride].

1. Regarding "Equal Wisdom" (*samatājñāna*): it is called "equal" because it elevates the essence of the Buddha-wisdom to realize emptiness and transcend all marks. 2. Regarding "attaining non-self": this explains the aforementioned Equal Wisdom.

3. Regarding "instruction" (*avavāda*): the following clarifies its activity; to teach others by means of what one has attained oneself so that they may enter together [into realization] is precisely the activity of Equal Wisdom.
4. By means of the sūtra, these three preceding points are applied; in terms of their wisdom-essence, they are identical.

The first six [verses] concern self-benefit, while the latter six concern benefiting others. Within this section: first, the skillful means of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) clarify the practice of benefiting others;

second, compassion clarifies the mind that benefits others; and finally, the last four clarify the wisdom that benefits others. Regarding the first [of these three], there are three parts: first, "saving" clarifies the Buddha-wisdom by presenting its essential nature;
second, "the four means of attraction transform beings" clarifies its functional activity; third, the sūtra passage provides the textual corroboration.
Within the five activities, there are three distinct phrases: first, "the Buddha’s wisdom is supreme" (*buddhajñānam anuttaram*) identifies the essence of that wisdom;
because compassion can eliminate obstacles such as anger and the like, it is termed "pure" (*śuddham*). Second, "it is pure" (*viśuddham*) below clarifies the activity of that wisdom;

since it gives rise to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) through a compassionate mind to rescue and save sentient beings, it is called "rescuing" (*tāraṇam*). Third, "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣam*) serves as a scriptural seal for the following four benefits.

His wisdom also consists of these four, which are likewise the five kinds of immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). The five immeasurables are: first, the immeasurable of sentient beings (*sattva-apramāṇa*), meaning knowing those to be converted;

second, the immeasurable of worlds (*loka-apramāṇa*), meaning knowing their places of birth and abode; third, the immeasurable of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-apramāṇa*), meaning knowing the dharmas such as good and evil that arise in beings;
fourth, the immeasurable of discipline (*vinaya-apramāṇa*), meaning knowing the faculties and natures of things; and fifth, the immeasurable of the methods of discipline (*vinayopāya-apramāṇa*).

The first immeasurable is the knowledge of the methods for counteracting [afflictions] and delivering sentient beings; it is supreme and without remainder. The second immeasurable is freedom from defilement;
it is the immeasurable of the world. The third immeasurable is awakened wisdom; it is the immeasurable of the dharma-realm, which is also its immeasurable of discipline.
The fourth is the skillful means of discipline; within the context of being without remainder, there are further distinct categories of phrases.

Third, regarding "knowledge of the remainderless" (*anupadhiśeṣa-jñāna*): first, it presents the essence of this knowledge; because it knows that birth has been exhausted, it is called "remainderless. Second, "the Buddha-eye" (*buddha-cakṣus*) below clarifies its function of knowledge.

The Buddha-eye has five types, beginning from the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) up to the Buddha-eye itself: the fleshly eye and the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) perceive the forms and colors of beings;
the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) can perceive the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings; and the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) can perceive the emptiness of sentient beings.

The Buddha’s eye of tranquility thoroughly penetrates the true nature of sentient beings; possessing these five eyes, one is able to see sentient beings and act for their benefit—this is the activity of the wisdom that is without remainder.
Third, regarding the section on "unstained wisdom" (*vimalajñāna*) from the sutra, there are five distinct points.
First, concerning the essence of unstained wisdom: because the mind has no attachment to the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), it is called "unstained."

Regarding "defilement," it should be stated according to the following [verse]: "unobstructed and undefiled. This presents one aspect; the second [aspect], "all worlds," explains the meaning of being undefiled.
Within the world, the severing of delusion is "unobstructed" and the extinguishing of craving is "undefiled. Third, "spontaneously" clarifies its activity:
because delusion and craving are exhausted, the wondrous response accords with the mind without requiring effort; this is called "spontaneous supernormal transformation" (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*).

Responding to conditions as they arise is called "responsive transformation" (*nirmāṇa*), which causes beings to turn toward virtue; this is termed "inspiring faith. Responsive transformation is the activity of that undefiled wisdom.

The phrase "the four wisdoms manifesting the previously unobstructed and undefiled virtuous wisdom" indicates the former state of being unobstructed, which is the liberation of wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
The phrase "unimpededness of mind" indicates the former state of being undefiled, which is the liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti*). Fifth...
The sutra commentary states "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*); the term preceding it is "pure" (*viśuddha*). "Undefiled wisdom" (*jñāna-asaṃkliṣṭa*) refers to the unimpeded nature of wisdom preceding it.
One should also say "mind," though it is omitted for brevity; were it fully expressed as a phrase, it should read "the mind of unobstructed pure wisdom.

Alternatively, since both wisdom and mind may be collectively termed "wisdom," within the context of awakened wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*), there are three distinct categories of phrases, the first of which is awakening.
The Buddha’s wisdom raises up the essence of that wisdom; because awakening is itself wisdom and cannot be named repeatedly, it is called "awakened wisdom.
The phrase "knowing with two moments of thought" below clarifies its activity: because he knows the phenomena of the mind, it is called "knowing the dharma-realm";

knowing this very mind is called "knowing subjugation. Third, the sutra provides a gloss: "Awakening to matters" refers to the matters of mental phenomena throughout the three periods of time, concerning their transformation.

Within the Dharma, there are four distinct categories of phrases. First, regarding the "Wisdom that Turns the Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra-pravartana-jñāna*): this raises the essence of the wisdom itself.

The Dharma taught by it is called a "wheel" because it can crush [the afflictions] and turn [the wheel]. The act of teaching and bestowing it is called "turning. Second, regarding "Liberation" (*vimukti*) and below: this clarifies its function.
The deliverance of sentient beings is termed "liberation. Because the Buddha turns the Dharma so that sentient beings may be liberated, it is called "turning the Dharma."
Because he is skilled in the means of liberation and can teach simultaneously in all places according to the needs of sentient beings, he is called "skillful.
[The following three hundred verses] explain this skillfulness. Fourth, by citing the sutra, it is stated that because he possesses mastery over knowledge, he is called "fearless.

Above was the first section, explaining the Buddha’s activity of wisdom; below is the explanation of the second [section], the arising of such a mind. First, the text reiterates the point before providing the explanation.
The phrase "giving rise to the mind" cites the sūtra as explained in the "Original Section" (Mūla-bhāga); it refers back to that [section] to clarify this [point].
Since the vow and the mind are non-different in essence, they refer to one another to mutually clarify their characteristics. Regarding the question "For what reason...

and so forth, the response analyzes and distinguishes why all virtues arise, yet why it speaks only of "giving rise to such a mind" and not "giving rise to wisdom. This is a single point: because wisdom and practice are distinct, wisdom is raised separately as the subject of the question.

Furthermore, the enumeration of the factors [of enlightenment] constitutes the second clause; since mindfulness, concentration, and so forth are not the primary leaders of the practice, they are collectively cited in the question and answer.
To clarify that the mind encompasses knowledge, abandonment, and so on, this corresponds to the first clause, which explains how the mind encompasses wisdom and all auxiliary paths.
To clarify the inclusion of the remaining enumerated factors, it corresponds to the second clause; therefore, they are not mentioned here. For now, this discussion follows one specific meaning.
If wisdom arises from clarity, it likewise encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in their entirety.
Regarding the question of why the first [clause] concludes the preceding and initiates the subsequent within the causal analysis:
the sūtra contains ten phrases; the first is the general [statement], while the remaining nine are the particulars. The phrase "this mind" refers to that which was previously produced.

Regarding the statement that "the bodhicitta has compassion as its foremost," the arising of the bodhicitta must rely upon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), with compassion serving as its guide and leader.
However, what is clarified here regarding the supramundane practice of accomplishment is that compassion and the vow arise simultaneously; in reality, there is no sequence of priority.

Nevertheless, for the sake of explaining their characteristics, it is said that compassion is primary and the mind [of awakening] arises in accordance with it. For what reason, then, is it stated specifically within the context of compassion that it is "as vast as the dharma-realm" and so forth?

The remaining points need not be discussed here, as they should all be understood by parity of reasoning; however, because compassion (*karuṇā*) is fundamentally what a Bodhisattva values, it is explained specifically.
In the treatise, the initial general phrase is first explained: "As for this mind," meaning this bodhicitta; "compassion is its head" means that the mind relies upon compassion.
Below, the remaining specific categories are explained. First, regarding the general category of compassion, the other nine specific types are opened up: "First," and so forth.

In the explanation of the nine [categories] following the listing of names: the first seven constitute the essence of compassionate practice (*karuṇā-caryā*), the next one constitutes the virtue of compassion, and the final one constitutes the capacity of compassion.

Regarding the first seven, the initial three are the "self-benefiting" (*svabhāva*) stages, while the subsequent four are the "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gāmin*) stages. Within these three self-benefiting stages, there is first, the wisdom that knows suffering;

second, the practice that uproots suffering; and third, the mind that rescues from suffering. Regarding the first of these—the wisdom—its excellence is listed as follows: its wisdom surpasses that of the mundane world.

Therefore it is said: "Supremacy" is derived from within great compassion; taking the general name and opening it into specific names, the principle of the great meaning applies similarly to all subsequent phrases, such as "subtle suffering" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "subtle suffering": the knowledge that exhaustively examines subtle suffering is called "knowledge of subtle suffering.
As for "supreme birth," because the knowledge of subtle suffering is termed "supreme," the manifestation of this supreme wisdom is designated as "birth."
Below, the sutra passage concerning "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is annotated: it refers to the superior cultivation of the knowledge of subtle suffering, which is the aforementioned superior birth.
Below, there is a further detailed analysis of the characteristics of wisdom. Now, regarding the explanation of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "wisdom," there are both general and specific meanings.

In their general sense, they are equivalent; in their specific sense, they differ. There are two types of this difference: first, knowing phenomena that exist is called "knowledge," while illuminating the emptiness of ultimate truth is "wisdom."
These are termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*). To know matters such as cause and effect, defilement and purity, and so forth, is called "knowledge.
To thoroughly comprehend the principles of existence and non-existence regarding the two truths is named "wisdom. Now, based on the latter category, these two are distinguished:

the wise cite the sūtras to judge that the contemplation of cause and effect, direct and reverse order, defilement and purity, karma, afflictions, and so forth, constitutes the "cause," while the retribution of suffering, pleasure, and so forth, constitutes the "result."

To speak of these as results, generally considered, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) that are capable of producing subsequent states are all termed "causes" (*hetu*);

when subsequent states arise from preceding ones, these are termed "results" (*phala*). To seek the cause by tracing back from the result is called "reversal" (*pratiloma*), while to infer the result based on the cause is called "conformity" (*anuloma*).

The causes and results of unwholesome (*akuśala*) phenomena are described as "defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭa*), whereas the causes and results of wholesome (*kuśala*) phenomena are judged to be "pure" (*viśuddha*).

"Thoroughly examining and discerning" refers to the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This is a restatement of the sūtra’s own phrasing. Regarding the distinction between "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*):

the existence of phenomena through causes and conditions is termed their "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*); the fact that these phenomena are of a single flavor—such as being empty—is termed their "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Because they are distinguished according to the division of these specific and common meanings, it is called "distinction. Alternatively, this wisdom does not perceive specific characteristics; rather, based upon those specific characteristics, it perceives the principle of emptiness.

Therefore, it is called "emptiness of specific and general characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); because names differ according to their designations, it is termed "differentiated contemplation," as explained previously.
Regarding the wisdom that knows emptiness, why is it taught alongside compassion? The explanation states:

because one knows that suffering is empty, yet sentient beings remain unaware and continue to wander in delusion within the realms of error, one gives rise to a compassionate mind; having already understood the nature of prior suffering, one must necessarily deliver and rescue them.
Therefore, next, the second [section] lists the names of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as "rescue" (*paritrāṇa*).

Below, it explains that skillfully extracting beings from suffering is called "rescue" (*paritrāṇa*), while being able to attract and bestow happiness is called "skillful means" (*upāyakauśalya*). Because there is that which is attracted, it is therefore called "that which is skillfully attracted.

Below, the sūtra provides a topical summary (*pratisaṃyukta*): the term "means" (*upāya*) summarizes the preceding "skillful means," and "attraction" (*saṃgraha*) summarizes the "means of attraction."

The postscript skillfully explains "pure and ultimate" (*chun-zhi*). Listing the names, "pure" (*chun*) refers to purity and thickness (*chun-hou*), while "ultimate" (*zhi*) refers to reaching the limit (*zhi-dao*).
Because compassion is predominant, it is called "pure and ultimate. The Sūtra says: "the straightforward mind, the profound mind, and pure and ultimate [mind].

Among these three, the former two are specific, while the latter one is general; since the name is taken from the general, it is called "pure and ultimate. Below, its characteristics are explained: "facing and permitting throughout all births."
"Acting for the benefit of others" explains the straightforward mind (*ṛjukatā*); this is the great compassion that intends to bestow happiness.
Specifically, when previously accumulating roots of goodness, one’s profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*) desired to benefit all sentient beings;

this is called the "vow at the time of proceeding," wherein one pledges to perform acts of benefit for the entirety of the realm of sentient beings. Because this intention to benefit all beings without partiality is free from crookedness, it is termed the "straightforward mind."

Regarding "compassionate mind" (*karuṇā-citta*): it explains the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*), which is the great compassion that uproots suffering. Because the sentiment of pitying suffering is earnest, it is called "profound. Regarding "superior" (*adhimātra*):

it explains "purity and sincerity" (*śuddha-sarala*) and "clarity and directness" (*vimala-ṛju*); together with "profound," these constitute "superior. The application of the sutra [passage] can be understood accordingly.

Within the section on "progressive advancement" (*viśeṣagamana*), the first phrase encompasses the power of the Buddha’s supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) to transform sentient beings and engender faith.

Next, regarding the first [section], "Skillfully Mastering the Faculties and the Appropriate Doses of Medicine," this refers to the method of bestowing the teaching; regarding the latter two, they refer to the methods of gathering [beings] that accord with and benefit them.

Within the first phrase, the "immeasurables" are listed by name to encompass the immeasurable powers, and their characteristics are explained—namely, the *Tathāgata-mahābhijñāprātihārya-sūtra*, which can be understood from its topical outline (*uddāna*).
The "decisive" [powers] list names to illuminate the capacities and natures of sentient beings, being clear and unimpeded.

The *Mahāvaipulya-nirdeśa-sūtra* (The Great Sutra on the Determination of Names) speaks of both "determination" (*niyata*) and "power of wisdom" (*jñāna-bala*). However, it mentions only "determination" by way of abbreviation and does not explicitly state "wisdom.
If it were expressed in full, one should say "the greatness of determined wisdom" (*niyata-jñāna-mahat*). Below, its characteristics are explained.

First, regarding the phrase "supremely excellent determined faith," this refers to knowing the vessel of sentient beings. Faith is that which is known; sentient beings are the vessels of faith. The Bodhisattva knows this and understands it with certainty.
Regarding the name "Decisive Faith": because it clarifies the superior within the midst [of phenomena], it is called "excellent, wondrous, and profound wisdom.
"Profound wisdom" refers to the understanding that is the knowing subject; "superior remedy" refers to the dharma-medicine that is the object known.

Within this stage of superior progress, because one knows the dharma-medicine, it is termed a "superior remedy. Within this phrase, there are three interwoven aspects: the knowledge of faith and the understanding thereof.
The understanding that consists of definitive knowledge as the remedy is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*); these two are mutually exclusive.
The understanding that consists of knowledge as the remedy for faith is called "supreme and wondrous"; this is explained as "profound," and these two are mutually exclusive.

The wisdom that knows the dharmas is called "profound," and the medicinal dharmas to be known are said to be "superior"; these three are mutually exclusive. Below, the sūtra provides the textual citations.
Regarding "certainty" (*niyata*): it refers to the aforementioned certainty concerning sentient beings, which is the conviction that one knows the capacity of sentient beings as vessels for faith.

It is called "power" (*bala*) because it is the supreme ability to know those who have a remainder [of potential]; it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it is superior to the aforementioned power and knowledge.

In the latter two phrases, the first concerns the skillful means of gathering the Dharma in accordance with enlightenment, while the second concerns the actual gathering of the Dharma and its bestowal upon sentient beings.
"Conforming to the enumeration of names" means conforming to right awakening (*samyaksambodhi*). "Explaining its characteristics" refers to the practice of cultivation leading toward the fruit;

thus it is called a *Sūtra of Conforming to Right Awakening*. The phrase "conforming to" (*anuloma*) is a gloss for "conforming. "Spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is a gloss for "right awakening. To awaken without relying on a teacher is termed "spontaneous.

Regarding the enumeration of names, "right reception" (*samyak-samādāna*) means that the grasping of the Dharma is without error; because one is able to grasp the supreme Dharma, it is called "right reception."

To explain its characteristics: "gathering" for the sake of one's own [enlightenment] within Buddhism is called "the capacity to take up" (*parigraha*); benefiting others is called "bestowing the scriptures. The text says "capable of receiving" (*pratigraha*), which refers to the superior Dharma;

"wisdom-transforming" (*jñāna-pariṇāmanā*) refers to the "instruction" (*avavāda*). The seven preceding phrases constitute the essence of the practice of compassion. Next, the most sublime qualities of that practice are clarified;
the enumeration of names and the explanation of the annotations can be understood accordingly. Below, the meaning of the practice acting as a cause is clarified.
"Abiding" refers to the enumeration of names; it is the cause of the fruit of impermanent craving, and because one receives retribution according to existence, it is called "abiding.
"Exhaustion" refers to the cause of its permanent fruit, for it extends to the limits of the future; thus it is called "exhaustion. The commentary on this may be understood accordingly.
*Ji-di-yi-ji* (Record of the Meaning of the Ten Stages),
Fascicle 2b–3a (This fascicle concludes the section on the precept against sexual misconduct within the Second Stage).
Exegesis by Jingying Huiyuan.
In the explanation of the benefits (*anuśaṃsa*), the first section concludes the preceding and introduces the subsequent.

In the sūtra, the initial passage clarifies the characteristics of the benefits of transcending the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and entering the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). The phrase "abiding in this Dharma" below summarizes the meaning of abiding.
Within the preceding section, there are nine phrases: the first is general, while the remaining eight are specific. Regarding the summary of abiding, as for the phrase "abiding in this Dharma":
The preceding explanation refers to abiding in the four aforementioned dharmas; this is called "abiding" (*sthiti*), which establishes the meaning of abiding.
Regarding "immovable" (*acala*), this explains the meaning of abiding: because that which has been attained does not regress, it is called "immovable.
Since it is immovable, it is termed "abiding. While those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward may be called "immovable," why is it already called "immovable" here?
There are five kinds of immovability (*akopya*): first, the non-destruction of the single seed is called the "immovable lineage";

having transcended this, it is called immovable. Second, the non-retrogression in the arising of practice is called immovable; from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, all are termed immovable. Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"From the first stage upward, like the moon in its bright fortnight, increasing day by night, one does not retrogress from wholesome dharmas. Furthermore...
Thus, the three emptinesses are called "immovable" when they are uninterrupted; from the seventh bhūmi upward, they are called "immovable.
When the four cultivations of the mind have matured and one is free from the movement of effort, it is called "immovable"; this refers to the eighth bhūmi and above.
When the ultimate is fully perfected and there is no further progress to be made, it is called "immovable," which exists only in the stage of Buddhahood. Now, regarding this...
The treatise states that "non-retrogression in the practice of arising" is what is meant by "immovability.
Within the text of the treatise, it first explains the initial general fault to demonstrate attainment; the noble path is its fundamental substance of benefit and merit.

By citing the faults of the ordinary stage, it demonstrates the attainment of the noble [stage]. Below, the remaining specific passages are explained; there are three distinct parts: first, opening based on the general;...

The second part provides a detailed explanation of the distinctions; the third part concludes the explanation. By showing that [the stages] are not identical, it demonstrates the meaning of the fault.

Of these eight points, the first seven establish the qualities of the respective stages (*svabhūmi-guṇa*), while the last one clarifies the maturation of the mind through further progress (*viśeṣa-citta-paripāka*).

"Entering the stage and receiving the name" (入位列名): this phrase clarifies the "ability to enter" (*praveśa*) by way of the stage (*avasthā*). To attain the supramundane path is called "entering the stage.

Within the general [category of] "transcendence," this "entering the stage" is opened out as a specific instance; taking the general term, it is designated as the "name for entering the stage. The meaning of "transcendence" (*ati-krama*) in the various subsequent phrases is likewise so.
Below, its characteristics are explained, first through the Dharma and then through a simile. First, the explanation of "entering" is established in contrast to what follows.
This is named the initial stage of transcendent understanding (*lokottara-adhigama*), which is illustrated by the metaphor of first dwelling in the womb.
Because the dharma and the metaphor correspond, it is called "resemblance" (*sādharmya*). The application of the sutra passage can be understood from this.

Regarding the faults of the household, the names are listed here; this phrase clarifies that [the practitioner] abides therein by means of the dharma. Since the Buddha-dharma is the family, why [is there a fault]?

Therefore, next, the distinction between the "actual" and the "semblance" is clarified: although worldly people may receive a womb-born existence, if they are born into an ordinary family, this is not yet considered superior;

it is only when one is born into a royal family that it is truly superior. In the same way, for a Bodhisattva, generating the aspiration for enlightenment within the teachings of non-Buddhists is not yet considered superior;
it is only when one generates the mind based upon the Buddha-dharma that it is truly superior. For this reason, it is explained next. As stated previously:

Having already stated that one "enters the stage of a bodhisattva," it is clearly understood that this is distinct from non-Buddhists; why then is this phrase used again to clarify the faults of their school?
Nevertheless, those non-Buddhists also constantly claim for themselves, "I am a bodhisattva. Since the term "bodhisattva" applies to them without distinction, it is clarified once more.

Regarding the phrase "born into the family" (*kula-ja*) and below, this is illustrated through a metaphor: because they are born into the family of the [Buddha] King, they are called "born into the family" (*kula-ja*). This is what is meant.

Because it is analogous to the same dharma, it is called the fault of "similar seeds. Listing the names, within the Mahāyāna teachings, the accomplishment of the auxiliary practices (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) is termed the fault of seeds.
Why? Next, it is explained as follows: although a person may be born into a royal family, they are not yet considered superior if they remain a slave or a servant;
only when they obtain the status of a prince is it a truly superior attainment. It is the same for the Bodhisattva: although they are born into the Buddha-family, [they must further... generate...

The minds of those of the two vehicles do not give rise to great benefit; only by initiating the practice of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) and being capable of continuing the lineage of the Buddhas is one truly sublime.

Therefore, following this, its characteristics are explained—first through a metaphor and subsequently through its application. One who attains the status of a king’s person is designated as his "son.

Because this metaphor accords with the Dharma, it is called "similar. Regarding the "birth of the Great Vehicle," this refers to the gathering and arising of all auxiliary factors based upon the Mahāyāna Dharma.

The practice of the Way is capable of succeeding to the rank of a Buddha, like a prince; because one obtains the seed of Buddhahood through the application of the sutra below, it is called "Noble" (*ārya*).
It is vastly different from the Small Vehicle, and thus there is no reason to begrudge the Way for being listed here. This phrase establishes its position to manifest its transcendence.
Why is the World-transcending called the Way? It is distinguished next [to the mundane] because although a person may possess the physical attributes of a king, [the true royalty lies elsewhere].
If one belongs to the realms of ghosts or animals, they do not surpass those who have received a human rebirth; only then can it be called a "transgression. It is the same for a Bodhisattva:
although they abide in the Mahāyāna, as long as they remain in the world among various classes of beings and have not yet abandoned them, it is not a supreme benefit.

Only when they abide in the supramundane state does it become supreme. Therefore, to clarify this "transgression of the path," the following explains its characteristics through first the teaching and then the analogy, concerning both the mundane and the supramundane.

Regarding "comprehended by what is comprehended": that which is prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is mundane, while that which is upon the stages is supramundane. Now, this Bodhisattva is not comprehended by the mundane, but is comprehended by the supramundane.
To clarify this through a metaphor of similarity with other paths: because the human path differs from the three evil destinies, it is called an "other path";

sharing common characteristics [with the supramundane] is called "similar. Below, the sutra provides the commentary: "transcending the world" comments on the phrase "not comprehended by the mundane," indicating entry into the supramundane.
The preceding section was the inclusion of those who have transcended the world. Regarding the nature of their excellence, the listing of names is as follows:

although worldly people may possess the human state, if their faculties are impaired and their karmic retribution is not superior, they are not truly excellent; only when their physical form is free from deficiency are they considered superior.

In the same way, although Bodhisattvas dwell in the supramundane, if they lack great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is incomplete, they are not yet sublime; it is only by possessing great compassion that they are truly so.
Since this is superior, it is explained next. Below, its characteristics are elucidated, first through the Dharma and then through a simile.

Regarding "compassion as the essence": this directly points to and excludes [the view that] it is for the sake of others. To explain: compassion is the essence; compassionate activity benefits others. Why is this taken as its own essence?
Because the mind of a Bodhisattva takes the benefit of others as primary; thus, performing deeds for the sake of others is itself a deed for one's own sake.
To "attain" is the essence [of the practice]. To illustrate this through an analogy of similarity with its own nature: just as a human body possesses common characteristics, it is called "similar.
As the Sūtra says, "dwelling in the dharmas of a bodhisattva," great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is precisely the dharma of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "If someone asks, 'In which stage does one dwell to be named a bodhisattva? one should correctly answer: 'One dwells in great compassion.'"

In this context, "place" (*sthāna*) refers to that which transcends the enumeration of names and does not abide within the sphere of conditioned activity; why is it that, following this, the analogy of a prince is used?

Although his faculties may be complete, if his dwelling place is base and inferior, his retribution is not superior. Only when one dwells in a palace and hall that is exquisitely adorned and transcendent of the world can one be called "superior.
Likewise, although a Bodhisattva possesses such a body of compassion, if they remain attached to the two extremes, they are not extraordinary.
Only when the function of supreme tranquility is unimpeded can it be called "supreme transcendence. Therefore, this non-abiding realm is clarified as being the locus of transcendence.
In the subsequent explanation, the principle is presented first, followed by the analogy. One who does not abandon the world does not abide in nirvāṇa through skillful means;
being unstained while abiding in the world, one is said to employ skillful means such that both the world and nirvāṇa are simultaneously present in the function of supreme tranquility.

Regarding "skillful dwelling based on names" (nāman), this is illustrated by means of a metaphor. Below, the sūtra provides the textual application (*pratisaṃyoga*). As for "dwelling in the proper place":

attachment to existence is the dwelling of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while dwelling in tranquility (*śama*) is the dwelling of the small [vehicle]. The "proper place" is the True Dharma (*saddharma*) of the Bodhisattva;

therefore, it is called the "proper place. Regarding "activity" (*karman*): the faults of activity are enumerated by name. Wisdom (*prajñā*) supported by emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is designated as "activity. Why is this explained next? It is because it is like a worldly king.
Although the dwelling place of a son [of the Buddha] may be magnificent, his food consists of coarse and inferior fruits rather than refined and exquisite delicacies;

yet, in sustaining himself in this way, he is truly superior. A Bodhisattva is likewise so: although he relies on these [conditions], he does not dwell upon them nor grasp at signs that defile the spirit;

thus, while not relying on the refined, he sustains his life through wisdom (prajñā-jīvita), and in this he is truly superior. Therefore, the faculty of hearing is explained next. Regarding the faculties that sustain [the path], within the subsequent explanation, the Dharma is presented first, followed by...

The analogy for one who accords with the wisdom of emptiness is that their darkened mind accords with the Way; this is called "accordance with emptiness. When it harmonizes with the true illumination of emptiness, it is termed "sage-wisdom" (*āryajñāna*).

"Life" refers to the similarity [of the metaphor]; borrowing the metaphor to reveal it, the sustenance of the retribution-body is called "life. That which shares the same dharma is termed "similar. Below, the sutra provides the textual application, stating:
"Those who enter the *tathatā* of the three periods of time" means that because their wisdom accords [with it], they are said to "enter"; this refers to contemplating the three periods of time.
The Dharma is equal and of one suchness; when the principles of expression and the ultimate meaning are presented together, it is called the "Suchness of the Three Times," which is like space.
When the names are definitively listed, the "Great Mind" is called "Firmly Established" (*niyata*). Why? Next, it is explained by analogy:

just as a prince, though his physical support and environment may be superior, if his essential nature and spirit are not established, he cannot succeed to the throne. Only one whose mind and will are firm and correct is capable of succeeding to the state and its ancestral sacrifices. The Bodhisattva is like this.
Although one may be fully endowed with these inherent virtues, if the mind is not firm and correct, one cannot definitively grasp bodhi;
it is only when the will is resolute that there is superior progress. Therefore, this is explained next. In the subsequent commentary, the Dharma is presented first, followed by the analogy:
the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage is the certainty of the cause; the attainment of ultimate nirvāṇa is the certainty of the fruit; and nirvāṇa is cessation.
In the sūtra text, it is stated that the fruit-path is the fruit of the skillful means of bodhisattva practice, and therein only bodhi is clarified.
Now, this treatise author cites nirvāṇa comprehensively because it ultimately achieves necessity; thus, it is called "ultimate accomplishment.

As for the term "resembling," it borrows a metaphor to reveal that just as a prince’s resolve is established and named "accomplishment," so too is this called "resemblance" by virtue of its shared qualities. Below, [the text] proceeds with the sūtra...
Within the category of the "conception" (garbhāvakrānti), there is the "definitive conception" (*niyata-garbhāvakrānti*), which is the uninterrupted path to ultimate bodhi;
this is the path to final nirvāṇa. Thus, the third section below explains the meaning of the fault of "dissimilarity.
It displays the births of ordinary beings and the births of Bodhisattvas, and by citing these two types of birth—beginning with their entry into the womb—it demonstrates their dissimilarity.
The meaning is to be inferred by analogy with the subsequent passage on "departure" (*niṣkramaṇa*), which distinguishes through dissimilarity (*visadṛśatva*).

This refers to the Bodhisattva who has already entered the noble abodes (*āryavihāra*) as being dissimilar to one who has not yet entered them, and so on, up to being definitively certain (*niyata*) as being dissimilar to one who is not yet certain; the same applies to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

Likewise, one who has entered the womb is dissimilar to one who has not entered it, and so on, up to one who has attained accomplishment (*abhinirvṛtti*) as being dissimilar to one who has not attained it. It is not that ordinary persons are different from Bodhisattvas; rather, it is the state of having entered [the womb] that is distinct.
Regarding the differences between the dharma, the analogy, and the application, what need is there for further discussion?

As for the statement that "entering the womb is not similar," this clarifies that the entry of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) into the womb is not like [the entry of those] with or without affliction; it reveals that the state of entering the stage of a Bodhisattva is likewise not similar.

Furthermore, as for the phrase "entering the womb is not similar," this generally clarifies both ordinary beings and sages (*ārya*). It indicates that while ordinary beings enter the womb in a manner that is not similar [to the noble], Bodhisattvas do not enter [in such a way].

However, there is a distinction between being with affliction (*sābādha*) and being without affliction (*anabādha*), which explains that the Bodhisattva’s entry into the womb is not like [ordinary] entry when afflicted, nor like it once entered when free from affliction;
this single principle runs through the subsequent sentence as well, for all are dissimilar due to the distinction between being with and without affliction.
Thus, the seven other points of dissimilarity are listed below. This concludes the explanation following the statement.
The scriptural text says: "Thus it is said that one who dwells in this stage is called a 'dweller'. The preceding forty phrases explain the practice while dwelling in this stage;
thus it is called "thus it is said that one who dwells in this stage. This explains that within the sutra, one who abides in such dharmas is called a "dweller.
This is the correct interpretation of the term "dweller" used in the sutra regarding the phrase "rejoicing and immovable"; the [remaining] words are not explained here in brief.
The commentary on the sutra may be understood through its four sections:

first, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent; second, briefly clarifying through question and answer; third, pointing out and refuting in accordance with the text; and fourth, providing an extensive explanation following the text.
The meaning of "abiding" has already been explained; how one interprets the names constitutes the first section.
How one explains what follows constitutes the second section. Within this, there are three questions and two answers. Furthermore, within the subsequent sutra passage, there are thirty phrases:

the first ten concern joy (*prīti*), the next ten concern mindfulness (*smṛti*), and the final ten concern the manifestation of mindfulness (*smṛty-abhimukhībhāva*). These correspond to the first ten phrases [of the preceding section].
There are two sets of question-and-answer pairs following the twenty single questions that lack answers;

however, when these will be explained below, it will be necessary to further provide question-and-answer analysis to distinguish between the mindfulness of the present and the mindfulness of what is to be contemplated. To avoid excessive redundancy, they are not answered here;

one must instead rely on the first set of question-and-answer pairs from the preceding section, which explains the "ground" (*bhūmi*) by means of "joy" (*prīti*), and the latter set, which demonstrates "joy" by means of the "ground."

"What is it that is called 'joy'?"—this is the first question. "How is it that among all the stages where one attains the state of a noble one (ārya), there is no lack of joy, yet this stage alone is specifically called 'Joy'?"—because of its great abundance of joy, it is designated by the name "Joy. This is the first answer.
In the subsequent scriptural passage, the first ten phrases are termed "abundant joy"; because of this abundant joy, this stage is revealed and named "Joyous" (Pramuditā).
The mark of joy (*prīti-lakṣaṇa*) is present in this initial stage; it is the beginning of the realization of holiness (*āryatva*). For this reason, there is much joy.

To the question "By what is this joy [produced]?"—the second inquiry—the preceding statement mentioned that the name "Joyful" (*pramuditā*) is indicated because of much joy, yet it was not known by what this much joy is produced.
The following answer clarifies this. Regarding the "joy" of this stage, it is pointed out in terms of its location within the subsequent scriptural text.
The first ten phrases state that a bodhisattva dwelling on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) achieves manifold joy;
this is because the joy of the bodhisattva on this stage is so named. Now, it is pointed out that the joy of this stage is its "manifold joy. Question:
Since there are thirty phrases in the text below, all of which constitute the joy of the bodhisattva on this stage, why is the name "joy" applied specifically to only the first ten phrases?

Regarding the joy of this stage, the commentary explains that the first ten [factors] are precisely the joy resulting from the practice of this stage; therefore, this stage alone is specifically named "Joyful" (Prāmodya).
As for the remaining twenty phrases, because joy arises only upon encountering their respective objects, they are given a different name and called "Mindfulness-Joy" (Smṛti-prāmodya).

Furthermore, what is meant by "mindfulness"? This is the third question. Moreover, it carries the sense of "again. Although [the practitioner] previously understood [the teachings], because there was much joy, [it is now called mindfulness].

It is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). By what further recollection is this stage named "Joy"? If one were to answer by way of the future, one should say it is because one will recollect the joy that is currently present;
thus, the stage is again named "Joy. This [point] is omitted from the answer here.
The section following "The initial exposition" constitutes the third segment, which briefly points to the text by correlating it with the initial exposition. Regarding "the first ten":
these refer to the ten phrases expounded in the subsequent sutra text, which clarify the "abundant joy" explained in the first two question-and-answer pairs. Regarding "the latter twenty":
these refer to the twenty phrases expounded in the sutra text concerning the "recollection of joy" asked about in the final question.

The fourth section is the word-by-word commentary. Within this, the first ten pairs clarify "joy" (*prāmodya*) by means of having previously accumulated a "thick body of merit" during the preceding stage;
the second pair clarifies the arising of joy for the sake of the higher meaning; and the third pair clarifies the arising of joy from previous benefit.
Since compassion (*karuṇā*) is a state of sorrowful pity and its characteristics do not accord with [the nature of] joy, it is not treated here to explain joy.
In the commentary on the first gate, there are ten phrases in the sutra: the first is general, and the remaining nine are specific. Regarding the treatise, there are two parts:

first, the inclusion of the specific joy-entrances within the initial general category; second, the establishment of the general [category] within the many joys. As for "joy" (*muditā*), this refers to the essence of the mind as stated in the sutra;

"faculty" (*indriya*) refers to the preceding six among the latter nine, which constitute the practice-body of self-benefit joy, while the final three concern transforming others and being free from the obstacles to joy.
Of the first two among the preceding [three], respect and affection are mental states associated with joy (*prīti-saṃprayukta-citta*), but they are not the actual substance of joy itself;

they are now subsumed under the general category and termed "joy of mind. The next three are the actual substance of the joyful mind, and when subsumed under the general category, they are termed "joy of substance.
The final one clarifies the meaning of the function of generating joy; it is explained as the "root" and is subsumed under the general category.
It is named "Root Joy" (*mūla-prīti*) because it possesses these three meanings; thus it is called "Abundant Joy. There are two explanations for the remaining distinctions.
First, regarding the general joy, the nine specific types are opened out. Next, they are explained individually. "Reverential Joy" (*gaurava-prīti*) refers to the listing of names:

honoring the Triple Gem is termed "reverence. This reverence is extracted from within the general joy to serve as a specific category; since the general term is applied to the particular, it is called "Reverential Joy" in the subsequent phrases.

The principle of "joy" (*muditā*) is likewise; "revering the Three Jewels" explains its characteristic. Because one personally realizes the essential nature of the Three Jewels on this stage and believes in their profound excellence, reverence arises.
Just as in the Lesser Vehicle, when entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one attains indestructible faith (*aveṇikī śraddhā*) in the Three Jewels, it is the same here.
The Sūtra says that "faith" implies reverence because of that faith; this refers to the higher object.

"Generating a mind of reverence" refers to those who are beloved; "enumerating their names" refers to those from whom one has personally realized the truth; "giving rise to love according to reality" and "contemplating with joy those who resemble them" explain their characteristics.

The application of these terms in the sutra can be understood accordingly. These two [phrases] pertain to the mind, while the following three are the actual essence and characteristics of *muditā* (sympathetic joy).

Because there are distinctions between the beginning, middle, and end, there are three phrases. "Celebration" (*qing*) refers to enumerating names; "celebration" (*qing*) is synonymous with joy. "Self-aware of being superior" means...
Emerging from that which is celebrated, one realizes the superior stage previously attained; this is called "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*).

The names are listed in order as the mind of joy (*muditā*) becomes increasingly superior, pervading both the internal and external body and mind. Because there is no suffering and one is free from anger and affliction, it is called "pliancy.

As for the statement that "the benefit of one's own body and mind is accomplished," joy is a dharma of gladness and benefit; however, because the preceding joy was subtle, it could only benefit the mind.
Now, as this [joy] increases further, it benefits the body and mind universally, causing them to leap with exultation; thus, it is named "Increasing and Flourishing" (*vṛddhi*).

Because its flourishing exceeds what came before, it is called "Leaping and Fulfillment" (*vṛddhipūrṇa*); this explains the term "leaping. Being capable of receiving the listing of names is "Joyful Practice" (*pramuditā-caryā*), for it can encompass enlightenment (*bodhi*);

thus, it is called "Capable of Receiving. Seeing for oneself that one is near means knowing that one's own practice is established and that the attainment of the fruit is close; this is being near to *bodhi*.

What is the difference between this and "recollecting what will be attained"? Recollecting what will be attained refers to the joy of anticipating the future fruit; here, however, it is joy because one can experience the present cause.

Above, [the practice of] self-benefit was explained; below, the three [remaining perfections] concern benefiting others. Having departed from the obstacles to joy, first the mouth, then the body, and thirdly the mind, we clarify the departure from malice and affliction.
Furthermore, the first [point] clarifies that when sentient beings seek the Dharma, one does not violate their intentions.

Next, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva transforms others so that they initiate practice without causing them distress; subsequently, it clarifies that when sentient beings act contrary to the Dharma, one should not give rise to anger and must not destroy their [virtuous] ranks.
It lists the names and explains their characteristics: "one's own mind is harmonious and supple" means the initial mind is free from hatred;
"discussing and explaining the immovable" means that when debating with others and explaining one’s own interpretations, the mind remains harmonious and free from contention.
Therefore, one does not cause disturbance because the mind is unmoving; one’s speech is necessarily gentle and does not destroy the intentions of others.

This may also be explained through discussion, as can be understood from the relevant passages in the Bodhisattva Sūtras. Having listed the names of those who do not cause affliction and taught them, the following explains their non-affliction:

when transforming and gathering others, they employ a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, with body and speech made supple and gentle; even upon seeing an evil person, they gradually transform them through the Path.
"Not vexing others" and "not being angry with them"—these two preceding phrases mean that one causes other sentient beings not to be ruined or vexed;

this clarifies that one's own mind does not give rise to anger. The subsequent explanation of their characteristics is as follows: seeing sentient beings who do not act according to the teachings means their minds deviate from the Dharma;
their deportment being improper means their bodies violate the Way. Although one sees such lack of discipline, one should regard them with compassion.

Therefore, having already explained non-anger and joy (*muditā*), [the text] now explains the subsequent mindfulness of joy (*muditā-anusmṛti*). Within this, first, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent section is introduced;

by referring to the text, its divisions are briefly enumerated. Having already explained "much joy," this concludes the preceding section; next, explaining "mindfulness of joy" introduces the subsequent section.
Regarding the second and third sets of ten phrases, the speaker refers to the text to point out that these are the two types of mindfulness. Below...
A brief enumeration of the categories consists of two parts: first, the enumeration of the numbers; second, the explanation of the names. Regarding the former, there are three types:

mindfulness of what is to be attained by conditions already present, mindfulness of what is to be attained by conditions yet to come, and mindfulness of what is currently being attained. These will be explained in detail below.
The explanation begins with the initial inquiry regarding what is to be attained.

According to the treatise, the sūtra is analyzed through two gates: first, the analysis of the general and the specific; second, the analysis according to the essentials through four gates. Regarding the first [the analysis of the general and the specific], there are ten phrases in the sūtra:

the first is the general, and the remaining nine are the specific. Regarding the second [the analysis according to the essentials through four gates]: the first is mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*); the second is mindfulness of... [text continues].
The Dharma consists of three recollections (*smṛti*) and the bodhisattva’s four recollections; that which is practiced refers to the latter seven phrases, all of which are subsumed under "practice.

The following treatise explains this based on these two gates. Within that fourth section on bodhisattva practice, the first phrase is the general [definition], while the remaining six are the particulars.
Among those six, the first is the essence of the practice, and the subsequent five clarify its successive cultivation and accomplishment. As for the term "recollection" (*smṛti*), it is as follows:

Regarding the phrase "coming to teach and transform the Dharma," this text is deficient by lacking the character "attain" (de). According to the treatise, it should state: "recalling that one attains the transformative Dharma.

This refers to the stage where, within one's own household, one shall attain the tenth bhūmi and obtain the Buddha’s transformative Dharma; it does not refer to recollecting the transformative teachings of other Buddhas.

In this treatise, there are two parts: first, an explanation by way of the general and the specific; second, an explanation of the specific which follows the requirements of the four gates starting from the first two together with the subsequent ones, thereby establishing the specific as the general. Within the former, we first explain the initial general mindfulness of the Buddha, and subsequently interpret the remaining specific aspects.
Regarding "How does one practice mindfulness?"—this is an interrogative inquiry intended to initiate the discussion. What doubt has arisen that prompts this question? Now, as for this mindfulness:
Having reflected thus, it is stated in the *Sūtra on the Future Realization*: "How does recollecting other Buddhas constitute the meaning of 'I shall realize'?

This question is asked because one wonders how recollecting others could result in one's own future realization. The answer to this previous question is: "Just as the Buddha has realized it, so too shall I realize it.

This means that by recollecting the fruit realized by the present Buddhas and thinking, "I shall be equal to them," one's recollection of other Buddhas becomes the recollection of what one will oneself realize in the future. One who recollects in this manner...

The concluding words of the summary state: "To contemplate others as being oneself—it is thus one contemplates. Regarding the explanation of the remaining individual [contemplations], first, based on the general contemplation, the remaining nine specific ones are opened up.
First, from the phrase "one" onwards, the general mindfulness of the Buddha is applied universally to the remaining nine;

within these nine phrases, each first lists the name and subsequently cites the sutra to correspond with the mindfulness of the Buddha. As for the "mindfulness of the Dharma," this precisely belongs to the section on the mindfulness of the Dharma within the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.

Opening this section on the contemplation of the Dharma, the general and specific names for the various phrases regarding the contemplation of the Buddha are presented together so that their mutual clarification may be understood.

Within the second section, there are briefly three pairs: first, establishing the initial contemplation of the Buddha by means of the contemplation of the Dharma; second, establishing the initial contemplation of the Buddha by means of the Bodhisattva;
and third, establishing the initial contemplation of the Buddha by means of the practices of those Bodhisattvas, which comprehensively subsume the remaining six [perfections].

The preceding section has three parts. First, a general summary of the previous two [sections] to demonstrate their shared meaning: regarding "among these," within these ten [practices], the first two are common;

that is, the mindfulness of the Buddha and the mindfulness of the Dharma among the ten are both considered "common" by the masters of the treatise, as they equally involve recollecting one's own future attainment of the Buddha’s virtues.
The same applies to the subsequent phrases. Second, following the mindfulness of the Buddha, the first [of the remaining items] is specifically raised.
Regarding the second [section], the initial statement "recalling the Buddha as the Buddha I have attained" cites the first phrase;
"recalling the Buddha" cites the sutra, while "as the Buddha I have attained" cites the treatise. Regarding "recalling the Buddha-dharma," this cites the treatise;
regarding "recalling the dharmas of all Buddhas," this cites the sutra. The third statement, "the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma," is the conclusion clarifying what preceded.
Second, because there is a distinction between the Buddha and the Dharma, the former was previously explained as being twofold.
Above, it was established through the Dharma that the first [type of] mindfulness of the Buddha consists of two aspects; this is the second gate.

Within the mindfulness of the Buddha, the mindfulness of Bodhisattvas is further divided into two, so as to manifest the duality for the sake of revealing their commonality. Why not clarify the common category above? It is permissible.
Knowing that it would be too cumbersome to elaborate extensively, within these three pairs, the first pair clarifies both [the individual] and their commonality;

this present pair clarifies the two while omitting the commonality; and within the final pair, the meaning of commonality is fully established while the two are omitted. Thus, the texts vary in their presentation.
As for "recalling the Bodhisattva," this is raised by citing the scriptural parallels; for what reason does it mention only the Bodhisattva and not the Buddha?
