This [section] concerns the supramundane bliss; as in the sutra, it follows the "Post on Peace" and precedes the "Post on Compassion.
Regarding all sentient beings, what has not yet been explained is not merely the post preceding [the section]; rather, it is raised by taking momentum from the preceding [discussion].

Below the section on cause and effect is the fourth segment, which clarifies detachment by means of the remedy (*pratipakṣa*). Within this, first, the preceding remedy is restated to manifest detachment from cause and effect.

In the middle, one seeks without inversion by restating the previous antidotes; because one bestows upon others the cause of goodness through a previously established mind of stability, one seeks without inversion regarding the cause.
Because one bestows upon others the fruit of happiness through a mind of loving-kindness, one seeks without inversion regarding the fruit.
Regarding [the abandonment of] killing for sacrifices and the like, one clarifies their abandonment by means of the antidote; thus, one seeks without inversion regarding the cause.

Therefore, one ultimately does not kill living beings for the sake of pleasure; because there is no inversion regarding the cause within the fruit, one likewise does not seek a pleasurable result by killing.
Thus, "abandoning the deluded mind that kills for sacrificial rites" is called "abandonment," which is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
As for the phrase "the antidote," it refers back to the aforementioned antidote; as for the phrase "called abandonment," it refers back to the abandonment of delusion.

Killing is the very thing that its antidote opposes; thus, the antidote is called "abstaining from killing. Therefore, it is named "the antidote" because it opposes and abandons [killing], thereby establishing the preceding section.
To further explain how that [antidote] can abandon the heavy [fault] of killing rooted in delusion, it is called "the antidote that opposes and abandons.

Within the commentary on the scriptural text, this addresses the statement regarding sentient beings to demonstrate that they are neither eternal nor subject to annihilation.

Following the section on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), it explains non-eternality and non-annihilation by means of the causes and conditions of the life-faculty. As for the eternally abiding dharma, it does not arise from causes;

In reality, the non-interruption of matter and mind in the present is called "life" (*jīvitendriya*). The karma of the past that is capable of producing this present life is termed the "life-faculty.
Because this faculty can produce and sustain the present life, it is called a "causal condition" (*hetupratyaya*).

Sentient beings obtain their present lifespan through the causal conditions of that life-faculty; therefore, it is not permanent. According to the *Abhidharma*, there exists a distinct entity that is neither matter nor mind.
Because life (*jīvita*) can cause form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) not to be severed, it is called the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*).

Because past karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) act as causes and conditions for the present life-faculty, they are called the "causes and conditions of life. Since the fruit arises in accordance with its causes, it is said to "follow" its causal conditions;

thus, one obtains a lifespan in the present. Therefore, it is not eternal. As for those who will be born in the future due to karma and afflictions, this explains that there is no annihilation (*uccheda*).

Furthermore, because it is severed, it does not continue; yet karma and afflictions are the causes and conditions for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) in future lives, and based upon this, that arises. Therefore, it is not severed.

Regarding the separation from the fruit and its activity, there are four distinct points: first, citing and stating the number; second, listing the names and defining their characteristics; third, a detailed enumeration.

first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as a sentient being; third, the intention to kill; and fourth, the severing of the continuity of life. This is the first [of these].

Within the conditions (*pratyaya*), excluding the divisions, there are two [points]. First, regarding "the body" (*kāya*): this distinguishes one's own body from the physical entity that is killed by another; thus, the body that is the object of the killing is called "the body. Second, regarding "the matter" (*vastu*):

Regarding "abstaining from stealing" in the sūtra on abstaining from stealing, this is the general definition; taking what is not given through improper means is termed "stealing," and its cessation is termed "abstinence.

Since it initially cites "insufficiency of the means of subsistence" (*upakaraṇa-vaikalya*) to clarify the cause of stealing—because the act of stealing arises from a lack of wealth—it is designated as a "cause.
Now, why is this not discussed here as a "cause" [of craving], but instead "insufficiency of the means of subsistence" is taken as the cause?

[This is because] while afflictions such as greed (*lobha*) are able to give rise to various karmas and are thus termed "causes," why is this not considered a cause here, but rather "insufficiency of the means of subsistence" is posited as the cause?
However, among the various causes of karma, there are those that are common and those that are uncommon. All such karmas take greed and other afflictions as their cause, which is termed "common.
Within the context of killing, using the strength of another animal, a staff, or similar implements as the cause; within stealing, the insufficiency of one's livelihood as the cause;
and within sexual misconduct, the insufficiency of one's own wife as the cause—these are termed "uncommon. As for those common causes, they have already been illustrated in the section on killing.
Other categories may be understood accordingly; they are not discussed here further. One must distinguish the specific causes for stealing that result in an insufficiency of resources for livelihood.
This section clarifies [the remedy]. Below, the sūtra is cited to demonstrate the abandonment [of this fault].

The following explains its characteristics: that which is called giving (*dāna*) is precisely the essence of the remedy.

Regarding these levels of coarseness and subtlety, there are three points concerning the non-giving of others from which one never takes anything oneself, analyzed through five conditions.

This "mind of volition" (cetanā) is precisely the essence of the karma of stealing.

it is coarse, vulgar, and must be permanently abandoned. Next, the following section explains the text concerning "improper conduct" (*agamyā*), which is divided into three parts:

first, an explanation through the contrast between other women and the wives of others; second, an explanation regarding those related by kinship; and third, an explanation based on identifying marks.

Regarding the "Threefold Protection" which explains the preceding words of the woman: first, the initial section sets forth the categories of the "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*) and the "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) as the headings.
The first heading, "shared protection," refers to the case of another's daughter, where there is the sense of mutual possession between oneself and others;
therefore, it is called "shared. The second heading, "unshared," refers to one's own wife or concubine, who is exclusively matched with oneself.
Since it has already been established that there is no principle for taking [a woman] as a common possession by either oneself or another, it is said that she is "not shared.

Next, this is explained: "Shared" refers back to the previous point; "protected by another" cites the scripture to clarify what is not shared; "another's wife" cites the scripture to specifically identify her.

Following the passage from the scripture below, the next section provides an explanation. Regarding "relatives by birth," the protection is indicated; first, the scriptural text concerning parents is cited.

"Relatives" (*jñāti*) refers to protection by kin; "clan" (*gotra*) refers to protection by lineage. Because one is not of a low clan when paired with a superior clan, it is called "protection by clan.

Regarding the explanation of the term *kṣetra* (field/land), it identifies that which is protected. Below, the sūtra provides the commentary: "a woman" (*stri*) refers back to the woman protected by another mentioned in the preceding sūtra.
Why is the word "person" (*puruṣa*) used instead of simply saying "woman"? Therefore, the following section explains this to exclude what is improper.
It is not out of fear of over-extending the definition to include all wood, stone, or women that we distinguish humans from these. "Human" (*pudgala*), "person," and "sentient being" are synonyms;
this category encompasses all realms of existence and is not restricted solely to the human path. Why was the protection by others not explained immediately previously, but only discussed here?
If the protection by relatives were not explained at this point, it would fail to manifest the specific nature of the person. Therefore, this is clarified now.
The commentary explains that the meaning of "person" (*pudgala*) is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "not at the proper time" (*akāla*), this refers to the second gate;

"time for the holy life" (*brahmacaryakāla*)—*brahma* being translated as "pure"—means constantly practicing pure precepts and never engaging in sexual misconduct. This can be understood from the application of the sutra text. Regarding the phrase "not in the proper place" (*adeśa*), this refers to the third gate;
"not by the proper way" refers to places such as the anus and so forth. According to this treatise, the term "not in the proper place" should be applied accordingly.

In this context, that sutra merely uses the subtle to illustrate the coarse; it is placed later only to clarify that [the former] was not for the sake of [the latter]. As stated in the following section of the sutra:
Third, we again cite the two preceding categories of the coarse and the subtle to demonstrate their ineffability. Regarding "subtle and coarse," we reiterate the meaning of the preceding category:
mental action (*manas-karman*) and bodily action (*kāya-karman*). We further cite the preceding explanation of their characteristics: mental action is what was previously called...
The mental and physical actions mentioned previously refer to the two kinds of detachment within the characteristics of the body; in contrast to these, detachment is manifested.
As stated in the sutra below, up to the point where it says "one does not give rise to thoughts or perceptions," this refers to transcending the coarse and elevating the subtle.

This phrase "up to" connects back to the previous section on detachment from mental action (*manas-karman*). How much more so for those of both sexes who, through their conduct, demonstrate detachment from physical action (*kāya-karman*)! This is the meaning.
If, when raising one's mind for even a single moment, there is already no such thought, how could there be the two physical forms of male and female to engage in the act of sexual misconduct?

How much more so in the case of an improper object (*agocara*)? Taking the right path as an analogy for the improper object: if one would not commit it even when the transgression on the right path is light, how much less would one do so when the transgression at an improper object is grave?
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Stages*, Scroll Three, End;
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Stages*, Scroll Four, Beginning (this scroll concludes with the Fourth Stage).
Compiled by Master Jingying Huiyuan.

Regarding "abstaining from false speech" and below, which concern abstaining from the four faults of speech: first, abstaining from false speech. In the sutra, the initial statement "abstaining from falsehood" is a general term;
that which does not accord with reality is called "false," and that which is spoken of is called "speech. To sever and eliminate this is called "abstaining.
"Always being truthful" and below are the specific [explanations].

In the treatise, the initial statement that "there are two ways of departing from delusion" cites the general principle and opens up the specific details; because within the verbal karma the cause and the remedy are combined, only two are mentioned.
Later, in the section on mental karma, there is only the remedy and no departure from delusion, as there is neither cause nor fruit for the mind, and no separate cause for speech.

This will be clarified in the subsequent discussion where it explains that the mind lacks both cause and fruit. Next, after listing the two names, the text provides a detailed analysis and explanation.

Regarding the "explanation of the remedy" (*pratipakṣa*), first, the explanation of the remedy is itself the cause of separation; subsequently, the explanation of the remedial text precedes the explanation of the remedy, which is itself the cause of separation.
Thus, the remedy within the cause of separation is collectively displayed as the cause. Why is this? Below, the question and answer provide a detailed explanation. One might ask:
"In all previous instances of bodily action, each had its own distinct cause; why is it said here that the cause is itself the remedy?"

The following response clarifies this by first providing a brief explanation and subsequently a detailed one. Within the brief explanation, it states that there are two causes for bodily action (*kāyakarman*) to clarify that the body differs from speech;

this refers to the two types of abstention regarding killing: the abstention from receiving and keeping [weapons] and the abstention from initiating [the act]. Regarding false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), the absence of "lower" [causes] demonstrates that speech differs from the body.

"There are no external objects" means there is no cause for receiving and keeping; "there is no cause for difference" clarifies that there is no distinct cause for the arising of such actions, such as greed (*lobha*).
Regarding the causes of volition (*cetanā*) within false speech, greed, hatred, and so forth are explained as its distinctions; this will be explained extensively below.

First, the extensive explanation of the absence of external and distinct causes; within that, there are two sections. The first clarifies that the body differs from the mouth, as in the case of abstaining from killing.
Within this, there are two types of causal reception. First, citing the aforementioned causes as they were explained: "abstaining from and discarding the blade."

Regarding the staff and the citation: having previously raised the point that there are two types of separation—separation from speech and separation from body—it is explained that within the context of false speech, there is no separation from the body.
This is because there are no external objects such as those two [implements], the sword and the staff; since these two do not exist, there is no cause for separation from them.

Below this, the text extensively explains the meaning of "no distinct cause" mentioned in the preceding section. Regarding "no distinct cause," the previous section is cited and then extensively explained. Within this, there are two parts; first, it says:
The killing of living beings through greed, hatred, and delusion explains how the body differs from speech; the two types of false speech below explain how speech differs from the body.
Within this, there are four sections: first, explaining the absence of distinct causes; second, establishing truthful speech by being free from those [causes];

third, establishing the absence of distinct separation based on what arises from them; fourth, the separation that is the antidote, which is itself the cause of separation, concluding with the absence of distinct separation.

Regarding the initial statement that false speech has "deception" as its cause: this is because the volition (*cetanā*) of the mind serves as the cause for speech; thus, it clarifies that non-attachment (*alobha*) and so forth function as distinct causes.

While afflictions such as greed (*lobha*) can give rise to all seven types of bodily and vocal karma, why then is it said that killing has greed as its cause and false speech has deception as its cause?
In reality, all karmas equally rely upon greed and other afflictions, and they share the same cause, which is volition.
However, because those various karmas arise with varying degrees of difficulty—since bodily karma is difficult to initiate, greed and so forth are clarified as its remote causes;
whereas mental and vocal karma are easy to manifest, volition (*cetanā*) is highlighted as their proximate cause for initiating karma.

This does not mean that afflictions (*kleśa*) are never causes at all. This second explanation is no different from the previous one regarding "separation," as it involves distancing oneself from them.
That is to say, truthful speech accomplishes clarity because its cause is "separation from [deception]," which is the antidote to separation.
This is because deception itself is the false cause; by abandoning that deceptive mind, one accomplishes truthful speech. Thus, truthful speech remedies the mind that deceives others.

Therefore, "separation" as the antidote is clarified as being identical to "separation" as the cause. Third, the conclusion establishes that there is no difference between them: based on that [antidote], this [cause] arises.
Therefore, there is no distinction, because this false speech arises based on that deceptive mind; thus, non-attachment and the other [wholesome roots] do not serve as distinct causes.

Fourth, the conclusion regarding the absence of distinction: In the section on "separation" (*viveka*), the antidotes are thus applied. That is, the separation from the cause is established because those antidotes are themselves separated from the cause;
they are not established separately. Above, the treatment was explained as being the separation from the cause; below, the text of the treatment is interpreted.
There are three types of speech: speech that accords with one's thoughts is speech that accords with the mind; as the Sūtra says, "truthful" means it does not contradict one's own mind.
Speech that results from careful reflection is speech that accords with the facts; as the Sūtra says, "real" means it is examined in accordance with the facts.
Speech that knows the proper time is speech free from faults; for there may be cases where the matter and the intent behind the words are both true, yet the words do not accord with the timing.
A Bodhisattva does not act otherwise; his speech is always appropriate to the occasion because it does not give rise to affliction for himself or others.
This indicates the preceding time [of speech]. Because he does not personally produce faults nor cause distress to others, it is said that "affliction does not arise.
The Sūtra speaks of "time," which refers to the time when neither oneself nor others are harmed. Regarding the separation from fruit and practice, first the coarse and subtle [aspects] are listed.
There are two ways of entering [the analysis]. Next, citing the sutra, we shall further distinguish the subtle [transgressions] within dreams.

Because speech is easily produced, even subtle mental transgressions are considered faults during dreams; thus they are termed "subtle. As for the fact that śrāvakas do not prohibit them while bodhisattvas avoid them even when awake—this can be understood.

Regarding those said to be "easy to recognize" through concealment and patience: although they are called easy to understand, they are still difficult to identify oneself; this is according to the *Vibhāṣā*.
Speaking falsely by concealing one's perception is called "concealing one's view. Speaking falsely by concealing one's mind is called "enduring one's view.

Regarding "concealing one's perception": this refers to concealing the object or event previously perceived. Having originally seen a certain thing, one’s own mind likewise gives rise to the thought that one truly saw it;
yet when asked by another whether one saw it, one answers, "I did not see it. This is a false speech in which the mind conceals and hides the matter one has personally perceived.
Therefore, it is said that "concealed seeing" refers to the mind that conceals itself yet is capable of seeing; though one originally does not see, one falsely gives rise to the perception of seeing.
When asked by another whether one sees, one answers, "I do not see. This false speech involves suppressing the mind that perceives within one's own house;
thus it is called "suppressing-seeing. The wisdom termed "seeing" cannot be illuminated by the eyes even in a dream.
Therefore, it is said that the discernment of cognition (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*), thought (*citta*), and perception (*mati*) is collectively termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*);

the act of illuminating is termed "vision" (*darśana*). Next, regarding the *Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka* on abandoning double-tongued speech: the initial statement "abandoning double-tongued speech" means that because words cause discord between this person and that, they are called "two";

because such words arise from the tongue, they are called "double-tongued. This phrase is the general [definition], while the subsequent sections provide the specific details. Regarding the first of these specific points:
The absence of breaking [the precepts], fearlessness, and the absence of a mind that causes affliction and disturbance constitute the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

Regarding "having heard this and below," this refers to the practice of the fruit (*phala-caryā*). "Being free from a mind that breaks [the precepts]" is the general summary within the antidotes. "A mind of harmony" is called "non-breaking.

"Fearlessness" and "the absence of a mind that causes affliction" are the specific details of the antidotes. Because one does not wish to cause others to have mutual fear, it is called "fearlessness"; because one does not wish to cause others... [to suffer].

Because they mutually afflict and disturb one another, it is called the "Treatise on Non-affliction" (*Anupaghāta-śāstra*). Within this, there are two parts: first, the general restatement followed by the detailed opening;

second, the enumeration of the two names followed by the extensive explanation and analysis. Regarding the first, the "non-destruction of practice," this means that the initial state of being unbroken, fearless, and non-afflicted is already included therein, and thus is not discussed separately.
Below, regarding the explanation of the "fruition-practice," the two names are first listed; the first is termed "mind" (*citta*).

The desire to transmit malicious words refers to the intention to cause division. Regarding the distinction of speech, it refers to the specific conceptualization at the very moment of causing division.
This is that which is to be abandoned; citing this serves to clarify the practice of abandonment. Below, first the section on "the mind" is explained, which is further divided into three parts:
(1) clarifying double-tongued speech; (2) attributing the fault to the mind; and (3) citing the sutra to demonstrate the abandonment of following what one has heard to others elsewhere.
"Speaking in another place" refers to the first phrase. "According to what one has heard" refers to the fault of the mind; this text is insufficient, for it should state:
"according to what one has heard, the mind receives and retains it," meaning that having heard the malicious words of both parties, one retains them in the inner mind with the intent to recount them.
"Going to another place" refers to the fault of the body; for the sake of recounting [the matter], the body goes there.

Regarding what was said about going to another place, this refers to the fault of speech. This second phrase below, concerning these two groups, restates the previous instance of divisive speech (*paiśunya*) and attributes the resulting fault to the mind.
"These two groups" restates going to another place for the purpose of causing dissension;

going there in person and feigning friendship toward both factions is called "the two kinds of groups. "The mind receives and retains" restates following what one has heard in order to cause division.

"Because it is destroyed," refers to the verbal karma of reciting and speaking what one has heard and retained; this reiterates what was previously stated. "Destroying the mind" attributes the fault to the mind.
Thus, the body follows the mind, the mind remembers, and the mouth speaks; because the mind is destroyed, as in the following sutra passage.

This is the third phrase, which cites the sutra to demonstrate detachment and clarify the absence of a destructive mind. "One who hears this does not speak it to another" correctly demonstrates the separation from both.

Regarding the tongue, as for the statement in the preceding text that "it goes to other places and speaks according to what it has heard, thereby causing destruction," the reason for not stating this is out of fear that the person before whom these evil words are spoken might be harmed or distressed by them, thereby causing their own ruin;

therefore, it is not stated in contrast to the "mind of destruction" mentioned in the preceding text. Why is it that the mental recollection and verbal expression of the two factions [of friends] are not discussed?

Regarding this phrase, since it merely restates what preceded it and contains no further distinct meaning, it is not addressed separately; that he did not speak [of other categories] can be understood by analogy with this.

Within the explanation of the distinctions, there are three separate points: first, citing the number based on the faults; second, listing the names based on the faults; and third, the analysis of the terms. Regarding "the destruction of the body" (*kāyabhedo*):

because one who has spoken their own words incites others to separate from them, it is called the "destruction of the body. Regarding "the destruction of the mind" (*cittabhedo*), it refers to the breaking [of the mind].

Regarding the meaning of "corruption" (*bhedana*): what is the difference between this and the previous "mind"? As for the "mind" mentioned previously, it refers to receiving harsh words from another and intending to propagate those words;
whereas the "mind" here refers to following that which is corrupted with the intent to cause separation—this is the distinction.
Regarding "corruption by action" (*karmabhedana*), it refers to corrupting others through verbal action by propagating malicious speech between them; therefore, it is called corruption by action.

What is the difference between "the destruction of the previous body" (*pūrvakāya-vināśa*) and "this present karma"? The former refers to causing others to break apart by proclaiming malicious words against them;
the latter refers to personally urging a separation rather than transmitting malicious words—this is the distinction.

Third, the detailed explanation cites the sutra to clarify that there are two types of "destruction of the body": first, the enumeration is stated as a heading, and then the categories of "not yet destroyed" and "already destroyed" are listed.

The second [category] is named "This Treatment" (*idaṃ-pratipakṣa*). Below this, the sūtra is cited to demonstrate the abandonment [of these faults]. First, regarding those who are already in agreement, one does not encourage their separation;

second, regarding those whose [relationship] has already been broken, one does not encourage further deterioration of the mind. These two points are restated to enumerate the categories, followed by the explanation of their characteristics.

This "Treatment" and below cite the sūtra to demonstrate the abandonment of the destruction of karma (*karma-bheda*). This also consists of two parts: first, the enumeration is restated, and then the names of the subtle and coarse [faults] are listed in reality.
Regarding "unreal" (*asatya*): this reveals that the fault of transmitting to others what one has heard as real speech is "subtle" because it is light;

whereas the fault of falsely fabricating it oneself is "gross" because it is heavy. Having explained this remedy, the following section cites the sūtra to demonstrate the abandonment of "not wishing to speak.

"Not wishing to speak" means not wishing to speak the real speech regarding what another has done; this remedies the aforementioned subtle fault. "Not wishing to act" means not personally fabricating it oneself.

This harsh speech is a corrective for the previous coarse speech. If the words were true, it would mean that such speech actually exists; however, the Bodhisattva does not speak of it, thereby revealing that the previous statement regarding non-speech was untrue.

If the words were false, it would mean that such speech does not actually exist; however, the Bodhisattva does not act upon it, thereby revealing that the previous statement regarding non-action was untrue.
These two pairs correspond to the aforementioned true and untrue speech.
Next, regarding the *Sūtra on Abandoning Harsh Speech*, the initial statement "abandoning harsh speech" is explained as follows: words that are coarse and vulgar are termed "evil" (*pāruṣya*);
because this evil issues from the mouth, it is called "harsh speech. This phrase is the general heading. Within the subsequent specific sections, there are two parts:
first, it clarifies the excellence and pleasantness of the fruit of the practice; second, it clarifies its antidote. Among all other verbal karmas, each begins by clarifying the antidote.
Now, for what reason is the fruit of practice (*phala-caryā*) explained first? To explain why it is not the sequence of cultivation, one might say that the explanation is concluded here;

furthermore, because the fruits of the various counteractive practices (*pratipakṣa*) are not sequentially correlated with one another, the clarification of the remedies is presented first, followed by the manifestation of the fruits.
Moreover, since these present counteractive practices are individually and specifically correlated with those fruits, the fruits are mentioned first.

Next, regarding the section on the practice of the fruit prior to the Meiji era, the initial part clarifies the practice of the fruit as described above; this concludes the clarification of the departure [from delusion] concerning the practice of the fruit.
Within this practice of the fruit, there are sixteen phrases. The meaning of their being of the same essence (*samatā*) is distinguished, rather than having separate essences.

These sixteen phrases are subsumed into four divisions: the first four constitute one division where the essence of the words is coarse and vulgar; the next four constitute one division that manifests the time of those words.
There are degrees of gravity regarding the faults of manifesting or not manifesting [the three types of misconduct]. Regarding the three categories of speech that can contradict conduct:
the first two types of speech contradict one's own and others' conduct; the last one, speech characterized by anger and vexation, contradicts the conduct of others and oneself.

Regarding the five categories of speech that can contradict feelings: the first four involve turning joy into anger; the final phrase contradicts happiness and leads to suffering. As for the preceding [analysis]:

Regarding the four [states]—the fire of the mind, the heat of the mind, the actual arising of anger, and the hearing [of the object]: when hearing it, the fire of the mind arises; when recollecting it, the mind becomes hot.
One does not love or delight in it, which explains the reason for abandoning anger. Because one does not love it upon hearing it, the fire of the mind burns;

because one does not delight in it upon recollecting it, the mind becomes hot and afflicted. These four phrases are not fixed in their sequence; here, the fire of the mind and the heat of the mind are explained first, followed by the manifestation [of the others].

Regarding "non-affection" (*apriya*) and "displeasure" (*arati*), in the commentary of the *Śāstra*, "mental fire" (*cittāgni*) is explained first; "non-affection" and "displeasure" are explained in the middle;

and "mental fever" (*cittopatāpa*) is explained last. In the subsequent section on remedies, there is a distinction: first, non-affection and displeasure are remedied, and subsequently, mental fire and mental fever are remedied.
In the final phrase, the term "unwholesome" (*akuśala*) directly indicates [the nature of the afflictions].
The essence of speech is capable of causing harm and obstruction; because it can cause harm and obstruction, it is called "unwholesome.

To destroy oneself and to destroy others, manifesting the characteristics of unwholesomeness by uttering evil words—such that when others hear them they turn away from oneself, one loses one's companions, which is termed "self-destruction";

and when others lose their friendship with me, it is termed "destroying others. As for the antidote, it is that which is free from these [faults], being beautiful, sublime, and pleasing to the ear. This generally clarifies the antidote, namely:

The following section provides a detailed explanation of the "lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). Regarding the first of these, within the general excellence, the essence is subtle and delightful, pleasing to the ear and harmonious with the mind.
Within this detailed exposition, there are twelve phrases according to their respective meanings. First, regarding the meaning of "essence": it does not mean that the essence itself is distinct;

rather, based on the preceding [analysis of] fruits and practices, they are subsumed into four. "Beneficial moisture" constitutes one phrase. As for the essence of speech being "gentle and soft," this corresponds to the first four phrases among the fruits and practices—namely, "gentle speech."

Exquisite speech (*suvaca*) is the second [of the four types of speech] among the practices corresponding to the fruit; it consists of words that are pleasant to hear, delightful to hear, enter the mind, and accord with reason.
Pleasant speech (*priyavāda*) is the third [of the three types of speech] among the practices corresponding to the fruit;

it consists of words that are pleasant to hear as opposed to those unpleasant to hear, delightful to hear as opposed to those not delightful to hear, and accord with reason as opposed to angry and vexing speech. It is for the sake of many people.
The final five [of the ten] constitute the fourth section, concerning the practice directed toward the fruit.

Within these, the first four reverse anger to produce joy, while the final one brings about happiness by overcoming suffering. Regarding the former four, they consist of speech that many people cherish and speech that many people delight in;

the reason they produce joy is that they remedy the previously mentioned speech that is neither cherished nor delightful. "Peaceful mind" (*citta-sānta*) and "joyful mind" (*citta-prāmodya*) precisely clarify this.
Regarding the phrase "producing joy," it refers to the sequence of speech that remedies the preceding mental fires of heat and affliction.
Among these, the final phrase—“that which can produce joy in one’s own mind and the minds of others”—is contrasted with the preceding speech that ruins oneself and ruins others.

Because one utters wholesome words, others come to associate with oneself, and by gaining such virtuous friends, one’s own mind experiences joy. This remedies the preceding state of self-destruction; because those [others] obtain me as a friend, they too experience joy.
To delight in speech that previously damaged the respect and faith of others is unwholesome.

This is because wholesome words are worthy of honor and trust, thereby giving rise to joy in one's own mind and the minds of others. In the concluding summary, "always speaking" means that one's speech is constantly wholesome;
"various kinds" means that wholesome speech is complete.

In the treatise, there are two sections: first, citing the headings to enumerate the items and listing their names; second, providing a detailed explanation of them. Regarding the first section, which involves the citation, it is explained extensively below.

Within that, one first explains the "fruits of action" (*phala-caryā*) and subsequently explains the meaning of "separation. In the explanation of the fruits of action, the first four items are explained together in a single passage.
Within this, one first explains "harming others. This refers to the initial category: "invasive, afflictive, and harsh speech that causes suffering to others."

This explains the speech that causes others to become angry and resentful. Next, using the sutra as a topical marker (*pāṭha*), the following section provides a detailed analysis of the sequence of these phrases.
First, "harming" (*viheṭhanā*) is cited because it is precisely the fault of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).

What kind of speech is harmful? It is coarse and abrasive speech (*pāruṣyavāk*). What constitutes being coarse and abrasive? It is that which causes suffering to others. What is meant by causing suffering to others?

The statement "he who is angry" is an explanation by means of synonyms (*paryāya*) for the four preceding types of characteristics. Because the meaning is one while the names differ, there is an explanation through synonyms.
This means that while the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the meaning is one, it manifests as different faults;

thus, although the names are divided into four distinct categories, the meaning is not merely that the four preceding meanings are one while the names differ—the meaning of the sixteen types of harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) is likewise not different. The subsequent four constitute a single section.
This is explained in one section. Within it, first, "confrontational speech" (*pratyakṣavāda*) is explained as speech that is present before one's face;

"non-confrontational speech" is explained as speech that is not present before one's face; "harsh speech" is explained as vile and evil speech; and "constant speech" is explained as uninterrupted speech.

Next, the sūtra is cited below for further detailed classification: therein, "present" refers back to speech that is present before one's face, and "vile and uninterrupted" refers to [the aforementioned qualities].

Because the verbal expressions directed toward another are coarse and heavy, they are called "harsh" (*pāruṣya*). Because they can act as a screen even when face-to-face and are constantly uttered, they are called "uninterrupted" (*anantarya*) and "not manifest" (*apratyakṣa*).
When it is stated that there is a slight interruption in what precedes, this is done by citing the subtle to reveal the coarse;

the opposite case can be understood accordingly. Based on this, one may verify the sūtra: the sūtra should also have stated that there is a slight interruption, but it was not mentioned because it is light. This applies to the next three sections as well.
In this section providing an explanation, first the [first] two [factors] are analyzed. Regarding "initially speaking thus" in reference to that which contradicts the precepts:
"speaking thus" refers back to what was previously stated. In general, it refers back to both manifest and non-manifest speech that is harsh and uninterrupted;
specifically, it refers back only to manifest, present speech that is harsh and uninterrupted. By means of this, one afflicts others.

Therefore, by violating one’s own precepts, one gives rise to suffering that provokes anger in others; this explains how [anger] subsequently fulfills the preceding [condition]. Because one was displeased at the time of hearing [the words], one causes suffering to arise in others;

because one was unhappy when recollecting them, one causes others to become angry. Since causing others to experience the suffering of anger violates one’s own precepts—just as the sutra’s subsequent sections state:

"displeasure" refers to suffering, and "unhappiness" refers to anger—the following explanation clarifies that by provoking anger and affliction, one violates the precepts of others and utters harmful speech.
Regarding "causing others to violate their precepts through anger and envy": anger and envy are one's own states of mental affliction;
based upon this mind, one utters evil words that cause others to become angry and afflicted, thereby causing them to violate their precepts. Below, the sūtra provides a gloss:

"afflicted speech" refers to speech arising from a state of mental affliction within one's own home that causes others to become angry and afflicted; this is called afflicted speech. The latter five [points] are as follows.

Section One: Distinguishing and Explaining the Two Causes of Others’ Anger. This section consists of two parts: first, restating the preceding [section] and opening the subsequent one; second, explaining that the first four items constitute a single category while the final one constitutes another.

Because the former causes anger to arise where there was joy, and the latter results in suffering where there was pleasure, it is said there are "two. Regarding "unbeneficial matters," the following explains their characteristics.

First, the first four are explained: causing those who were not yet angry to become angry. This refers to the fire of the mind; because anger arises upon first hearing [the words], it is called "not yet" (i.e., previously).
Birth can give rise to anger; at the time of hearing and at the time of recollecting, there is no love and no joy. This explains the latter two [terms].

"At the time of hearing there is no love" explains the absence of affection for the speech; that is, at the initial moment of hearing, it is not something to be cherished, which completes the "fire of the preceding mind.

"At the time of recollecting there is no joy" explains the absence of delight in the speech; that is, when recollecting repeatedly, it is not something to be craved or enjoyed, which completes the "heat of the subsequent mind," whereby the chest and heart are constricted.

The term "desirable" (*iṣṭa*) refers to *nirvāṇa*; being free from peril, it is called "peaceful" (*kṣema*). From within the preceding category of the "desirable," these two [the desirable and the peaceful] are distinguished;
because they are both subsumed under the general name "desirable," they are so designated. Below, their characteristics are explained:

"desirable" reiterates the former category, referring to those who follow the paths of humans and gods, which describes the wholesome dharmas of the world that give rise to the two kinds of fruits pertaining to humans and gods. "Peaceful" reiterates the latter category, referring to those who follow *nirvāṇa*.

This explains that which is supramundane, wholesome, and conducive to *nirvāṇa*. Below, the sūtra provides the following applications: "delight in hearing" (*śrutautsukya*), "delight in wishing to hear" (*śrotukāmatā*), and "delight in entering the mind" (*cittapraveśautsukya*).
Regarding the preceding [section], it is "conducive to humans and devas" and "conducive to principle. Regarding the latter, it is "conducive to *nirvāṇa*.

Within these five phrases, the first two explain the causes for the arising of delight and the arising of joy; they are explained in one place. [The remaining three] explain the many types of persons—enemies, relatives, and neutral persons.

It is also said that "when hearing, joy arises" (*śrutvā prītir jāyate*) and "when recollecting, joy arises" (*smṛtvā prītir jāyate*); these phrases from the *Sukha-vihāra-sūtra* can be understood accordingly.
Below, the three [sections] correctly clarify the arising of joy and the arising of bliss, explaining them together in one place.

This statement, "this speech can produce two kinds of benefit," reiterates what precedes and introduces what follows; it means that the aforementioned speech of affection, joy, and delight can produce the two kinds of benefit: joy and bliss.
Below there are three phrases: the first two produce joy (*prīti*) and are combined as one benefit; the last one produces bliss (*sukha*) and constitutes a single benefit.
The following provides a detailed explanation: "Causing others who have not yet produced anger not to produce it" explains pleasant speech (*sākhilya-vāk*).
"Anger not arising when one has not yet become angry" explains a peaceful mind (*citta-sāntva*). "Producing joy" explains a gladdened mind (*citta-prāmodya*). Furthermore, three [benefits] arise.
The commentary explains that the mind becomes universally joyful; because the mind is joyful, the body experiences pliancy and bliss;

because the body experiences pliancy and bliss, one is able to give rise to samādhi. These two [joy and bliss] arise sequentially: first joy is produced, and subsequently bliss is explained as being produced through intimacy.
This is because hearing wholesome words, one becomes intimate with the Bodhisattva; thus, through the intimacy of friendship and harmony, joy arises within one's own person.
The following explains the phrase "reverent faith. It is because the essence of speech is worthy of reverence and faith that one manifests it oneself and others likewise revere and believe it;
when one transmits one's own words to others, they too revere and believe them. Because of this reverence and faith, [the mind] becomes intimate. The subsequent lines apply the Sūtra:
"a mind of harmony and joy" refers to ensuring that anger which has not yet arisen does not arise, and causing joy to be produced. "Universal gladness" refers to the subsequent arising of *samādhi*.

Furthermore, the sections concerning "the joy of oneself and others," "those previously born with whom one was intimate, respectful, and trusting," and "the constant discourse on what one currently does for oneself and others" are the concluding remarks of the preceding text;
that they were not explained earlier was not because they were not part of the text, but because they were brought up by way of momentum following the previous discussion.
In the *Prapañca-vivāda-sūtra*, one who abandons frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) is so called because their words are improper, much like variegated colors; thus it is named "frivolous.

Because such speech involves various discourses, it is termed "frivolous speech" (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). This phrase is the general definition, while "well-considered" (*su-cintita*) and what follows are the specific details.
Within the treatise, there are two sections: first, citing the headings to enumerate the items and listing the two names;

second, providing a detailed explanation and analysis of them. Regarding the first section, there are nine distinct phrases which, when grouped together, form three parts: the first two concern "teaching" (*śāsanā*), instructing and transforming others so that they may give rise to faith;

the next three concern "instruction" (*avavādā*), teaching and directing them to initiate practice; and the final four concern "admonition" (*anuśāsanā*), earnestly exhorting them to perfect their virtues. Within the first of these [three], the initial phrase is now explained.

Later, by means of the sutra passage, it is explained that "knowing well the time for speaking" refers to relying on both others and oneself. This clarifies that when speech is appropriate, there is no harm to self or others and wholesome dharmas arise;
this is called the "time for speaking. Because one constantly contemplates this time, it is said that one "knows well.

This interpretation explains that "constantly contemplating" means relying on both others and oneself. This is the explanation of "speech": "others" refers to sentient beings, and "oneself" refers to the individual; thus, it means relying on both others and oneself.
Beneficial dialects that are not unbeneficial and do not constitute speech of inferior timing clarify the essence of transformative speech.

The initial statement, "exhortation and arousal," refers to the time of uttering words to encourage the recollection and practice [of the Dharma]. "Exhortation" (kuan-fa) refers to the beginning; it means encouraging others to abandon evil and arousing them to cultivate goodness, which is termed "exhortation.
Generally speaking, the meaning is consistent; "recollection" (yi-nian) follows next, as it relies upon that exhortation for those sentient beings.
To gather all dharmas within the mind is called "recollection" (*smṛti*); to cultivate practice based on what has been recollected is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
From "If one sees... onwards, this correctly clarifies the transformative speech: "seeing" refers to the teaching to abandon evil so that one does not continue it;

"abiding securely in wholesome states" refers to transforming beings toward goodness. From "At that time... onwards is the conclusion: "at that time" concludes the preceding exhortation to initiate cultivation, while "transformative teaching" concludes the subsequent [section].
It causes non-virtuous sentient beings to abandon [non-virtue] and abide in virtue. The lower section applies the sūtra to the constant reflection;

the preceding "knowing" refers to the time of speaking, while the subsequent "speech" applies to the time of addressing others. It exhorts them toward practice so that they may abandon non-virtue and dwell securely in virtue.
Within the lower section on instruction, there is first the explanation and then the application. Furthermore, "not inverted" explains truthful speech in contrast to the aforementioned teaching.

It is called "repetition" (*punaḥ*) because it refers to conduct and demeanor; it is said to be "non-perverted" (*aviparīta*) because it bestows actual benefit. This phrase is the general [statement], while the subsequent sections are the specific [explanations].

It is the time when speech is uttered through successive instruction. Because one first received instruction from others and now, in turn, instructs others, it is called "successive instruction" (*pāramparyopadeśa*).

Because it inspires the arising of wholesome conduct and admonishes one to depart from evil, it is termed "instruction" (*upadeśa*). These two terms refer to both the meaning (*artha*) and the dharma (*dharma*).

This clearly explains that the instruction on exhorting oneself to undertake practice is termed "words of meaning" (*arthavāda*). "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to benefit; because they are able to benefit sentient beings, they are called "words of meaning.

Once one has received this exhortation and desires to initiate practice, yet does not know the method for practicing, the proclamation of the methods for practice found within the sūtras and their transmission to others is termed "words of dharma" (*dharmavāda*).
Below, the sūtra is cited to substantiate the reality [of these words], while the non-erroneous meaning is cited to substantiate the "words of meaning."
In the section on "Dharma-Edicts" and "Dharma-Speech" regarding the administration of instruction, there are five distinctions according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:

(1) prohibition (*niyama*), (2) permission (*anujñā*), (3) formal censure (*codanā*), (4) subduing (*nigraha*), and (5) causing joy (*saṃpraharṣaṇa*). That treatise explains: "One prohibits those who have committed offenses and permits those who have not.
Regarding prohibitions and permissions, one should formally censure according to the Dharma those who violate them; for those who repeatedly commit transgressions, one should apply subduing."
Regarding the four lines beginning with "When one remembers those who possess real virtue, one should praise them so as to gladden them": the first two lines are general;

if distinguished specifically, the first line presents [the subject] while the latter line effects subduing. Within the latter two lines, the first line concerns listening, while the latter line concerns gladdening.
As for the first two lines, which govern the meaning of transgressions, they are explained together in one place. Within this, first there is the explanation, followed by the citation of the sutra.
Regarding the "mutual" (*kṣepa-kṣepa*) method for settling disputes through the accusation of offenses during the time of training: when speech is uttered, there may be both offense and dispute;

because they mutually accuse and settle one another, it is called "mutual. Seeing that another has committed a transgression and accusing them according to the Dharma is termed "accusing of an offense" (*āpatti-udbhāvana*).

This is to manifest their fault in order to expel them. As stated in the Vinaya: if one does not see [the fault], does not repent, or if evil views are not eliminated, one shall accuse and cast them out from the assembly.
To govern others externally and now to bring this person to light for the purpose of removing their offense—this is the first instance of speech that accords with the Path.
When it is said that "disputes are extinguished," it means that when the four types of disputes arise, they are pacified and eliminated in accordance with the Teaching;

this is the second instance of Vinaya speech. Regarding the phrase "at the time of training and practice," the preceding two are collectively termed the "time of training. This is because [the offense] has been formally raised...
The path that causes cessation to increase is called the "practice of training. At such times, speaking in accordance with the Dharma (*yathādharma*) is the essence of correct speech;

speaking in accordance with the Dharma refers specifically to the speech used when censuring faults. Because one censures faults while being fully endowed with virtue, it is called "in accordance with the Dharma.

There are five distinct virtues: namely, acting with a mind of loving-kindness rather than with anger; benefiting others rather than harming them; being gentle rather than coarse; and being truthful [rather than false].
Knowing the proper time through non-delusion and not acting at an improper time—possessing these five virtues is called *āgama* in accordance with the Dharma;

this is the discourse for settling disputes. Settling disputes by relying on the teaching is termed *āgama*. Below, the Sūtra provides a topical summary (*uddāna*) that accords with the Path, which summarizes the preceding discourse in accordance with the Dharma.
These five virtues constitute the Path; to rely upon them when raising a charge is termed "accordance" (*anuloma*). This is the topical summary of the Vinaya.

The first phrase refers to the *Āgama*, meaning that the teaching capable of extinguishing disputes is called *Vinaya*. The following two phrases—“listening” (*śruta*) and “the good meaning” (*artha*)—are explained together as a single unit;
first they are explained individually and then summarized. Regarding the term “words of inclusion” (*parigraha-vākya*), this is a brief explanation.

The latter two refer to the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma to include and sustain sentient beings, which is termed “words of inclusion. The subsequent detailed explanation of the latter two concerns the inclusion through the preaching of the Dharma.

This refers to the time when [the Buddha] initiates speech. Because the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to gather in sentient beings and cause them to initiate practice, it is said that he "preaches the Dharma to gather in and lead them to cultivation.

The practice that arises from birth and brings benefit is called "meaning" (*artha*); because it is intended to bring joy, its cultivation is described through various metaphors, which is termed "speech conforming to meaning" (*anulomārthavāda*).

Below, this is applied by means of scriptural citations (*sūtra-paṭṭhāna*), weighing them according to the occasion; applying them to proper deportment (*īryāpatha*), and applying them to knowing well the inclinations of the mind.

Regarding the explanation of "speech conforming to meaning," within the section on the fruit of practice (*phala-caryā*), there are two types of fruit-practice: first, the enumeration is set forth by citing the number; second, they are listed in terms of their coarse and subtle aspects.

The name "Distant" (Dūra) below clarifies the departure from frivolity, as in the sutra passage below which states: "One does not engage in frivolous or ornate speech," thereby clarifying the departure from subtle [faults].

Furthermore, the phrase "much less intentionally" clarifies the departure from coarse [faults]. This text is inverted; if it were correct, it should say: "Even one does not engage in frivolous or ornate speech, much less intentionally.
Since even light [faults] are not committed, how could there be intentional acts that cause distress? Light [faults] are still not committed; how much more so those that cause turmoil?
[One engages] in frivolous speech with the mind.

Regarding the abandonment of greed, among the lower three [unwholesome paths], one first clarifies the abandonment of the three mental perversions; therein, only the antidotes for abandoning [greed] are clarified.

Subsequently, the same applies to the categories such as non-anger and so forth. Furthermore, among the various courses of action (*karmapatha*), there is also a gradation of priority; first, within the bodily actions—
Regarding the three types of abstention from the four verbal karmas, there is no distinct cause for "abstention with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa-virati);

regarding the two types of mental karma-paths, there is only "abstention through antidote" (pratipakṣa-virati) and "abstention without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa-virati). This is because greed and the other roots of karma have no further basis;

thus, they are not "resultant conduct" (*phala-caryā*). Since they are not results, it is impossible to establish a distinct cause in opposition to them; therefore, there is no "causal conduct" (*hetu-caryā*).
Because it is not a fruit, that which is free from greed and the like is not called "separation from the fruit. Because there is no cause [for its non-existence], it cannot be removed;

thus it is taught as being "separated from the cause. The Sūtra states that "separation from greed" generally clarifies that the absence of seeking desire is called "the abandonment of greed," while "separation from others" refers to specific instances below.

In this treatise, there are three sections: first, citing the enumeration to state the number; second, listing the three names; and third, explaining the "object" (*vastu*). Regarding "object," it distinguishes another's property from one's own wealth.
Regarding "the entity of the object" (*vastutva*), it identifies the specific substance of that which is craved. These two constitute the objects of craving.
While craving actually extends to matters such as wealth and sensual pleasures (*kāma*), here it is discussed specifically in relation to wealth. As for the term "distinction" (*viśeṣa*):
The non-greedy mind: within the middle phrase of "non-greedy mind," there are four distinct sections. The first is the general [explanation], while the latter three are the specific [explanations].

Because they are presented according to their distinctions, they are called "differentiated. Regarding the matter of the extensive explanation below, it comprises the functions and restates the initial general explanation.

Within this, there are two further specific [sections]. Having stated the number, the "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) section lists their names; the "appropriation" (*parigraha*) section concerns the utilization [of these names].

Regarding the perception of "presently protecting material wealth": although the objects are not currently manifest, they belong to someone else; one causes that person to protect them by formally entrusting them.

Second, there are two [types of] "use" (*paribhoga*), which are enumerated and explained below. As for "use," it refers to gold, silver, and so forth—objects that cannot directly sustain the body but can be utilized.
As for "sustenance" (*upabhoga*), it refers to food, clothing, and so forth, which can directly support the internal retribution (*ātmabhāva*).
It is called "the nature of non-greed regarding requisites. The following explains the third section of the sutra, which first presents a general statement and then specific details.
First, "the nature of non-greed" reiterates the initial general statement; since this general non-greed is the essence of non-greed, it is termed "nature.
"Counteracting greed" generally clarifies the state of detachment. Below, the remaining specific phrases are explained; there are four such parts, the first of which is a brief enumeration.

This refers to the three types of greed categorized according to their specific meanings as the antidotes to them: first, the initial seeking is called "desire" (*kāma*); second, the wish for it to belong to oneself upon attainment is called "acquisition" (*lābha*);
and third, the final thought of taking it away is designated as "seizure" (*ādāna*). These three distinctions are termed "gateways" (*dvāra*).

Furthermore, because they can collectively bring about the karma of theft, they are called "gateways"; because they arise together, they are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*); and because they can initiate the karma of theft, they are called "formations."

Third, regarding the antidotes, the sutra reveals these antidotes by distinguishing between the lower and the uplifting. Among these, the first two faults of the lower realm of concentration—the subtle—are described as "subtle" because they are difficult to separate from;
the latter one fault, being more grave, is described as "coarse."
In the *Vairāgya-sūtra*, "freedom from hatred" (*vairāgya*) is the general term for the abandonment of anger; "the severance of hatred" refers to freedom from all [forms of it].

Within the subsequent specific sections, there are three parts: first, six phrases concerning the mind that remedies hatred; second, the section beginning with "resentment" which clarifies the obstacles to freedom from hatred;
and third, the section beginning with "whatever" which concerns the benefits of the remedial practice.

In the treatise, the section explaining the mind of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-citta*) first has two distinct parts. First, it provides a general clarification that the counteractions pertain to five types of sentient beings.
As will be shown in the text below, there are six types of sentient beings, and the counteracting minds are likewise six; why, then, does this passage speak only of five?
It is because the two minds that arise toward those who are impoverished and those who are suffering are combined into one, and thus they are said to be five.
Second, by separately citing the five types of beings and contrasting them with their respective antidotes, one reveals the method for subduing enemies:

for those who provoke resentment, one cites the generation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as the antidote to reveal the subduing of enmity, because such people are characterized by much anger; thus, one generates a mind of loving-kindness, as shown in the subsequent passage of the sutra.

Regarding evil sentient beings, one cites the generation of peace and security (*kṣema*); this cites the sutra to reveal the subduing of desire, seeking to transform them through goodness so that they may be led away from it.
Because of fear and dread, it is called "settling the mind. Regarding those who are poor and suffering:

to cite their circumstances, a lack of favorable conditions (*anuloma-pratyaya*) is termed "poverty," while being oppressed by adverse conditions (*pratiloma-pratyaya*) is described as "suffering. As for the mind of compassion and joy, the Sūtra is cited to clarify their remedies.

However, these two minds, when considered in relation to that poverty and suffering, have both general and specific meanings. Generally, these two minds arise together toward them; specifically, however—
Previously, compassion was directed exclusively toward the poor and the desire for happiness was directed exclusively toward suffering beings; now, the universal application is established.
Regarding those who seek happiness, one must benefit them in the very areas where they are attached; since they already possess their own happiness, what need is there to provide further profit?
Because they are negligent and defiled by afflictions, the mind that seeks to provide profit is illustrated by citing the sutra to demonstrate its remedy through virtue.

To cause [beings] to abandon negligence through benefit is called "profitable profit. When sentient beings give rise to the resolve for awakening, one inspires them by describing their deeds, causing them to conceive the intent of the three vehicles;
this is collectively termed "arousing the resolve. This birth is precisely the point where the Bodhisattva’s benefit is applied, designated as that which is required within the course of practice.

Because of weariness, one must provide benefit; for if they were to arouse the resolve on their own, what need would there be for further assistance? It is because of such weariness that the three vehicles [are established].

The Way is called "immeasurable practice. When sentient beings who have resolved their minds on awakening repeatedly give rise to indolence and retreat within this practice, it is termed "diligent weariness" (*sāta-parikheda*);
here, *sāta* means "repeatedly," just as in the three obstacles, the repeated arising of afflictions is termed *sāta*. Regarding "gathering and benefiting":
the sutra cites this to manifest the remedy for gathering those weary sentient beings; initiating the Path for them is termed "benefit. Now, this...
Among the five [objects], those who are enemies, those who commit evil deeds, and sentient beings suffering from poverty must be benefited exclusively;

therefore, it does not clarify that they must be "benefited" (hita) [in the sense of being made happy]. This is because joy and the initial arousal of the bodhicitta already involve a preference for goodness that manifests the meaning of benefit (*hita*). For this reason, it is necessary to clarify "beneficiality" (*artha*).
Following this, the text explains the distancing from the obstacle of anger (*dveṣa-āvaraṇa*); therein, it first analyzes malice, resentment, envy, harm, and false conceptualization.

Regarding the meaning of "defilements" (*mala*), following the explanation of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the subsequent explanation of "all" (*sarva*) is as follows. First, there are five pairs established in relation to their respective practices, which constitute obstacles:

namely, the six types of obstacles to the six qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Second, regarding the relationship between obstacles and their remedies, it is clarified that these apply generally rather than specifically;

that is, the six obstacles obstruct the six remedies collectively, not by way of specific individual correspondences. "Not individually" means they are not distinct from one another; "not common" means they do not pertain to both [the remedy and the obstacle] simultaneously. "Not two" refers to the three types of obstacles.

They are collectively obstructed by a single remedy, not by two or three; since they are collectively remedied by a single [antidote], they are not distinct. "Not one-to-one" means they do not correspond individually.
These six types of obstacles are not matched one-to-one with the six minds. This is explained in detail within these six statements, which are subsumed into three pairs.
The first pair—taking oneself as the point of reference relative to others—clarifies the nature of hatred, resentment, and enmity in contrast to intimacy.

Because they are explained with reference to oneself, the next two pairs are interpreted solely in relation to oneself to clarify envy (*īrṣyā*) and malice (*pradāśa*); the latter two pairs are explained solely in relation to others to reveal the defilements of falsehood (*mṛṣā*).

Within the first pair, the arising of resentment toward those who have not yet caused harm is called anger (*krodha*), while harboring a grudge against those who have already caused harm and increasing that grudge once it has arisen is also anger;
however, this does not apply to those who have not yet become kin, nor to the non-arising or non-increasing of a grudge once it has arisen.
This is resentment (*upanāha*). Within the second pair, that which obstructs the good is called envy (*īrṣyā*), and that which increases evil is called malice (*vihiṃsā*).
That good dharmas have not yet arisen and do not arise, or that those already arisen are caused to perish, is the fault of envy.

That unwholesome dharmas have not yet arisen and do arise, or that those already arisen increase, is the fault of malice. Within the third pair, causing others suffering and destroying their happiness is called defilement (*daurmanasya*).
To cause that which is undesirable in another’s body to arise when it has not yet arisen, or to cause it to increase once it has already arisen, is deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Regarding suffering, because one desires to cause others to suffer through undesirable things—thereby causing them to decline and fall below oneself—it is an extreme perversion and confusion;

among all faults, it is the most grave, and thus it is specifically termed "deluded conceptualization. Furthermore, regarding that which is desirable in another’s body, one does not wish for it to arise when it has not yet arisen.

That which has already arisen does not increase—this is its defilement (*mala*). To envy excellence is a defilement. The above constitutes the third section: the detailed explanation according to the text.

Fourth, [the section] on applying the sūtra and correlating it with the treatise to clarify their sequence: this means that the six phrases of the text in this sūtra were explained in the preceding treatise in their respective order.
Below is the explanation of the word "etc. (*ādi*): these evil practices, such as hatred (*dveṣa*), are the root.
Because these six types, such as anger and so forth, can produce immeasurable afflictions and evil karma, they are called "roots.
By mentioning these, one includes the misconduct produced by them; thus, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used. "They all abandon" explains the phrase "all abandon" in the sutra.
The remainder, starting from "recollection," explains the third benefit of the remedial practice. The rest is designated as the subsequent portion of the sutra text.

As for "others," it refers to those sentient beings who are the objects of one's thoughts; since these objects of thought are not limited to a single type, they are collectively described as "various.

"All" means that one benefits them entirely with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*); because one gives rise to a beneficial loving-kindness toward all those sentient beings who are the objects of one's thoughts, this is called the intention to bestow happiness upon all. This state of loving-kindness comes first, as it is the direct antidote to hatred (*dveṣa*).

Because they serve as the basis for the attainment of peace and happiness, these [two] are specifically mentioned; however, in principle, this also applies to the arising of minds such as compassion (*karuṇā*).
The practice that accomplishes the benefit of others is termed "benefit" (*hita*). Below, the sutra provides the following correlations: the word "all" correlates with "all [beings]";
"conforming to loving-kindness and compassion" correlates with the "mind of loving-kindness" (*maitrī*); and "skillfully cultivating and accomplishing the practice" correlates with "benefit."

In the *Prasādapratibhodbhava* (or *Dṛṣṭāntamālya*), "abandoning what is wrong" (*mithyā-vivarjana*) is the general term for that which deviates from reason; "wrong seeking" is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).

To sever and eliminate these by means of right wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*) is termed "abandonment. Following this, there is the detailed classification of the "restraints of the day and night" (*rātri-divasa-saṃvara-śīla*). Within this second major section on the ultimate maintenance [of the precepts], it concerns the constant ability to refrain from transgressions.
In this treatise, there are two parts: first, a general explanation of how right view serves as the antidote to the seven types of wrong views;
second, a specific explanation of the seven wrong views through their respective opposites to reveal their antidotes. Regarding these seven types, they are categorized by means of two gates.
First, the classification according to practice: the first is the wrongness of aspiration, because it aspires to the Hīnayāna. Next...
The first [verse] is for the purpose of resolving false and inverted views; the next one is for the purpose of concealing actual faults through deceit while falsely manifesting virtue;

and the final one is for the purpose of generating faith in what is false, namely, worldly [views]. Second, regarding the classification of persons according to their inclinations, there are three types of persons:

first, those seeking the holy life (*brahmacarya*); second, those seeking sensual desire (*kāma*); and third, those seeking existence (*bhava*). Among these seven [categories], the first four are those seeking the holy life, and the subsequent two are those seeking sensual desire.

Regarding the latter one that seeks existence among the preceding four, the first is the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) of the same dharma, while the latter three are the heterodox paths of those with false views.
For those who hold these as distinct from the Mahāyāna—clinging to names and views—this [text] serves as an antidote.
Below this, the sūtra is cited to demonstrate the antidote for those who follow the right path; "following the Mahāyāna path" refers to the next three phrases.
The first is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the second is attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the third is attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Wrong view and attachment to precepts and observances are mentioned together as independent views (*mukhyadṛṣṭi*), while attachment to views is mentioned separately as the view that stands upon them. Question:

Is it not the case that attachment to precepts and observances lacks a view standing upon it, and that within attachment to views there is no independent view? Why then do you say that attachment to precepts and observances is an independent view?

Regarding the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), it is "standing upon" views. The commentary explains that the view of holding to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of two kinds:
first, independent views; second, views standing upon [other] views. Taking precepts, vows, and ritual offerings to be the true path is called an independent view.
Relying on various views and taking those views to be the path is called a view standing upon [other] views, because it uses those various views as its feet and support.
Within the category of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), there are also two types: first, that which exists independently (*mukhya*), which proclaims saṃsāra to be pleasant, pure, and so forth;
second, that which is "based upon" (*pādastha*), which arises from various views and takes those views as supreme.

While the independent type is more common within the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it is cited here specifically [in that context]. Within the adherence to views, however, the "based upon" type is more common, and thus it is discussed here specifically.

Regarding the first two of these [eight] bases, false discrimination constitutes wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), not knowing that results arise from causes, falsely engage in divination and omens;
such views that do not accord with the Dharma are called false discrimination. This is a minor form of wrong view, distinct from the views of causelessness and resultlessness.
The "view of purification through precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) refers to the notion that purity is attained through precepts; here, "precepts" are that which is grasped.
"Purity" refers to the two meanings established [in this context]; since both are raised together, it is termed "the view of purification through precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

In reality, however, the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) generally encompasses all contaminated phenomena—including precepts, offerings, and various views—regarding them as purity.

Why, then, is it specifically named "clinging to precepts"? In truth, while the clinging to precepts generally encompasses all dharmas, it is specifically so designated because of those non-Buddhists and Buddhist practitioners who...

Because people mostly grasp at precepts as the true path, this is spoken of in general terms as "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Thus, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya* states that one should say "clinging to precepts and so forth.
Although the sutras and treatises omit "and so forth," they simply say "clinging to precepts" because one grasps these precepts and the like as being capable of purification;
hence it is called the "view of purification. To counteract this, the following passage from the sutra is cited to demonstrate the remedy for those who cling to signs.
"Treating false discrimination and abandoning evil precepts" refers to treating the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*).

When non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) observe the "crow-and-cock precepts" and so forth, which do not effectively prevent transgressions, these are called "evil precepts. To perceive and cling to such evil precepts as being pure is called the "view of evil precepts.
Regarding the "view of evil precepts," the sutra text is cited again: "those who grasp at views" refers to those who grasp at the evil precepts according to their own subjective perspectives.

To regard that which is the path to purification as being correct is the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). To take what is inferior to be superior and what is not correct to be correct is called clinging to views;
however, in reality, clinging to views generally takes all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as supreme, not merely views alone.
Nevertheless, because those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) mostly cling to their own views and hold them to be superior, the name is established based on this majority.

Therefore it is said: "Because of the grasping at views. The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states that one should say "the grasping at views and so forth," though the sūtras and śāstras abbreviate this by mentioning only "grasping at views.
To claim something as correct means to regard one’s own false views as right views. Regarding the antidote below, a sūtra is cited to demonstrate the remedy:
