"Right wisdom is the abandonment of grasping; this is called cultivating rectitude. The four preceding lines concern the seeking of liberation by sentient beings.
The following two lines concern those who, while seeking gain, conceal their faults and feign virtue during their pursuit;
this is termed "conduct contrary to desire. The meaning is the same as when these are mentioned together and contrasted. "Concealing" refers to hiding one's own faults;
"feigning" means falsely appearing to possess virtues that one actually lacks. To counteract this, the sutra is cited below to demonstrate the remedy.
"Free from deceit" means being free from concealing one's previous views; "free from flattery" means being free from subsequently feigning what is not real.
Regarding those with impure views who seek the pleasures of sentient beings and are attached to the three realms of existence (*trisaṃsāra*), they lack pure faith in the Three Jewels.

This refers to those who distinguish their views by believing in and delighting in the mundane world as ultimate. To counteract this, the following passage from the Sūtra is cited to reveal the remedy.
Thus, the following explains the second [section], "Constantly Protecting Day and Night," which consists of three parts:

first, connecting the preceding with the subsequent to provide an introduction; this has already been stated as the connection of the preceding. Next, the explanation of the increase is the generation of the subsequent.
Second, the explanation of the words: "uninterrupted" does not mean causing a total severance; "without omission" does not mean a temporary suspension.

This clarifies the constant protection and maintenance that is free from faults. This clarifies the third [category], the gathering of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), through three points:
first, citing the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, pointing out and refuting according to the text; and third, explaining in accordance with the text.
Regarding "thus, all these natures are accomplished," this cites the aforementioned accomplishment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-siddhi*). Ten.

"Difficult to kill" and so forth refers to the non-interruption [of the precepts]. Furthermore, it demonstrates this by restating what was previously mentioned: that one constantly guards the ten wholesome paths throughout day and night; this is the restatement of the preceding.

Next, the "gathering of wholesome qualities" is explained as that which arises subsequently. This means that, below, the text provides specific explanations in accordance with the following passages. (The phrase "as for the Bodhisattva... refers to the subsequent text. Below, the text is interpreted according to its sequence.
The distinctions in phrasing consist of five meanings, and the distinctions in meaning consist of four points, which are subsumed into two statements.

Regarding the fivefold phrasing, as shown below in the text, it cites the sūtra at five locations to provide specific explanations. Regarding the fourfold distinctions in meaning: first, wisdom; second, aspiration; third, contemplation; and fourth, practice.
First, reflecting that sentient beings fall into the evil realms entirely due to unwholesome courses of action constitutes wisdom. Therefore, I shall...

"First, 'abiding well in the lower' is his vow (*praṇidhāna*). Furthermore, 'deeply contemplating the lower' up to 'the ten wholesome actions of the Tathāgata are pure' is his contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Therefore, 'I should practice so as to make all things pure' is his conduct (*caryā*).
Regarding the first wisdom, there is a threefold distinction: first, what is known? It is knowing that sentient beings have fallen into the various evil realms.
All [this suffering] arises from unwholesome [karma]. How is this known? It is known from the preceding discipline (*vinaya*):

one knows that evil is severed, yet because one does not cease [the thought of] sentient beings, one falls into the various evil realms. Third, why is it known that the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) practiced by Bodhisattvas is the foundation?

Whatever wholesome qualities they gather are all for the sake of [other] beings; therefore, one knows that the suffering experienced in birth is due to karma, while the gathering of wholesome qualities is for the sake of [beings].
Within the vow, there is also a threefold distinction: first, what is the object of the vow? It is the vow to abide in goodness oneself and to cause others to abide in it as well.

Second, what is the cause of the vow? Because one previously knew that birth and falling into the evil realms arise due to karma, one gives rise to the mind of the vow to abide in goodness oneself and to cause others to abide in it, thereby severing unwholesome karma and departing from the evil paths. Third, for what reason is the vow made? It is because [the vow] is the foundation of contemplative practice.
Since all arise from vows, the vows are clarified. Within the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), there is also a threefold distinction: first, what is contemplated;
that is to say, one contemplates the obstacles and their remedies, wherein the remedies refer to the five kinds of ten wholesome paths of action. Second, by what cause is it contemplated?

It is because of the preceding mind of aspiration, wishing to abide in goodness oneself and causing others to abide in it as well; for if one does not recognize goodness, how could one know where to abide? Thus, the mind of contemplation is clarified.
"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is synonymous with "understanding. Why is there contemplation? It is because one contemplates the wholesome as being subsumed by the desire to initiate practice.
Within this practice, it is also analyzed by means of three phrases: first, what is practiced—namely, practicing the fivefold ten paths of wholesome action;

second, by what cause one practices—because through the aforementioned contemplation, one sees that the fivefold wholesome dharmas can serve as antidotes, and thus initiates cultivation; third, for what purpose one practices.

Because one practices for the sake of relying on one's own goodness to gather others with goodness, one subsequently gathers sentient beings through wholesome dharmas to cause them to leave the ten unwholesome actions;
only at that time can it be called the essential core of the original vow.

Regarding the two pairs [of the four immeasurables], in the first pair, wisdom serves as the skillful means and the subsequent arising of the correct vow follows; in the latter pair, contemplation serves as the skillful means.

The *Pratipattisāra* (Treatise on Subsequent Right Practice) relies upon these two aspects to provide an interpretation. First, it explains the initial pair; then, observing what follows, it explains the second pair.
Regarding the first pair, the sutra first clarifies that "wisdom" is the result and "falling into evil" is the cause—the unwholesome—while "thought" (*cetanā*) applies to both.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the vows within the section on "aspiration," the first vow is stated first, followed by its explanation: "Therefore, I shall first abide in wholesome dharmas."

"To cause others to abide" refers to the correct arousal of the vow. Since all these sentient beings fall into the evil realms due to unwholesome karma, I first abide in the wholesome and transform them, causing them to abide in it so that they may sever and abandon unwholesomeness and not fall into the evil paths. Why [is there a question]?
The word "why" is a question. [The text] previously considered that sentient beings fall into the evil realms because of karma; therefore, one should properly first arouse the vow.

Regarding the phrase "causing others to abide in the wholesome," why is it said, "I shall first abide [therein] myself"? This explains the reason why a bodhisattva must first abide [therein] themselves.
If one does not practice it oneself while attempting to cause others to abide in it, such a thing is impossible. Because it is impossible, one must necessarily abide in it oneself;
the meaning of the words is thus. In the text, the phrase "if a person" is used as a general term, and "not practicing it oneself" refers to the failure to act accordingly.

If one lacks the skillful means from the beginning, there will be no completion at the end; if one speaks for the sake of others, it is the beginning of benefiting beings, and if one causes others to abide [in the path], it is the final completion of transforming others.

There is no principle that allows for anything other than this, which is called "impossible. Conversely, if one accords with the teaching by personally practicing and personally fulfilling [the path] for oneself, and then speaking it for others to cause them to abide [in it], this is "possible."
In this treatise, the section beginning with "The Bodhisattva, having contemplated the profound stillness of wisdom" first explains the falling into the various evil realms;
subsequently, it explains the causes for the accumulation of the ten unwholesome actions.

Regarding the latter, the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva, having thus distanced himself" explains the contemplation that sentient beings all [suffer] because they do not abandon [unwholesomeness]. Within the first of these sections:

There are three [types of] falling into the evil realms (*durgati*). To cite the sutra and state their number: those who ride upon evil and proceed toward it explain its doctrinal meaning (*mārgārtha*). Evil conduct leads a person to a result; this is called the "path" (*mārga*).

The bitter retribution of the three miserable states (*tripatana*) is the result reached by that path. Because the name of the cause is applied to the result, they are called "paths of evil" (*durgati*).

In the sutras, they are also sometimes referred to as "evil destinies" (*durgati*); the name is established in contrast to the cause, for the result is the destiny reached by the cause, and thus they are called "destinies."

Some say that the "three paths" (trayadhvā) are termed "paths" (*tú*) because they are places of suffering like poisoned darts; they are called "paths" because suffering arises based upon the body, which explains their meaning as "evil.
Because one creates evil causes and effects that do not depart from oneself, it is said to be "based on one's own body.

Since the body is a vessel of suffering and can give rise to the mind of suffering, it is called "arising-suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Because suffering is thus named "evil," one constantly falls into its characteristics; this explains the meaning of "falling."
The immeasurable characteristics of suffering are termed the "various three miserable realms" (*tridurgati*). To fall into these places is called "falling into cyclic existence" (*saṃsāra*);

to describe this as having no end is to call it "eternal. Regarding the subsequent explanation of the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*), first there is the interrogation, followed by the exposition, and finally the conclusion.
Below, the sutra and the treatise are further distinguished in relation to one another. The question, "Why are they called the ten unwholesome actions? constitutes the initial interrogation.
That which encompasses all categories of evil results is termed "explanation" (*vyākhyā*). Reaching the meaning of the karma of explanation is called "result" (*phala*);
arriving at the result is called "reaching" (*prāpti*). Their meanings are identical. "All evils" explains "unwholesome" (*akuśala*);

"evil" and "unwholesome" differ only in terminology. "Result" is explained as the retribution; it is the path that leads to that result, and because it can reach the result, it is called the "path" (*mārga*).

"Number" (*saṃkhyā*) means ten; it refers to those paths of action (*karmapatha*), which are counted as ten. Regarding the term "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) mentioned at the beginning: it refers to reaching the enumeration of the results of evil.
It is called "comprehension" because the names of the ten unwholesome paths found in that sūtra differ from these, yet their substance is one—the distinct categories are subsumed into one.

This is similar in meaning to what was stated in the "Fundamental Section" regarding being "determined by the vow" and "comprehended by true wisdom"; this point will be further addressed in the subsequent sūtras and śāstras.

Since the meaning is naturally revealed through the correlation [of scripture and treatise], the following section concludes by correlating the scripture and the treatise, first generally and then specifically.
Regarding the enumeration that encompasses all evil fruits: "generally citing the treatise" refers to stating the ten unwholesome actions;
"citing the scripture to correlate with the enumeration" refers to citing the scripture to manifest the correspondence between the enumeration and the number ten.

Because the names are distinct while the substance is one, it is said that "it encompasses the unwholesome. This [phrase] restates the treatise; "because it is unwholesome" cites the sutra to clarify the correspondence.
If one follows the preceding and following sections, one should also say "it encompasses the concise"; however, the results are not discussed here.

"Because they are despicable, such as falling into hell," etc., refers to the fact that [actions] can cause one to fall into the three miserable realms, manifesting that karma is the path. That which is fallen into is extremely evil, and thus is termed "despicable."

Regarding "reaching," this refers to the *śāstra*; regarding "grasping," this refers to the *sūtra*. To clarify the meaning of "grasping" (*saṃgraha*), it is shown to be the same as before. Above, the ten unwholesome paths were explained in detail;

next, the meaning of the "causes and conditions for accumulation" (*saṃcaya-hetu-pratyaya*) will be explained. As for "accumulating causes," this cites the *sūtra*. Regarding the phrase "because of receiving and practicing":

"receiving" (*pratigraha*) refers to understanding well; "accumulating" (*saṃcaya*) refers to the name given to the accumulation of results; "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) refers to the name given to the gathering of results. Since their meanings are similar, one may use the term "receiving" (*pratigraha*).

The explanation establishes the meaning of "causal practice" (*caryā-hetu*). Because the meaning of producing a fruit from a cause is similar to the meaning of proceeding toward a fruit, it is appropriate to explain "cause" by means of "practice.
Next, the contemplation (*manasikāra*) is explained through the sense of "non-separation.

The Bodhisattva distances himself from causelessness and erroneous causes; this explains "contemplation. Previously, it was said that sentient beings fall into the various evil realms due to such [erroneous] thoughts.

All [suffering] arises from unwholesome causes and is not without cause; for by means of the ten unwholesome paths, one falls into the various evil realms. Regarding the phrase "born from inverted causes":
"inversion" refers to sentient beings who, through their own volition, perform evil karma and dwell in what is not the Dharma (*adharma-sthāna*). This is explained according to its meaning:

the three miserable states (*durgati*) are not places where one experiences happiness, and thus they are called "places of non-Dharma. Because one attains those states through one's own actions, it is not without cause.

Because one dwells in the commission of evil, it is not the cause of non-perversion; nor is it non-existent, for it is precisely this [evil]. Thus, all [faults] arise from the ten unwholesome paths of action.

One cannot distance oneself from them, for one does not understand how to remain detached. The following explains the text of the vow. "Contemplating the profound and tranquil" reiterates what preceded to initiate what follows. This passage refers to perversion;
if it were correct, it should have stated that the Bodhisattva, having contemplated his own name in profound tranquility, [the previous thought] would have fallen away.
All [this] arises from volition (*cetanā*) that is unwholesome. Because volition relies upon a quiet place, it is called "tranquil volition" (*śānta-cetanā*).

When one’s volition is not erroneous, its expression is termed "profound. Having concluded the preceding section on naming oneself, the following section provides the correct interpretation of the vow-text for the purpose of rescuing others.

To rescue those beings, one must first know that one is capable; this is explained as: "I shall first establish myself in the wholesome and cause others to abide therein. Only by knowing this is one truly capable.

Therefore, having first established oneself [in the practice], one then observes the lower stages; this provides a broad explanation of the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Within this, first the two gates of contemplative practice are presented, and subsequently they are explained according to the text.

Regarding the former, from the beginning up to "the highest of the high" (*uttarottara*), the latter gate of contemplation is presented to give rise to a superior resolve (*adhimukti*) for seeking training;

the subsequent section on the gate of conduct (*caryā*) follows. Within the gate of contemplation, there is further observation of obstacles and their remedies, briefly presenting the gate of contemplation.
Having previously contemplated the causes and effects of unwholesome states, one now again gives rise to contemplation; therefore, it is called "further contemplation.

Unwholesomeness is named an "obstruction" to the wholesome, and its "remedy" is the counteraction of unwholesomeness. Below this, there is a further analysis of the unwholesome states and their results that were previously the obstructions, as well as the wholesome paths and their results—extending even to the highest levels—which were previously the remedies. Within these remedies, there are two types: first, the mundane.
Second, mundane wholesome karma and its fruits belong to the world; those that are superior and superior-to-the-superior belong to the supramundane.
"Superior" refers to the wholesome dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; "superior-to-the-superior" refers to the wholesome dharmas of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Since the wholesome dharmas of the Two Vehicles are superior when contrasted with ordinary beings, and the wholesome dharmas of the Mahāyāna are superior even to those, they are called "superior-to-the-superior. This is the general explanation.
There are five grades of goodness: first, ordinary goodness; second, that of the śrāvaka; third, that of the pratyekabuddha; fourth, that of the bodhisattva; and fifth, the goodness of the Buddha.

These five grades of the ten wholesome paths of action are explained in detail in other chapters and should be discussed fully here. Below, the "Gate of Practice" is presented for those who, having aroused the superior mind (*adhyāśaya*), seek to train in and cultivate [the path];
this refers to the gathering of the virtuous mind. It is the pure practice of the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts for gathering wholesome dharmas).
This refers to the gathering of wholesome conduct (*kuśalasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*). Furthermore, seeking and practicing with a superior mind is that which is capable of gathering;
the pure practitioner of the precept for gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*) is what is gathered.
In the commentary on the text, the initial contemplation is first explained; therefore, from "I should thus practice" onwards, its actual practice is explained.

Within the aforementioned contemplation, the obstacles of unwholesome karma, the wholesome dharmas that serve as their antidotes for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and *śrāvakas*, and the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*) for *pratyekabuddhas*, *bodhisattvas*, and *tathāgatas* are explained together in one place.

Why are the initial obstacle of unwholesomeness and the wholesome antidotes of ordinary persons and *śrāvakas* explained together? It is explained that this is because *śrāvakas* employ the obstacle of unwholesomeness [as their primary concern].

Furthermore, because the wholesome dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) serve as the objects of observation and require one another in their logical force, they are explained together in this single section.
Within this sutra, four gates of analysis are distinguished according to the differences in meaning: First, the analysis of obstacles and antidotes:

The ten unwholesome actions that lead to rebirth in the evil realms are the obstacles; the lower [levels of] the wholesome paths are the antidotes. Second, the distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*).
Separately, from the beginning up to birth in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the wholesome dharmas of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are clarified in contrast to evil;

furthermore, by means of the upper and lower [realms], the wholesome dharmas of the noble Śrāvakas are clarified. Regarding the differentiation of the three objects and practices: first, the causes and fruits of good and evil are clarified as being the domain of the Śrāvakas;
moreover, through the upper and lower [realms], these are the practices of the Śrāvakas. These four pairs are distinguished according to their superiority and inferiority.
The analysis proceeds from the beginning up to the stage of integration (*samāpatti*). In contrast to the lower, the superior is manifested; in contrast to the higher, the inferior is revealed.

Among these four gates, this treatise relies on the latter gate for its analytical exposition of the first three, rather than discussing them by contrasting the former with the lower to manifest superiority.

Within that [latter gate], from the beginning up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the inferior is cited to manifest the superior; furthermore, this constitutes a distinction of superiority based on the upper and lower realms.
The "inferiority surpassing the former inferiority" refers to the object of contemplation; the "subsequent superiority" refers to the practice that contemplates it.

Having first raised the inferior, the subsequent deep reflection upon the intermediate stage corresponds to the aforementioned contemplation on falling into evil due to karma; this is explained as what is further contemplated, through which the causes and effects of good and evil can be known.

In the subsequent analysis of superiority, the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) are explicitly raised as the essence of goodness, while the preceding section clarified [the preliminary stages].

Since we are now further discussing the excellence of the noble ones (*ārya*), the word "furthermore" (*yu*) is used. The goodness of the noble ones surpasses that of ordinary persons and is thus designated as "superior.
For one who practices in conjunction with the contemplation of wisdom, it is explained why this is superior: because it is in harmony with wisdom, it attains the status of being superior.

When one is free from killing, stealing, and so forth within the mind of wisdom, this is called "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*). To initiate goodness based upon wisdom is termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*); the following section clarifies this.
Regarding the five distinct categories of inferior and middling verses, they clarify those of inferior pratyekabuddhas and those of the Mahāyāna.

In the treatise, there is first an explanation of the scriptural passage that demonstrates superiority by contrasting it with what is below; this passage has two parts: first, clarifying the causes and effects of good and evil for ordinary beings;
second, clarifying the ten paths of wholesome action of the śrāvakas along with their wisdom. The commentary on this has three parts: first, the transcendent explanation of wisdom.
The first [section] explains the two [types of] ordinary beings’ causes and effects of good and evil; the third explains the ten paths of wholesome action of the śrāvakas along with wisdom.
Why are these explained first? Because they transcend [ordinary understanding], and because wisdom is the master of the śrāvaka’s ten wholesome paths, it is explained first.
Furthermore, one wishes to clarify the objects of contemplation—the truths of suffering, origin, and so forth—in contrast to this, and thus explains them first. Within this, the initial [part]...

Regarding the term "contemplation of wisdom," it refers to that which transcends the scriptural text; as for "contemplation of the true reality (*dharmatā*)," the Four Noble Truths constitute the true reality of all phenomena.

That the Śrāvakas illuminate and perceive these is called the "contemplation of true reality. Next, the second explanation follows: the causes and effects of good and evil for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are taken as the dharmas of true reality.
The causes and effects of unwholesomeness are explained as the two truths of Suffering and Origin; however, [the truths of] Cessation and the Path do not exist within the sūtra.

The meaning of the text clarifies this by explaining the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) in terms of the causes and effects of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. The commentary discusses this through both words and meaning:

"separation from the proclivities" (*visamyoga-prahāṇa*) refers to the extinction of unwholesome dharmas because their substance (*svabhāva*) has been eliminated; thus, it is not called the "extinction of proclivities.

As for wholesome [dharmas], their substance is not severed, but rather the proclivities of affliction (*kleśa*) within the wholesome are removed; therefore, it is called "separation from the proclivities. This is truly because the Śrāvakas do not understand what is wholesome.
Because the mind arises through the conceptualization of dharmas, it is not extinguished; that which serves as the antidote to this is the path within each respective excellence.
Next, the ten wholesome actions and wisdom are explained in sequence. Regarding "contemplating together with wisdom":
the wisdom of the śrāvakas contemplates both types of the Four Noble Truths mentioned above. This clarifies the wisdom upon which the ten wholesome actions rely.
The essence is the cultivation of non-discrimination; this explains the term "conjunction" in the phrase "practicing the ten paths of wholesome action.

Practice arises from the accumulation of wisdom; this explains the term "practice" (*bhāvanā*) within the sutra. Wholesomeness conjoined with wisdom is called "non-discrimination"; this explains the term "conjunction" (*yoga*) within the sutra.
The preceding explanation demonstrates superiority in relation to what follows; the subsequent explanation reveals [the meaning] in relation to what precedes it.

Regarding the four points on being inferior to those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): first, the designation of the person and the enumeration of the number; second, the listing of the five names;

among these five, the first three clarify the inferiority of the *bodhisattva*, while the latter two phrases clarify the inferiority of the *pratyekabuddha*. As for the term "accumulation due to causes" (*hetu-saṃcaya*): it refers to the narrow and inferior roots of goodness practiced in the past that can produce present conduct;
this is called the "cause. Because one relies upon this to accumulate the path, it is called "accumulation. As for the term "fear" (*bhaya*): [it refers to the fear of the suffering of saṃsāra].
"Regarding suffering": it refers to the present state where the mind is timid and weak, fearing and wearying of future suffering, and thus seeking its swift cessation.

"Regarding the mind of relinquishment": it refers to seeking only one's own deliverance while abandoning sentient beings. "Regarding reliance": it refers to attaining deliverance by relying on a teacher, which differs from the Pratyekabuddha who attains self-enlightenment.

"Regarding contemplation": it refers to contemplating that the provisional names of sentient beings are not as profound as the Pratyekabuddha’s contemplation of the three marks of dependent origination.
This is a general summary of the scriptural text, referring to persons by way of their limited and inferior nature and so forth; these constitute the "śrāvaka mind.

The sūtra contains five phrases, with "limited" (*parītta*) at the beginning and "and so forth" (*ādi*) following it; thus, it says "limited and so forth. The four [subsequent phrases] provide a detailed explanation.

Having cited the preceding section, the following section explains the practice: practicing few roots of virtue refers to the inferiority of one's own conduct; it relies solely on benefiting oneself rather than transforming others.

The narrowness [of the path] can be understood from the preceding scriptural citation; the fear [of the path] can be understood from the preceding scriptural citation regarding the gate of relinquishing;

the relinquishing of life is explained based on the scriptural citation. Regarding the two gates of reliance and contemplation, both the commentary and the scriptural citations follow the preceding scriptural citations.

"Relying on the teacher’s instruction" means relying on the Buddha’s teaching. Regarding the gate of reliance and contemplation, the subsequent explanation begins with "mindfulness. As for "mindfulness of sound," this is the explanation.

Hearing arises from sound and gives rise to understanding; this is called "recollection of sound. Because one recollects the sound, it is conventionally described as "hearing," though it is not heard by the ear.
Why is this? Below, the text explains that sound is merely a name because it arises [from causes]; thus it is called "sound" (*śabda*).

In this way, "that" refers to the conceptual understanding derived from the explanation of sound. The preceding statement that there are five kinds of characteristics of the *śrāvaka* now restates them.

For that reason, it is said: "Thus, that person relies on the provisional [teachings] to realize emptiness; they are called 'entering through the interpretation of sound' because they give rise to the realization of the non-self of persons.
Within the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, this establishes the entry into the realization of the non-self of persons for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle;

it does not establish the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), nor does it establish the other two types of non-self. This is explained in detail in a separate chapter, which should be consulted here for a full discussion. Below, by...

The "Sūtra-seal" (sūtra-mudrā) refers to hearing sounds from others; the "seal of reliance" (niśraya-mudrā) refers to understanding through hearing sounds and so forth; and the "seal of subsequent observation" (paścāt-pratyavekṣā-mudrā) refers to what follows.
Among the wholesome states of the Pratyekabuddhas, the "superior wholesome" is the general category, not derived from the inferior or the specific.
In this treatise, there are four sections: first, identifying the person and stating the number; second, listing their names; third, explaining according to those names;

and fourth, distinguishing their similarities and differences relative to the śrāvakas. Regarding the term "pratyekabuddha," it identifies the person. The meaning of "pratyekabuddha" is analyzed through two gates: first, the explanation by translating the name;
second, the distinction of its characteristics relative to the śrāvakas. As for the pratyekabuddha, [he is] the one of middle [capacity].

The term used in this country is translated as "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer). There are two explanations: first, the twelve links of dependent origination are called "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*);
one who attains awakening within these is termed a "Pratyekabuddha. Second, because one attains the Way by relying on the causal conditions of present phenomena, they are named a "Pratyekabuddha.
Regarding the distinction made in contrast to the *Śrāvaka* (Hearer), there are two types of *Śrāvakas*.
There are two types of śrāvakas: those who follow the voice of the śrāvakas and those who follow the voice of the pratyekabuddhas. There are likewise two types of pratyekabuddhas:

those who follow the path of the pratyekabuddhas and those who follow the path of the śrāvakas. This distinction arises because the Dharma differs according to the individual. Regarding the difference in the Dharma:

first, the difference in the gates of the Dharma that are observed, namely the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; second, the difference in the conditions for attaining the Way.
The distinction refers to the fact that they rely on verbal teachings and present conditions; because these causal conditions and characteristics are not identical, there is this difference.
As stated in the *Pratyekabuddha-nidāna-sūtra*, there are such differences among persons, and their characteristics are as follows:

regarding the two types of Śrāvakas, there are those who have sought the path of a Śrāvaka since ancient times, who delight in contemplating the Four Noble Truths, and who encounter a Buddha in their final body.
For him, the teaching of the Four Noble Truths was expounded, through which he awakened to the Way. This person was originally of the *śrāvaka* lineage;
now, having again heard the voice [of the Dharma], he has attained the fruit of the Way. For this reason, he is called a *śrāvaka*.

There are some who have sought the path of the *pratyekabuddha* since ancient times, constantly delighting in the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). In their final birth, they encounter a Buddha, who for them expounds the twelve [links].
One who attains awakening through conditions based on the teachings is as follows: this person was originally of the *pratyekabuddha* lineage, but now awakens by means of sound;
for this reason, they are called a *pratyekabuddha-śrāvaka*. Among the *śrāvakas*, there are these two distinctions. As for the second type of *pratyekabuddha*:

there is a person who previously sought the path of a *pratyekabuddha* and constantly delighted in contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), yet in their final body, they did not encounter [a Buddha].
In the Buddha’s world, some obtain the Way by relying on present circumstances and conditions. Such a person was originally of the *pratyekabuddha* lineage;
now, by relying on present conditions, they attain the fruit of the Way. For this reason, they are called *pratyekabuddhas*.

There are also those who previously sought the path of a *śrāvaka*, contemplated the Four Noble Truths, and attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*); however, because their faculties were dull, they did not attain [the higher fruits] within their present lifetime.
One who attains nirvāṇa after being reborn seven times among gods and humans, and having completed those seven births,
attains the fruit of the path in a world devoid of a Buddha by relying on present conditions— this person was originally of the śrāvaka lineage,
but because they now attain the path by relying on present conditions, they are described as a śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha; this is explained here specifically in terms of their pratyekabuddha nature.
Because this person excels in wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*), there are three types of exaltation (*utthāpana*); they are listed here in sequence by name.

Regarding those who are "self-awakened" (*svayambhū*)—those who do not rely on a teacher’s instruction, cannot speak [the Dharma], and lack the skillful means of compassion, observing only a limited range of objects—there are two general explanations. First, the narrow sense:

that which is observed by the *pratyekabuddhas* consists of the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*) within the twelve links of dependent origination; it is so called because it lacks the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*). Thus, the name is established.
Regarding "narrow and few": "subtle and few" refers to the profound and subtle objects of observation of the *pratyekabuddhas*, which are described as "few.

Now, what is discussed here is that "profound and subtle" is termed "few"; this will be explained below. In the explanation of the first section, "not depending on the Buddha’s teaching or the explanations of various bodhisattvas, but awakening by oneself from another" clarifies "self-awakened right enlightenment" (*svayaṃsaṃbuddha*); the application of the sutra text can be understood accordingly. This concludes the explanation of the first point.

Regarding those two [types of persons], one who does not give rise to the thought [to teach] lacks the understanding of compassion; because they lack compassion, they have no desire to speak and are incapable of providing an explanation.

One who lacks skillful means (*upāya*)—such as a *pratyekabuddha* appearing in the world—is incapable of preaching the Dharma because there are no ninefold scriptures (*navāṅga-dharma-pravacana*) and because they lack skillful means.
This can be understood from the scriptural citations. Regarding the third [point], the commentary on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* explains that it penetrates the subtle and understands profound causes.

Regarding the "object-condition" (*ālambana-viṣaya*), this explains and establishes the *Pratyekabuddha-yāna* sūtras; the details may be understood from below, where it contrasts with the *Śrāvaka* to distinguish their similarities and differences.

Among the five characteristics previously mentioned for the *Śrāvaka*, three are the same and two are different. First, it is said that [the *Śrāvaka*] "fears suffering due to the accumulation of causes and abandons birth";

the *Pratyekabuddha* also possesses these, which demonstrates their similarity. If the two vehicles were equal in terms of attaining the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), why is this not explicitly stated?

The commentary states: Although the Śrāvakas have attained the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), their vision is not clear; the Pratyekabuddhas, however, observe subtle causes and conditions and thus see emptiness with clarity and precision.
Because they surpass the Śrāvakas in this regard, they are not said to be equal to them. Having already explained this superiority, the text now explains the difference in their clarity:

namely, that while they are superior to the Śrāvakas in being able to personally awaken to and contemplate subtle causes and conditions, they are inferior to the Śrāvakas in their inability to preach the Dharma.
Why is it that they are not said to speak? It is explained that although Pratyekabuddhas are unable to teach, this does not mean they are inferior.

Why is this so? Because when Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, there are no formal teachings upon which to rely; therefore, they are unable to speak. It is not that their wisdom is deficient or weak such that they are incapable of preaching the Dharma.
In fact, their wisdom surpasses that of the Śrāvakas, such as Śāriputra, whom they cannot even reach. For this reason, they are not discussed [in this context].
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states that the supreme purity is fully perfected by summarizing the mind as a whole and then detailing its aspects.
In the treatise, it first states that there are four types of bodhisattvas, thereby indicating the number of persons; next, it enumerates their names.

Among these four, the first constitutes the cause, while the latter three constitute the qualities. Within these qualities, the first two pertain to the benefit of others (*parārtha*), and the last one pertains to self-benefit (*svārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "the accumulation of causes": it refers to the roots of goodness practiced in the past, which are explained as the cause; because one relies upon them to accumulate practice, they are called "accumulation.
Regarding the "function": this is the mind that seeks to benefit others. Because it can provide benefit by taking suffering as its object, it is termed "function. Regarding the phrase "that power":

it refers to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as skillful means for the practice of benefiting others. Arising based on the aforementioned compassion, it is the second compassionate function of the household power.
These two stages of benefiting others are called "stages" (*bhūmi*) because they are the places where one's own virtuous conduct is perfected;
this will be explained below. First, regarding the explanation of the cause within the *Samuccaya*: first is the explanation, followed by the conclusion, and finally the application of the sūtra.

Regarding the practice arising from goodness: all roots of goodness of the great mind are the causes practiced in the past; based on those wholesome causes, present goodness is now gathered and produced.

The phrase "named 'arising in practice'" clarifies the greatness of one's own practice. The phrase "relying on all sentient beings to benefit those who practice" explains the broadness of the expansive mind;
this clarifies the vastness of benefiting others. The statement "the Mahāyāna mind is broad and immeasurable" restates the previous "greatness.
Regarding the explanation of "immeasurable," it refers to the great assembly. The phrase "relying on the good to arise in practice" restates the previous "broadness."
It is based on conduct that benefits all who are born; because these two [aspects] are profound and yet vast, they are called "immeasurable.
This is the concluding summary of the lower section. Following the sutra’s lower passage, in explaining its application, one first provides an exposition and then offers a concluding summary.
One sees that by accumulating the causes of suffering through unwholesome conduct, although the suffering has not yet been experienced, it will be far from avoided; therefore, this too is pitiable.
When experiencing suffering, one has already received the retribution; regarding these sentient beings, one gives rise to a mind of compassion and pity.

Based on that, the following section is introduced and concluded. As in the sutra, the subsequent passage explains that power: first the introduction, then the explanation, and finally the citation from the sutra.

Regarding that power, within the preceding two sections, there is first the explanation and then the conclusion; for the following two sections, there is first the introduction and then the explanation.

The commentary on the left and right ears explains this as follows: according to the sutra, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) function as skillful means (*upāya*) capable of gathering [beings];

therefore, they are called "gathering through skillful means. The commentary below explains that within the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three. Having cited them to indicate the number, the distinct stages are ten, which are summarized into three.
From the first to the seventh stage, their meaning regarding functional application (*prayoga-artha*) is the same; thus, they are combined into one.

The eighth, ninth, and second [eighth] stages, which are characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*), are further combined into one, the tenth stage; this is the ultimate culmination within the path of training and is likewise treated as a single unit.

A detailed explanation follows: the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) is enumerated prior to the first seven stages. These seven stages are termed the "pure profound mind" because they eliminate obstacles and incline toward reality.
The ten vows are so named because the *Śāstra* harmonizes with the *Sūtra*. If the preceding seven stages constitute the pure profound mind, [the remaining stages follow accordingly].
Why is it that the sutra does not speak of "arousing the pure and profound ground of mind," but instead speaks of "arousing the vow"?
This is because the speaker refers to the ten vows of that first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) when designating the name; thus, it says "arousing the vow.

However, if one considers the general name, it is also appropriate to say "the pure and profound ground of mind," as the subsequent section of the sutra lists the stages from the eighth stage onward as being within the "flowing water of the Dharma" (*dharmasrotas*) where there is no regression.
Because they advance spontaneously, they are called "non-regressive. Having attained quiescence (*śamatha*), they do not abandon liberation. This commentary reconciles the sūtra:
why is it that from the eighth stage upward one is called "irreversible" (*avaivartika*) in the sūtras, yet here it says "not abandoning liberation"?
It is because, having attained profound quiescence, they do not abandon the realms of existence (*bhava*). They deliver sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation.
Therefore, the Sūtra states that not abandoning sentient beings is the constant function of tranquility (*śānti*).

Thus, by correlating this with the *Avaivartikacakra-sūtra*, one may understand that "receiving the position" refers to being named in the tenth stage (*daśamī bhūmi*), while "receiving the office of Buddha-wisdom" refers to receiving the position below that stage.

Regarding the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), there are three parts: first, the explanation; second, the correlation; and third, the detailed analysis. Therefore, "seeking to realize vast wisdom" explains its characteristics.

This is because the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) is the stage for receiving the position; thus, one seeks to realize the Buddha-wisdom. "Seeking" refers to the seeking through contemplation, while "realizing" refers to the realization through practice.
The Buddha’s vast and great wisdom is that which is sought and realized. "Vast" means broad; "great" means deep.

In the second fascicle, the passage on the "vastness and greatness of contemplative wisdom" precedes the section on "seeking," as the Buddha-wisdom is broad and deep, and is therefore termed "vast and great. This occurs below the stage of the Bodhisattva.
The preceding passage serves as the proof. It begins from the first stage (*bhūmi*) and extends through the ninth stage, wherein the stages are purified; hence it is said that "the stages are pure.

The virtues practiced within those various stages are called *pāramitās*. Because the practices of the ten stages are accomplished by relying on what preceded them, the present text cites the former to manifest the latter accomplishment.
Entering into the profound and vast accomplishment is precisely the accomplishment of the realized practice of the ten stages.
Because the Buddha’s wisdom is great, it is termed "profound and vast," as explained previously. Bodhisattvas of the ten stages accord with and realize this Buddha-wisdom, which is called "entry";
when realization is perfected, it is called "accomplishment. From this point downward is the third section, which further analyzes [the subject].

Within this, first is the question, followed by the explanation of the intent of the teaching, and finally a detailed analysis correlating the sutra and the treatise. Here, it is sufficient to speak only of the broad accomplishment.
Why is it said again that "the purity of the bodhisattva stages and the purity of the perfections" constitute the first question?

Now, since this [first question] is intended to clarify the accomplishment of profound and vast practices within the tenth stage, this alone should suffice. Why, then, is it stated again that "the purity of the bodhisattva stages from the ninth stage downward and the purity of the perfections"?
The intention of the question is as follows: the word "again" (punar) is used because what was previously clarified [in the first question] has already been explained.
Regarding the "pure deep mind stage" and the "non-retrogressive stage," these are now reiterated by citing those practices and stages; thus it says, "furthermore, it is explained.

From this point downward is the second section, which explains the intent of the explicit teaching. These are cited to manifest that the profound and vast practices have been perfected within the tenth stage;
hence, it is "furthermore explained. "Supremely pure" refers to the purity of the stage itself, such as from the first stage up through the ninth stage.
"Transcending obstacles with increasing excellence is called 'superiorly superior purity' (uttarottara-viśuddhi); this supreme purity is the *pāramitā*.
Because this *pāramitā* is preeminent among those that transcend obstacles, it is termed 'supreme purity. Since one can enter the realm of the Buddha by means of these two purities, it is said:

'It reveals the accomplishment of profound and vast conduct. This concludes the section on the relative distinction between the Sūtra and the Śāstra regarding the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), which reiterates what was previously stated in the treatise.
The meaning of "the first dharma" (prathama-dharma) is the same as that of "dharma. The meaning of *pāramitā* is elucidated by citing the sūtras for comparison;

the meaning of *pāramitā* taught in the sūtras constitutes the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) within this treatise. However, simply by saying "the first" is *pāramitā*, one knows that it is progressively superior (*uttarottara*) and belongs to the stages of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), without depending on further verbal explanation.

In the *Buddhasūtra-śāstra*, the "superior-to-superior" (*uttarottara*) is the general [category], while within all the "inferior-to-inferior" (*adhodha*) specific [categories], there are four phrases:

first, the purity of all aspects; second, the power of the ten powers (*daśabala*); third, the establishment of the factors for the attainment of awakening; and fourth, "therefore, practicing accordingly," and so forth.

Among these four, the first three are exclusively subsumed under the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*), whereas the meaning of the final phrase has a dual application. If one correlates this with the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*), it can...
Seeking with the mind to manifest the excellence of the sought-after Buddha-dharma belongs to the preceding gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);
if one takes the seeking mind of the second stage (*bhūmi*), it then belongs to the gate of practice (*caryā*). Now, first, regarding the contemplation, its four distinctions are as follows:

the first pair contrasts the ordinary person with the manifestation of purity; the second, the ten powers, contrasts the small light with relinquishment; the third, the gathering of dharmas, applies to those who bring [the practice] to fulfillment.

The first phrase cites all the stages (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattvas to manifest the perfection of the Buddha, because by practicing the Buddha-dharma throughout all the bodhisattva stages, one brings them to fulfillment;

thus, the Buddha’s virtues are perfected. The fourth phrase separately cites two specific stages to manifest the excellence of the Buddha, because in those two stages there is an insatiable seeking; thus, the Buddha’s virtues are supreme. This is truly so.
Because this stage of the second bhūmi is its specific locus, it is singled out to manifest its excellence. If one explains the text according to this meaning:

"Therefore, I should practice the ten wholesome actions equally to purify and perfect them" means that because the Buddha’s ten wholesome actions are entirely pure, and because of the power of the ten powers (*daśabala*), he gathers all dharmas to bring them to fulfillment; thus, "I should practice them equally."
Regarding the phrase "bringing the ten wholesome paths to purity and completion," if explained according to the gate of practice (*caryāmukha*), the text states:
"Therefore" means that because the five types of ten wholesome paths observed above can serve as antidotes by abandoning unwholesomeness,
I should practice these five types of ten wholesome paths so as to bring them to purity and completion.

In this treatise there are five sections: first, restating the initial section to provide a general summary; second, specifically demonstrating its establishment; third, listing the names according to their respective categories;

fourth, providing extensive explanations according to those names; and fifth, corroborating with scriptural citations. Regarding the phrase "the supreme of the supreme" (*uttarottara*), it restates the initial general summary.
The statement "there are four kinds" serves to demonstrate the nature of the supreme by citing specific instances. Below, the names are listed, beginning with: [The first...]
"Cessation" refers to the manifestation of purity for the sake of ordinary beings; "second abandonment" refers to the abandonment of the two vehicles to manifest its uniqueness.
As for "expedient means," this is a general reference to all practices performed by bodhisattvas to manifest the Buddha’s fulfillment.

This is why the practices of those bodhisattvas are termed "expedient means": because the Buddha’s virtues are perfectly complete and inexhaustible due to the bodhisattvas' cultivation of expedient means.

Regarding "the feet," this separately cites the seeking-mind of two stages to manifest the supreme excellence of the Buddha’s ten wholesome paths of action reaching their ultimate consummation. Next, the text explains them:

"The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of unwholesome courses of action are extinguished" explains the initial "extinguishing. Unwholesome actions are the primary evils, while habitual tendencies are their residual traces;

because it mentions the primary [actions] while including the tendencies, they are termed "conjoined. All of these are completely extinguished, and one attains mastery over wholesome karma, surpassing even the *śrāvakas*.
"Equanimity" (*upekṣā*) refers to the aforementioned relinquishment; "mastery" (*vaśitā*) is the meaning of its power. Because the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) lack this, it is called "relinquishment.
Regarding the term "expedient means" (*upāya*), it restates the third section. As for the phrase "skillful in the Bodhisattva vehicle," it explains the meaning of expedient means:
it means that by being skillful in the Bodhisattva vehicle, one practices all Buddha-dharmas so as to bring them to completion.

Regarding the phrase "Thus, the Buddha is perfectly complete," the following explains the fourth [point], "the remainder who are insatiable. This remaining portion of the sūtra constitutes the fourth [point], "insatiability.
"Insatiability" explains the passage beginning with "Therefore, I should practice the ten wholesome paths," meaning that because one seeks them without ceasing, it is called "insatiability.
The phrase "attaining mastery within omniscience" explains the term "all-aspect" (*sarvākāra*), signifying that one becomes fully endowed with it.
The "feet" refer to that which is sought: the Buddha-wisdom, called "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*). Within that wisdom, being fully perfected and thoroughly matured, it is termed "sovereignty.

"Purity in all aspects" (*sarvākāraviśuddhi*) means to purify every aspect. As in the subsequent section of the sutra, the first "purity in all aspects" refers to the cessation of unwholesome habits through shared practice.
The "ten powers" (*daśabala*): regarding the term "power," the second phrase refers to wholesome karma.
The third phrase, "The mastery [of the Śrāvakas] and others abandon and gather all dharmas so that they may achieve accomplishment," refers to their skillfulness regarding the Bodhisattva vehicle.
The following section, "Therefore... and so forth, constitutes the fourth phrase, "lack of satiety.

The passage beginning with "subduing Māra" further explains the meaning of the ten powers (*daśabala*) by abandoning the two vehicles; "subduing the enemies of Māra" refers to the capacity and power of those powers.
Regarding the statement that the *Dharmasaṃgraha* (or *Kṣitigarbha-sūtra*) says "because of subduing Māra," it means that by abandoning all Māras and attaining victory, it is called "power" (*bala*).

As for the statement that the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) acts as the predominant condition (*adhipati*), this is said in contrast to the inferior to manifest the superior; that is, in relation to that Lesser Vehicle, the functioning of the Tathāgata’s ten powers is predominant, thereby manifesting the power of the Buddha-dharma.
This concluding virtue of the qualities belongs to the person, in relation to the functioning of the Tathāgata’s ten powers as compared to that Lesser Vehicle.

Because it was stated above that the ten powers (daśabala) are exclusively the Buddha-dharma and not the dharma of the Lesser Vehicle, the phrase "should be known" serves as a concluding exhortation to understand that one should know the ten powers are exclusively the Buddha-dharma and not the dharma of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, they are described here as being relinquished.

The second section, the precept of gathering wholesome qualities (*śīla-saṃgraha*), is now concluded. Following this, the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha*) is clarified; the scriptural text contains two parts:
first, a detailed exposition of gathering sentient beings, and second, a summary of gathering sentient beings beginning with "By relying on the power of upholding the precepts, one is well able...

This twofold structure exists in the Sūtra, and the Treatise follows it accordingly. Within the preceding detailed exposition, there are three sections: first, a general presentation of the arousal [of the mind]; second...

Opening the five gates, the threefold extensive explanation of the words follows the sequence above: the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha-śīla*) is "next superior" (*uttara*) in comparison to the preceding precept of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśala-saṃgraha-śīla*).

That which is adjacent to the preceding is called "next" (*uttara*); that which surpasses the preceding is named "superior" (*uttara*). While the former concerns only one's own goodness, this includes others;

therefore, the mind that gathers sentient beings is called "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*), and the arising of practices to gather others is termed the "precept of gathering sentient beings," which is "increasingly superior" (*uttarottara*). Below.

Opening the five gates, there are five enumerations: wisdom that discerns [the path], and so forth, which are collectively termed "gathering sentient beings. Thoroughly knowing the fruits of karma is called "wisdom.
From wisdom arises "vow," because one vows to abide in goodness oneself and to cause others to abide in it as well;

thus it is called "vow. Based on vow comes "practice," which refers to correct conduct; since one first desires to gather sentient beings through one's own practice, one first gives rise to compassion. Compassion...

Because it is able to gather and initiate activities for the benefit of sentient beings, it is called "accumulation" (*saṃbhāra*). Based on the previously accumulated mind, one gives rise to the practice of gathering (*saṃgraha-vihāra*);
because this practice arises based on accumulation, it is termed the "fruit of accumulation. This will be explained in detail below.

Within the exposition of the wisdom of understanding, first the chapter headings are opened, followed by the Sūtra and then the Śāstra. In the preceding opening of the chapters, there are three types of wisdom;

these are cited to state the number, and "time" (*kāla*) and so forth are listed as their names. Regarding the differentiation of time: in contrast to the fruit, the causes and effects are clarified across three periods of time;

in relation to these, the causes are distinguished and termed the "differentiation of time. Regarding the differentiation of retribution (*vipāka*): in contrast to the cause, the fruit is clarified as the ten unwholesome karmas.

The various distinct results obtained are called "the fruit of the differentiation of retributive habitual tendencies" (*vipāka-vāsanā-prabheda-phala*). This applies generally to both retribution (*vipāka*) and the residual energy of that retribution, which is termed "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*);
it does not refer to the intensification of habitual tendencies.
In the sutra, the preceding section extensively explains the distinctions between time, retribution, and habitual tendencies; all that follows is a summary of the causes of suffering.
Regarding the two aspects of the preceding Chinese text, there are three distinct points: first, the distinction between the phrasing and the meaning;

second, within the phrasing, the first part is general while the latter is specific—the ten unwholesome karmas as the cause for the upper realm of hell, the cause for animals in the middle, and the cause for hungry ghosts in the lower realm constitute the general section, while the remainder constitutes the specific section;
third, regarding the meaning, within the former general section the distinctions of time are clarified, and within the latter specific section the retributions and habitual tendencies are clarified.
The two different types constitute the third [point].

In the treatise, the broad explanation is first expounded, followed by the resolution of the concluding text. Within the former, there is first an explanation of the temporal, retributive, and habitual latencies;

subsequently, returning to these, their distinctions are clarified. Within the explanation of the temporal, there is first a restatement of the preceding section concerning the superior, middling, and inferior causes and effects of unwholesome karma.

The commentary clarifies their characteristics: regarding the explanation of the retributive fruits (*vipāka-phala*) based on the Sūtra, the preceding section provides a general summary while the present section provides a specific enumeration.

The former establishes the sequence of cause followed by effect; within that temporal sequence, the ten types of karma are generally explained. Among these, the causes for rebirth in hell, the causes for rebirth as animals, and the causes for rebirth as hungry ghosts are termed "general.
Following this, within the explanation of the retributive fruits, the ten types of karma are individually specified according to the distinct results each obtains; this is termed "specific."

The phrase "all evil states" explains and reveals their characteristics; below, the scriptural citation regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) restates the third section on humans, while the subsequent explanation clarifies that unwholesome habitual tendencies also exist among devas, though the text specifically addresses humans because these ten [categories] all possess habitual tendencies.
Thus it says "one by one," and following the scriptural citation, it again addresses the preceding points to clarify their distinctions.

First, the distinctions of suffering are clarified by way of time and retribution (*kāla-vipāka*). Regarding the distinction of time and retribution, this is presented as a general heading to demonstrate the profound gravity of suffering.
To explain how this is demonstrated: below, it is shown through specific details. Next, its distinctions are manifested through the perspective of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The phrase "reaching the path of the virtuous" refers to the time prior to reaching the path of the virtuous; through both time and retribution, the profound gravity of suffering is made clear.

Now, these habitual tendencies manifest suffering that is difficult to escape; there is also the aforementioned explanation of the "extensive" (*vistara*) and the following interpretation of the "knots" (*grantha*).

As for the combination of the general and the specific: the former refers collectively to what has been stated above. The difference in time is the general, while the retribution is the specific; because these two are weighty, they are singled out.
The combination of the general and the specific is termed "synthesis" (*saṃgraha*), wherein one contemplates them collectively. At this time, the retribution is experienced within the evil realms.
It is called "immeasurable great suffering within the evil realms" (*durgati*); since it is termed "evil realms," it is clear that they are not "wholesome paths.

Because the distinctions among their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are slight, they are not discussed. In the sutra, only the ten unwholesome karmas are summarized as the causes and conditions of suffering;
the commentator merely explains them as the causes and conditions for the great mass of various sufferings, omitting further detailed exposition as they are easy to understand.
Regarding the section on the vow (*praṇidhāna*), first the inquiry is raised, followed by the citation of the scriptural passage: "I abandon unwholesome vows" means to leave behind evil;

"vowing to delight in practicing the Dharma" means to accumulate goodness. "Delighting in relying upon the Great Dharma" is called "delighting in practicing the Dharma," and "delighting in giving rise to great practices" is called "delighting in practicing.
Below, the treatise explains the vow by restating the preceding categories; "delighting in the Great Dharma" is the explanation of "delighting in practicing the Dharma."
"Acting for the benefit [of others]" refers to the practice of benefiting sentient beings, which is subsumed under the practice of benefiting others;
"gathering wholesome dharmas" refers to the practice of self-benefit. This can be understood from the context of the sutra.

Within the section on practice, first the question is posed, followed by the citation of the sutra text: "Dwelling in seclusion" constitutes the practice for one's own benefit, while "causing others to dwell [therein]" constitutes the practice for the benefit of others.

Below, the commentary explains: "Dwelling in wholesome dharmas oneself" provides a general explanation of self-benefit; "secluding oneself from those obstacles" explains the abandonment of unwholesome states;
and "practicing the remedies" explains dwelling in the ten wholesome paths of action. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "also causing others... explains the benefit of others.

The arrangement of the sūtras can be understood from the headings. Within this collection, first come the questions, followed by the sūtras, and finally the śāstras. Regarding the śāstras, there are two parts: the first provides a general clarification for the purpose of generating the ten kinds of mental states.

Based on the aforementioned compassion, one previously contemplated suffering through wisdom and gave rise to superior compassion; now, relying upon that, one gives rise to the mind of origination (*samudaya-citta*).
It is also said that those who give rise to the ten minds for the sake of sentient beings do so because their respective actions differ; thus, the ten minds are distinguished and revealed separately.
Among these ten, the first eight take the lower realm as their object, while the latter two take the upper realm as their object.

Since the objects of the former eight are identical, they are explained in one place; since the latter two are similar, they are explained together. In explaining the first eight, there is first a general clarification.
These are collected into eight categories of sentient beings; subsequently, the eight pairs are explained individually within this collection.

First, among these, the six types of mind previously discussed in the context of "freedom from hatred" are distinguished according to their similarities and differences. Then, the text is interpreted. As for the similarities and differences, there are four kinds of distinctions:

first, the difference in combination and separation. The previous category of "sentient beings of evil conduct" is here divided into two, namely: "sentient beings of evil conduct" [and "sentient beings of good conduct"].
Regarding the gathering of sentient beings through the vow for awakening (*bodhicitta-praṇidhāna*), this section is divided into two:

those who practice together and those who are gathered for the sake of awakening. While the former involves giving rise to two types of minds—namely, compassion (*anukampā*) and the wish to bestow happiness—toward impoverished and suffering sentient beings in a general manner, here they are distinguished specifically; [these two minds] arise toward suffering sentient beings individually.
Regarding those who are happy, he gives rise to compassion toward the poor; thus three types of mental states arise, which differ from the previous ones.

Whereas previously he gave rise to a mind of pity (*anukampā*) toward the poor, now he gives rise to a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) toward the poor. Why is this so? Previously, he gave rise to a mind of pity because he pitied their suffering;
now, this Bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of compassion because he wishes to uproot their suffering. Furthermore, as for the former [state], it was directed toward sentient beings who were happy...
Regarding the arising of the mind of profit and the arising of the mind of compassion: why is it thus? The former [mind] arises to cause [beings] to abandon negligence and abide in wholesome dharmas;
the present [mind] arises as compassion because one considers that they shall undergo the retribution of suffering.
Fourth, the former and latter differ: in the former case, these were sentient beings of the second grade of evil conduct, whereas here they are of the first grade. The former... [text ends].
Those who are suffering from the four types of affliction constitute the second; those who were previously the first—enemies and rivals—constitute the third;
those who were previously the third—those in poverty—constitute the fourth. Apart from these four differences, all else is similar.
Next, I shall explain the text: in each of the subsequent phrases, one first mentions the birth, then clarifies the accumulation of the mind, and finally cites the sūtra.

The application of the "exhortation to the unwholesome" (*pāpa-udghaṭana*) is intended to cause one to abide in the wholesome; it is explained in relation to the mind of accumulation (*saṃcaya-citta*) below by means of the Sūtra.

The application of the "exhortation to suffering" (*duḥkha-udghaṭana*) is intended to cause one to find joy in [the cessation of] that which is not exhausted; it is explained in relation to the mind of accumulation below by means of the Sūtra. The application of the "exhortation to resentment" (*vaira-udghaṔana*) is intended to prevent the thought of seeking retribution;

it is explained in relation to the mind of accumulation below by means of the Sūtra. The application of the "exhortation to poverty" (*dāridrya-udghaṭana*) is intended for what was previously called "suffering," which refers to being oppressed by adverse conditions (*vipakṣa-pratyaya*).

Regarding this statement on poverty: "insufficiency of conditions" refers to the desire to bring about the cessation of suffering; "the mind directed toward the accumulation [of merit]" is clarified below by the scriptural citation. Regarding compassion:

"compassion for their poverty and suffering" refers to the practice of joyful engagement so that one does not become negligent; "the mind directed toward the accumulation [of merit]" is clarified below by the scriptural citation.
As ordinary beings often give rise to negligence when obtaining pleasure, [the text] instructs them to abandon it; "pity" refers to the following scriptural citation.
Those who are negligent shall undergo suffering. To cause externalist sentient beings to believe in the Buddha-dharma, he cites their own actions as a contrast to clarify the mind of accumulation;
because externalists slander erroneously, this causes them to believe in the Dharma. Below, the sutra provides a scriptural citation to likewise cite their actions.

For the sake of small-vehicle sentient beings who practice the same path as the Buddha-dharma, it distinguishes them from the aforementioned externalists; thus it says "practicing together" to cause them not to regress. This is done in contrast to [the former case].
The "Clarifying the Mind of Gathering" (ming ji xin) means that according to what one cultivates, one teaches, transforms, and protects others so that they do not regress;
it uses the sutras as a binding to encompass the vow for bodhi, raising up all that is done. From this stage onward, those who seek the Mahāyāna are said to "encompass the vow.

Because the vow raises everything equally, it is called "taking all as one's own body"; through the "Clarifying the Mind of Gathering," one gathers sentient beings so that they are identical [to oneself].
Because his body remains as it was, he is said to be "as himself. That all these sentient beings are none other than my own body—this explains "as himself.
Dwelling in the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), he desires to serve as a place of reliance for sentient beings; those who have resolved their minds likewise serve as a place of reliance for all.
Since what they do is no different from what I do, it is said that they are "identical" [to me]. Therefore, the benefit and assistance provided is as such.
"Being no different from oneself" refers to the sutra passage below; "generating the remaining two" refers to the subsequent explanation of the latter two minds.

First the mention, then the explanation: "surpassing oneself" means excelling within the Bodhisattva-dharma; "gathering and possessing virtue" means reaching ultimate fulfillment in the stage of the Tathāgata.
As the sutra states below, citing the scripture to reveal the mind: regarding those who advance, one gives rise to the mind of a teacher and becomes capable.
Because it instructs me, I give rise to a mind of reverence toward those possessed of virtue, for their virtues are worthy of honor.
Within the collection of results, there is first a general summary and later a specific detail; that which is subsumed by supreme compassion constitutes the general summary.

The former collection of the mind is termed "supreme compassion," while the latter collection of results is termed "desire," because one desires to rescue and deliver the ten classes of sentient beings.
It is called "the superior basis for desire" because desire arises based on compassion; thus it is said to be "subsumed. Furthermore, what follows below constitutes its specific analysis.
Within this analysis, first there is a brief presentation, followed by a detailed explanation. Regarding the brief presentation, it is cited according to the Sūtra.

In the Sūtra, each of the ten sections first clarifies the sentient beings to be converted and subsequently demonstrates the benefits of the conversion. The author of the treatise now first [proceeds with]...

Having collectively presented the ten types of sentient beings within the sutra, he subsequently analyzes the ten types of sentient beings to be transformed through the ten modes of transformative benefit;
these categories are neither fixed nor exhaustive. Now, according to one specific approach, we shall discuss these ten types.

Among them, the first is the sentient being of wrong understanding, while the remaining nine are sentient beings of wrong practice. Regarding the phrase "furthermore" (*punar-aparam*): previously, the cultivation of the mind was explained; now, this further clarifies it.

The fifth [section] is called "Fruit" (*phala*) because it refers to the fruition; thus, it is said "again. As for what is called "reliance" (*āśraya*), it is so termed because the transformation relies upon the ten births; thus, it is said "reliance.
Regarding the "predominant inversion" (*adhipati-viparyāsa*), it is the first among the ten, as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) overturns the objective realm and is named "inversion.

Because it is the most extreme among delusive inversions, it is called "predominant. The first of the ten is called the "head. Next, the remaining wrong practices of sentient beings are explained; therein, first—

According to their essentials, they are threefold; within these three, when enumerating them, the names are listed as the pursuit of sensual desires (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*) and so forth. Seeking the five external objects of desire is called the "pursuit of sensual desires" (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*).

Seeking the fruit of the primary retribution within the three realms of existence is called the "pursuit of existence" (*bhava-paryeṣaṇā*). Seeking the path of transcendence is called the "pursuit of the holy life" (*brahmacarya-paryeṣaṇā*).

The first three of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) constitute these [three pursuits], making nine in total. The pursuit of sensual desires is divided into five, while the pursuit of the holy life is divided into two, each further subdivided into two.
Regarding the first part of the section on desire, it is divided into two: first, the number two is presented; next, two names are listed.

That which refers to the faults arising from the enjoyment of the five objects of desire currently present is called "the time of enjoyment. That which refers to the faults arising when seeking the five objects of desire not yet obtained is called "the time of pursuit.
The second part is further divided into five: first, regarding enjoyment, it is divided into three. As for that which is not shared, it refers to what has already been obtained.
When one does not share material things with others at the time of expenditure, the fault of anger arises; when there is no contentment while seeking, the fault of greed arises from insatiability;
and when one receives and accumulates, the fault of increasing delusion arises as the three poisons develop in accordance with the objects stored and not used.
These three phrases describe the faults that give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*); hereafter, they are categorized according to the stage of pursuit.
Regarding the two types of pursuit: for those who pursue present retribution and practice unwholesome deeds, they engage in misconduct because their pursuit of the present is irrational;
for those who pursue future retribution and practice wholesome deeds, they do not obtain the wholesome fruits of future happiness, and thus their practice of wholesome deeds leads toward danger.
Therefore, these two phrases refer to the faults arising from the undertaking of karma. Below, this is further categorized according to the division of "seeking."
The first two lines refer to the fault of transmigrating through the six realms of existence; the next two lines refer to the fault of the difficulty of escaping the three realms.
These two [sets of] phrases concern the fault of increasing suffering. Below, regarding the pursuit of Brahma, they are further divided into two:
