the fault of seeking erroneously through heterodox paths, and the fault of the narrowness and inferiority of the same Dharma (the Hīnayāna). These two types constitute the fault of deviating from the Path. [End of] Upper Collection.
In the mind, one universally takes as objects sentient beings who have resolved their minds toward the Mahāyāna, up to those endowed with merit;
why then is it that here the ordinary person and the Hīnayāna are clarified while the Mahāyāna is not explicitly highlighted?

It is because those Mahāyāna practitioners who are weary of the world must also be transformed, and thus they are not discussed here due to brevity. Furthermore, the intention of the compiler to benefit others is vast in its scope, extending even to...
Because the Buddha also gives rise to the thought [of awakening], this collection of fruits uses the Dharma to rescue and deliver them;

beyond the Mahāyāna, there is no other Dharma superior to it that can encompass and transform beings, and thus it is omitted from discussion here. Below, the manifestation of benefits for those sentient beings is shown:
regarding the ten types of sentient beings previously listed who follow such paths, each of these ten types of sentient beings has—

Regarding "the antidote according to the destination," this means bestowing the remedial dharma upon one after measuring what is appropriate for them. Regarding "abiding in what is suitable," this means bestowing the path upon one after measuring what is appropriate;
it cannot be defined by a single fixed term. "According to what is suitable" refers to the following section, which explains and analyzes based on the sequence of the preceding ten [categories].

In the first section of the introductory gate, there is first a question that initiates the discourse. Within the scripture, the faults are first presented, followed by the explanation of their remedies.
Regarding the fault of falling into error, it is generally explained as "perversity" (*viparyāsa*). Seeking outside the [true] principle is called "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);

"falling" refers to descending into evil, while "evil intention" (*akuśalacitta*) specifically clarifies the practice of perversity. Below, it is shown that the aforementioned false views serve as the cause for all faults. For whom does [this apply]?
"Practice" (*caryā*) refers to acting within the dense forest of the evil paths; the subsequent commentary explains this as follows:

the "true path of remedial practice" treats the previous falling into error by establishing one in right view, while it treats the previous evil intentions and evil minds through the "Dharma as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-dharma*), which serves as the remedy for proceeding toward the dense forest of evil practices.

In this treatise, first the refutation is explained, followed by the exposition of the antidote. Within the refutation, first the general [definition] is explained, and subsequently it is combined with the citation of the sutra.

Regarding "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): this term is cited to introduce the initial general category, referring to the four perversions (*viparyāsa*). To point out its specific characteristics, the meaning of perversion is explained in detail in other chapters;

this should be discussed in full there. Next, its specific types are explained. This perversion is twofold: citing the general category to open up the specific, these two perversions arise from a malicious intent.

Because the practitioner who focuses their mindfulness observes the conditions of "name" (nāma), and because it arises within the conditions of the two inversions—permanence and bliss—it is called "mind" (*manas*).

That which contradicts reality is termed "evil"; it is produced by the mental application (*manasikāra*) that gives rise to afflictions, and thus it is called "the practice of focused mindfulness. These two inversions—the evil mind—are not [mere] focused mindfulness;
their fundamental arising and gathering is the meaning of "mind. Compared to the preceding [inversions of] permanence and bliss, the two inversions of self and purity [are further removed].
Because it is the fundamental source of all arising, it is called "mind" (*citta*). The self (*ātman*) is eternal and fundamentally pure; this is the origin of bliss.

These two natures are established as such and do not arise through volitional effort; they are termed "non-contemplation" (*amanasikāra*). However, within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the beginning and the end are not one, for there are nine stages:
first, true mind (*tathatā-citta*) is the root, and ignorance (*avidyā*) is the branch. Thus, Asvaghosa said: "Based upon True Suchness (*tathatā*), there exists its non-existence."

1. It clarifies that the two types of ignorance—the ignorance of the cause of defilement and the ignorance of habitual perfuming—are the root, while the three inversions of mind, thought, and view are the branches. 2.

Among these three inversions of mind, thought, and view, the inversion of mind is the root and the inversions of view and thought are the branches, because the four inversions arise based upon the three inversions. 3. Within the four inversions, the inversions of self and purity are [the root].
1. Taking "eternal," "blissful," "self," and "pure" as the root, and taking the arising of the six and four inversions based on these as the branch; 2.

Taking the evil destinies produced by the aforementioned [inversions] as the root, and taking the dense forest of those evil destinies as the branch; 3. Within that dense forest of evil destinies, taking the specific evil destinies as the root and the dense forest itself as the branch; 4.
Furthermore, taking the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the nature of the dense forest as the root and their manifest arousal as the branch; 8. All afflictions (*kleśa*).

The fundamental cause consists of the various karmas, while the derivative effects consist of the nine afflictions and karma; these together constitute the root, with the fruit of suffering being the derivative.

Here, for the time being, we are merely distinguishing between root and derivative according to the fifth gate. Below, in the explanation of the "dense forest of evil conduct" within the Sūtra, the term "that" refers to the aforementioned four inverted views.
The phrase "dense forest of conduct" signifies that which is not the correct path of practice; it does not refer to the meaning of practicing with correct understanding.
This is precisely as in this sutra: the evil realms are designated as "evil dharmas" according to their meaning, and being biased and deviant, they are called the "non-right path.

Because those four preceding inversions can act as a dense forest (*gahana*) of what is non-right, they are called "conduct" (*caryā*); because they give rise to that [forest], they are termed "causes" (*hetu*), which clarifies the sense of the preceding "conduct," for conduct is like a cause.
The following explains the meaning of the "dense forest of the evil realms. It is not... [the end of the fragment].
The formal restatement of the preceding [passage]—"these various afflictions" (*kleśa*)—refers to the dense forest (*gahana*) of manifest afflictions such as greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*).

The restatement of the preceding "afflictive proclivities" (*anuśaya*) is because all afflictions, having long been practiced until they become inherent dispositions, constantly follow sentient beings and act like servants;

therefore, they are called "proclivities. Because these many proclivities form a forest and their accumulation is difficult to distinguish, it is called "dense. The application of the Sūtra [to this] can be understood from below.

The commentary by Shi Zhizhong first provides an explanation and subsequently offers a topical summary (*pratīka*). Regarding the term "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*): because the Dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) can remedy the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), it is called the Sublime Dharma.

This explains the passage in the Sūtra concerning "practicing the true path to remedy previous faults. First, regarding the general explanation of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*):
in order to avoid confusion with other views, the Sūtra uses "right mindfulness" as its heading for the passage on "abiding in the path of right view."

Distinguishing their characteristics, these are explained as the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) which constitute right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*); therefore, they are called right mindfulness and right view.

Among these, they serve as remedies for the faults of the preceding [false views]: the evil intentions and evil minds. Within the four foundations of mindfulness, mindfulness of the body remedies [the false view of] purity; mindfulness of phenomena remedies [the false view of] self; mindfulness of the mind remedies [the false view of] permanence;
and mindfulness of feelings remedies [the false view of] pleasure—each respectively countering the corresponding evil intention. Thus, they emerge from [the afflictions].
The "Worldly Dharmas" (*lokadharma*) explain the dharmas as they truly are within the sūtra. They treat the dense forest of evil deeds committed during the preceding transgressions.

Regarding the explanation of the "unshared" [dharmas], there is first a question and then the sūtra text, which consists of two parts. First, regarding the treatment of transgressions following the lapse:

the phrase "mutual destruction of common characteristics" (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa-vināśa*) generally clarifies the destruction and the analytical distinction of common disputes; the subsequent section, beginning with "destruction by day and night," lists the specific instances of destruction.

This section summarizes and concludes [the discussion on] the bond of resentment (*upanāha*) that persists day and night; it follows the previous analysis of the unceasingly blazing bond of anger (*pratigha*), which arose from prior strife and contention.
Because anger constitutes a fault, it is remedied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

This treatise analyzes the remedies according to the faults and provides two interpretations. Within the first interpretation, there is first an explanation, followed by a citation, and finally a further detailed analysis.

Regarding "experiencing what is not shared," this restates the preceding section. Regarding "mutually refuting one another," this cites the general category to clarify that "mutual" (互) is equivalent to "shared" (共).
Next, its specific distinctions are explained; there are two types of destruction. This refers to opening up the specific from the general. Next, their names are listed:

"hostility toward the mind" means anger resides in the mind, explaining the aforementioned "discrimination"; "quarreling in speech" means divisive contention resides in the mouth, explaining the aforementioned "constant quarreling."
Thus, having explained the destruction of bonds and the formation of general mental enmity and verbal strife, the following section explains the concluding text.
"Reflecting on retribution" means resolving resentment; because of resentment, one reflects on seeking revenge.
"The words and deeds are blazing" explains "blazing up"; "increasing" explains "not ceasing. The application of these terms in the sutra is clear.
In the lower section, "Detailed Analysis Regarding the Mind that Confronts the Enemy," the preceding treatise (*śāstra*) is cited and analyzed.

By distinguishing between "self" and "other," this sūtra passage employs the term "analysis" (*vibhaṅga*) to demonstrate that the same term is used in the treatise for the mind that confronts the enemy.
Furthermore, this phrasing accords with foreign (Sanskrit) terminology; strictly speaking, it should be stated that this term "demonstrates" refers to the analysis within that treatise.
The phrase "words toward an enemy" demonstrates the analytical discourse found in the Sūtra; the subsequent phrases demonstrate that the same applies by analogy.
Regarding "strife in speech," the preceding treatise is cited: "Constantly engaged in strife. Below, the Sūtra is cited in contrast to clarify the intensity of the karmic formation of thought.

Regarding "the intensity of resentment," the preceding treatise is cited: "Resentment is intense. Below, the Sūtra is cited in contrast to clarify the antidote; herein, first there is the explanation, followed by the application.
Regarding the first question among the "insatiable riches," the scriptural text consists of two parts: first, the transgression; second, the subsequent remedy.

Within the section on the transgression, "one whose mind is insatiable" refers to one whose inner heart is difficult to satisfy, who constantly seeks the wealth of others through deception of body and speech, and who maintains a wrong livelihood—this summarizes the transgression.

Within the section on the subsequent remedy, "purifying body and speech" remedies the aforementioned constant seeking [of wealth], while "purifying mental karma" remedies the aforementioned insatiability.
Right livelihood treats the previous wrong livelihood of self-sustenance.

The treatise divides this into two parts according to the faults addressed: first, the explanation; second, the application of the sutra. Regarding "insatiability," it refers to the two previously mentioned categories:

first, the mind seeking desire; second, the body and speech [engaging in it]. As for "greed in the mind," it refers to the initial state of the mind seeking desire; as for those [involving] the body and speech...

"Deceiving and seizing through skillful means" (upāya): the following explains its characteristics. "Weighing with a false scale" refers to falsehood of the body; "false speech with a false scale" refers to falsehood of the mouth.

To cause someone to lose [property] without their awareness is called "seizing through skillful means. The mention of "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*) is omitted here without further explanation, as it can be understood from the context of the sutra. The commentary on the treatment [of this topic] is clear and may be understood.

Regarding the accumulation of wealth, there is first the initial inquiry and then the sutra. Within the sutra, there are two parts; the first concerns the subsequent treatment of faults. This section contains three phrases:

first, "the cause" refers to the first phrase, which generally clarifies the fault of taking the accumulation of wealth as a cause; second, "following after" and so forth specifically clarifies its function as a cause;
third, "constantly being" and so forth concludes by establishing the fault of delusion—being repeatedly burned by afflictions and failing to know how to seek liberation.
Therefore, it is called the affliction of delusion; because it can burn, it is described as fire. Regarding the placement in a cool place among the remedies mentioned below:
Nirvāṇa is that cool place, established as a cool place in contrast to the aforementioned fire.

The section on "Treating Faults According to Their Occurrence" is divided into two parts. Regarding the explanation of the preceding faults, the phrase "receiving and accumulating" restates the fault of the previously mentioned gateway of greed and other afflictions;
this explains the first cause. Because the accumulation of wealth can give rise to the three poisons of greed and so forth, it is called "accumulation of wealth.

This serves as the essential nature of the cause. The reason why it is a fault is that it gives rise to the three poisons. The passage beginning with "that defiled attachment" explains the second [cause].
"Pursuing greed and the like" refers to those who are stained by attachment; "giving rise to anger through dissipation" refers to those who follow after aversion;
"treasuring, enjoying, and delighting in objects of pleasure" refers to those who follow after delusion. "Treasuring" means holding them as precious; "treasuring and enjoying" means cherishing them.
Those sentient beings, regarding the objects of the five sensual pleasures they enjoy, hold them dear and cherish them, never knowing weariness or detachment.
The phrase "therefore this is the category of delusion" explains the third point; "the category of the fault of delusion" establishes the conclusion.

"Burnt by" explains being consumed by various fires. "Neither seeing nor seeking" is an exegesis of the sutra; "unable to resolve upon seeking the essential way" can be understood through the commentary.
The explanation of the remedy is easy to understand.

Regarding the first inquiry within the section on seeking results in the present life, there are two parts in the sutra. First, the fault of past transgressions and their subsequent treatment; this contains four points:
(1) the fault of the mind being shrouded by delusion—because one seeks slight pleasure in the present, one creates many causes for sin and will undergo great suffering in the future;
this is due to ignorance (*moha*). (2) The fault of entering the great abyss and increasing unwholesome dharmas while distancing oneself from wholesome dharmas. (3) Falling into the great abyss.

Regarding the suffering of retribution, following the four [preceding points], the text below clarifies the fault of remorseful vision at the time of death. Within this section, there are three phrases:
first, transforming sentient beings so that they may attain the eye of wisdom; second, seeing the true reality of dharmas with the eye of wisdom;
third, by seeing reality, one immediately attains the unobstructed wisdom-eye of suchness. This is the understanding that illuminates emptiness; because of this understanding, [the following occurs].

To see that phenomena are empty and quiescent is called knowing the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Because one sees reality, one accomplishes the Buddha-wisdom, thoroughly penetrates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and attains unimpeded knowledge.
Realizing that [wisdom] arises from one's own mind without depending on a teacher’s instruction is called "not following others.
Because one sees the reality of phenomena, one no longer delights in practicing various evil deeds.
The treatise, following the faults to be remedied, divides [the section] into two gates. Within the section on faults, the initial statement "pursuing and practicing evil" cites the preceding gate;
below, its characteristics are explained. There are four kinds of faults, which are explained in sequence. In explaining the first fault, there are four distinct parts:

(1) citing the sūtra to manifest the fault; (2) the explanation; (3) the application; and (4) the further differentiation. Thus, from "since there is... up to "the fault of being covered," [the text proceeds].
The first section here cites the sutra to reveal faults; therein, "delusion" (*moha*) constitutes the essence of delusion, while "darkness" (*tamas*) is its characteristic.

Because the deluded mind is like darkness or obscurity, it is called "darkness. Since [false views] such as "erroneous views" are the faults of delusion that can cover and obstruct, these are termed "faults" (*doṣa*).
This refers to the fault of practicing unwholesome conduct; thus they are called "faults. The meaning of "fault" in the subsequent phrases follows this same pattern.
However, in the second explanation, the phrase "the fault of being obscured by delusion and so forth" merely explains the obscuration;

"those who falsely perceive pleasure" explains false perception (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), for while pleasure does not exist in reality, they falsely claim it does. "Not seeing the future fruit" explains the "thick gloom" (*ghanatamas*);

because they are currently practicing unwholesome deeds and will consequently undergo great suffering, they do not see this due to their ignorance (*moha*), hence it is called "thick gloom. "Not seeing the present" [is explained as follows:]...
This explains the obscuration of darkness (*tamo-āvṛti*). Because one does not recognize the reality of suffering due to delusion (*moha*), it is called "obscured by darkness";
this can be understood from the citation of the Sūtra. Below, there is a further analysis of delusion, which restates the first phrase and names it "darkness" (*andhakāra*);

this is used to clarify the preceding [explanation] by manifesting the characteristics of the darkness of delusion. "False view" (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) restates the Sūtra; "perverted desire for pleasure" cites the Śāstra to contrast and clarify that perverted view. Just as... [text continues].
The previous [section] was a false view regarding pleasure. "Thick obscuration" (*thūla-andhakāra*) cites the Sūtra to show that future results are not seen;

citing the Śāstra, this is contrasted with the Sūtra to clarify it. "Darkness" (*andhakāra*) cites the Sūtra to show that present results are not seen; citing the Śāstra, this is contrasted with the Sūtra to clarify it. In the second fault, there are also four parts:

first, stating the fault; second, explaining it; third, applying it; and fourth, citing the Sūtra and Śāstra to comparatively distinguish this fault. This fault has two aspects: first, increasing evil.
Regarding the two aspects of the Dharma: first, it is the cause of delusion that fulfills the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) which increase the faults of evil;

because this mind of delusion acts as the cause for the latent tendencies, it is called the "cause of delusion. The nature of greed, hatred, and so forth, which arise based on delusion, is termed "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*);

when these latent tendencies are fully present, they are called "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*). Because this fulfillment of latent tendencies is the habituation of evil faults, it is called a "fault" (*doṣa*). Furthermore, it is because it distances one from the sphere of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
This refers to that which is distant from the wholesome and transcends the supramundane noble path; it is called the "outflow-free state" (*anāsrava-pada*).

To be "deluded and averse" to this is what is meant by being "distant. Next, [the text] explains this: "obstructing those wholesome practices" explains the subsequent "separation from the outflow-free state.

"Conforming to the unwholesome" explains the aforementioned cause of delusion—the "sufficiency of the outflows" (*āsrava-paryāpti*) and the "enablers" (*anuśaya*). Below, the sūtra passage "entering the dark forest" serves as a gloss for the aforementioned cause of delusion—the sufficiency of the enablers.
The "Passing Beyond Darkness" section concerns the cause of delusion; the "Great Section" concerns fulfillment; and the "Thicket" section concerns causing entry.

As for the single character "one" (之) mentioned previously, it was not understood as a section heading. Rather, it is brought forward by way of the preceding momentum to clarify that those who practice evil deeds enter that forest arising within the black darkness;
it is not that they enter a "Black Darkness Forest" from which darkness is produced. For this reason, it is called the "Thicket of Black Darkness."

The "Forest" (*vana*) refers to the light of wisdom that is far removed from it; the "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the locus of profound knowledge. Below, there is a detailed analysis of the "dense forest" (*gahana*). Citing the Sūtra:

This is the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) caused by delusion (*moha*). Raising the treatise (*śāstra*) to clarify: All underlying tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśa-anuśaya*) arise based on the cause of delusion.

By citing the root, the branches are indicated; therefore, they are called the "underlying tendencies caused by delusion. Here, we take the underlying tendencies belonging to the category of the cause of delusion to correspond with the preceding "dense forest," rather than taking delusion itself.

Regarding the phrase "because the great cause fulfills the sūtra": this cites the treatise (*śāstra*) to clarify that the locus of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is easy to understand, as it does not correspond to the third fault.

Within the text, there are three distinct sections: first, citing the fault; second, applying the sūtra to it; and third, distinguishing between the sūtra and the treatise through mutual correspondence.
To correspond with the faults, one cites those faults. Because it is capable of receiving the fruit, it is called [the cause].

Because the name "fruit" (vipāka) refers to that which is received, and because the evil fruits one receives are characterized by many obstacles and impediments, they are called "obstructions" (pratigha). Being "extreme" in their obstruction, they are termed "great";

this refers to the fault of practicing evil, which results in receiving these great obstructions. The term "affliction" (*pīḍā*) is merely another name for "fault," as can be understood from the corresponding passage in the Sūtra.

Regarding the subsequent detailed analysis of "obstruction," the text cites the treatise; the phrase "darkness" (*andhakāra*) is raised to illustrate the meaning through a scriptural parallel, thereby demonstrating it.
The term "darkness" (*tamas*) indicates a great counterpart (*mahā-pratipakṣa*). Just as in the darkness below, this explains the sūtras and harmonizes them with the śāstras;

thus the title of the scripture is the *Tamaḥ-śāstra*. Why is it called a "great counterpart"? It must be explained that darkness establishes the meaning of its counterpart. For example, when walking in the dark, there are obstacles everywhere;
this is explained by means of a metaphor to clarify "hindrance," which is like a counterpart. In this way, through similarity, the meaning is revealed by means of the metaphor.

The phrase "the Dharma explains this great counterpart" refers to the explanation of "reception" (upādāna) down to its establishment as the meaning of "falling" (pātana). "Reception" is the great counterpart that establishes the explanation;

the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms (tridurgati) is its great counterpart. Because the causal matter of receiving that great counterpart is accomplished, it is called the "accomplishment of the matter of reception.

The phrase "reaching the various evil destinies" explains the term "reaching" (gati). The previous mention of the "great counterpart" and the current mention of "evil destinies" are stated in alternating fashion.
Because one hears [this], it is called "falling. By means of this reception, the "falling" spoken of in the sūtra is established.
Regarding the fourth fault, the explanation of "committing many sins" has three distinct parts: first, citing the fault; second, applying the sūtra to it;

third, analyzing the causes for committing many sins up to the point of repentance and insight. This is the citation of the fault. Within that, there are five phrases, the first of which is "committing sin."
First, the two [causes]; second, at the time of death; third, seeing the signs of retribution; fourth, the arising of remorse in the mind; fifth, this is the vision itself.
Now, it is precisely to clarify that seeing has its causes that the commission of offenses is explained; since seeing necessarily occurs at a specific time, the moment of death is clarified.

Regarding what is beheld at the time of death: it refers to seeing the signs of retribution. Seeing that which can give rise to remorse is called "remorseful vision. This remorseful vision serves to habituate one to the faults of evil.
Below, the scriptural passage is cited according to what is seen; "rectifying the vision" refers to what kind of vision it is—namely, the vision of reaching various perilous paths.
Below, there is a detailed analysis of seeing the perilous paths, which restates the scriptural text.

Regarding "because of rectifying the vision," this cites the treatise to clarify that when one sees the perilous paths, one is able to give rise to a mind of repentance; therefore, that vision is called "the vision of repentance."
Having seen the signs of one's fundamental offenses, as detailed in the preceding treatise, one frequently creates the causes for further offenses;
seeing the signs of retribution for evil, one is unable to gather the means for their remedy, and thus fails to reach the realization of the sūtras.

With the eye of wisdom that illuminates emptiness, which is the power of correct view, being weak and unable to arise through gathering, and because there is no remedy, one falls into perilous paths according to what is perceived. This is cited from the sūtra text regarding the time of death.

The phrase "the one who" is used at the conclusion of the treatise to clarify by way of contrast. Below, in the explanation of the "remedies," "real dharmas" refers to the remedial dharmas of emptiness and selflessness.
"Unobstructed" below clarifies that within these remedies, non-obstructive wisdom is the resultant wisdom (*phala-jñāna*), while the "pure eye of wisdom" is the causal wisdom (*hetu-prajñā*).

In the section concerning the seeking of future retribution, there is first the question and then the sutra text. The sutra text has two parts; the first concerns the subsequent treatment of faults, which contains twelve distinct phrases.

The very first phrase functions both as a general heading and as a specific detail: it serves as the general heading because it can accord with [the fault], and it serves as the specific detail because it is that which is followed.
Here, in order to clarify the fault of falling into a perilous path while practicing wholesome dharmas, the term "that which can accord" is stated to serve as the general heading.
That which is followed is the very nature of the perilous path; it is designated as "distinct" because it differs from other obstructions.

Within the fourfold analysis of the remedy, the phrase "I pull them out from the various sufferings of birth" constitutes the first clause, meaning one pulls them out from the sufferings of the three miserable realms where they have fallen.
The phrase "delivering them from the world" constitutes the second clause, meaning one delivers them from the hardships of the human and celestial realms where they might otherwise fall.
Abiding in the state of fearlessness is the third phrase; in contrast to the previous [phrase] which clarifies the extraction from suffering, this clarifies abiding in nirvāṇa.
Omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the fourth phrase; in contrast to the aforementioned transcendence of the world, this clarifies the attainment of bodhi.
Since omniscience refers to all-knowing wisdom, it is described as a "city" in contrast to the previous "perilous path."
The treatise divides the section on "remedying according to faults" into two parts. Regarding the first fault, the phrase "practicing wholesome conduct" cites the preceding category.

In the subsequent explanation, it first clarifies the initial general fault of being "conducive": the term "perilous path" refers to the good destinies of humans and devas being on the verge of falling into the three miserable realms, much like a dangerous road in the world;
thus it is called a "perilous path. To practice wholesomeness in order to seek those [good destinies] is termed "conducive."

Following a precipice is not peaceful; thus it is known from the sutra passage that this is a fault. There are three types of precipices, which will be explained by categorizing them according to what they follow.
First, the enumeration of their number; second, the listing of their names. The essential nature of the precipitous path is called its "substance" (*tattva*).
Because it is difficult to emerge from it, it is called an "obstruction. Because dwelling therein causes one to lose the wholesome dharmas of renunciation, it is called a "loss."

The following provides a detailed explanation of its substance. The first section, which states "the world," precisely identifies its essential nature; this is what is being followed in accordance with that initial phrase.

The phrase "lacking roots of goodness" clarifies the meaning of its treacherousness: because it takes meager roots of goodness as its basis, one is easily prone to falling and tumbling, and is thus called a "treacherous path.
Since this was already presented previously, it is not restated here. Next, the second section is introduced; it contains eight points, and the number is first stated.

The following provides a detailed explanation of these eight points: the first two are delusions regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); the next two are delusions regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); the next two are delusions regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*);

and the final two are delusions regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Within the first pair of statements, the former refers to the existence of suffering, while the latter refers to being deluded regarding suffering yet seeking its exit.

This is termed "worldly sentient beings" who, out of weariness and detachment from the three miserable realms, perform wholesome deeds in pursuit of happiness; this is called "seeking exit," yet it remains in accordance with worldly concerns.

"Falling into the three evil realms" explains and reveals their faults. Below, the sutra provides the illustration: "Like a perilous path in the world on the brink of a precipice about to fall"—the future three miserable paths are like deep pits.
Although one has not yet fallen from the good paths of humans and devas, the fall is not far off;
therefore, it says "about to fall. "Entering the net" lists their names: they are like the tangled weeds and vines of a perilous path in the world, where there is no way to advance or traverse.

The matter of the perilous path of birth and death is likewise so; because it is difficult to emerge from wrong views, it is called "suffering upon entering the net," which explains the nature of falsely conceiving pleasure where there is none.
That humans and devas actually experience suffering yet falsely conceive the notion of pleasure can be understood from the scriptural citations.

In the following two lines, the first line refers to delusion regarding the origin (*samudaya*), while the latter line refers to the creation of that origin. "Enveloped in darkness" lists their names, just as a worldly perilous path is overgrown with wild thickets and shrouded in gloom.
One cannot look about at will on the perilous path of birth and death; the matter is likewise so. Because delusion (*moha*) clouds the mind, it is said to be "covered.

Following that delusion, its characteristics are explained below. "Due to" (*yīn*) means "by means of. Regarding the explanation of delusion as darkness and the "proliferation" (*papañca*) of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) such as greed:
these are what constitute the "proliferations. Because they cover the mind, they are called "non-awakening. Below, this is corroborated by a scriptural citation.

Because the latent tendencies of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*) are not singular, they are described as "various. To enumerate these inverted practices, it is like a worldly dangerous path with many narrow byways that are difficult to traverse;
the situation on the dangerous path of birth and death is likewise. Evil dharmas fill the world, making it difficult to rely upon for progress in learning.

To abandon the bliss of the supramundane and practice the evil paths of the world explains their characteristics. Because one abandons the bliss of transcendence (*lokottara-sukha*) to practice the evil paths of the world, it is called "erroneous conduct" (*mithyā-caryā*).
The passage below explains that those who follow deluded paths do so by relying on false teachings; those who practice inverted conduct give rise to false karma.

In the subsequent two phrases, the first indicates the absence of the essence of the Path, while the latter indicates the absence of the conditions for the Path. "Blind and dark" is a descriptive term: it is like a person in a precipice who has lost their sight and finds it difficult to escape.
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are likewise so called because they lack the eye of right wisdom; thus, they are "blind and dark," being blinded by craving for the fruits [of existence].
The commentary explains its characteristics: those who are attached to the fruits of human and celestial rebirths and whose minds of wisdom are shrouded by craving are said to be "blind.

This can be understood from the scriptural passage. Regarding the listing of names for those who lack guidance: just as it is difficult for one in a precipice to ascend the right path without a guide to lead them, so too are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

because they turn their backs on the Great Sage, it is difficult for them to realize the right path. Therefore, they are called "far removed" [from enlightenment]. The following section explains its characteristics in detail.

Being born in the evil realms refers to the three miserable paths (*tiryag-yoni*, *preta*, and *naraka*). The "difficulties for those who are heedless" among gods and humans refer to the difficulties of Uttarakuru and the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyus-deva*), as well as other places where gods and humans commit transgressions.
Even if one encounters the era of a Buddha, not seeing or hearing [the Dharma] refers to those such as the congenitally blind and the congenitally deaf.
Because these individuals turn their backs on the Noble Ones (*ārya*), they are termed "far removed. This can be understood from the two subsequent lines of the sutra passage.
The first phrase refers to delusion regarding cessation (*nirodha*), and the latter phrases refer to having obstacles, seeking, and pursuing different destinations; these are listed by name.
It is like being lost on a perilous path, where it is difficult to escape; ordinary beings are likewise deluded regarding *nirvāṇa*, finding it difficult to emerge from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Those who seek *nirvāṇa* all loathe suffering and desire its extinction. As for those who pursue different destinations, they falsely claim that the Brahma-heaven is *nirvāṇa*.

"Creating merit and seeking its name" refers to "going to different places. The following explains its characteristics: it refers to the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of the first dhyāna, such as the Brahma heavens, and so forth;
"taking the superior" means including the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) of the Brahma realms, which is the environmental fruit (*adhiṣṭhāna-phala*) of the first dhyāna, and so forth.
This means taking those karmic rewards as the cause for transcending the world. Regarding "right view," the sutra clarifies that these are not the definitive means of liberation (*niyyāna*).
The fruit of Brahma is not the cause of emergence, nor is it the essential path. That which is called "emergence" refers to the fruit as the state of emergence and the cause as the essential path.
As for the enumeration of enemies and thieves: just as when a person is in a perilous place and beset by enemies and thieves, it is difficult to escape;

so too is it for ordinary beings who are beset by evil Māras, making it difficult to attain Nirvāṇa. Below, its characteristics are explained: those who traverse the realm of Māra have the five desires as their [obstacles].
The mental object of the affliction-māra is called "conduct"; it is the attachment to various desires that robs one of merit. Greed is the essence of Māra;
because greed opposes wholesome dharmas, it is said to "rob merit. It causes what has already arisen to perish and prevents what has not yet arisen from being accumulated.

Below, the sutra passage follows the preceding discussion on the māra-path of conduct. The section on "enmity" subsumes the preceding "robbing by desire. This concludes the enumeration of the three [types of robbers].

The following explains its characteristics: the first phrase concerns the loss of the person, while the latter two concern the loss of the Dharma. "Departing from the good guide" means relying on those who are not virtuous;

"departing from the Buddha guide" means dwelling in the midst of evil. Regarding the subsequent loss of the Dharma, "relying on the ground of enmity" refers to losing the separation from all afflictions that constitute evil dharmas;
this is called the "ground of enmity" because it is the dwelling place of Māra. As for "entering," according to the words of the Sūtra, it means to follow [the path].

The "preface" (*pūrvapīṭhikā*) means reliance; the "afflictions" (*kleśa*) mean enmity; the "dense forest" (*gahana*) refers to the ground of the dense forest. Because these give rise to a mind that accords with Māra, they are called the "forest of Māra’s intent.
To enter into this forest is called "entering the forest of Māra’s intent. The "ground of spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the loss of wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha acts as a spiritual friend for sentient beings; the wholesome dharmas appearing in the world are the dwelling place of the Buddha.
The stage of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmi*) is called "distant" because it is contrary to that [lower] stage. Regarding the scriptural statement, "because it is far removed from the Buddha's intention":

wholesome supramundane dharmas arise in accordance with the Buddha's mind, which is termed the "Buddha's intention. To be contrary to those wholesome dharmas is to be "far removed from the Buddha's intention.

For what reason is it not said to be "far removed from the Buddha"? "Far removed from the Buddha" is the first phrase mentioned previously; here, in the section on the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), [it refers to the opposite].
First the explanation, followed by the application.
Within the section on the differentiation of the path, there are two parts in the scriptural text. First, regarding the subsequent treatment of transgressions, there are thirteen distinct phrases;

the first is the general [statement], while from "according to one's desire" onwards are the specific [details]. Within the subsequent application of the antidote, "generating great compassion" refers to the mind of benefiting others.

By means of the roots of goodness, one practices the conduct of benefiting others; this conduct consists of four phrases: the first phrase is to rescue and deliver [beings] by means of the roots of goodness;
the second is to uproot their evil causes so that they may attain [the lower realms]; the third is to cause them to attain nirvana and depart from the lower [realms];
and the fourth is to cause them to depart from the fruits of suffering and abide in [the higher realms], ultimately attaining bodhi.

The section on "Treating Faults According to Their Occurrence" is divided into two parts. First, regarding the statement that there are distinctions among those who seek the Way, this reiterates the preceding category.
Below this, in the explanation, the first point—the general fault of being submerged in the river—is interpreted. The drifting and drowning within the six realms of existence is like a great river;

one seeks existence and is submerged therein, which is why it is a fault. In the subsequent explanation of the specific details, there are three types of torrential waters, which reiterate the general principle and open up the specific categories.
Regarding the "difficulty of penetration" and the "loss of the path," their names are listed as follows: afflictions constitute the substance of the river of the six realms of existence;
because they are full of harm in their location, they are said to be "difficult to penetrate. Because they cause one to depart from the path leading out [of saṃsāra], they are termed a "loss.

Below, this is explained in detail. There are five types of self-nature. First, the number is stated; then, for those that are profound, the names are listed: just as a river in the world is called "great" because it is deep, so too are these called "great afflictions."
"Immeasurable waters" explains its profound meaning: because it is profoundly possessed of the four currents (*ogha*), it is called "immeasurable.
The Dharma is named after this metaphor, just as one speaks of "water. As for the phrase "following desire and so forth," it refers to sentient beings who possess seeking following the four currents.

The fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm, excluding ignorance and [wrong] views, are called the "current of desire" (*kāma-ogha*). The fetters of the two upper realms, excluding ignorance and [wrong] views, are likewise [the current of existence].
The various views of the three realms are called the "outflow of views" (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*); the ignorance of the three realms is called the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Regarding these "outflows," this explains their continuity. Just as a river, though deep, may run dry if its flow is not continuous, because its flow is continuous, it cannot be exhausted;
the afflictions (*kleśa*) are likewise difficult to exhaust because they constitute a flow. This will be explained further below.

Below, the names of those who have drifted along with the sutra and its commentaries through the ages are listed; those renowned for their great fame are recorded because their illustrious names have manifested the greatness of the River.
As for those submerged by the waters of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), their names are extracted. Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are manifold, why is craving alone designated as "water"?
It is because craving has the power to moisten, drift, and drown most forcefully; thus it is singled out for emphasis. Those who have drifted are listed by name.
This clarifies urgency: it should be like a flowing stream; if one is slow, a person can easily exit [the water], but if it is urgent, it is difficult to cross.

Afflictions (*kleśa*) are likewise: if they arise slowly, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) can be produced; if they arise incessantly and without interval, the Noble Path is difficult to manifest, and one cannot achieve liberation.
The following explains their characteristics: "not abiding from moment to moment" clarifies that there are obstructions; "not seeing the bank" clarifies that there is no remedy.

Because it flows continuously, one cannot see the further shore of Nirvāṇa. [The following] uses a scriptural passage to explain "flowing" before the section on "not abiding from moment to moment," which explains that one cannot correctly contemplate because of this lack of stability.
Regarding "wide": if the name is listed as being like a river, then if it is narrow, though swift, it can be crossed;
but if it is wide, it is difficult to traverse. Afflictions are also like this. The following explains their characteristics, such as conforming to desire and so forth.

Regarding the "extensive" nature of the awakening-factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): desire is the awakening-factor of desire; by including "and so forth," it refers to the awakening-factors of anger and malice.

These—desire and the rest—are termed the awakening-factor of mindfulness because mindfulness is the act of recollecting, and "awakening" refers to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), which are one and the same.

Since sentient beings constantly follow after desire and the other [afflictions] rather than being singular [in their focus], they are called "extensive. The Sūtra states, "They always possess the awakening-factors of desire, anger, and malice," which reiterates the aforementioned desire and so forth.
The phrase "the awakening of mindfulness" refers to the extensive [treatment of] unwholesome conduct mentioned previously.

The first three awakenings are designated as unwholesome conduct, as in the *Bhūmivastu*, where there are eight kinds of awakening, as detailed in a separate chapter; this should be discussed in full, but here we shall briefly discuss three of these eight.
There are four difficulties in raising the objection, which are enumerated as follows: among these four, the first is the affliction of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
The next two [afflictions] are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and the last one is pride (*māna*). Regarding the listing of these names as "clinging" (*parigraha*), the following provides the explanation:

falsely grasping at a presiding spirit is called the "view of self-clinging" (*ātma-grāha-dṛṣṭi*); taking the aggregates (*skandha*) to be the dwelling place of the self is called "clinging to a cave-dwelling.

Because it cannot be subdued, it is called "immovable" (*aniñjya*); because it cannot be extinguished, it is called "inseparable" (*avinirbhoga*). Below, the Sūtra is cited to apply the terms "craving" and "view" to these names.
This refers to the mind of views (*dṛṣṭi-citta*) grasping at names and craving; it is not dull craving.
The metaphor of the *rākṣasa* in the water is used to name "views" because they are able to grasp objects, being similar to the *rākṣasa* in the water. Therefore, it is called the "water-rākṣasa.

Among the subsequent two types of craving, the first is the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of greed, while the latter is its active manifestation (*samudācāra*). It is listed among the "returning" [floods] and named the "river," for it involves returning [to saṃsāra].

The difficulty of emerging from this state is the same as that of emerging from afflictions. The following explains its characteristics: first, one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to suppress the fetters and is reborn in the higher realms;
this is called "having abandoned desire. Later, because one falls back and gives rise [to afflictions] again, it is called "re-entering the midst of desire-thoughts.

Here, "desire" refers to the mind of craving within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); alternatively, the minds of craving belonging to all stages (*bhūmi*) are termed "desire-thoughts. As the Sūtra says, "one enters in accordance with [them]."

Regarding "returning to the forest of desire": because the various forms of craving and desire are as dense as a forest, it is called a "forest. Because one abandons [the path] and returns to enter therein, it is called "returning.
Furthermore, because one becomes attached within it, its names are listed like those of a river; for just as a demon entices a person and makes it difficult to escape, so too is affliction (*kleśa*).

It delusively delights the mind, making it difficult to abandon or leave. In the explanation below, "seeking desire" refers to initially seeking the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), while "delighting in attachment" refers to...

"Having attained [them], they become attached. The scriptural passage "seeking desire" (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*) refers to those who are deeply enamored; "attached" (*abhiniviṣṭa*) means "delightfully attached. Regarding the "continents" (*dvīpa*):

these are listed by name as the continents, meaning the islands of the six realms of existence. Since the great river has already been used as a metaphor, there are thus two afflictions: water and land.
For sentient beings dwelling on the mountain peak of liberation, water is explained as a disease; for those dwelling in wholesome dharmas, it is likewise explained.
The beings in the water speak of the land as a source of affliction; the preceding "love" and "view" were metaphors for the water.

Now, it is clarified that pride (*māna*) is like a high island. To explain its characteristics: when engaged in activity, those who think "we are superior" give rise to much conceit based on their skills;
therefore, it says "at the time of activity. This refers to *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"), by which *abhimāna* (conceit) and *adhimāna* (great pride) are also included.

It is said that because one considers oneself alone to have emerged [from the world], it is called "supreme. The following section further clarifies this through three types of *māna* (pride), which manifest the three types of pride mentioned previously—namely, *asmimāna*, *māna*, and *abhimāna*—as explained in the context of the first three stages. Specifically: to hold oneself as superior to those who are inferior is called *asmimāna*;
to hold oneself as superior to those who are equal is called *abhimāna*; and to lack reverence toward those who are superior is termed *māna*.
Since all forms of pride arise based on the notion of "self," they are now discussed collectively as the three types of *asmimāna* (pride of self).

As explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, there are eight types of pride, which are detailed extensively in other chapters; here, we shall discuss them fully. Within these eight, we will briefly discuss three.
To exalt oneself and disparage others is to manifest one's own superiority. This is illustrated by the following scriptural passage: "Pride is like being on high ground."

Because the water of the Dharma does not moisten them, they are said to be "scorched and withered. Regarding the three types of loss: first, the phrase "the loss of rescue in the evil realms" cites the number and presents the first of the three;
second and third, the phrases "no exit and no rescue in the good realms" list the names. The subsequent explanation of these losses concerns the lack of rescue in the evil realms.
Within the latter two points: first, there is the absence of the cause for exit within the good realms; second, [the absence of rescue] within the good realms.
"Those who lack the intention to emerge from their conditions for emergence" lists their names; "those who have no mind to emerge within the wholesome path" explains their characteristics.

Below, the sutra provides a commentary on the six villages: among humans and devas within the wholesome path, the locations upon which the eye and other faculties and consciousnesses depend are called the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). "Unable to stir or initiate" comments upon the absence of a mind to emerge.
"Movement" (*i*) is the beginning; "arising" (*fa*) is the proceeding. Since both the beginning and the proceeding are non-existent, it is said that they cannot be differentiated.
The enumeration of names gives rise to difficulties; this does not encounter the explanation of their characteristics. Longevity and Uttarakuru—these are places of various difficulties.

Being born there, one is far from the Buddha; therefore, there is no emergence or liberation. Below, the sutra applies [the principle] to oneself: being separated from wholesome conduct, one is born in a place of difficulty where there is no correct deliverance.
The *tiē* (annotation) does not correspond to the Buddha’s own explanation; within the commentary on the *zhìzhōng* (treatment), the explanation comes first and the annotation follows later.

Within the section on the distinctions of boundaries (*jiè chābié*), there is first the question and then the sutra. Within the sutra, there are two parts: first, the transgression (*guò*), and second, the treatment (*zhì*). Within the transgression, there are six phrases;
the first phrase, "shutting in a secure prison," is the general statement, while the subsequent many afflictions are the specific details.

The section on "Treating Faults According to Their Occurrence" is divided into two parts. Regarding the first fault, the phrase "distinctions of the realms" (*dhātu-viśeṣa*) restates the preceding category and provides a detailed explanation below.
The "fault of the prison" (*kārā-doṣa*) explains the initial general summary: the difficulty of escaping the three realms is like a prison; because grasping at signs is firm, it is called "shut.
Seeking [existence] in accordance with this is why it is a fault. Below, the remaining specific faults are explained.

Within the section on "Distinctions," first, regarding the analogy of the prison, there are five faults; these five faults are necessarily present within the prison, hence they are said to be "pursuing" [the inmates].
As for the phrase "should be known," it means one should know that within the prison there are necessarily five faults:

first, "suffering matters"—referring to the scourging with whips and canes, which is termed "suffering matters"; second, "exhaustion of resources"—referring to the depletion of the necessities of life, termed "financial ruin."
Because one's kinsmen are dispersed, it is called "separation from loved ones. Because shackles and fetters are fastened upon the body, they are termed "bonds.
Because there is no means by which to escape, they are termed "obstructions. Next, these are combined; this demonstrates the distinctions among the five kinds of difficulties.

Generally, the preceding metaphors are used to illustrate the subsequent phenomena. First, and so forth, regarding the phenomena, the five are extensively revealed; therein, the first three clarify their retributive suffering.

Regarding the latter two afflictions, there are eight distinct types of suffering; here they are summarized as three: first, the suffering of illness; second, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and third, the suffering of separation from what is loved.

As for the "difficulty of being free from illness": freedom from illness is happiness. The suffering of illness obstructs that happiness of being free from illness, and is thus called the "difficulty of being free from illness.
The various types [of suffering] are explained below: the "various sufferings of illness" refer to physical illnesses, such as delusions, grief, and mental distress.
This is a mental affliction; because one falsely grasps at what is favorable and unfavorable, giving rise to sorrow and distress, it is called "false sorrow and distress.

As the Sūtra says: "Suffering much, afflicted by many illnesses; much distressed by false imaginings, [afflicted] by false sorrow and distress. Regarding "difficulties in the means of subsistence": poverty constitutes a difficulty for those means of subsistence.
Regarding "bound by attachment and aversion toward the pleasant and the unpleasant": material wealth is that which is cherished as a pleasant thing.
The poverty of craving for existence is an undesirable thing; its rejection is called "hatred. Because it is never absent from the mind, it is termed a "bond.
Regarding the difficulty of separation from loved ones: it is difficult to part from those one loves and difficult to reunite with them.

As for the sorrow of separation from loved ones, it is because when relatives are dispersed, great grief arises. The Sūtra says "together" because when there is separation from loved ones, the members of the household grieve together.

It may also be called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), for sorrow and grief are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that arise together with the mind. They are termed "common" because they arise simultaneously.

Regarding the two subsequent phrases, the first—craving (*rāga*)—is an obstacle to ethical discipline (*śīla*), while the latter—delusion (*moha*)—is an obstacle to wisdom (*prajñā*). As for the difficulty of maintaining discipline, breaking the precepts constitutes an obstacle to those who uphold them.
The following explains their characteristics: in the form and formless realms, one temporarily abandons [the defilements] that violate [discipline]; in the higher realms, one is free from...

Because of a lack of shame and dread of blame, one does not give rise to the restraint that subdues the fetters of transgression; since this higher rebirth is not a permanent departure, it is called a "temporary separation.

One who is bound by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of craving for precepts cannot avoid falling back and giving rise to desire and evil, nor can they achieve permanent liberation because they are bound by the latent tendencies of craving for pure precepts.
Regarding the statement that "view is difficult," delusion poses a challenge to right view; the following explains its characteristics.
"Obtaining worldly knowledge that is obscured by its contrary tendencies" refers to the wisdom of the eight dhyānas and so forth;

because it is covered by ignorance, one cannot emerge from them. The subsequent passage "entering the three realms" applies to worldly knowledge, while "covered by ignorance" applies to the latter obscuration.
The explanation of their remedy can be understood accordingly.

Among the heterodox outsiders, there is first the Questioning Sūtra and then the Scripture Sūtra. Within the Scripture Sūtra, there are two parts: the initial [section on] transgressions and the subsequent treatment of those transgressions.

Within the treatment of transgressions, there are seven phrases; the first is general, while the remaining six are specific. Regarding the treatment, the first phrase—the path of emptiness and non-self—is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) that treats [the affliction].

The initial "mark of self" refers to *nirvāṇa*, which extinguishes all obstructions and causes one to realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); this is the treatment. The subsequent six phrases are as follows:
The section on "Treating Faults According to Their Occurrence" is divided into two parts. Within the first part, the initial phrase "erroneous non-Buddhists" cites the preceding category;
"those who cling to the fault of a self" explains the initial general statement. The phrase "the root of other views" explains the underlying principle behind the contradiction:
why is it that the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is singled out as the fault? It is because it is the root of all other views, and it is upon this view of a self that they rely.

Because it gives rise to immeasurable views such as eternalism and nihilism, it is called the "root. Below, the sūtra provides the commentary; in explaining the remaining distinct sections, there are six phrases.
Of these, the first three clarify the departure from the bliss of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), while the latter three demonstrate the presence of various sufferings.

Within the former group, the first phrase indicates the failure to initiate skillful means from the beginning, the middle phrase shows that the practice performed is incorrect, and the final phrase [indicates the result].

In the end, they fail to reach the truth. As for the initial statement that those who desire to attain nirvāṇa cannot move from their "dwelling" within the five aggregates because they still cling to a self:
although these non-Buddhist beings have the intention to seek liberation and attain nirvāṇa, those beings seek the extinction of the self;
yet because sentient beings conceive of a self, they ultimately do not depart from the aggregates. Therefore, they are unable to stir from or emerge out of this dwelling within the aggregates.

The aggregates (*skandhas*) are the dwelling place of the spirit; therefore, they are called "abodes. The following passage from the Sūtra uses the term "nest" (*āśraya*) for the five aggregates to refer to these "aggregates-abodes.

"Not emerging of its own accord" refers to being unmoving and unaroused; it means that one must rely on the teaching of another, as it cannot be relinquished by oneself—this is termed "not emerging of its own accord.

To wish to practice the right path while practicing a wrong path means that although one's actions are not upright, one seeks correctness in the fundamental mind; this is termed "desiring the right path."
Because of inverted perceptions, one erroneously seeks a divergent path; this is called "practicing a deviant path. Below, the Sūtra provides a gloss:
for one who practices an inverted path, the dharmas such as permanence and bliss grasped by an inverted mind are called the "inverted path.

Relying upon the notion of a self (*ātman*) while desiring to reach Nirvāṇa—wherein false views of a self reside within the six sense bases—one ultimately pursues that which is not real; seeking extinction for the sake of a self is what is meant by "pursuing Nirvāṇa."
Because they see me, they seek the retribution of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)—such as that of Brahmā or Maheśvara—as a divine abode;

this is called "dwelling in the six sense bases. Entering [them] is like entering a village, hence it is called the "Sūtra on the Village of the Six Sense Bases. The term "reliance" (*niśraya*) in the verse refers back to the aforementioned "dwelling.

"Empty village" refers back to the aforementioned "village of the six sense bases. It is said to be "empty" because there are only the sense bases and no person (*pudgala*); this is explained in the latter three lines of the verse.

The first two [of the four types of suffering] are internal suffering, while the last one is external suffering. Within the internal, the first phrase clarifies that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are mutually discordant, and the subsequent phrase clarifies that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are subject to transmigration and oppression.
Regarding the four great elements, the mention of aging, illness, and so forth clarifies the gravity of suffering. Aging exists because the four great elements undergo decay and transformation;
illness exists because they are impaired and diminished; and death exists because they disintegrate. Birth is also suffering, but it is not mentioned here because its nature is subtle.
Because of attachment to a self, one undergoes these various sufferings; the intent of "wishing to distance oneself" clarifies that suffering is profound.
All people loathe suffering and thus desire to be free from it, yet because they calculate [the existence of] a self, they continue to receive bodies without interruption.

Since these bodies are all greatly formed, one cannot escape them; they constantly follow the person. The Sūtra says "constantly" (*chang*) means "always following" (*hengsui*). The "four snakes" that inflict harm refers to old age, sickness, and so forth.
The analogy of the four great elements coming and going is like that of poisonous snakes; their increase and decrease give rise to suffering, which is termed "affliction.
The phrase "the enemies of the aggregates follow" clarifies the suffering of the five aggregates as they shift and press upon one another. Why are the five aggregates specifically called "enemies"?

Because all people delight in dwelling [in peace], yet within the five aggregates, consciousness, sensation, perception, and formations arise in succession—each subsequent arising pressing upon the preceding, and each moment perishing as it arises.

Because it contradicts human nature, it is described as the arising of enmity; since this exists from the very moment [of birth], it is said that one does not abandon various sufferings—these are external sufferings.
The explanation and treatment thereof can be understood.

Within the sutra text concerning the faults of the Hīnayāna, there are two parts: first, the subsequent treatment of the faults, and second, the preceding faults. Within the preceding faults, there are three distinct sections.
"Being cautious, narrow-minded, and inferior, not seeking the Great Vehicle" is the first phrase.

"Not seeking the great cause" is the general [description], while "cautious, narrow-minded, and inferior" is the specific [description]. "Not seeking the Great Vehicle" manifests that narrow-mindedness;

it means not seeking the two types of practice—benefiting oneself and benefiting others—within the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. "Remaining far removed from the unsurpassed omniscience" is the second phrase.

"Not desiring great fruits" refers to the faults of the mind in seeking [results] in the two preceding lines. "Equally there is emergence" refers to the third line, which concerns the faults of initiating practice.
Regarding the subsequent treatment, the phrase "I should cause [beings] to arise and abide in the subtle and wondrous Dharma with a vast mind" remedies the two faults following the initial one;
the treatment for the latter two is not briefly analyzed here. Thus far, the characteristics of the precept for gathering sentient beings have been explained in detail.
The following summarizes this: that which extensively gives rise to practice in accordance with the power of morality is termed the "preliminary vow" (*pūrva-saṃvara*);

this is subsumed under the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-kuśala-dharma-śīla*). Because it arises based upon morality and is produced in accordance with the power of that morality, it is said to be "well able to extensively give rise to practice."

The section on "Treating Faults According to Their Occurrence" is divided into two parts. Within the first part, the phrase "one who correctly practices the holy life" (*brahmacarya*) cites the preceding category;
"seeking minor faults" generally indicates the nature of the fault. Below, there are three specific types: first, the fault of the mind, which is not seeking the great cause;
second, the fault of the vow, which is not seeking the great fruit; and third, the fault of conduct. Regarding the first of these faults, the term "minor intention" (*parītta-cetanā*) is used.
Citing that sutra, the initial general statement regarding the two types of small minds is followed by an explanation of the two types of narrow-mindedness.

After listing their numbers, their characteristics are explained. "Small mind" refers to the inferiority of one's own practice. "The mind retreats and sinks from the vast Buddha-dharma" explains its characteristic.
"Subtle and wondrous" means the realization of the profound Dharma; "vast and immeasurable" means the breadth of teaching and practice.
"Extensive" refers to the first through the sixth grounds; "great" refers to the seventh ground;

"immeasurable" refers to the eighth, ninth, and tenth grounds—all of these are the dharmas that serve as the causes for Buddhahood, and are therefore called the Buddha-dharmas. To abandon these and seek the Lesser Vehicle is why it is called "narrow-minded.
"Narrow" refers to the limited scope of transforming others. The explanation is clear. Below, the sutra provides a gloss, stating: "Narrow-minded."
The preceding "small intention" is narrow; the preceding "narrow and inferior" is narrow. The preceding "small" does not seek the Mahāyāna vehicle, yet it brings forth its momentum.
As for what was previously stated—that this is not the preceding [state]—it is because the vows of those who pass beyond [the world] do not seek the fruit of Buddhahood.

Therefore, this is a vow for the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). To distinguish and explain its characteristics: below, according to the sutra, those who cultivate their transgressions and list their names are born into the *aniyata-rāśi* (the indeterminate group).

There truly exists the Mahāyāna, yet those who practice the Hīnayāna—those whose faculties are dull from the stage of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) and below—are called the "indeterminate group" (*aniyata-rāśi*), because the Great Vehicle truly exists and is not in vain;
thus it is said "truly exists. To abandon it and practice the Lesser Vehicle is therefore a fault. Below, the sūtra provides the commentary:

"Equal" means that there are equal [faculties for] the mundane and supramundane practices of both the Great and the Small Vehicles. This phrase comments on the preceding statement: "there truly exists the Mahāyāna," while "delighting in the Śrāvakas, etc. refers to the Lesser Vehicle.
The subsequent application is minor; below, in the commentary on "governing the midst," one first explains and subsequently applies them so that their mutual manifestation may be understood.

Regarding the explanation of the concluding text: "relying on those who uphold the precepts" means relying on the *vinaya* vows; "attaining the power of the precepts" means attaining the power of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśala-saṃgraha*).

That *kuśala-saṃgraha-śīla* arises from the *vinaya* vows; because it is the power inherent in the *vinaya* family, it is called "the power of the precepts. Furthermore, gathering wholesome qualities can give rise to gathering sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called "the power capable of skillfully initiating all practices," which is the precept for gathering and producing [beings].

"Capable of performing the good" means being able to perform those wholesome dharmas that benefit others; this explains "capable. "Skillful" refers to skillfulness in transformative application (*nirmāṇa-prayoga*).
"Initiating all practices" means initiating the aforementioned practices that benefit others. Below, the sūtra provides the scriptural citation for the "precept of compliance":

"Adhering to the power of the precepts" means adhering to the power obtained from the precepts previously mentioned. "Skillful" means being adept at adhering and capable of extensively initiating practice.
"Initiating various practices" refers to the commencement of all forms of conduct.

Within the first of the three fruits discussed below—according to both the Sūtra and the Śāstra—the section on the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) consists of three major parts: first, the characteristics of pliancy; second, the causes of pliancy; and third, the fruits of pliancy. Regarding the characteristics of pliancy: [text follows].
Second, the distinct practices of the stages (*bhūmi*) are explained in three parts: first, the conditions for initiating practice by beholding the Buddhas;

second, the ability to refine the practice; and third, the purity resulting from that refinement. Within the section on the conditions for initiating practice by beholding the Buddhas, there are three further points:

first, making offerings; second, dedicating the merit (*pariṇāmanā*); and third, receiving the practice of the Dharma. Because this is the stage of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one receives the ten wholesome paths of action.

Regarding the purity cultivated therein, for those who maintain the purity of the precepts throughout immeasurable eons, there is ultimate detachment; the analogy and its application may be understood accordingly.

Among the characteristics of the distinct stages, "loving speech" (*priyavāditā*) is the practice for benefiting others. Since the maintenance of the precepts on this stage involves being free from the four verbal transgressions and is subsumed under loving speech, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) characterized by the predominance of loving speech is the practice for one's own benefit. Why was it not [emphasized] in the preceding stage?
Regarding the ability to refine practices, the specific practices of the stages are now clearly distinguished; it is only after this refinement is complete that they are explained.

Since the practices for refining within those preceding stages inherently contain both self-benefiting and other-benefiting practices, the superiority of these two types of practice is clarified therein to distinguish them from the other stages.
Among these, making offerings to the Buddha is the practice of self-benefit, while transforming sentient beings is the practice of benefiting others.
However, although this present stage of training in conduct consists only of self-benefit and lacks benefit for others, it is not here that the excellence of conduct is analyzed;

rather, it is at this point that the two types of conduct are clarified. Since this is the conclusion of the cultivation of conduct through such refinement and flexibility, it is here that the summary is provided.
In this treatise, there are three parts. First, the statement "the fruit and benefit are like those of the first stage" is made in contrast to what preceded it to demonstrate their commonality.

Second, regarding the phrase "possessing [them] as below," this cites both presence and absence to encourage the knowledge that while the maturation of the faculties (*indriya-pariśuddhi*) and the wisdom of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*) are shared with the preceding stages, the actual setting forth toward this [stage] is absent;

this should be understood. Third, herein, the superiority over the lower is distinguished specifically by means of the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-pariśuddhi*), thereby clarifying the excellence of the higher and the inferiority of the lower.
Within this, there are two parts: first, distinguishing superiority and inferiority by way of the Dharma; second, distinguishing superiority and inferiority by way of analogies.

Regarding the first [part], there are three sections: first, distinguishing superiority and inferiority; second, at the beginning of the first stage (*bhūmi*), citing the inferior to manifest the superior;
third, from "If that were so" onwards, a question-and-answer analysis. Within the first section, "superiority here" serves as a general heading, while what follows provides the specific details.

This reveals the superiority [of this practice] over being free from stinginess and breaking precepts throughout immeasurable eons; it explains the accomplishment of generosity and morality as the antidote.
This section cites the preceding text to demonstrate that superiority. The second part is self-evident. Within the third section, the question is raised:
"If this generosity is so superior, why is giving (*dāna*) said to be supreme at the first stage (*bhūmi*)? This is answered by contrasting that [first-stage teaching] with what follows.
The explanation of the general statement has two parts: first, establishing the thesis to distinguish its superiority; second, explaining the name to manifest that superiority.
Regarding the first part, "establishing the thesis to distinguish its superiority," the phrase "this [perfection] is superior" is not intended as a refutation of the preceding stage.

Although it was stated in the previous stage that the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is predominant, this [present] perfection of giving is even more excellent because it encompasses all ten perfections.

Regarding the distinctions among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), why is it that within this context the two practices of giving (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are proclaimed as superior? There are three ways to distinguish these practices: First, to manifest their differences individually:
from the first stage, giving alone is predominant, up to the tenth stage, where wisdom alone is predominant. Second, to distinguish the superiority of one over another:
the giving of the first stage is superior, while the others are not equal to it; and so on, until the tenth stage, which is fully endowed with all [virtues], whereas the preceding [stages] are not.
Furthermore, each subsequent stage necessarily includes the three preceding ones; according to the actual practice, every single bhūmi is complete with all ten pāramitās.
Now, because this is explained according to the gate of distinguishing superiority over inferiority, it speaks of giving and discipline as being superior to what preceded them.

Why, then, are the subsequent stages not explicitly shown to include the preceding practices? It is because these two stages mark the beginning of the distinction from what came before, and thus they are treated specifically.
