therefore, they are called "refuge" (*śaraṇa*). Furthermore, because this practice accords with and leads toward the non-arising wisdom (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) of the eighth stage, it is also termed "refuge."

Regarding this refuge, it is established by name as "refuge in the Dharma" based on the meaning of the Dharma that serves as its support. To explain below what constitutes the supramundane support for this refuge:

this refuge is the conduct and virtue accomplished on the four stages (*bhūmi*) and above; when that conduct arises, it relies upon the supramundane wisdom-Dharma to be established, and is thus named "relying on the supramundane.
This follows the sequence of the sutra regarding the conduct and virtue of the wisdom-cultivation practiced from the eighth stage upward.
The name "conformity to the Buddha’s liberation" refers to the practice of conforming to the Dharma by relying on liberation; this is a brief explanation of its characteristics.

This conformity is the merit of the practices accomplished from the eighth bhūmi upward. When those practices arise, they rely upon the liberating Dharma of all Buddhas and are thus called "relying on liberation.
The subsequent section further clarifies these characteristics by distinguishing between the seeker and that which is sought.
In this context, "seeking practice" reiterates the first phrase [of the previous section], and "constantly seeking to hear the Dharma" reiterates the second phrase.
These two initial items together restate the preceding two points: "showing the one who constantly practices" refers to the constancy of night and day in the second stage;

"showing the one who practices with diligence" refers to the intensified diligent cultivation mentioned in the first phrase. This constitutes the practice of seeking the Dharma in the third stage, consisting of the nine phrases beginning with "joy."
To demonstrate correct practice refers to the method of correct cultivation sought by him. Next, the cause for the practice of seeking the Dharma is explained.

Within this, first, through a brief question-and-answer, his constant and diligent practice is revealed. As for the phrase "by what cause," the two preceding lines—which describe the practice of seeking—are cited to inquire about its cause.
To "demonstrate reverence and exhaustion" is the general answer that reveals the cause; it is because of the presence of respectful veneration.

Because he initiates the practice of seeking the Dharma, it is called "reverence" (*gaurava*); this reverence serves as the cause for the practice of seeking. The ultimate limit of this reverence is termed "exhaustive.
To manifest the characteristics of this reverence, the text states that for that bodhisattva, "wealth is primary.

This means that for the bodhisattva seeking the Dharma in the third stage, the value of the Dharma is first demonstrated by being weighed against material wealth; finally, it is distinguished through five specific points concerning his own person.

Because wealth and material affairs are the beginning, they are called the "foremost of wealth"; these are distinguished individually below within the section on wealth and treasures. The first calculation concerns the station of kingship;
the second calculation concerns the title of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), which is termed "kingship" or the state of being born in heaven;
the third calculation concerns what is known as Śakra, the pure realm of the world; and the fourth calculation concerns the Brahmā King.
Being free from the defilement of desire is described as purity; this constitutes the fifth comparison with one's own person.

Regarding the weighing of factors by means of the Dharma, it means that when comparing and measuring against the aforementioned five matters, the Dharma is the most weighty. This clarifies that the preceding two [matters] are the causes for seeking through practice;
however, in the subsequent sutra, it does not merely clarify these causes for seeking through practice, but also reveals the remaining nine causes for what is sought through practice.
Now, this commentator has omitted it for brevity.

In the Sūtra, the first part clarifies the cause of constant and diligent practice—the arousal of diligence; the subsequent part clarifies the remaining causes of correct cultivation, such as joy and so forth.

Within the category of "wholesome" (*kuśala*), there are five distinct meanings, as differentiated in the previous comparison of the five matters. Regarding the first of these, material wealth (*āmiṣa*), there are seven distinct points.

The first phrase, "initially encountering what is difficult to find," refers to being able to relinquish all material things; herein, one does not conceive of difficulty when initially encountering [the teacher], but rather seeks the Dharma by giving away wealth.
Regarding the speaker, one treats the person as weighty and the teaching as precious; there is no external wealth that one would not give up—this is the second phrase.
Being able to relinquish fields and houses, there is no internal wealth that one would not give up—this is the third phrase.
To be able to renounce wife and children and practice every deed that ought to be done is the fourth phrase.
To be able to renounce one’s own body to serve as a messenger for the Dharma, yet not renounce pride and the like, is the fifth phrase.

To renounce a haughty mind and seek the Dharma with humility—being disrespectful toward superiors is called "haughtiness," while grasping at a self within inferior realms and looking down upon others is likewise so called.

That which is called "self-conceit" (*asmimāna*) regarding those equal to oneself, and "great conceit" (*abhimāna*) regarding those superior to oneself—all these are abandoned because they lack the quality of being noble and upright;

this explains the abandonment of pride. "There is no suffering one does not undergo" is the sixth line; seeking the Dharma through a body of suffering results in supreme wealth—this is the seventh line, meaning that one is able to relinquish great wealth in order to seek the Dharma.
Knowing that the Dharma is the supreme provision is what is meant by "supreme wealth. This refers to the mind.

That which is not a mere precious object is called "supreme wealth. The seven preceding phrases together constitute the first section, which demonstrates the gravity and superiority of attaining the status of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
The second section compares and measures the superior attainment of Śakra Devānām Indra. The third section compares the station of Brahmā. The fourth section begins with "If there were a person...
and so forth, comparing and measuring [the merit]. The fifth section begins with "If a person were to say... and describes the act of offering oneself by casting oneself into fire.
Under the heading "Provisionally Making Essential Statements," it clarifies that the bodhisattva’s concentrated mind seeks the Dharma by casting himself into the three thousandfold world-system;

though the transgressions are grave, he makes a solemn vow to have no fear of the fire-pits. The Dharma should be fully received, for through the Dharma one attains self-liberation and does not shrink from various sufferings.

Because the Great Compassionate One acts for the sake of sentient beings, dwelling in suffering to seek the Dharma, this is the proper deportment of a bodhisattva; hence it says, "The Dharma should be [received]. Next, the correct practice of the cause is clarified.

Thus, for one who has thus resolved to advance and cultivate all dharmas, relying on the aforementioned joy and so forth to advance in correct practice is called "arousing diligence" (*vīrya*) to cultivate all true dharmas.
For one who contemplates in a quiet place, this is the cause for initiating practice in accordance with the Dharma. What is it that is contemplated which can serve as the cause for practice?
It means that the practitioner must truly attain the Buddha-dharma; it cannot be attained through mere verbal expressions alone. It is through purity [of realization] that one attains it.
Because these give rise to practice, they serve as the causes for practice.

In the treatise, the explanation of the causes for the practice of seeking the Dharma is first presented; this section is divided into two parts: (1) an explanation according to the text, and (2) a discernment of the distinctions among the dharmas sought.
Within the first part, the explanation follows the sequence of those five types of comparison. Regarding the explanation of the first gate:

The seven phrases of the sutra are explained in sequence: first the explanation, followed by the conclusion. Within the explanation, the initial statement, "For the sake of honoring the Dharma, one relinquishes everything," explains the first phrase.
The phrase "one can relinquish wealth, its source of acquisition, fields, and houses" explains the second phrase;

since movable wealth is easy to give up while fields and houses are difficult to part with, they are clarified next. Furthermore, it clarifies that one can also relinquish internal things for the sake of that [Dharma].

The third phrase is explained as follows: those aforementioned material goods are all spoken of as "internal phenomena" (*adhyātma-dharma*) for the sake of human beings; because the former encompasses the latter, they are described as being "together with" external wealth.
Furthermore, while external wealth is easy to relinquish, one's wife and children are difficult to part with; therefore, they are discussed next.

The fourth phrase, "and that which is done [by them] can also be relinquished," explains that it is not merely a matter of relinquishing the two types of wealth—internal and external—but rather that these internal and external riches [are themselves what must be relinquished].
That which is for one's own sake can also be relinquished; this explains the practice of offering oneself as service.

As for its characteristics, other things are easy to give away, but one's own body is difficult to part with; therefore, it is explained next. The phrase "Who, regarding this," explains the fifth line.

It clarifies that those who are able to obtain and able to relinquish these things are manifesting their pride and haughtiness; whereas the intention to relinquish [the body] clearly demonstrates the capacity to abandon bodily reverence, which is easily done.
Because mental pride is difficult to dispel, it is clarified next. Regarding the sixth phrase, "one does not fail to undergo suffering":

because mental pride is easy to subside while physical suffering is difficult to endure, the latter is raised next. Regarding the seventh phrase, "obtaining much...": the three thousandfold layers of precious jewels are most difficult to relinquish;
therefore, this is discussed last. The preceding seven sections have been sequentially arranged above; below, it says, "this is called..."

Regarding the "Supreme among Wealth," this summarizes the preceding seven points, including the three lower sections, the questions, and the explanations, as well as the application of the sūtra passages.
Because these are easy to understand, they are not discussed further. As for how kings and others ask questions to initiate the discourse, this refers to the "Wheel-Turning Kings" and so forth;

the subsequent explanation regarding Śakra and Brahmā refers to the Bodhisattvas. The following response to these questions serves to clarify the application of the sūtra passages, as should be understood. This concludes the fifth section.
First, having explained and subsequently applied the extensive exposition of the five gates of comparative evaluation above, we shall next distinguish the dharmas sought therein.
These consist of the phrases and verses, which are the teachings (*śāsana*), and the meanings, which are the practices (*pratipatti*).

Thus, regarding the three types of practice—seeking through hearing, reflection, and cultivation—as they correspond to those sought through practice, their causes have been explained; one should now likewise manifest reverence toward that very hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

Now, for what reason is it said here that one seeks the Dharma of the teachings, and that hearing [the Dharma] is accomplished by relying on the teachings? Therefore, seeking the teachings is for the sake of accomplishing that [hearing].

Next, the causes for correct practice will be explained. First, regarding the inquiry into the arousal of thought in a secluded place, the response to the question is analyzed and explained, followed by the citation of the sutra.

In the section on the "Analysis of Disenchantment" (*nirveda-vibhāga*), the initial question and answer briefly clarify the nature of the inquiry. From the passage beginning with "Having heard all phenomena...

and below, the response to the question briefly clarifies the subsequent points. Within the text of the sutra, there are three distinct parts: first, citing the prior hearing of the Dharma and reflecting in a quiet place to give rise to subsequent disenchantment;

second, elucidating the essence of disenchantment; and third, clarifying the intent of entering [the path], which is to practice in accordance with the Dharma without attachment or delight. Now, as for what is being said:
"Having heard [the Dharma], one knows it; having known it, one practices as taught, and thereby attains the Dharma"—this cites the first section of the latter sutra.
"Entering dhyāna, the formless realms, the immeasurables, and the supernormal powers"—this cites the essence of aversion from the latter sutra.

While dhyāna and the formless realms may be considered the essence of aversion, the immeasurables and supernormal powers are the fruits of that aversion. Why are they cited? It is because they likewise consist of practicing according to the teaching.

Because they are included [within the category], they are mentioned collectively; that "not delighting" refers to the third section of the subsequent sutra passage concerning the intent of entering dhyāna.
That "not delighting in abiding therein" means being unstained by it; this refers to not taking pleasure in or becoming attached to the eight worldly dhyānas (*laukika-dhyāna*).
These are not places where a bodhisattva finds delight or craving; therefore, one must certainly not give rise to affection or defilement toward them.
The author [states] that because one practices in accordance with the Dharma in the subsequent sutra, and because this conforms to immeasurable dharmas and so forth, it must necessarily be performed.
The three sections of the sutra are fully detailed as previously analyzed. Having heard all the dharmas, one reiterates the previous hearing of the Dharma to subdue the mind and bring it low.

The preceding section restates the correct contemplation of the mind in a quiet place; "subduing the mind in a secluded place" clarifies the abandonment of the fault of distraction, while "subduing that mind" clarifies the departure from faults of the mind.
"In a solitary place, departing from bodily faults" clarifies the removal of physical transgressions. "The mind forms a thought" below clarifies the arousal of the Path;
"below, wearying of the body and abiding therein" clarifies the stage of dwelling in weariness, for it is based on this that one practices the skillful means of weariness as taught.
That which follows "detachment" (*viveka*) constitutes the essence of revulsion (*nirveda*). Regarding the definition of the eight dhyānas, it is extensive as explained in a separate chapter.

Within the first dhyāna, the phrase "detached from desires, evils, and unwholesome states" refers to detachment from obstacles (*āvaraṇa-viveka*). This explanation has four aspects: (1) An explanation by way of general characteristics:

because one eliminates the evils and unwholesome states of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is called "detached from desires, evils, and unwholesome states. (2) According to Nāgārjuna... [text continues]

The explanation is as follows: being far removed from the five desires is called "freedom from desire" (*vītarāga*); severing the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is called "freedom from unwholesomeness. Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:

"One who proceeds toward the first dhyāna distances himself from five things and severs five things. Thirdly, according to the Abhidharma, one is called "freedom from desire" because of being detached from the five desires;
it is called "freedom from evil" because of severing the ten unwholesome paths of action; and it is called "freedom from non-restraint" because of removing the five hindrances.

The perfection of the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*) and the actual severance of the mind of craving is called "detachment" (*vairāgya*). Because of this detachment, one also abandons killing and so forth;
this is called "abandoning evil and unwholesome states. That which possesses *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) is the antidote.

Gross thinking is called *vitarka*, while subtle thinking is called *vicāra*. Therefore, Nāgārjuna said: "For example, when a bell is rung, the coarse sound is a metaphor for *vitarka*, and the subtle sound is a metaphor for *vicāra*."

Contemplating the joy and bliss born of seclusion is its benefit; because one turns away from desires and evils, joy arises. Because faults are abandoned and there is tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), it is called bliss.
Entering the dhyāna practitioner is the essence of concentration, which is the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). Why is this alone termed "dhyāna-practice"?
Because the essence of dhyāna is one-pointedness of mind, it is called dhyāna-practice. Within the second dhyāna, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are extinguished.

This refers to the cessation of the two types of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) within the first dhyāna that obstruct it: first, those occurring within the concentrated mind;

second, the coarse and moving *vitarka* and *vicāra* within the three bodies of consciousness at the time of emerging from concentration. Both of these are minds of distracted movement. In the superior stillness of the second dhyāna, both are extinguished.
As for "inner purity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), it is the essential nature of the antidote; if there were the turbidity and disorder of *vitarka* and *vicāra*, [this purity would not exist].

This dhyāna is called "inner purity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) because it is superior and tranquil, having abandoned external distractions. It is said to be "one-pointed" (*ekāgra*) to manifest its characteristic of cultivation;
because that mind of inner purity abides in a single object and no longer follows other conditions, it is called "one-pointed. Thus, the *Śāriputrābhidharma* states:
"In the stages of the desire realm, mental activity operates across six locations, as the six groups of consciousness apprehend the six sense objects."
Therefore, in the stage of the first dhyāna, mental activity operates in four locations, because the four bodies of consciousness operate upon four objects;

since the first dhyāna and above lack the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses, it is said to be "four. From the second dhyāna upward, mental activity operates in a single location, because only the body of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the dharma-object as its condition.
Furthermore, because this continuity is uninterrupted and unceasing, it is also called "one location," as explained in the lower treatise.
That this middle [dhyāna] possesses these two meanings yet lacks vitarka and vicāra reveals its capacity for remediation; it can remedy vitarka and vicāra.

By stating that vitarka and vicāra have previously ceased, it directly demonstrates the transcendence of faults, just as the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is described as being without outflows (*anāsrava*). Here, by emphasizing the remedy itself, it is said to be without vitarka and vicāra, just as the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is described as being without outflows.
"Joy born of concentration" (*samādhi-ja-prīti-sukha*) constitutes its benefit, as was previously explained regarding the first dhyāna.

Because one abandons the intermediate [joy] and the desire for evil, there is joy (*prīti*); because one experiences the arising of joy from within this dharma in the present dhyāna, there is bliss (*sukha*).
The explanation is the same as before. Entering the second dhyāna is the branch of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*) of that dhyāna-samādhi.

Regarding the phrase "abandoning joy" in the context of the third dhyāna, it refers to the cessation of obstacles; the joy of the second dhyāna arises from conceptualization (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*), which is highly agitated and distracting.

Because the mind becomes even more tranquil than this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is called "cessation. Equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are its antidotes.

Regarding "equanimity": it is the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃskāra-aṅga*). It means the mind is balanced; because it abandons the fault of that [previous] joy (*prīti*), it is named "equanimity. This is the mental factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃskāra*);

it is distinguished from the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), which is why it is specified as "activity" (*saṃskāra*). Regarding "mindfulness": it is the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃskāra-aṅga*), which keeps in mind the previous joy.

Because it maintains the one-pointedness of mind, it is called "moment-to-moment" (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*). It is spoken of together with mindfulness (*smṛti*) as its companion; thus it is said to be "mindfulness and recollection" (*smṛti-anusmṛti*).

Recollection (*anusmṛti*) is able to trigger awakening and assists mindfulness with great strength; therefore, they are mentioned together. Alternatively, one may speak of mindfulness itself as recollection, just as the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) are in essence wisdom (*prajñā*) yet are named "mindfulness.

This case is likewise the same. As for "settled wisdom" (*samprajanya*): *Note: The provided text contains a complex discussion regarding the relationship between *smṛti* (mindfulness) and *anusmṛti* (recollection), and how they function together to maintain mental focus and cognitive clarity.*
This refers to the branch of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*). It is explained as being wisdom (*prajñā*) by way of discerning the excellence of joy (*prīti*).

"Wisdom" and "tranquility" are names for the body; experiencing pleasure is what is meant by "benefit. When this pleasure is thoroughly pervasive within the mind, it is called "mental feeling" (*caitasika-vedanā*).

When this superior feeling pervades both body and mind, it is designated "bodily feeling" (*kāyika-vedanā*) based on its point of pervasion, using the peripheral term. Now, according to the latter sense, pleasure is actually mental.

Because this dharma increases and pervades both body and mind, it is called "bodily sensation" (*kāyika-vedanā*) to manifest the predominance of bliss; "bliss" here signifies the mental sensation (*caitasika-vedanā*) of the mental factor of bliss.
Without relying on further discourse, it is said that the noble ones (*ārya*) are able to describe "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). This bliss is profound and supreme;
only the noble ones can declare it to be a fault and are capable of relinquishing it. It is not something that ordinary people can manifest as bliss.

Regarding the statement that one who deeply contemplates and experiences joy enters the third dhyāna (*tṛtīya-dhyāna*), this refers to the essence of that dhyāna: the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).

This means that by reflecting upon the faults of experiencing joy within one's own stage, one enters into one-pointedness. Within the context of the four dhyānas, the cessation of suffering and pleasure, and the extinction of sorrow and joy, constitutes the "elimination of obstacles.

By severing these four types of feeling (*vedanā*), the immovability (*āniñjya*) of the dhyāna is clarified. As for the mention of "severing suffering," it is because suffering actually exists [in the lower stages].
The cessation within the second dhyāna is taught for the purpose of manifesting that this is the "unshakable" (āneñja) dhyāna, so as to avoid the interruption of the four types of feeling;

thus, it is also described here as "abandonment. Furthermore, because the bliss of the third dhyāna can be pointed out as suffering, the abandonment of the bliss of the third dhyāna is termed the "abandonment of suffering.
Why is this so? Because that bliss of the third dhyāna is called "bliss" when compared to those with coarse minds, but it is [suffering] when compared to the subsequent state of tranquility.
The mind itself is great suffering, just as in the world when one points with a finger and strikes wood:
to one who is awake, this is called pleasure, but to a sleeping person, it is considered great suffering. It is the same in this case; therefore, it is said that "suffering is abandoned.

When it says "pleasure is abandoned," it refers to abandoning the pleasure of the third dhyāna, because that pleasure is coarse and agitated, and thus it is abandoned. "First, sorrow is extinguished" means it is extinguished in the first dhyāna.

Regarding the statement "sorrow and joy are extinguished first," this refers to their extinction in the third dhyāna; they both cease prior [to the cessation of other factors], and for this reason it is said they are extinguished first.
Since these are not the [ultimate] cessations [of the path], why discuss them? It is also for the purpose of clarifying this immovable dhyāna.

If it were argued that sorrow and joy are designated as extinguished first because they are severed in the preceding stages, then suffering (*duḥkha*) is also extinguished first—why is it not said to be extinguished first? The explanation states that even if one clarifies the principle of what comes first, there is no logical fault.
The *Śāstra* merely clarifies this: although suffering was extinguished first, the pleasure that opposes suffering is severed within this [context];

therefore, the suffering that opposes pleasure cannot be said to have been extinguished first. If one were to say that suffering and pleasure were both extinguished first, people would claim that the pleasure was also extinguished first;
thus, it does not manifest that sorrow and joy are both extinguished first as the opposer and the opposed. Therefore, it is said "first."

The cessation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure constitutes its specific benefit. In the other dhyānas, the elimination [of suffering and pleasure] is explained first; why, then, is the benefit explained first here?

It is because it follows upon what was previously clarified—the abandonment of pain and the abandonment of pleasure. By contrast with those, the state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure is made manifest, and since explaining the meaning of this benefit is convenient, it is discussed first.
The actual practice, however, remains subsequent. This is because the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) differs from suffering.
Because it is pleasant, it is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Why is it not called "neither-sorrowful-nor-joyful"? There are three explanations:
first, because this dhyāna correctly abandons the feeling of pleasure while also being free from pain, it is contrasted with those two; therefore, it is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Second, because in the preceding text suffering and pleasure were previously abandoned, it is specifically contrasted with them to clarify that it is "not painful. Third, [it is so called] because it transcends both sorrow and joy.

The "joy" (*prīti*) and "pleasure" (*sukha*) within the three feelings are distinguished by the names "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) and "joy" (*saumanasya*); these two names are subsumed within the categories of suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*).
Because suffering and pleasure are broad [in scope], the term "neither-suffering-nor-pleasure" (*aduḥkhāsukha*) is used as their counterpart. Regarding "equanimity, mindfulness, and purity":

equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-aṅga*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-aṅga*). Since there is pleasure present in the first three dhyānas, equanimity and mindfulness are not [present there].

Because these [defilements] are now absent, there is purity of equanimity and mindfulness; entering the practice of the fourth dhyāna constitutes its essential body (*dharma-svabhāva*), namely the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).
The definition of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) is extensive, as detailed in other chapters, and this should be discussed therein.

Regarding the textual passage on the four formless attainments, for one who practices in accordance with the Dharma (*anuloma-dharmācārin*), because they rely upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to give rise to the immeasurable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth, they enter the various dhyānas.
It is certainly not a matter of attachment.

Below, the treatise explains this; within it, only the essential nature and characteristics of the practice of revulsion are analyzed, while the first and last sections are easy to understand and thus not commented upon.
Within the treatise, there are two parts: first, questions and answers to clarify the purpose of entering [the path]; second, a word-by-word analysis and explanation of the meaning.
Therefore, when entering into the inquiry that initiates the bodhisattva’s proper cultivation of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and other paths leading out [of saṃsāra], one might ask:

"Why is it that these are the dharmas of ordinary beings? The intention behind this inquiry is as follows: at this point, one should properly inquire about the meditative concentrations and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Why, then, are the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) mentioned together? By means of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the intent behind entering the meditative concentrations and formless attainments is clarified; for this reason:
The general question is answered below by first clarifying that dhyāna and so forth serve as the Dharma-gates for five types of sentient beings.
Within the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), there are two purposes; therefore, there are five kinds [of practitioners]. Below, these are specifically elucidated:

regarding those who enter the various dhyānas through pride, there are some who, having cultivated and attained the four mundane dhyānas, either become attached to the bliss of dhyāna or give rise to arrogance and loftiness, making them difficult to transform.

Because of the Path, one manifests entry into the formless realms to transcend what has been attained, to turn away from that which is clung to, and to still the mind of pride; this is transformation through the Path.
For those who possess pride regarding the formless, there are some who cultivate and attain the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and claim them to be *nirvāṇa*.

Relying on their own attainment, they are difficult to gather through the Path; therefore, it is necessary to manifest entry [into the formless] to still that mind of pride, as it is [otherwise] suffering.

The term "beings" generally clarifies that the purpose of the two practices of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is to extract them from suffering. Loving-kindness bestows happiness; how does it extract them from suffering?

By applying the remedies [to their causes], one causes them to be separated from suffering. Below, this is specifically revealed: "peaceful and virtuous" refers to establishing them in the virtuous cause;
"bestowing happiness" refers to granting them the fruit of happiness—this is the benefit of loving-kindness. "Relieving suffering" refers to... [relieving] their... suffering.

To cause those who have not yet experienced [the results] to not experience the fruit of suffering due to the causes of suffering—this is the benefit of compassion (*karuṇā*). For this reason, one must enter into compassion.
To liberate those who enter into joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), one rejoices in their liberation from suffering with a joyful mind and relinquishes them [to that state].

Regarding the statement "to enter into superior penetration for the sake of those who have taken refuge in what is false": because there are sentient beings who have taken refuge in heterodox paths and external teachings, one enters [into superior penetration].

The second section, following the text, provides a detailed explanation of attaining the meditative concentration (samādhi) named "Non-retrogression" and the explanation of the "Stage of Radiance" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*) within the Sūtra.
It states that by abiding in this Stage of Radiance, one is able to give rise to dhyāna; because of this stage of samādhi, one is able to produce dhyāna.

This is not to say that the preceding stages lack such distinctions, for they are characterized by the superior and the inferior. Below this, the causes [for this attainment] as explained in the Sūtra are interpreted.

Regarding the statement that "practice is the departure from desire, evil, and so forth," this is a general classification of the distinctions between the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

The text consists of four parts: first, the detailed analysis and explanation; second, among the four dhyānas, the initial opening of the topical headings; third, the enumeration of their number; and fourth, the listing of their names.

"Departure from obstacles" refers to what is eliminated by meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Antidote" (*pratipakṣa*) refers to the practice that remedies those obstacles. "Benefit" refers to... [text fragment ends]

That which is accomplished by the "beneficial" (*anuśamsa*) is the welfare for those two bases; the essence of one-pointed concentration (*ekāgra-citta*) serves as the basis for the two practices of counteracting (*pratipakṣa*) and benefiting (*anuśamsa*).
Why is it not said that this is the basis for the removal of hindrances? Because that [state] directly abandons faults and possesses no further functional essence (*carita-rūpa*);

therefore, it is not mentioned here. Below, the first dhyāna is specifically identified and distinguished, which can be understood. Within the second dhyāna, the removal of hindrances is clear regarding the internal [state].

Within the *Śuddhaka-sūtra*, there are three phrases: first, internal purity; second, the two minds in one place; and third, the absence of vitarka and vicāra. The commentary explains these in four parts:
first, regarding "internal purity," this refers to the antidote; by citing the initial phrase on internal purity, it introduces the discussion to clarify the antidote.

Second, regarding "the cessation of vitarka and vicāra," this explains the absence of vitarka and vicāra to establish the meaning of the antidote. Third, the application of the sūtra text. Fourth, the explanation of "one place. First [the explanation of "one place"].
The passage "dwelling in the application of the sūtra and cultivating the untainted" (*anāsrava*) refers to the actual antidote, which is the practice of the untainted path.

It may also be said that one cultivates both the mundane and the untainted; as for the term "uninterrupted," this is based on the cultivation of liberation (*vimukti*). If there were interruptions between the preceding and succeeding moments, it would not be "one place" or "uninterrupted";

therefore, it is said to be "one place. Regarding "practicing a single object" (*ekālambana*), this is stated in terms of the object to clarify the "one. From the second dhyāna upward, one is detached.
The five groups of consciousness take only mental objects (*dharmārambaṇa*) as their domain; this is called "focusing on a single object" (*ekālambana*). The rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the explanation of the abandonment of the obstacle of joy (*prīti-āvaraṇa*) within the third dhyāna: the first dhyāna is the most inferior, as it merely eliminates desire and unwholesome states; the second dhyāna is progressively superior, as it eliminates the applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) that are the antidotes within the first dhyāna.

Because this [third] dhyāna is even more excellent, it eliminates the benefit of joy (*prīti-anuśaṃsa*) belonging to the second dhyāna. The rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding the explanation:
Regarding the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the opening of the chapter first states that there are likewise four; this indicates their number.
Below, the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) were termed *samādhi*, whereas here the four formless attainments are termed *samādhi*. Next, the four names are listed;
their explanations are the same as those above. However, since they are omitted in the subsequent sutra text, the Master [Vasubandhu] has categorized them here based on the preceding analogy.

In the section specifically identifying and refuting [misconceptions] within the explanation of the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and the cessation of hindrances, there is first an explanation followed by a conclusion. Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, "Transcending form...
up to not attending to perceptions of diversity," the commentaries provide different interpretations.

According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, "transcending the perception of form" means distancing oneself from the perceptions of color, odor, taste, and tangibility; "ceasing resistance" (*sapratigha*) means further ceasing the perceptions of color, odor, taste, and tangibility.

Because those [objects] such as form (*rūpa*) possess resistance (*sapratigha*), they cease; one does not recollect them separately. As for the perception (*saṃjñā*) of sound, it ceases because sound arises by depending on various conditions and being struck [by them];
therefore, it is said to be distinct. This explanation is incorrect. Why is it incorrect? Because there are six kinds of form:
namely, visible form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and the unmanifested form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). These are the six kinds of form.
To summarize, these are threefold: first, that which is visible and resistant, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, which are the objects of the eye;

second, that which is invisible and resistant, which are the objects of the ear, nose, and so forth; third, that which is invisible and non-resistant, which is the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) that is the object of the mind.
Since one contemplates these three types, why would the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) not be extinguished in the concentration of emptiness?

Regarding the statement that "form is merely extinguished," the commentary explains that the meditative concentration on emptiness has both cause and fruit; the fruit is the cessation of form, while the cause is not so.
This is because that cause—the stage of earth—arises through cultivation without having abandoned the shape of form; thus, the affliction of the perception of form is not yet extinguished.

Since the affliction can be severed, why does one extinguish the perception of form but not consciousness and the other mental factors? While it is specifically stated that "perception is extinguished," in principle, this applies universally.

Because the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) through the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā*) is predominant, it is explained specifically in this way; the interpretation in the *Abhidharma* does not differ from this.

"Transcending the perception of form" (*rūpasaṃjñā*) refers to the citation of the scriptural text. "Transcending the perception of eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñānasaṃjñā*) refers to the cessation of the first aforementioned perception of form.
"Cessation of the perception of ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses" refers to the cessation of the second aforementioned perception of form. "Perception" (*saṃjñā*) and... [text ends]

Because it is co-existent with the mind, it is called "conjoined" (*saṃprayukta*). "Not recollecting" refers to the sūtra’s mention of the cessation of mental conceptualization; this means the cessation of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) belonging to the third stage above.
Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discriminates all phenomena, it is termed "distinctive"; this is because its distinctive characteristics are concealed. To explain further:

the perception of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna-saṃjñā*) perceives only form and does not understand other phenomena. When one attains the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the entire body [is transformed].

Being entirely devoid [of the object] is not termed "distinct" (bhedya); the same applies to the ear and other senses. The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) universally takes all dharmas as its objects;

therein, when it apprehends the aspect of taking form as its object, the emptiness-concentration (śūnyatā-samādhi) ceases. When it takes other dharmas as its object, the emptiness-concentration does not cease.
By citing that which ceases to distinguish that which does not cease, it is said to be "distinct. Among these three phrases, the first phrase states "exceeding" (atikrānta), while the second...
It is said that the third [dhyāna] is called "cessation" because one does not attend to variegated speech. Question:

Since the perceptions of the two objects—odor and flavor—have already been eliminated in the first dhyāna, and the perceptions of form, sound, and touch have already been detached from in the second dhyāna, why is it now said that they are "ceased" in the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)? Answer: There is a reason for this.

Although the perceptions of odor and flavor have indeed ceased in the first dhyāna, what is here termed "cessation" refers to four types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*): first, the antidote of destruction (*bhedana-pratipakṣa*).
1. Antidote as the path of means (*upāyamārga*) refers to the contemplation of the suffering, impermanence, and other [aspects] of the contaminated states (*sāsrava*) of the lower realms.
2. Antidote as the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) refers to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*), which correctly abandons the faults of the lower realms. 3.

Antidote as maintenance (*dhāraṇamārga*) consists of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and all subsequent paths of non-obstruction and liberation, which maintain that unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) so as not to let it be lost or destroyed. 4. Antidote as distancing (*dūribhāvamārga*) consists of the path of liberation and... [and so forth].
Subsequently, all unimpeded liberations cause prior obstacles to never arise again;
this present concentration on emptiness is their remote antidote, and is therefore said to "extinguish" the perceptions of form, sound, and touch. Regarding the phrase "the two dhyānas extinguish":

although the perceptions of form, sound, and touch do not exist in their own respective levels from the second dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, one perceives them by means of the three consciousnesses belonging to the first dhyāna.

Because hearing, perceiving, and touching exist, even within the fourth dhyāna this perception still persists; only upon attaining the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) can it be extinguished.
Therefore, it is said that "emptiness extinguishes" it. This is called the general conclusion. The subsequent explanation clarifies the remedy.

First, there is the general statement; next, the explanation; finally, the conclusion. "Such a remedy" is the general statement. It is called "such faults" because it reveals the remedy in contrast to what preceded it.

The following section explains the characteristics of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for form and so forth. Among these, there are three phrases that explain one another in sequence. "Transcending the perception of form and so forth" is the first phrase.
Now, regarding those forms, according to their essentials, they are only three, which are broadly divided into six: namely, visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and phenomena (*dharma*).
As for "phenomena," this refers to unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*). The mental objects that take these as conditions are called the "objects of form and so forth."

The perception of the elements is also empty because one is detached from this; therefore, it is said to be a fault. "Not discriminating form" is the second phrase, which clarifies the aforementioned fault.
Because one contemplates the emptiness of form, there is no discrimination. Because one perceives non-self (*anātman*), this is the third phrase, which clarifies the absence of discrimination.
That form has no intrinsic reality is called "non-self"; this is stated as "non-self" based on its actual remedy. This...

The preceding section was explained in sequence; this concluding summary is called "concluding the names. Regarding these antidotes, there is no explicit text in the Sūtra, but they are established through the meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*).
This applies to all four *ārūpyas*, and the rest may be understood accordingly.

In the section explaining the fruits of detachment (*vairāgya-phala*), there are two distinct parts: first, concluding the preceding [section] and posing a question regarding the subsequent one to briefly indicate the headings;

this concludes the summary. What is the question? It asks: "What are the immeasurable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)? This is a brief indication of the headings. "Immeasurable" refers to the fruit of the skillful means (*upāya*) of practice;

the "five supernormal powers" refer to the fruit of functional efficacy (*kārya*). Although the supernormal powers generally comprise six types, here, in these three stages, they manifest in the world.
Because the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is concealed therein, only five [powers] are mentioned;

these two are explained according to the text. Within the sūtra, there are three parts: first, clarifying the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); second, clarifying the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and third, summarizing the mastery (*vaśitā*).

This treatise explains the three [immeasurables] in their proper sequence. Regarding the first of the immeasurables, after posing the initial question, one should first explain the meaning of "immeasurable" at length, as detailed in a separate chapter;
subsequently, the text itself will be analyzed. First, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is clarified, followed by the exposition of the other three.
Within the section on loving-kindness, there are thirteen distinct phrases; the first phrase is the general heading, namely, that loving-kindness arises in accordance with sentient beings.

The eleven intermediate sections specifically clarify the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), while the final section, which universally covers the world, clarifies the practice of loving-kindness as having the sense of being "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because it is all-pervasive;
thus, the treatise explains only loving-kindness, and the other three can be understood by analogy. There are three [types of objects]: first, the enumeration of the number;

second, the listing of the three names; and third, regarding "recollection of sentient beings" (*sattvānusmṛti*), this refers to recollecting all sentient beings with the desire to grant them happiness. As stated in other sūtras and śāstras:
"Mindfulness of sentient beings" means that the mind takes them as its object, just as one is mindful of this [present] thought.

"Mindfulness of phenomena" refers to knowing the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and their various attributes of sentient beings, as well as the wholesome and unwholesome phenomena that arise within them, in order to use these for the purpose of teaching and transforming them.

"Mindfulness of non-thought" refers to knowing that the essence of sentient beings is empty, thereby transforming them so that they may enter [the path]. Below follows a detailed analysis and explanation; first, within the initial section, the categories are enumerated.
Next, regarding the four names: "giving happiness" refers to the function of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is its ability to bestow happiness;
"remedy for obstacles" refers to the practice of loving-kindness being impartial, which remedies the obstacle of partiality; and "purity" refers to the purity of the essence of loving-kindness.

One should know that what was previously called "remedy for obstacles" is also pure, and what is here called "purity" is likewise the remedy for obstacles; therefore, it is termed "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*) in the sūtras.

These are merely stated as alternating pairs for the sake of distinguishing between the two gates. Regarding "the purification through the treatment of hindrances" (*āvaraṇa-pratipakṣa-viśuddhi*): this refers to the function of equality, wherein one employs the function of equanimity toward enemies and kin to treat and eliminate hindrances;

thus, it is called "purification through the treatment of hindrances. However, from the perspective of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), this is the dhyāna that serves as the basis for wholesome fruits.

Since it is the dhyāna that first gives rise to the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) by treating the evils of the lower desire realm, and not loving-kindness itself that acts as the treatment to dispel those evils, it is not termed "treatment."

Because its essence is free from defilement, it is termed "pure. Regarding the inclusion of the fruit within the verbal expression, the benefits of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*) will be explained extensively below.

Within the section on the object of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), there are eight phrases in the sutra: the first four bestow happiness; the next two are the remedies for obstacles; the next one is purification;

and the last one is the inclusion of the fruit. What is the bestowing of happiness? This is the question regarding the first gate. "Bestowing" refers to the enumeration of the three types of happiness. "Bestowing the happiness of desire" (*kāmasukha*)... [text continues].
Regarding the statement that this [joy] is "identical to joy" (*saumanasya*) with all the pleasures of the five desires of humans and devas in the desire realm:
in the first and second dhyānas, pleasure (*sukha*) and joy coexist; therefore, it is called "identical to joy. What is this pleasure that is identical to joy?
It is all causes and effects within the first and second dhyānas, which are collectively termed "pleasure. That which is not identical to joy refers to the third dhyāna and above.
All forms of happiness are discussed here in a general sense; it is not only the experience of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) that is called "happiness. Below, happiness is analyzed by way of two gates:
that which is called "leaving suffering" refers to the desire realm and the [first] dhyāna, where one leaves suffering and shares in joy (*prīti*);

that which is called "leaving joy" refers to the [second] dhyāna and above, where one does not share in joy. From the third dhyāna onward, because joy is regarded as a affliction (*ādīnava*), leaving it behind is called "happiness. This explains [the term] extensively.
The statement that "the three phrases of the immeasurable are also non-dual and likewise vast" explains non-duality (*advaya*).
When the three aforementioned joys are bestowed upon sentient beings without discriminating between self and other, they are called non-dual.

Alternatively, while the former [section] distinguished "vast" and "immeasurable" based on the joys themselves, this [section] differentiates them according to the three types of those to be converted; therefore, it says, "likewise," meaning they transform the beings of the desire realm.

That which is called "vast" (*vipula*) refers to transforming all sentient beings of the first and second *dhyānas*; that which is called "great" (*mahat*) refers to transforming all sentient beings from the third *dhyāna* upward;
that which is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) should be understood as non-dual because it is identical to the aforementioned vastness and so forth. Thus it is said:

"Furthermore," [the text] applies the sūtra to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) in accordance with its nature, rather than directly applying it to the preceding "vast. Because the desire for happiness is expansive, it is termed "vast."

The *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) agrees with this; it is called "Great Immeasurable" because its joy is superior to that which precedes it. It is called "Immeasurable Non-dual" because its joy is not like that which precedes it, being profound.
Regarding the explanation of the obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*), what is the question? Next, in distinguishing the characteristics of the obstacles:
"being unloved" (*apriya*) is one type of obstacle. "Inflicting harm upon an enemy" is termed "being unloved. As for "being loved" (*priya*): [the text continues].
This is the second hindrance: bestowing happiness upon one’s kin is called "bestowing affection. [The text] cites the scripture below to demonstrate the remedy for this.
"Being without resentment" remedies "not bestowing affection," while "being without opposition" remedies "bestowing affection. If one has partiality toward kin, there will be enmity and opposition;
because there is no enmity, there is likewise no opposition toward those who are partial kin. This is non-dual with what was stated previously.
What is the distinction? Previously, non-duality was explained solely in terms of pleasure (*sukha*); here, it is explained by means of the mutual exclusion of suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure.
Regarding the explanation of purity, what is the question? The subsequent statement concerns the correct abandonment of the lack of harmony in body and mind and the departure from unwholesome karma.

Because the body is not harmonious, one gives rise to killing and other such [actions] through the conceptualization of form and mind; since speech is also termed the "lack of harmony in body and mind," [it is included].
He has completely severed all unwholesome mental karma; he has severed sleep and so forth, which clarifies that his mind is free from the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
Regarding "sleep, restlessness-and-regret, and the various hindrances," this mentions the first two types while including the remaining three by the term "and so forth.

The meaning of the five hindrances is explained extensively in a separate chapter; it should be discussed in full there. Here, being free from these five is termed "purity. Below, the sūtra provides the scriptural citation.

Regarding the term "unobstructed," compassion arises based on dhyāna, being free from the obstructions of desire and unwholesome states. As for the inquiry within the section on the "fruits of mastery": why is it asked?
It is because the fruit of mastery in the desire and form realms arises based on dhyāna; thus, one receives its direct fruit in the form realm.
Through the residual force of the practice of compassion, one is subsequently born in the desire realm and receives its fruit of mastery. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
One who cultivates loving-kindness sleeps in peace and awakens in peace; they are protected by the devas and loved by humans; they are not harmed by poisons or weapons, nor by water or fire;
they suffer no loss, and their sleep is free from evil dreams; upon death, they are reborn in the Brahma-heaven. Such are the benefits obtained therein.

Regarding the absence of suffering, this explains the meaning of the *Jieyi hui jing* (Sūtra on the Assembly of Liberation): because one has correctly cultivated the two fruits [of the path], there is no occurrence of suffering. Thus, the sūtra says that there is no affliction or harm.

Regarding the mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), how is it questioned? Its characteristics are explained generally as applying to all places, and below they are explained specifically. As in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, taking the dharmas that benefit sentient beings as the object is called "taking dharmas as an object" (*dharmālambana*). In the *Bhūmivastu* (or *Dharmasaṃgraha*), taking all sentient beings—who are merely the causal factors of the five aggregates—as the object is called "taking dharmas as an object. Herein, both [meanings] are complete: first, knowing the five aggregates; second, knowing the dharmas that benefit sentient beings. Thus, these two meanings are fully contained within the mindfulness of dharmas. Furthermore, the term "dharma" has many meanings: it refers to the Buddha-dharma, the twelvefold scriptures, the three jewels, the four truths, the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the nine successive stages of meditative concentration, the ten powers, the eleven knowledges, the twelve links of dependent origination, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth. All such things are called "dharmas. Therefore, the mindfulness of dharmas is established based on these various meanings. Moreover, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking internal dharmas as an object; second, taking external dharmas as an object. Taking internal dharmas as an object means taking one's own body, sensation, mind, and dharmas as objects. Taking external dharmas as an object means taking the bodies, sensations, minds, and dharmas of others as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking conditioned dharmas as an object; second, taking unconditioned dharmas as an object. Taking conditioned dharmas as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements as objects. Taking unconditioned dharmas as an object means taking space, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the desire realm as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the form and formless realms as an object. Taking the dharmas of the desire realm as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the desire realm as objects. Taking the dharmas of the form and formless realms as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the form and formless realms as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking wholesome dharmas as an object; second, taking unwholesome and indeterminate dharmas as an object. Taking wholesome dharmas as an object means taking the roots of goodness, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as objects. Taking unwholesome and indeterminate dharmas as an object means taking the unwholesome and indeterminate dharmas of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the past as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the future and present as an object. Taking the dharmas of the past as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the past as objects. Taking the dharmas of the future and present as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the future and present as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the internal sense bases as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the external sense bases as an object. Taking the dharmas of the internal sense bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal sense bases as objects. Taking the dharmas of the external sense bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the external sense bases as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the internal elements as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the external elements as an object. Taking the dharmas of the internal elements as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal elements as objects. Taking the dharmas of the external elements as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the external elements as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the internal sense fields as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the external sense fields as an object. Taking the dharmas of the internal sense fields as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal sense fields as objects. Taking the dharmas of the external sense fields as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the external sense fields as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object. Taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal bases as objects. Taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the external bases as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object. Taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal bases as objects. Taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the external bases as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object. Taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal bases as objects. Taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the external bases as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object. Taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal bases as objects. Taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the external bases as objects. Furthermore, there are two types of "taking dharmas as an object": first, taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object; second, taking the dharmas of the external bases as an object. Taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal bases as objects. Taking the dharmas of the internal bases as an object means taking the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements of the internal bases as objects.
