Regarding the two knowledges of the phenomena that constitute sentient beings and the arising of their minds: all phenomena are employed for the purpose of transforming and delivering sentient beings.

Within these phenomena that constitute sentient beings, there are both mundane and supramundane. What is now mentioned—the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, and so forth—refers to the mundane phenomena of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

Those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are the supramundane phenomena. The causal practices of the Three Vehicles are called "those in training," while the ultimate fruits of the Three Vehicles are [the state of those beyond training].
Those called the "dharmas of non-learner beings" (aśaikṣa-sattva-dharma) and so forth, which encompass both ordinary persons and noble ones, are all termed "dharmas of sentient beings.
Furthermore, all that arises from the conceptualizing agent—the mind—such as wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, is termed "conceptualizing agent dharmas" (vikalpa-kartṛ-dharma).
As for those who cite the names of these dharmas, they are not [true] persons. One is able to recollect and know all such dharmas; as the Sūtra says, they "pervade everywhere."

Regarding "the world-spheres," it is understood that all sentient beings within the world-sphere are fully known. The commentary on "non-thought" asks: "How is this so? There are two [points]: first, the enumeration;

second, the explanation of their characteristics. Citing the sutra to clarify these two, the first concerns the contemplation of the emptiness of the essence of phenomena, while the second extensively clarifies the limits of emptiness.
"Lacking self-characteristics" lists the initial name; it refers to the distinctness of form, mind, and so forth.

To say that the essence of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is empty is called "non-illumination" (*wu zhao*). To know this through mindfulness is truly wisdom; it is designated by the term "mindfulness.
To contemplate the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) explains "non-thought" (*wunian*); to understand non-self explains "non-contemplation" (*wuguan*), which in turn explains "mindfulness.

Regarding "the most excellent in the world," this is an exclamation used to manifest its superior character. While there are worldly principles, none surpass it; thus, within the world, it attains the status of being the most excellent.
Below, by means of the method of applying the sutra, one applies it to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Because non-self (*anātman*) is the nature of all phenomena, it is called a "realm" (*dhātu*).

That which is supreme in the world applies to the most pervasive and inexhaustible within the world; this clarifies its boundaries. Its principle is universally pervasive and vast, and thus it is described as "inexhaustible.
When the contemplation of the mind reaches ultimate illumination, it is called "pervasive arrival"; the sutra speaks of "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*).
The citations extend everywhere; the citations of emptiness are inexhaustible. The three preceding conditions have separately clarified the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*);

from here below, the meaning of "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) is summarized. Regarding the phrase "because one universally practices throughout all worlds": this means that because the mind of loving-kindness is universal toward all sentient beings in the world, it is called "immeasurable.
Below, the sūtra uses the citation of "pervasive covering" to correspond to "universal practice," and further corresponds to "practice."
"All worlds" refers to the world of sentient beings; the remaining three categories are not further analyzed here.

Below, the meaning of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) is explained in detail as it applies universally across all six, as extensively treated in a separate chapter; this [section] should discuss them fully.

In the main text, the commentator first distinguishes the general meaning of the powers and subsequently explains the scriptural passage. Within the initial analysis of the meaning, there is a twofold classification: first, the essential nature of the powers; second, the clear wisdom of the four types of powers.

The fifth section clarifies that while the essential nature of all five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is wisdom (*jñāna*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is specifically termed "seeing" (*darśana*). This is because its illumination is distinct and clear;

thus, setting aside its essential nature, it is designated according to its faculty (*indriya*). If this is so, why is the divine ear not likewise designated as "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) according to its faculty?

It should indeed be consistent with the same principle. However, since the nature of wisdom is seeing, and the eye is also seeing—whereas the meaning of "seeing" accords with wisdom—it is designated as "seeing" in the case of the divine eye.
These are explained as "seeing" because hearing is not included; thus, they are not called "hearing. Regarding the initial analysis of the two types of karma: first, there is a brief classification.

The first supernormal power (*abhijñā*), which transforms physical form and appearance, is called "purity of bodily action" (*kāyakarman-viśuddhi*). The powers of the divine ear and knowledge of others' minds can give rise to speech, and are thus called "purity of vocal action" (*vākkarman-viśuddhi*).

As for the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), these involve knowing events of the past and future; since such matters across different lifetimes are difficult to know, they are known only by the mind.

"Understanding names" refers to the purity of mental action (*manas-karman*). The five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are wisdom; since all wisdom is mental action, these are here categorized according to their functional characteristics.

Below, this is further elucidated: first, regarding the supernormal power of the body (*rddhi-vidyā*), one can reach places of birth; therefore, it is called the purity of bodily action (*kāya-karman*).

Within the category of vocal action (*vāk-karman*), the two supernormal powers of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) and knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) are first cited, followed by an explanation of what is encompassed by the divine ear and knowledge of others' minds.

To know that which can know the meaning of the sounds of the Dharma teachings is what is known by the ear; the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) is able to hear the various dialects of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, which is called "knowing.
Because one uses those dialects to proclaim all dharmas, these dialects are termed the "sounds of the Dharma teachings.
With the divine ear, one is able to hear the Dharma taught by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to being able to know the meaning of the Dharma teachings; knowing the minds of others is the object known through the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*).

Below, it clarifies how speech is initiated based on these two types of objects of knowledge. Within this, first, speech is correctly initiated based on what is known by the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*);
subsequently, knowing the minds of others, one is able to preach in accordance with sentient beings, initiating speech that follows their various dispositions.
"Knowing all sounds completely" refers to the aforementioned divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) being able to know the various sounds of the teachings.
"Based on this meaning" means that based on the meanings of the Dharma known by the aforementioned divine ear, one explains them using different names;

that is, one uses the various verbal expressions previously known to explain those aforementioned meanings. Each of those individual meanings is manifested through various verbal expressions; these are called "different names."
Regarding the explanation of the function of "arising in accordance" (*anupapatti*): this is explained based on the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

It is called a "function" because it refers to the Bodhisattva’s verbal activity (*vākkarman*) that accords with things and accords with sentient beings. Alternatively, it may be explained as the "function of arising in accordance" by virtue of causing others to rely upon that function.

The subsequent explanation concerns the mental activity (*manaskarman*). Regarding the phrase "knowing the past and future, and knowing whether [beings] are mature or immature": "past" refers to the previous life.
The knowledge of past roots is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which knows the transformations that will be accomplished in future lives.

The following section explains the scriptural text. Regarding the question, "What is the supernormal power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*)?"—this inquiry is raised to introduce the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). First, the question is posed;

next, the scriptural text is cited, first clarifying the sentence regarding the supernormal power of the body, which consists of eleven distinct parts. The first states: "The Bodhisattva manifests immeasurable power."

One phrase is the general [statement], while the remaining ten are the particulars. Within the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*), the phrase "the ear is purified, surpassing that of humans" briefly sets forth the heading;

the section beginning with "hears everything" clarifies the characteristics of surpassing human capacity. Within the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*), there is first the general [statement], followed by the particulars, and finally the summary.

The phrase "knowing the mind and its mental factors" constitutes the initial general statement. "The essence of consciousness is the mind, while greed and so forth are the mental factors" represents the particulars within the scriptural text.

There are thirteen phrases in this treatise, which are subsumed under eight meanings and ultimately reduced to three categories. First, there are four phrases concerning the mind of affliction (*kleśa-citta*);

second, four phrases concerning the mind of retribution (*vipāka-citta*); and third, five phrases concerning the mind that initiates karma (*karma-pravartaka-citta*). Within these five, the first three are pure minds, while the latter two are impure.
Regarding the impure, the first phrase refers to covetous seeking and the last to haughty pride; thus, these two minds are greed and pride.
What is the difference between this and the aforementioned greed (*lobha*) and so forth, such that it is explained again?

Although its essence is not distinct from what preceded, the previous instance was cited to clarify the specific nature of the afflicted mind (*kleśa-citta*), whereas the present instance is cited to clarify the different ways in which karma is initiated. Therefore, it is presented again within the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
First, one generally knows the places of birth; furthermore, one is able to recollect the various specific characteristics of past lives. Finally, it concludes with a general summary.
Regarding this knowledge of past lives, from the very beginning up to immeasurable *nayuta* kalpas, one clearly knows the objects of knowledge.

First, concerning the objects of knowledge, one extensively understands their characteristics; within that, first, regarding internal retribution, one knows one life, two lives, and so on up to immeasurable [lives].
Subsequently, regarding the limits of the formation and destruction of worlds, one can know from one kalpa up to immeasurable [kalpas].

In the first part of the second section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one first knows the eight types of phenomena of the past, and subsequently knows the manner of their mutual circulation.
Regarding these eight phenomena, they are largely the same as those in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, though there are slight differences. As for how these characteristics differ:

the fourth [phenomenon] here, "such form" (*rūpa*), is not present in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*; that text instead divides the limit of life within the category of vitality (*āyus*) into a separate item. Furthermore, there is also [a difference regarding] the following.
Eighth: Furthermore, in this text, the eighth [section] concerning suffering and pleasure is the fourth; there is only this difference, while all else is similar.

In the concluding summary, various characteristics are explained, including the signs of one's lineage (*gotra*) and so forth. Regarding the analysis in the *Śāstra*, within the section on the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), there are four distinct parts:
first, a general clarification that the divine eye is pure and transcends that of ordinary humans; second, the specific details regarding the arising of vision; third... [the text continues].
The purity of the eye surpasses that of humans. This concludes the preceding general text on the four characteristics; below, the specific text begins with "lineage" (*gotra*) to conclude the above.
First, the general section is clear. Second, within the specific section, there are eight distinct points. The first four clarify the objects perceived;
the latter four clarify the modes of seeing and knowing regarding those aforementioned objects. What distinguishes the first four? The first concerns the birth and death of sentient beings.

1. Seeing the total retributive fruit; 2. Seeing the wholesome and unwholesome as the causes of total retribution; 3. Seeing poverty, low status, wealth, and nobility as the fruits of individual retribution; 4.
Seeing that one encounters the causes of individual retribution according to the specific karma created. Regarding the four phrases within the section on characteristics, what is their distinction?

The first phrase refers to the accomplishment of evil karma of body, speech, and mind through the cause of creating evil; this is "evil discipline" (*duḥśīla*). It also refers to slandering the noble ones.
The noble ones achieve the accomplishment of wrong view; this is an evil view. Second, regarding "and wrong view": it refers to the lower views that result in the fruit of suffering.

It is not merely the cause of seeing [suffering], but one also sees the undergoing of its fruit; therefore, the word "and" is used. As for the term "wrong view," it restates the previously mentioned wrong view, citing it here because of the continuity with the preceding context.
Regarding "karma," it restates the previous karma of body, speech, and mind. Regarding "causes and conditions," it refers to wrong view.
Furthermore, karma can act as the causal condition for the evil realms (*apāya*). Those who fall into the evil realms include those born among ghosts and animals;

those who fall into hell receive the retribution of hell. Because the retribution of hell is so grave, it is discussed separately. Regarding the three types of bodily wholesome [karma], the lower [level] involves seeing and practicing wholesome causes, which should be understood as the inverse of unwholesome [karma].
Fourth, regarding right view and the lower [level], one receives the fruit of happiness, which should be understood as the inverse of suffering.
"Born into the good realms" refers to those born into the human realm and the various heavens; this is the celestial destiny (*devagati*).

The above constitutes the second section, which specifically clarifies what is seen by the eye-purity that transcends that of humans. This concludes the first general summary and begins the preceding specific details.

Within this, it first presents the characteristics, names, and lineages of the beings he will see in the future, and then, based on those characteristics and so forth, it clarifies how the Bodhisattva perceives them.
The physical characteristics, surname, and given name are identical in meaning to those described in the account of past lives; the only difference is the time period.

Regarding "physical characteristics," this refers to [the marks one will have] in a future life, a second life, or even for immeasurable *nayuta* kalpas. "Surname" refers to having such a surname in the future.
"Given name" refers to having such a name in the future. This follows the previous account of past lives, with the omission of the character "characteristic" (*xiàng*).
"Characteristics" refers to future birth, form, food, lifespan, suffering, pleasure, and so forth, up to dying here and being born there;
this explains the first of the "objects seen," from beginning with poverty and wealth. "Birth and death, beauty and ugliness" summarize the results of retribution.
"Wholesome and unwholesome actions" summarize the causes of retribution. "Poverty, low status, wealth, and nobility" summarize the specific results of retribution.

The causes for separate retribution are briefly not concluded here; this follows the principle of receiving results according to karma, which concludes the second section on the characteristics of seeing and knowing mentioned previously—namely, that one receives suffering or pleasure based on having seen good or evil, which is termed "receiving according to karma. Below this begins the third section, concluding the meaning of mastery over dhyāna and so forth.
There are two types of mastery: first, mastery over the entering and emerging from dhyāna and so forth, which refers to the ten types mentioned previously.
The intense mind within deep reflection and the radiant, flourishing mind—these two being manifested as accomplishments—constitute mastery over not following along with rebirth in lower realms;
this is the aforementioned ten kinds of intense mind within deep reflection, which is the mind of profound maturity, now manifested as accomplishment.
Below, the commentary explains that "the body of speech" (*vāk-kāya*) refers to the first gateway; this is the general introduction to attaining supreme mastery.

The phrase "should be known" (*veditavya*) means that one should know the mastery [of power]. This explains the "immeasurable powers manifested in the sutra. Below, the remaining specific points are explained as being threefold:
the number is raised as three because there are ten phrases in the sutra—the first two each constitute one, and the latter eight constitute one—thus making three.
Below, its characteristics are distinguished: the listing of world-systems is explained by "capable of shaking," while the listing of one's own body is explained by "scattering" and so forth.
Following this, the Sūtra provides the topical headings: "one body as many" corresponds to the preceding "scattering"; "many bodies as one" corresponds to the preceding "merging";

"appearing and disappearing" corresponds to "concealment"; and "returning and emerging" corresponds to "manifestation. The listing of activities explains that based on the body, transformations are manifested for the sake of performing specific deeds.
The phrase "the name of karma resides herein" is the general heading; there are eight [points] below, which first state their number and are then explained in detail.
Seventh, regarding the great majesty and virtue of the sun and moon: "swift in their movement" means they travel rapidly; "of great power" means their majestic radiance is magnificent.
In the eighth sentence, "up to the Brahma-world" refers to the primary retribution fruit of the First Dhyāna; as for the "receptacle world," it is...
This is the fruit of the environmental retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*) based upon the first dhyāna. "Transforming at will" means being able to effect transformations within that Brahma-world;
because it performs functions belonging to a different realm, it is called "mastery.

Regarding the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*): this is the heading for the second [power]. In the explanation, one first clarifies that the purity of the ear surpasses that of humans, and according to its capacity, it can hear.

"This is the divine ear" means that what is heard is the sphere of sound heard by the ear. This explains the "ear-element" (*śrotradhātu*) as it is truly manifested, which is the understanding of its purity.
That what is heard is not erroneous is called "as it truly is" (*yathābhūta*); because hearing it is clear and distinct, it is said to be "manifested.
The term "purity" clarifies the aforementioned manifestation, while "hearing with truth" (*satya-śravaṇa*) clarifies the aforementioned "as it truly is."

Regarding the term "surpassing human" (*atikrānta-mānuṣya*) in the Sūtra: it is widely known that this surpasses the sound of humans. To distinguish this from the sound of humans below, it is called "surpassing human sound.
As for the sound from a distant place, it is so named because it cannot be heard by humans. From the bottom down to the Avīci Hell, looking downward to distinguish what is surpassed;

looking upward, one should say it reaches the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; looking sideways, one should say it extends to the eight directions. These are now omitted and not discussed, as they can be understood from the application of the Sūtra text.

Regarding the lower explanation, "he hears all sounds of humans and devas," etc.: first there is the explanation, followed by the application. This means that he hears both the loud sounds of humans and devas as well as the faint sounds of mosquitoes and the like.

As for the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), it is the third [power] indicated; in the subsequent explanation, first the number eight is raised, and then the eight names are listed.

The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are those that arise following primary afflictions according to conditions; they are called "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*) because their nature is established as afflictions that follow along with persons.
These two types of afflictions give rise to the retribution-mind (*vipāka-citta*), while the latter five are the karma-initiating minds (*karmākṣepaka-citta*).
Among these five, the first three are pure minds (*viśuddha-citta*); within the pure [minds], those acquired through study are the concentration-minds (*samādhi-citta*).
The stage of seeking is called "learning," and the stage of completion is called "attaining liberation. This wisdom is followed by two [stages]: deluded conduct and correct conduct.

Deluded conduct refers to the mind of external ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) who greedily seek; being free from greed is called "correct. "Correct" is not a defiled state, as it is established in contrast to the defiled.

Other ordinary beings who increase their pride are internal ordinary beings (*adhyātma-pṛthagjana*). Those who are external ordinary beings are called "correct ordinary beings," while those who are internal ordinary beings are simply "that" [internal class].

Those remaining among the outer ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana) who have not yet attained that noble path (āryamārga) but claim to have attained it are called "those with overweening pride" (abhimāna);

this will be explained extensively below. Following the first category [of the classification], regarding the "conjunction with greed and so forth," the essence of the mind (cittasvabhāva) is conjoined with those enumerated factors such as greed (rāga), hatred (dveṣa), and delusion (moha).
The Sūtra states that greed and so forth are secondary afflictions (upakleśa), whereas the abandonment of greed, hatred, and so forth is not itself an affliction (kleśa).

Because they arise in relation to one another, the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) are described as the second [category]. To explain this, the Sūtra states that "being defiled" (*saraṇa*) is precisely the essence of the *anuśayas*, whereas being free from defilement (*vītarāga*) is not an *anuśaya*.
Because they arise in relation to one another, the third category consists of the two deliverances (*vimokṣa*) of the formless realm, which are termed "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).

Among the four dhyānas, the first two are the "emptiness" (*ākāśa*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) bases; because these extensively take space and consciousness as their objects, the cognizing mind is called "immeasurable."
The latter two are not "immeasurable trainings" because they involve abbreviated observation. Regarding the fourth [category], "the distracted and the undistracted":

"undistracted" refers to training, while "distracted" refers to that which is not training; these are presented here as opposites. The Sūtra says: "concentrating the mind" refers to the undistracted mind, and "not concentrating" refers to the distracted.

This introduces the fifth [category]: "one who has entered meditative absorption" refers to the mind in a state of concentration; this correctly explains "attainment," whereas "one who has not entered meditative absorption" refers to the opposite.
The mind prior to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the mind before entering concentration; the mind arising from concentration is the mind after concentration.

Because the states prior to and after concentration do not correspond to the attainment of *samādhi*, the Sūtra speaks of "abiding in concentration" to refer to the mind while in concentration, and "not abiding in concentration" to refer to the minds when not entering or having arisen from concentration.
The phrase "attaining liberation" restates the sixth section concerning the presence or absence of bonds to explain its characteristics.

"Being unbound is liberation; being bound is not liberation"—this arises from the relativity of opposites. Thus, regarding the seventh gate, "false practice" and "correct practice," within the context of seeking fame, one manifests a longing for it.
To summarize the characteristics of these faults: "conformity" and "non-conformity" refer to the aforementioned characteristics of fault.
To manifest a longing for fame in accordance with those faults is false practice; to not conform to such longing is correct practice.

The Sūtra says that "seeking the mind" is compliant with what precedes it, while "not seeking the mind" is non-compliant. Regarding the remaining ordinary persons who increase their pride, as recorded in the eighth section:
the pride of external ordinary persons (bāhyapṛthagjana) is coarse, while the pride of internal ordinary persons (antarapṛthagjana) is subtle.

This subtle pride is a remnant of that coarse [pride]; thus, it is called "coarse-subtle. By contrasting the subtle with the coarse, one does not grasp that [external] coarseness; this subtlety is its [remnant].
Because it is the residual energy of coarse [defilements], it is called "habitual practice" (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, knowing that this is not pride, I shall briefly omit a detailed explanation.
Regarding the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), the fourth [power] is first indicated;

below, in the explanation, I will first interpret the initial general [statement] regarding who is able to ask, followed by the specific explanation. As in the sutra, there are two sections: first, the matters to be recollected.
Regarding the second point, "the characteristics of mindfulness and knowledge," the question is: "What is the object of mindfulness? The initial section of the text is as stated in the Sūtra;

the subsequent passage cites the Sūtra to clarify it. The question "How does one practice mindfulness? refers to the second section. The explanation below has two parts: first, an explanation based on the text; second, a further analysis.
Within the preceding explanation, the phrase "due to names" explains the first term. That which is past is described as the "cause" in relation to the present.
To know that [name] within the cause is the differentiation of names. The Sūtra says, "I [am such-and-such]," which refers to the name of the cause.
Such a name is the differentiation of the name; the differentiation of the family refers to the family of one's parents. The Sūtra says, "clan" (*gotra*), which refers to the lineage.

To speak of "noble and lowly" refers to the Kṣatriyas and so forth. "Beautiful and ugly" refers to the physical form (*rūpa*). "Provisions" refers to the secondary retribution (*upabhoga-pratyaya*). As for "karmic activity," it refers to...
Life is the cause [of suffering]. The Sūtra says: "A lifespan may be middle-aged, or one may meet with premature death; thus one dwells for a long time until life reaches its limit.

This includes heaven and the calculation of years, as well as suffering and pleasure, birth and death—all occurring in a single location. To explain: decline is suffering, and gain is pleasure; completion is birth, and destruction is death.
The application of these principles in the Sūtra can be understood. What follows provides a detailed analysis, specifically explaining these four phrases; the remainder is easy to understand.
The second section of the Genealogy explains that one may know [the status of] noble and base. The third section explains that one may know their karmic conduct.
This is the sixth and seventh [points]. Regarding "timely" and "untimely": when one's life is exhausted according to the celestial lifespan, it is called a "timely death.

This explains that living for a long duration and then meeting with an early demise in middle age is called an "untimely death. This explains that the limit of one's lifespan is as described in the *Dharaṇī-śvara-rāja-sūtra* (or *Bhūmi-vyavasthāna*).

How does this differ from what was stated previously? Dying as a youth is termed a "limit of lifespan"; dying in middle age is termed "long residence"; and dying in old age is described as "longevity.
Regarding the various characteristics in the subsequent section on the resolution of the knots (*granthi-vimocana*), there are two interpretations in the treatise:

the first interpretation restricts [the text] only to the passage beginning with "I have resolved the knot at such-and-such a place," while the second interpretation applies it generally to both one lifetime and two lifetimes.
Regarding the passage from "even unto this death and birth in that interval" and so forth:

first, as for how the various characteristics are cited from the sūtra text, the phrase "all characteristics" refers to everything from "such-and-such a name" up to "this death and birth in that interval";

this sentence provides a general summary, while the subsequent section provides specific summaries. As for the term "proponent," it specifically summarizes the eight [categories] among those mentioned in the sūtra.
Regarding the phrase "thus named" and "the scribe records the family name and so forth": the family name is recorded as a collective unit, and the family lineage is recorded as a collective unit;
this extends from the production of form (*rūpa*) up to its further production. Furthermore, there is another interpretation below:

within the Sūtra, the physical characteristics (*liṅga*) are separately recorded for one lifetime up to hundreds of thousands of *nayuta* kalpas; within the Sūtra, the name, family name, and so forth are separately recorded as eight distinct categories of phenomena.
In the sutra, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are separately concluded regarding birth-and-death; now, based on this meaning, I shall explain them in sequence.
"Recalling one lifetime, etc. cites the preceding sutra text; "this is called the characteristic" is the conclusion made in contrast to it. The phrase "the speaker cites...

refers back to conclude that while there is a name and clan mentioned in the sutra's concluding passage, they are omitted here because [the names] such as "name" and so forth are abbreviated. This concludes the preceding section and introduces the names of the conclusions.

Regarding the "clans" (gotra), they are further categorized by clans; as for the remaining [factors] such as birth and so forth, the phrasing of the summary is omitted. As for the characteristics, these are citations from the sūtra’s text on the "summarizing" (saṃgraha) section;
"I, regarding that... and below, it concludes in contrast to what precedes it.

Regarding the supernormal power of knowledge of birth and death (*cyutyupapādābhijñā*), it is designated as the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*) based on its faculty, but is referred to as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) based on its object. This is the fifth sūtra cited.

Regarding the "knowledge of birth and death" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), it is said that one sees the present realm with the eye of wisdom; having seen it with the eye, one knows that one will die here and be born there in the future.
This is called the knowledge of birth and death. Below, this is explained in detail. The sutra has four sections;
first, the initial section on the "purity of the eye" (*cakṣurviśuddhi*) is explained. Then, the question is raised: "Who is able to see beyond human [capacity]? to initiate the discourse.
Regarding the question of whether the eye can see, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun) refutes this by asserting that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is what sees.
One master claims that wisdom (*prajñā*) is what sees, while another master maintains that it is the conjunction of various mental factors (*caitasika*) that sees, as stated in the *Abhidharma*.

Now, when we say "the eye sees," we agree with the *Abhidharma*; however, we clarify that the scripture speaks of "pure seeing" (*viśuddha-darśana*), and we explain this purity through careful examination.
"Transcending humans" refers to the sutra passage on "seeing far beyond. Having explained the general meaning, the following section interprets the specific text.

"What is seen? asks about the objects perceived, namely birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and so forth; their characteristics may be briefly explained as they can be understood from the sutra's application.

"How is it seen? asks about the mode of seeing; this is clarified by citing the sutra text below. The final two concluding passages are omitted here without explanation. Regarding the remainder... [and so forth].

To reiterate and clarify this in contrast to what was previously seen—namely, that birth-and-death and so forth are termed the "subsequent" good and evil retributions—and as in the case of the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*), it is as explained in the section on the "Precepts for Gathering Virtue" (*kuśalasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*) in the second stage:

because the ten unwholesome paths lead to rebirth in the hells and so forth, while the causal conditions of the ten wholesome paths lead to rebirth among humans and devas. Therefore, the present passage refers back to that [second stage] to clarify this current stage. This concludes the commentary on the text.
The four dhyānas are called *dhyāna* because they can give rise to all meritorious qualities; this is translated here as "grove of merit.

The four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are subsumed within the four liberations among the eight liberations, and are thus called "liberations" (*vimokṣa*). The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) are the right concentration of a bodhisattva, and are thus called "samādhi";
this is translated as "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*), though other sources often refer to them as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
It is held that each samādhi manifests according to its respective meaning; the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) manifesting in function are called samāpatti.

This is translated as "the function of concentration manifesting before one. Regarding the entry and exit [of meditative states], when citing the sūtra, it says: "At the very moment the mind arises, the function manifests before one.

This means that at the very moment one gives rise to the thought of wishing to enter or the thought of wishing to emerge, one is able to enter and emerge; this is called "the function manifesting before one. This, then, is what was mentioned previously.
Among the ten types of profound mindfulness (*adhimukti*), the mind of intense clarity is accomplished here. It does not follow the lower dhyānas; this is a citation from the sutra.
That "pure and thick" (*puruṣa*) mind is accomplished here: among those ten preceding types of profound mindfulness, the eighth—the pure and thick—is accomplished at this point.
Because that mind is accomplished, one is not reborn according to the dhyānas, but follows the vision (*darśana*) that can fulfill the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The citation of the scriptural passage stating that one is born in the same place as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is explained from the perspective of one's own practice (*svayam-caryā*):
it means that by seeing for oneself the realm of the Dharma where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are born, one is born there together with them, thereby increasing one's own path.

In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, this is explained from the perspective of benefiting others (*parārtha*): having seen according to the perceptions of others, one goes to the realm of the Dharma where they have been born and is born there together with them, thereby increasing their path.
The scriptural citations can be understood from the preceding text.

It is frequently observed that following the Buddha’s exposition, his specific stage (*bhūmi*) and its fruition (*phala*) are clarified. Regarding the fruition, there are three types; their sequence is the same as before.

Within the "Fruition of Refinement" (*praśrabdhi-phala*), there is a broad classification into four parts: first, the practice of refinement; second, the merit of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*); third, the specific practices of the stages; and fourth, the conclusion.

Regarding the explanation of the characteristics [of the practice], there are four parts within the section on the Dharma (the first of the three sections: Dharma, Analogy, and Application): first, seeing many Buddhas as the condition for initiating practice;
second, "making offerings" and below, clarifying the refining practice; third, "desire being thin" and below, clarifying the thinning of defilements and hindrances;

fourth, "immeasurable kalpas" and below, clarifying the purity resulting from refinement. Of these four, the first two are both presented together and explained together, while the remaining text [explains] the latter two.
To summarize and explain the two preceding sections: seeing the Buddha is the same as previously described in the section on "refining practice.

First is the offering; next, the dedication is clarified; finally, the practice of receiving the Dharma is explained. Offering and dedicating toward the various stages (*bhūmi*) are analogous to receiving the Dharma and practicing it, though each stage differs from one another.
Reverence for the Buddha is "associating with a spiritual friend"; listening with single-minded devotion is "hearing the Dharma"; and receiving [it] is...
"Holding" (dhāraṇī) refers to the binding of mindfulness and thought; "cultivation" (bhāvanā), as it is said, refers to practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

"Cultivating practice" (pratipatti) is the general contemplation of all things, while the following specifically reveals the characteristics of cultivation: the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is that which is neither arising nor ceasing;

the contemplation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is that which exists by way of causes and conditions. These two gates mutually establish one another: because there is no arising or ceasing, it is merely that which exists through conditions, and because there are causes, it is [the conventional].
Because existence is conditional, there is no fixed arising or ceasing. Why is this so? Regarding arising and ceasing, one contemplates that dharmas are neither born nor extinguished.

Although the meaning of arising and ceasing is explained in various ways in general, what is clarified here is that defiled dharmas, being capable of being severed, are described as "ceasing," while pure dharmas, being capable of being cultivated and brought forth, are described as "arising.
To contemplate this arising and ceasing is itself ungraspable; it is called the mark of non-arising and non-ceasing.

What is its nature? First, it is explained from the perspective of ordinary beings, and subsequently from the perspective of the sages. Ordinary beings falsely construct thoughts, gathering and giving rise to defiled phenomena;

they speak of this defilement as "arising. They obscure pure phenomena and designate this purity as "cessation. One should know that this arising is non-arising, for it is arising-as-non-arising, and thus is not truly arising.
Cessation is likewise: it is non-cessation, for it is cessation-as-non-cessation, and thus is not truly cessation. It is like a deluded person who grasps...
The South is taken as the North; the North arises according to the mind and is explained as birth, while the South is hidden from the mind and explained as cessation.
That which is born—the North—is non-birth, yet it is called birth; that which is extinguished—the South—is non-extinction, yet it is called extinction.
According to the mundane, it is thus; but as for the noble, how is it? The arising of noble wisdom is described as the relinquishing of deluded defilement.

As for this, the extinction of the root is hidden while the beginning of purity is revealed; what is called "arising" is the purity of that which is produced, and non-arising is the arising of arising.

Thus, where there is no arising, there is no extinction, and it is likewise with extinction. It is like being lost and then finding the way: when one abandons the direction one was lost in, saying "north" is extinction;

when one first realizes the correct direction, saying "south" is arising. Where there is first arising, there is south; where there is no arising, there is the arising of arising, and thus there is no arising.

Cessation is likewise so. The essential principle of delusion and awakening lies herein: taking non-arising as arising and non-cessation as cessation is the existence of causal conditions through counteraction;
taking arising as non-arising and cessation as non-cessation is the non-arising and non-ceasing that is the object of contemplation.

This non-arising and non-ceasing is the true nature of phenomena, which is called the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the characteristics of arising and ceasing phenomena are called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

This is for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); now, in these three stages, because one enters the supramundane while still within the world of fulfilled desires, one relies upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to give rise to this contemplation of reality.

Subsequently, in the four stages, one gives rise to the wisdom of the practice of non-arising (*anutpāda-caryā-prajñā*). Therefore, the previous statement that "one gives rise to the contemplation of wisdom within meditative concentration" is based on this text.
Within this treatise, there are three parts: first, explaining that the Bodhisattva contemplates defiled and pure phenomena and perceives neither arising nor ceasing, but only dependent origination;

second, distinguishing how phenomena establish contemplation; third, citing the sutra to corroborate the statement that "all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished," which refers to the nature of the defiled and pure phenomena being contemplated, and explains that within pure phenomena, one perceives no increase—this clarifies the contemplation of non-arising and the perception of no decrease.

Those who understand the contemplation of non-extinguishing [realize] that the collection of causes and conditions is what is contemplated; those who understand the contemplation of conditions [realize] that there is something spoken of because of the collection of causes and conditions.

Because of the collection of causes and conditions, there is neither increase nor decrease; because of the collection of causes and conditions, there is increase and decrease. From here below is the second section, which distinguishes the purity of the contemplation established by the Dharma:
within the absence of increase, it establishes the non-seeing of increase; within the absence of decrease in delusion, it establishes the non-seeing of extinction; ultimately, there is nothing.

Therefore, it is said that there is not a single dharma that can be increased or decreased. Nevertheless, when prajñā manifests through the abandonment of the defilements of affliction by means of its antidote, it constitutes the aforementioned accumulation of conditions.

The word "however" (*ran*) is a term used to turn back from the former [point] and accord with the latter; although it does not exist [inherently], it exists by virtue of the causal conditions of the antidote.
This may be understood from the application of the sūtra.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the bonds of desire," it has already been analyzed above in the *Vyākhyā*. Here, I shall only explain the characteristics of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and the virtue of patience (*kṣānti*).

Other practices specific to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the concluding summary are easy to understand and thus not explained. Within the explanation of the characteristics of pliancy, I first explain the teaching by way of Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), followed by the interpretation of the parable.
A single sentence combining the parable with its application is omitted here as it is easily understood. Regarding the preceding section on the Dharma, the sūtra consists of four parts.

The first two sections have already been explained above; now the latter two will be explained. Within these, we shall first explain the attenuation of the various fetters (*bandhana*), and subsequently explain the meaning of the purification through refinement.
Now, these five fetters are precisely the afflictions of the five stages (*pañca-vāsa*) mentioned in the sutras;

the meaning of these five stages is as extensive as discussed in a separate chapter and should be fully treated therein. For the present passage, we shall first explain desire (*kāma*) and the others.

The four bonds (*bandhana*) become attenuated; next, the bond of views (*dṛṣṭibandhana*), which was previously eliminated, is further addressed. Subsequently, by means of the sutra, all bonds of desire (*kāma-bandhana*) become even more attenuated.

This refers back to the sutra text: regarding the initial reference, it simply mentions "bonds of desire," but if stated fully, one should say "the bonds of desire, form, and existence (*rūpa-bhava-bandhana*), as well as the bond of ignorance (*avidyā-bandhana*), become even more attenuated. In the preceding stage, the partial abandonment [of these bonds] was first cultivated.
Now, because one further grows weary of and abandons it, surpassing the previous state, it is said to become "thinner" (*tanu*). Why is it not said to be "exhausted" (*kṣīṇa*), but rather "thinned"?
This is because this is not yet the ultimate limit of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); since it has not been attained, it cannot be called "exhausted.

For example, within the Śrāvaka vehicle, the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin is described as "thinned" when six categories of desire are eliminated. Within the subsequent explanation, there are two distinct sections: first, distinguishing the differences in cultivation.

Seeing that both are equally non-existent within ignorance, [the text] distinguishes the subtle from the coarse. These four [afflictions] can obstruct both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Those that obstruct the path of seeing are eliminated at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*); since what is severed here belongs to the path of cultivation, it is necessary to distinguish this cultivated affliction from those of the path of seeing.
Furthermore, within the path of cultivation, there are both coarse and subtle types: the coarse are eliminated in the preceding two stages, while the subtle ones belong to this stage.

Because they are to be abandoned, one must distinguish them as subtle and different from the coarse. When it says "abandoning the afflictions of the desire realm, the form realm, and so forth" during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it refers to abandoning the fetters (*bandhana*) of the desire realm, the form realm, and so on that obstruct the path of cultivation.
"Desire" refers to the desire realm; "form" refers to the form realm; and "formless" refers to the formless realm. The afflictions of the desire realm are the fetters of desire;
the afflictions of the form realm are the fetters of form; and [the afflictions of the formless realm] are the fetters of the formless.

The afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute both the bondage of existence (*bhava-bandhana*) and its cause; because the bondage of ignorance (*avidyā-bandhana*) precedes and encompasses the latter, the word "and" (*ca*) is used.
However, since the bondage of ignorance is able to produce the three bondages of desire (*kāma*) and so forth, and the afflictions serve as its root, they are called its "cause.

The preceding phrase distinguishes [afflictions] from the view of cultivation (*bhāvanā-dṛṣṭi*), which shares the same nature as ignorance; the following phrase distinguishes the subtle from the coarse, thereby excluding them.

Among the four bonds (*bandhana*), how is it that those which arise coarsely are produced through mental attention (*manasikāra*), while the distinct entities of the four bonds are subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)?
The four bonds share the same essence and reside together within a single mind; they are dull ignorance (*avidyā*) which, upon grasping, becomes the nature of craving (*rāga*).

This is explained as the bond of desire, form, and existence (*kāma-rūpa-bhava-bandhana*). However, since these words state that they are identical to the habitual tendencies of ignorance, one knows that they are not [the bonds] that arise coarsely.
Because the four bonds (*bandhana*) share the same essence, they are called "identical. To distinguish their identical nature:
ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the bond of ignorance, while the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) are the three bonds of desire and so forth. Why is ignorance not called a "residual impression"?
It is because the first three bonds are the coarse arising of afflictions; those that arise coarsely are termed "active outbursts" (*paryavasthāna*), whereas [ignorance] is subtle.
The theory of "residual habit-energy" (*vāsanā*) holds that the essence of ignorance (*avidyā*) is an innate, subtle affliction, while its coarse manifestations are called "increased habit-energy.
Its subtle aspects are termed "fundamental proclivities" (*anuśaya*). Since what is being severed here is this subtle fundamental proclivity of ignorance, it is not called "habit-energy";
rather, one is entirely freed from the ground of this ignorance as well as the habit-energies of desire and so forth. (The preceding sentence.)

Within this [passage], first its abandonment is manifested, followed by the emergence of that which is abandoned. Regarding the four fetters of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), in this present sentence, first the ignorance (*avidyā*) and its residual impressions (*vāsanā*)—that which is to be relinquished—are raised, and subsequently the state of being free from them is manifested; the text merely shifts its perspective.

As for the statement that "the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭibandhana*) are severed at the time of seeing in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*)," this explains that the fetters of views are first eliminated. According to tradition handed down from of old, [this occurs] in the third stage.
Having returned [to the path], it is called "seeing the truth" (*satyadarśana*). By verifying this through the text, one can know that the words of people are certainly erroneous;

this may be understood from the arrangement of the sutra. It will not be further explained below. Regarding the fourth point, the purification through refinement: as for the phrase "no longer manifesting the severance of false greed and so forth," this cites the scriptural text.
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "false," but those that currently arise are said to be "false" because their delusive nature is coarse and manifest.
Regarding the statement "this delusion is false": since delusions such as craving have already been eliminated in the preceding stage, they do not manifest or accumulate here again.
The phrase "the antidote eliminates delusive craving and so forth, severing the habituation to unwholesome states, rather than severing the coarse" explains its characteristics.

This clarifies that within this stage, the manifest accumulation of antidotes severs only the habituation to the unwholesome roots such as craving, rather than severing the coarse arising; the term "coarse afflictions" refers to those of the preceding stage.

Regarding "abandonment," the obstacles to the aspect of seeing the meaning [of reality]—namely, the three fetters such as desire—are already abandoned from the first bhūmi onward. As for the coarse obstacles to cultivation, they are eliminated from the second bhūmi;

therefore, it is said that "the lower are abandoned previously. This is confirmed by the sūtra. Furthermore, all afflictions necessarily fall into two categories: first, those that are unwholesome, such as those arising in ordinary worldlings;
second, those that are wholesome, which the Buddha named "craving" (rāga)—referring to attachment to the Buddha and aversion toward the world. It is this [latter category] that is spoken of here.
Regarding the discrimination of existence and non-existence arising from anger, it is taught that ignorance is an unwholesome affliction. There are three stages for its abandonment:

first, at the initial arising [of the path] during the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), it is exhausted; second, the habitual arising—namely, the afflictions of violating the precepts through a mistaken mind—is abandoned during the Second Ground;
and third, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the three unwholesome roots, which have become established by nature, are gradually eliminated from the Third Ground upward.

Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), time (*kāla*), and the exhaustion of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), there are also three [points]: first, when one correctly arises upon the stages (*bhūmi*), the afflictions of the eight stages are gradually severed and exhausted at that time;
second, when one has already practiced and arisen beyond the eight stages, they are gradually and successively severed and exhausted at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*);

third, as for their latent tendencies (*anuśaya-svabhāva*), they are exhausted only upon reaching Buddhahood. Now, since this [text] speaks only of severing the nature of unwholesomeness (*akuśala-svabhāva*), it says they are "not manifest" when severed.
Regarding the false craving and so forth, there are four distinct sections in the explanation of the analogy: first, the presentation of the analogy;

second, the indication that it does not diminish, which reveals the intended meaning of the analogy; third, the aversion to the world, which is superior to what preceded and is free from loss, wherein the Dharma is revealed through the analogy;

and fourth, the explanation of the Dharma being identical to the analogy. In this stage, one cultivates wholesome qualities and develops a weary detachment from the lower realms, remaining without retrogression, just like that pure gold.
Furthermore, it is like refining gold with fire; its weight does not diminish by even two *liang*. This can be understood through the four scriptural citations.

From "Patience" (*kṣānti*) onwards, the explanation of the phrase on the practice of patience is divided into twelve sections, which are subsumed into four pairs. The first pair briefly clarifies the practice of patience as peace and happiness.
Next, there are five phrases that form another pair, expanding upon the two preceding practices. Finally, there are three phrases that constitute yet another pair.
Regarding the two lines at the end that clarify the causes for patience and the bliss [of practicing it], they form another pair.

To explain the removal of obstacles to the practice of patience and its bliss, first, within the initial pair, there is first a presentation, then an explanation, and finally a citation from the Sūtra.

Below, patience and bliss are further distinguished; "the purity of the transformation" is the presentation of the Sūtra. "Others... and so forth is the explanation of the infliction of harm and insult.
It is also capable of receiving and enduring; because one can endure insults, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). It is well-protecting the minds of others, which explains "peace and happiness.

The application of this in the sutra is as can be understood. Below, there is a detailed analysis: "not changing even when evil is added" restates the first phrase, while "well-protecting the minds of others" restates the latter phrase.
To provide a detailed demonstration, these two phrases are used to analyze the patience and peace and happiness within the sutra.
Delighting in adding further harm yet not ceasing [one's practice], one discriminates through patience to skillfully protect the minds of others and discriminates for their peace and happiness.

In the first two lines of the second pair, the former "peace and happiness" is expanded upon; in the latter three lines, the aforementioned "patience" is expanded. Regarding those who commit evil and harbor doubts:
those sentient beings who previously caused injury and affliction to the Bodhisattva are termed "those who do evil"; reflecting that one possesses [the capacity to endure]...

Because the Bodhisattva harbors malice and suspicion, it is said that he "harbors doubt. To manifest as a companion means that the Bodhisattva protects his own person while sharing the same affection as the other;
"guiding through speech" refers to compliance with their words. The Sūtra says "harmonious companion," which refers to a companion; "gentle and soft" refers to conciliatory speech.
In the subsequent three phrases, "maliciously not being angry" refers to when sentient beings inflict harm upon him with their bodies.
A bodhisattva does not give rise to anger toward them; hearing abuse, he does not retaliate.

When those beings before him revile the bodhisattva with their mouths, the bodhisattva neither retaliates nor feels distress. Although his own body and speech do not respond in kind, his inner mind might fluctuate;
yet the bodhisattva is not so—he remains composed and without further agitation, and thus he feels no distress. As the Sūtra says: "He is without anger."
"Not being angry" means not being moved; "not responding" means not retaliating; "not being turbid" means not being distressed by grief.
In this third pair, the first phrase is the cause of peace and happiness, while the latter two are the causes of patience (*kṣānti*).
Having abandoned past pride, one practices respect and conduct, personally engaging in kind speech; with a present mind that is humble and gentle, because of this humility, one [attains] oneself...
Regarding the practice of speaking kindly to those sentient beings, the *Sūtra on Kind Speech* states that one should not be haughty or overbearing, nor should one be arrogant or condescending;

rather, one should speak kindly after first humbling oneself. Of the latter two phrases concerning the causes for practicing patience: the first phrase refers to transforming others without desiring their respect, while the second phrase refers to bestowing kindness without expecting a reward.
If one harbors a desire for respect or a reward, even the slightest failure to receive what one expects will lead to dissatisfaction.

One gives rise to anger because of a lack of expectation; yet, because one does not disrespect others and is able to endure without retaliating or becoming angry, these two are taught as the causes of patience (*kṣānti*).
The intended meaning is as follows: one who does not expect respect transforms others through the Path, seeking no honor for oneself.
As the Sūtra says: "One whose mind does not expect [recompense] for what is done toward sentient beings performs acts of benefit and transformation among them."
To have a mind of reverence and hope regarding one's actions while not seeking recompense means to perform deeds for the benefit of others without expecting a reward.

In the first pair [of verses], the first line clarifies the abandonment of obstacles to the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*), and the subsequent line clarifies the abandonment of obstacles to patience (*kṣānti*).
"Not with a lack of sincerity" explains "without guile" (*amāyāvitā*); "and without partiality" explains "without crookedness" (*aśaṭhatā*). One acts with a peaceful mind and humility.

The preceding section followed the characteristics of things because of crookedness and flattery; now, it clarifies reality while remaining impartial. "Not low" is glossed by the scriptural passage on being "not flatterous";

"not crooked" is glossed by the absence of partiality; "free from subtle defilements" means that all subtle habitual tendencies of anger have been severed and abandoned—this is the purity of the practice of patience.
The following section, "not a dense forest," is glossed by the scriptural passage.
"Free from subtle defilements and with the obscured mind transformed into clarity and purity" is the concluding summary of these various phrases.

From this point onward, regarding the retribution received, it differs from the previous two stages. How do their distinct characteristics differ? In the first two stages, the former clarifies the householder state and the latter clarifies the renunciant state;
from here onwards, within the results of retribution received, there is no longer any mention of renunciation. This is because [the inhabitants] are all devas.
Since there is no renunciation, and since renunciation does not exist, how can one ground be divided into two?
First, those with superior bodies, such as the kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; second, those with superior fruits who are able to eliminate the greed and other afflictions of sentient beings.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the practice of one's own level; second, "always remaining below," which refers to the practice of further advancement (*viśeṣagamana*). Of these, the former clarifies the mind of further advancement.
Furthermore, from this reflection, one generates diligence; the subsequent stages are all to be judged in the same manner as the "Progression of Luminous Excellence" (Vimalaprabhā-pracāra).
This should be noted and understood.
End of the fourth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Completed on the first day of the sixth month in the first year of Eihō.
In the autumn of the fourth year of Shōryaku (the year of Gengshen), I had the four fascicles copied at a command in Tango Province.
Based on a single manuscript, I exerted myself despite my lack of ability to complete this work for Zenrin-ji.
